glossary.readjustment of seats after census: The Article 82 requirement that, after each census, Lok Sabha seat allocation among States and constituency boundaries within States be readjusted by an authority and method Parliament fixes by law.
glossary.Delimitation Commission (readjustment au: The body Parliament has historically established by law to carry out the Article 82 readjustment of parliamentary seat allocation and constituency boundaries after each census.
glossary.readjustment not affecting current House: The first proviso to Article 82, ensuring that any constituency readjustment does not alter the composition or representation of the currently sitting House of the People — it applies only from the next dissolution onward.
glossary.delimitation freeze until post-2026 cens: The third proviso to Article 82, which — paralleling Article 81(3) — suspends the obligation to readjust Lok Sabha seat allocation and constituency boundaries until the first census after 2026 is published.
glossary.Council of States is a permanent body: The Article 83(1) rule that the Rajya Sabha is never dissolved as a body, distinguishing it structurally from the Lok Sabha, which has a fixed term and is dissolved either on term expiry or earlier.
glossary.one-third retirement every two years (Ra: The Article 83(1) mechanism by which approximately one-third of Rajya Sabha members retire every second year on a staggered basis, per rules Parliament makes by law, preserving the House's institutional continuity.
glossary.five-year term of the House of the Peopl: The Article 83(2) rule fixing the Lok Sabha's term at five years from the date of its first meeting, after which it automatically dissolves unless dissolved earlier — a figure that was briefly extended to six years by the 42nd Amendment (1976) and restored to five by the 44th Amendment (1978).
glossary.Emergency extension of Lok Sabha term: The proviso to Article 83(2) allowing Parliament to extend the Lok Sabha's five-year term by law during an operating Proclamation of Emergency, in increments of up to one year at a time, capped at six months after the Emergency ends.
glossary.citizenship and pre-election oath (Parli: The Article 84(a) qualification requiring a prospective Member of Parliament to be an Indian citizen and to make and subscribe the prescribed Third Schedule oath or affirmation before an Election Commission-authorised person before candidacy.
glossary.thirty years minimum age (Rajya Sabha): The Article 84(b) minimum age of thirty years required for a person to be chosen to a Council of States (Rajya Sabha) seat.
glossary.twenty-five years minimum age (Lok Sabha: The Article 84(b) minimum age of twenty-five years required for a person to be chosen to a House of the People (Lok Sabha) seat.
glossary.other qualifications prescribed by Parli: The Article 84(c) residual power allowing Parliament to prescribe, by ordinary law (chiefly the Representation of the People Act, 1951), further qualifications for Parliamentary membership beyond citizenship, oath, and age.
glossary.summoning of Parliament: The Article 85(1) Presidential power to summon each House of Parliament to meet at a time and place of the President's choosing, subject to the mandatory maximum six-month gap between sessions.
glossary.six-month gap rule between sessions: The Article 85(1) requirement that no more than six months elapse between the last sitting of one Parliamentary session and the first sitting of the next, guaranteeing Parliament meets at least twice a year.
glossary.prorogation of Houses: The Article 85(2)(a) Presidential power to formally end a Parliamentary session (prorogue) without dissolving the House, distinct from dissolution which ends the House's very existence.
glossary.dissolution of the House of the People (: The Article 85(2)(b) Presidential power to dissolve the Lok Sabha specifically — a power that cannot be exercised against the permanent Council of States under Article 83(1).
glossary.President's right to address Parliament: The Article 86(1) discretionary power of the President to address either House or both Houses assembled together on any occasion, with power to require members' attendance.
glossary.President's power to send messages to Ho: The Article 86(2) power of the President to send messages to either House on any matter, Bill-related or otherwise, obliging that House to consider the message's subject with all convenient despatch.
glossary.President's Special Address: The mandatory address under Article 87(1) that the President must deliver to both Houses assembled together at the start of the first session after each general election and the first session of each year, informing Parliament of the causes of its summons.
glossary.commencement of first session after gene: One of the two mandatory triggers under Article 87(1) for the President's Special Address — the opening of Parliament's first session following a fresh general election to the House of the People.
glossary.commencement of first session of each ye: The second mandatory trigger under Article 87(1) for the President's Special Address — the opening of Parliament's first session of every calendar year.
glossary.Ministers' right to speak in either Hous: The Article 88 right of every Minister to speak in and otherwise participate in the proceedings of either House, any joint sitting, and any committee they are named to, regardless of which House (if any) they are a member of.
glossary.Attorney-General's right to speak in Par: The Article 88 right of the Attorney-General for India, though not an elected member of either House, to speak in and participate in the proceedings of either House, joint sittings, and named committees.
glossary.no voting right by virtue of Article 88: The express limitation in Article 88 that the right to speak and participate it grants does not itself confer any voting right — a Minister or the Attorney-General votes only if independently a member of the relevant House.
glossary.Deputy Chairman of the Council of States: The presiding officer the Rajya Sabha elects from among its own members under Article 89(2), distinct from the ex officio Chairman (the Vice-President), governed as to tenure and removal by Article 90.
glossary.automatic vacation of Deputy Chairman of: The Article 90(a) rule that a Deputy Chairman of the Council of States automatically vacates that office on ceasing to be a member of the Council for any reason.
glossary.Deputy Chairman resignation to Chairman: The Article 90(b) mechanism by which a Deputy Chairman of the Council of States may resign by writing under his hand addressed to the Chairman.
glossary.removal of Deputy Chairman by Council re: The Article 90(c) removal mechanism — a simple-majority resolution of all then members of the Council of States, moved only after at least fourteen days' advance notice.
glossary.Deputy Chairman performing Chairman's du: The Article 91(1) rule that the Deputy Chairman performs the Chairman's duties whenever the Chairmanship is vacant, or whenever the Vice-President is acting as or discharging the functions of President under Article 65, with a further fallback to a President-appointed Council member if the Deputy Chairmanship is also vacant.
glossary.acting Chairman during a sitting: The Article 91(2) fallback for mere absence (not vacancy) of the Chairman from a specific Rajya Sabha sitting — the Deputy Chairman acts, or failing that a person determined under the Council's rules of procedure, or failing that a person the Council itself determines.
glossary.no presiding over own removal resolution: The Article 92(1) natural-justice rule barring the Chairman from presiding while a resolution for the Vice-President's removal is under consideration, and barring the Deputy Chairman from presiding while a resolution for his own removal is under consideration.
glossary.Chairman's speaking right without voting: The Article 92(2) rule permitting the Chairman to speak and participate in debate on a resolution for the Vice-President's removal, while completely denying him any vote at all — on that resolution or any other matter — during those proceedings, overriding the general voting rule in Article 100.
glossary.Speaker of the House of the People: The Lok Sabha's chief presiding officer, elected from among its own members under Article 93, whose tenure and removal are governed by Article 94, including a special continuity rule during dissolution.
glossary.Deputy Speaker of the House of the Peopl: The Lok Sabha's secondary presiding officer, elected from among its own members under Article 93 alongside the Speaker, whose tenure and removal are governed by Article 94.
glossary.automatic vacation of Speaker/Deputy Spe: The Article 94(a) rule that a Speaker or Deputy Speaker of the House of the People automatically vacates that office on ceasing to be a House member, subject to the Speaker's special dissolution-continuity proviso.
glossary.resignation of Speaker to Deputy Speaker: The Article 94(b) mechanism by which the Speaker resigns by writing addressed to the Deputy Speaker, and the Deputy Speaker resigns by writing addressed to the Speaker.
glossary.removal of Speaker by House resolution: The Article 94(c) removal mechanism — a simple-majority resolution of all then members of the House of the People, moved only after at least fourteen days' advance notice.
glossary.Speaker's continuity despite dissolution: The second proviso to Article 94 uniquely protecting the Speaker (not the Deputy Speaker) from automatically vacating office on dissolution of the House of the People — the Speaker continues until immediately before the newly constituted House's first meeting.
glossary.Deputy Speaker performing Speaker's duti: The Article 95(1) rule that the Deputy Speaker performs the Speaker's duties whenever the Speakership is vacant, with a further fallback to a President-appointed House member if the Deputy Speakership is also vacant.
glossary.acting Speaker during a sitting: The Article 95(2) fallback for mere absence (not vacancy) of the Speaker from a specific Lok Sabha sitting — the Deputy Speaker acts, or failing that a person determined under the House's rules of procedure, or failing that a person the House itself determines.
glossary.no presiding over own removal resolution: The Article 96(1) natural-justice rule barring the Speaker from presiding while a resolution for his own removal is under consideration, and barring the Deputy Speaker from presiding while a resolution for his own removal is under consideration.
glossary.Speaker's limited voting right during ow: The Article 96(2) rule permitting the Speaker to speak, participate, and vote in the first instance during debate on his own removal resolution, while denying only the tie-breaking casting vote he would otherwise exercise under Article 100 — a narrower restriction than the Rajya Sabha Chairman's total voting ban under Article 92(2).
glossary.salaries of presiding officers (Article: The Article 97 rule fixing salaries and allowances for the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Council of States and the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People, as Parliament determines by law or, absent such law, as specified in the Second Schedule.
glossary.separate secretarial staff for each Hous: The Article 98(1) default rule that each House of Parliament has its own separate secretariat, protecting Parliament's administrative independence from the executive.
glossary.common posts between the two Houses: The proviso to Article 98(1) permitting the creation of staff posts common to both Houses of Parliament, despite the general rule that each House has a separate secretariat.
glossary.Parliament's law-making power over secre: The Article 98(2) power of Parliament to regulate by law the recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed to either House's secretarial staff.
glossary.President's interim rule-making power fo: The Article 98(3) power allowing the President, after consulting the Speaker or the Chairman as relevant, to make interim rules on secretariat recruitment and service conditions until Parliament legislates under clause (2), with such rules always subject to any later Parliamentary law.
glossary.oath of office (Member of Parliament): The Article 99 requirement that every Member of Parliament, before taking his seat, make and subscribe an oath or affirmation before the President (or a person appointed by the President) in the form set out in the Third Schedule — distinct from the Article 84(a) oath taken before candidacy, and backed by the Article 104 penalty for non-compliance.
glossary.majority of members present and voting: The Article 100(1) default rule that, except as otherwise constitutionally provided, all questions in either House of Parliament are decided by a majority of the members present and voting, excluding the presiding officer.
glossary.presiding officer's casting vote: The Article 100(1) rule that the person presiding over a House of Parliament does not vote in the first instance but exercises a casting vote in the case of an equality of votes — contrasted with the narrower version of this rule discussed under Article 96(2).
glossary.validity despite vacancies: The Article 100(3) rule that the proceedings of Parliament remain valid notwithstanding that it is later discovered some person who was not entitled to do so sat, voted, or otherwise participated in a House's proceedings.
glossary.validity despite ineligible participatio: The Article 100(3) safeguard preserving the validity of Parliamentary proceedings even where an unqualified or disqualified person sat or voted, protecting legislative business from retrospective invalidation.
glossary.quorum for Parliament (one-tenth rule): The Article 100(3) default quorum — one-tenth of the total membership of the House — required to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament, subject to Parliament's power to prescribe otherwise by law, coupled with the presiding officer's Article 100(4) duty to adjourn or suspend the sitting when quorum is lacking.
glossary.no simultaneous membership of both House: The Article 101(1) bar on a person being a member of both the Council of States and the House of the People at the same time, with Parliament empowered to make laws on vacating one seat if elected to both.
glossary.no simultaneous membership of Parliament: The Article 101(2) bar on a person being a member both of Parliament and of a State Legislature simultaneously, subject to a grace period Parliament prescribes by law for vacating one seat, after which the Parliament seat becomes vacant automatically.
glossary.seat vacation on disqualification (Artic: The Article 101(3)(a) rule that a sitting member's seat automatically becomes vacant upon incurring any of the disqualifications specified in Article 102.
glossary.resignation of parliamentary seat: The Article 101(3)(b) mechanism by which a member resigns his seat by writing addressed to the Chairman or the Speaker as applicable, with the seat becoming vacant upon acceptance, subject to the presiding officer's inquiry into the resignation's genuineness.
glossary.presiding officer's inquiry into genuine: The proviso to Article 101(3)(b), added by the 33rd Amendment (1974), empowering the Chairman or Speaker to withhold acceptance of a resignation if satisfied, after such inquiry as he thinks fit, that it is not voluntary or genuine — a safeguard against coerced or fraudulent resignations.
glossary.sixty-day absence seat vacation: The Article 101(4) rule that a House may declare a member's seat vacant if he is absent from all its sittings for sixty days without the House's permission, excluding periods of prorogation or adjournment for more than four consecutive days from that computation.
glossary.office of profit disqualification (Parli: The Article 102(1)(a) disqualification of a person holding any office of profit under the Government of India or a State (other than an office Parliament by law declares does not disqualify), subject to the Explanation exempting Ministers from being deemed to hold an office of profit by reason only of their ministerial office.
glossary.unsound mind disqualification: The Article 102(1)(b) disqualification of a person of unsound mind, so declared by a competent court, from being chosen as or remaining a Member of Parliament.
glossary.undischarged insolvent disqualification: The Article 102(1)(c) disqualification of an undischarged insolvent from being chosen as or remaining a Member of Parliament.
glossary.foreign citizenship or allegiance disqua: The Article 102(1)(d) disqualification of a person who is not an Indian citizen, or who has voluntarily acquired foreign citizenship, or who acknowledges allegiance or adherence to a foreign State.
glossary.Parliament-prescribed disqualification (: The residual Article 102(1)(e) disqualification ground allowing Parliament to prescribe further disqualifications by law, chiefly exercised through the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
glossary.Tenth Schedule disqualification (anti-de: The Article 102(2) disqualification for defection under the Tenth Schedule, inserted by the 52nd Amendment (1985), which operates as a separate self-contained disqualification regime with its own Speaker/Chairman-centred adjudication procedure distinct from Article 103's Election Commission-based procedure for Article 102(1) grounds.
glossary.President's decision on Article 102(1) d: The Article 103(1) rule that questions on whether a sitting member has become subject to any Article 102(1) disqualification are decided by the President, whose decision is final.
glossary.mandatory Election Commission opinion (A: The Article 103(2) requirement that before deciding any Article 102(1) disqualification question, the President must obtain and act according to the Election Commission's opinion — making the Commission the real decision-maker in substance despite the formal vesting of the decision in the President.
glossary.penalty for sitting/voting without oath: The Article 104 penalty of five hundred rupees for each day a person sits or votes as a Member of Parliament knowing he has not complied with the Article 99 oath requirement, or knowing he is not qualified or is disqualified for membership — recoverable as a debt due to the Union.
glossary.freedom of speech in Parliament: The Article 105(1) guarantee of freedom of speech in Parliament, subject to the Constitution's other provisions and to the rules and standing orders regulating Parliamentary procedure.
glossary.immunity from court proceedings for parl: The Article 105(2) absolute immunity barring any court from instituting proceedings against a Member of Parliament in respect of anything said or any vote given by him in Parliament or any Parliamentary committee.
glossary.immunity for authorised publication of p: The Article 105(2) protection extending court-proceeding immunity to any person for publishing, under the authority of either House, any report, paper, votes, or proceedings of that House.
glossary.residual powers privileges and immunitie: The Article 105(3) provision defining the powers, privileges, and immunities of each House of Parliament and its members and committees as those Parliament defines by law from time to time, and until so defined, those of the House of Commons of the UK Parliament as they stood immediately before the commencement of the Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment position) — the 44th Amendment (1979) having removed an earlier evolving-UK-precedent link in favour of this fixed pre-commencement baseline.
glossary.extension of privileges to non-member pa: The Article 105(4) provision extending the Article 105 privileges and immunities to persons who, though not members, are entitled under the Constitution (such as the Attorney-General or Ministers under Article 88) to speak in and otherwise take part in the proceedings of a House or its committees.
glossary.salaries and allowances of Members of Pa: The Article 106 rule that Members of both Houses receive salaries and allowances as Parliament determines by law, defaulting — absent such law — to the rates payable to Constituent Assembly of the Dominion of India members immediately before the Constitution's commencement, rather than to any Second Schedule figure (unlike the salary defaults for the President, Ministers, and presiding officers under Articles 59, 75, and 97).
glossary.dual-origin of Bills: The Article 107(1) default rule that an ordinary Bill may originate in either House of Parliament, subject to the Money Bill and financial Bill restrictions in Articles 109 and 117 which confine those categories to the House of the People.
glossary.prorogation does not lapse a Bill: The Article 107(3) rule that a Bill pending in Parliament survives the prorogation (formal ending) of a session and carries over to the next session, contrasted with dissolution which is generally fatal to a pending Bill under Article 107(4)-(5).
glossary.dissolution lapses Lok Sabha-pending Bil: The Article 107(5) rule that a Bill still pending in the House of the People, or passed by it but still pending in the Council of States, lapses upon dissolution of the House of the People — subject to the Article 108(5) exception where a joint sitting has already been notified.
glossary.deadlock between the two Houses: The Article 108(1) trigger conditions for a joint sitting of Parliament — outright rejection of a Bill by the second House, irreconcilable disagreement over amendments, or six months' inaction by the second House after receiving the Bill.
glossary.President's notification of joint sittin: The Article 108(1) discretionary power of the President, once a deadlock trigger arises, to notify both Houses of his intention to summon them to a joint sitting to deliberate and vote on a Bill — unavailable for Money Bills.
glossary.joint sitting majority (both Houses comb: The Article 108(4) voting rule at a joint sitting — the Bill passes if agreed to by a majority of the total membership of both Houses present and voting together, a mechanism that numerically favours the larger House of the People.
glossary.amendments admissible at a joint sitting: The restrictive proviso to Article 108(4) limiting amendments at a joint sitting to those made necessary by delay or those addressing points of continuing disagreement between the Houses, with the presiding officer's ruling on admissibility being final.
glossary.joint sitting survives intervening disso: The Article 108(5) exception to the general dissolution-lapsing rule — once the President has notified an intention to summon a joint sitting, a subsequent dissolution of the House of the People does not prevent the joint sitting from being held and the Bill passed.
glossary.Money Bill introduction restricted to Lo: The Article 109(1) rule that a Money Bill can only be introduced in the House of the People, never in the Council of States.
glossary.fourteen-day recommendation window (Rajy: The Article 109(2) strict time limit within which the Council of States must return a Money Bill to the House of the People with its recommendations, after which the Bill is deemed passed in its original form under Article 109(5).
glossary.Lok Sabha's power to accept or reject Ra: The Article 109(2)-(4) rule giving the House of the People unfettered, unreviewable discretion to accept or reject, wholly or partly, any recommendation the Council of States makes on a Money Bill.
glossary.deemed passage on expiry of fourteen day: The Article 109(5) fallback rule that a Money Bill not returned by the Council of States within fourteen days is automatically deemed passed by both Houses in the form the House of the People originally passed it.
glossary.Money Bill definitional test (Article 11: The exhaustive, closed-list test in Article 110(1) under which a Bill qualifies as a Money Bill only if it deals exclusively with the seven listed fiscal matters — taxation, government borrowing, the Consolidated/Contingency Funds, appropriation, charged expenditure, and Union/State audit-related receipts — or matters merely incidental to them.
glossary.'contains only provisions' requirement: The restrictive word 'only' in Article 110(1), which makes the Money Bill definition exhaustive — a Bill mixing a genuine fiscal matter with any substantive non-fiscal provision fails the Money Bill test even if fiscal matters predominate.
glossary.carve-outs from Money Bill status (Artic: The Article 110(2) exclusions clarifying that a Bill is not a Money Bill merely because it imposes fines, pecuniary penalties, licence or service fees, or because it deals with local-authority taxation for local purposes.
glossary.Speaker's certification of a Money Bill: The Article 110(4) mandatory endorsement — the Speaker of the House of the People's signed certificate that a Bill is a Money Bill — required when the Bill is transmitted to the Council of States under Article 109 and when presented to the President for assent under Article 111.
glossary.finality of Speaker's Money Bill classif: The Article 110(3) rule declaring the Speaker's decision on whether a Bill is a Money Bill to be final — textually conclusive, though its practical finality has been contested in modern litigation over Bills bundling fiscal and non-fiscal provisions (e.g., the Aadhaar Act, 2016 and later Finance Acts).
glossary.Presidential assent to Bills: The Article 111 act by which the President formally approves a Bill passed by both Houses of Parliament, upon which it becomes an Act of Parliament.
glossary.Presidential withholding of assent: The Article 111 option available to the President to decline assent to a Bill outright, an option that — unlike the return-for-reconsideration proviso — carries no textual obligation to explain or to act within any timeframe, and has never been formally exercised against a Bill re-passed after reconsideration.
glossary.President's power to return a Bill for r: The proviso to Article 111 permitting the President, for any Bill except a Money Bill, to return it once to the Houses with a message suggesting reconsideration or specific amendments, without indefinitely blocking it since re-passage compels assent.
glossary.mandatory assent on Bill's re-passage: The concluding rule of the Article 111 proviso — once Parliament re-passes a returned Bill, with or without the President's suggested amendments, the President is constitutionally barred from withholding assent any further.
glossary.annual financial statement (the Union Bu: The Article 112(1) formal name for what is popularly called the Union Budget — the President's mandatory annual statement to both Houses of Parliament of the Government of India's estimated receipts and expenditure for the coming financial year.
glossary.expenditure charged on the Consolidated: The Article 112(3) closed list of expenditure items — including the President's and presiding officers' emoluments, public debt servicing, higher judiciary and CAG salaries/pensions, and court/arbitral award payments — that are insulated from an up-or-down Parliamentary vote under Article 113(1), though open to discussion.
glossary.revenue account vs. other expenditure: The Article 112(2) requirement that the annual financial statement distinguish expenditure on revenue account (recurring/operational spending) from other (typically capital) expenditure, in addition to the separate charged-versus-voted distinction.
glossary.exemption of charged expenditure from vo: The Article 113(1) rule that expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India is not put to a Parliamentary vote — it may be discussed in either House but cannot be approved, rejected, or altered by vote.
glossary.demands for grants: The Article 113(2) mechanism by which non-charged ('voted') expenditure estimates are placed before the House of the People department-by-department for its assent, refusal, or reduction — the constitutional basis of the Indian Budget session's grant-voting and 'cut motion' practice.
glossary.House of the People's power to reduce or: The Article 113(2) rule that the Lok Sabha may assent to a demand for grant in full, refuse it, or reduce the amount specified — but has no power to increase any demand beyond what is proposed.
glossary.Presidential recommendation precondition: The Article 113(3) requirement that no demand for a grant may be made in the House of the People except on the President's prior recommendation, reinforcing exclusive executive initiation of spending proposals.
glossary.Appropriation Bill: The Bill required by Article 114(1), introduced after grants are voted under Article 113, that formally authorises withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund of India of the moneys needed to cover both the voted grants and the fixed charged expenditure.
glossary.bar on amendments varying grants or char: The Article 114(2) rule barring any amendment to an Appropriation Bill in either House that would alter the amount or destination of a voted grant, or vary the amount of charged expenditure, with the presiding officer's ruling on inadmissibility being final.
glossary.no withdrawal from Consolidated Fund wit: The Article 114(3) bedrock rule that no money may be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India except under an appropriation made by law passed under this article, subject only to the interim/exceptional mechanisms of Articles 115 and 116.
glossary.supplementary grant: An Article 115(1)(a) grant topping up an existing sanction found insufficient for the current financial year's purposes, processed through the same Article 112-114 statement/vote/appropriation machinery as the original Budget.
glossary.additional grant: An Article 115(1)(a) grant funding a genuinely new service that arose during the current financial year but was not contemplated in the original annual financial statement.
glossary.excess grant: An Article 115(1)(b) grant that retrospectively regularises money already spent on a service beyond the amount originally granted for that service and year, typically processed after Comptroller and Auditor-General audit and Public Accounts Committee review.
glossary.excess demand for a grant: The Article 115(1)(b) mechanism by which the President causes a demand for the amount of excess expenditure already incurred to be presented to the House of the People for after-the-fact regularisation.
glossary.vote on account: An Article 116(1)(a) advance grant of funds for part of a financial year, made pending completion of the full Article 113 grant-voting and Article 114 Appropriation Bill process — the standard mechanism used when a full Budget cannot be passed before the financial year begins.
glossary.vote of credit: An Article 116(1)(b) grant for meeting an unexpected, large-scale, or indefinitely-described demand on India's resources that cannot be itemised with the detail an ordinary annual financial statement requires — typically used for emergencies such as war.
glossary.exceptional grant: An Article 116(1)(c) grant funding expenditure that forms no part of the current service of any financial year — a one-off appropriation outside the ordinary annual Budget categories.
glossary.financial Bill (Article 117): A Bill touching one or more Article 110(1) fiscal matters but also containing substantive non-fiscal provisions, failing the strict 'only' test for a true Money Bill under Article 110 — still requiring Presidential recommendation and Lok-Sabha-only introduction for its fiscal provisions, but otherwise processed as an ordinary Bill through both Houses (unlike a Money Bill's Rajya-Sabha-recommendation-only regime under Article 109).
glossary.Presidential recommendation for fiscal-m: The Article 117(1) requirement that a Bill or amendment dealing with any Article 110(1)(a)-(f) fiscal matter cannot be introduced or moved without the President's prior recommendation, and cannot be introduced in the Council of States.
glossary.proviso for tax-reduction amendments: The proviso to Article 117(1) exempting amendments that merely reduce or abolish a tax from needing fresh Presidential recommendation, since such amendments carry no additional expenditure risk.
glossary.Presidential recommendation for expendit: The independent, broader Article 117(3) requirement that any Bill at all — whether or not a 'financial Bill' under clause (1) — that would involve expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India needs the President's recommendation before either House passes it.
glossary.each House's power to make its own proce: The Article 118(1) grant of internal autonomy allowing each House of Parliament to regulate its own procedure and conduct of business by its own rules, subject always to the Constitution's overriding provisions.
glossary.transitional pre-Constitution standing o: The Article 118(2) bridge provision carrying over the Dominion Legislature's pre-Constitution rules of procedure and standing orders, as adapted by the Chairman or Speaker, until each House made its own rules under clause (1) — now a spent transitional mechanism.
glossary.President's rules for joint sittings and: The Article 118(3) power of the President, after consulting the Chairman of the Council of States and the Speaker of the House of the People, to make rules governing the procedural mechanics of joint sittings and communications between the two Houses.
glossary.Speaker presides at joint sittings: The Article 118(4) default rule that the Speaker of the House of the People (or his rules-designated substitute if absent) presides over any joint sitting of both Houses, regardless of which House originated the Bill under consideration.
glossary.Parliament's law-making power over finan: The Article 119 power allowing Parliament to regulate by ordinary law the procedure and conduct of business in either House specifically for financial matters and Appropriation Bills, aimed at ensuring timely completion of financial business.
glossary.statutory override of internal House rul: The Article 119 rule that a law made under this article prevails over any inconsistent internal House rule made under Article 118(1) or transitional standing order under Article 118(2), for financial-business matters specifically — a narrow, purpose-limited exception to each House's general procedural autonomy.
glossary.language of Parliamentary business: The Article 120(1) rule fixing Hindi and English as the languages in which Parliament's business is ordinarily transacted, overriding Part XVII's general official-language scheme but subject to Article 348.
glossary.mother-tongue proviso: The proviso to Article 120(1) permitting the Chairman or Speaker to allow a member who cannot adequately express himself in Hindi or English to address the House in his mother tongue.
glossary.fifteen-year sunset on English (unless e: The Article 120(2) clause that would have automatically dropped English as a permitted Parliamentary language fifteen years after the Constitution's commencement, but which Parliament has continuously overridden by law (notably the Official Languages Act, 1963), keeping English available indefinitely.
glossary.bar on discussing judicial conduct in Pa: The Article 121 general prohibition on Parliament discussing the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court Judge in the discharge of his duties, protecting judicial independence from routine political scrutiny.
glossary.removal-motion exception: The sole exception to Article 121's discussion bar — a formal motion for presenting an address to the President praying for a Judge's removal, following the procedure Article 124(4)-(5) establishes for Supreme Court Judges (and its High Court equivalent).
glossary.non-justiciability of Parliamentary proc: The Article 122(1) rule that courts cannot invalidate Parliamentary proceedings merely on the ground of an alleged procedural irregularity, distinct from and narrower than immunity from substantive constitutional review of legislation.
glossary.immunity of presiding officers for proce: The Article 122(2) immunity shielding any officer or member exercising constitutionally-vested powers to regulate Parliamentary procedure, business conduct, or order from being subjected to court jurisdiction over the exercise of those specific powers.
glossary.Presidential Ordinance-making power: The Article 123(1) power allowing the President, acting on Council of Ministers' aid and advice, to promulgate Ordinances with the full force of an Act of Parliament when immediate action is necessary and Parliament is not in session.
glossary.recess precondition for Ordinances: The Article 123(1) requirement that the Ordinance power can only be exercised when both Houses of Parliament are not simultaneously in session — it is unavailable while Parliament is sitting.
glossary.six-week expiry after Parliament's reass: The Article 123(2)(a) automatic sunset rule under which an Ordinance ceases to operate six weeks after Parliament reassembles, unless converted into a permanent Act or earlier disapproved by both Houses, with the clock running from the later reassembly date if the Houses are summoned on different dates.
glossary.disapproval resolutions by both Houses: The Article 123(2)(a) mechanism by which an Ordinance can be terminated earlier than its six-week default expiry if both Houses of Parliament pass resolutions disapproving it, with the Ordinance ceasing to operate upon passage of the second such resolution.
glossary.Ordinance void if beyond Parliament's le: The Article 123(3) rule that an Ordinance is void to the extent it contains any provision that Parliament itself would lack constitutional competence to enact as an ordinary law.
glossary.composition of the Supreme Court of Indi: The Article 124(1) rule establishing the Supreme Court as consisting of a Chief Justice of India plus other Judges, a ceiling originally fixed at seven but expandable by Parliament by law and now standing at thirty-three additional Judges under the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2019.
glossary.appointment of Supreme Court Judges: The Article 124(2) process by which Supreme Court Judges are appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal — textually described as requiring 'consultation,' but in practice governed by the judicially evolved collegium system requiring the Chief Justice's effective concurrence following the Second and Third Judges Cases.
glossary.sixty-five-year retirement age (Supreme: The Article 124(2) mandatory retirement age of sixty-five for Supreme Court Judges, higher than the sixty-two-year retirement age fixed for High Court Judges under Article 217, with clause (2A) letting Parliament by law determine the authority and manner for resolving age disputes.
glossary.Supreme Court Judge eligibility criteria: The Article 124(3) qualification requirements for Supreme Court appointment — Indian citizenship plus at least five years as a High Court Judge, or at least ten years as a High Court advocate, or being a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion.
glossary.distinguished jurist route to Supreme Co: The Article 124(3)(c) eligibility route allowing a person who is, in the President's opinion, a distinguished jurist (rather than a career judge or advocate) to be appointed a Supreme Court Judge — a route rarely if ever actually exercised in practice.
glossary.removal of a Supreme Court Judge (impeac: The Article 124(4) quasi-impeachment removal procedure for a Supreme Court Judge, requiring an address by each House of Parliament supported by both an absolute majority of total membership and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, presented to the President in the same session, on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
glossary.proved misbehaviour or incapacity standa: The sole constitutional ground under Article 124(4) for removing a Supreme Court (or, via Article 218, High Court) Judge — misbehaviour or incapacity that must be proved, with Parliament empowered under clause (5) to regulate the investigation and proof procedure by law.
glossary.post-retirement practice bar (Supreme Co: The Article 124(7) permanent prohibition on any person who has held office as a Supreme Court Judge from pleading or acting in any court or before any authority within India's territory after leaving office.
glossary.National Judicial Appointments Commissio: The six-member body — the CJI, two senior Supreme Court Judges, the Union Law Minister, and two eminent persons — that Article 124A (inserted by the Ninety-Ninth Amendment, 2014) would have created to replace the collegium system for judicial appointments and transfers.
glossary.NJAC struck down as unconstitutional (20: The Supreme Court's ruling in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) declaring the NJAC scheme (Articles 124A-124C and the companion 2014 Act) unconstitutional as violating judicial independence under the basic structure doctrine, restoring the pre-existing collegium system as the operative appointment mechanism.
glossary.NJAC's recommendation functions (inopera: The Article 124B description of the NJAC's intended duties — recommending appointments to the CJI-ship, Supreme Court and High Court Judgeships, and inter-High-Court transfers, plus screening for ability and integrity — rendered legally inoperative by the 2015 NJAC judgment.
glossary.Parliament's law-making power for NJAC p: The Article 124C power that would have let Parliament legislate the NJAC's detailed appointment procedure and authorise the NJAC to frame its own regulations, exercised via the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, 2014 — struck down together with Article 124A-124C in 2015 and no longer in legal force.
glossary.salaries of Supreme Court Judges: The Article 125(1) rule that Supreme Court Judges' salaries are fixed by Parliament by law, defaulting to the Second Schedule figures absent such law.
glossary.Second Schedule default (Judges' salarie: The Article 125(1)-(2) fallback mechanism under which, absent a Parliamentary law fixing salaries, privileges, allowances, leave, or pension for Supreme Court Judges, the Second Schedule's specified figures apply by default — the same drafting pattern used for the President, Ministers, and presiding officers.
glossary.non-disadvantageous variation rule (Judg: The proviso to Article 125(2), guaranteeing that a Supreme Court Judge's privileges, allowances, leave-of-absence rights, and pension rights can never be varied to his disadvantage after his appointment — a structural financial-independence safeguard against retaliatory pay or benefit cuts.
glossary.acting Chief Justice of India: The Article 126 mechanism by which the President appoints one of the other Supreme Court Judges to perform the Chief Justice of India's duties during an actual vacancy in that office or the sitting CJI's temporary inability to perform duties — conventionally the senior-most puisne Judge, though the text leaves the choice to Presidential discretion.
glossary.ad hoc Judge (Supreme Court): A High Court Judge duly qualified for Supreme Court appointment, temporarily designated under Article 127 to sit with full Supreme Court jurisdiction and powers when the Court lacks a quorum of its own Judges to hold or continue a session.
glossary.quorum shortage trigger for ad hoc appoi: The Article 127(1) precondition for appointing an ad hoc Judge — an actual absence of the quorum of Supreme Court Judges needed to hold or continue any session of the Court.
glossary.retired Judge recalled to sit (Supreme C: A retired Supreme Court Judge, retired Federal Court Judge, or retired/qualified High Court Judge specially requested under Article 128 to sit and act as a Supreme Court Judge, exercising full jurisdiction and privileges during that engagement without becoming a permanent Judge of the Court.
glossary.consent requirement for recalled retired: The proviso to Article 128 making a retired Judge's own consent mandatory before he can be required to sit and act as a recalled Supreme Court Judge — the recall cannot be compelled.
glossary.Supreme Court as a court of record: The first limb of Article 129, designating the Supreme Court a court of record whose proceedings and judgments carry perpetual, unimpeachable evidentiary status when produced elsewhere — a status mirrored for High Courts under Article 215.
glossary.contempt power (Supreme Court): The second limb of Article 129, granting the Supreme Court a direct constitutional (not merely statutory) power to punish for contempt of itself, protecting the Court's dignity, authority, and the due administration of justice, supplemented but not created by the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.
glossary.seat of the Supreme Court: The Article 130 designation of Delhi as the Supreme Court's default sitting location, subject to the Chief Justice of India's power, with Presidential approval, to appoint other places from time to time — a provision underlying ongoing but unimplemented regional-bench proposals.
glossary.Chief Justice's power to appoint alterna: The Article 130 power vested in the Chief Justice of India, exercisable only with the President's approval, to designate places other than Delhi where the Supreme Court may sit from time to time.
glossary.original jurisdiction of the Supreme Cou: The Article 131 grant of exclusive first-instance jurisdiction to the Supreme Court over genuinely federal disputes — Centre v. State(s), Centre-with-States v. other States, and State v. State — where the dispute turns on the existence or extent of a legal right.
glossary.exclusive federal-dispute jurisdiction: The Article 131 rule that no court other than the Supreme Court may entertain a qualifying Centre-State or inter-State legal-right dispute — this jurisdiction is exclusive from the outset, not merely appellate.
glossary.legal-right-dependent dispute requiremen: The Article 131 threshold requirement confining original jurisdiction to disputes involving a question of law or fact on which the existence or extent of a legal right depends, excluding purely political or policy disagreements between governments.
glossary.pre-Constitution treaty/instrument exclu: The proviso to Article 131 excluding from Supreme Court original jurisdiction any dispute arising from a treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement, sanad, or similar instrument executed before the Constitution's commencement and still in operation, or which itself excludes this jurisdiction — a legacy carve-out from the princely-state integration era.
glossary.constitutional appeal (Article 132): The Article 132 appellate route to the Supreme Court from any High Court civil, criminal, or other proceeding's judgment, decree, or final order, available whenever the case involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, regardless of the underlying subject-matter.
glossary.substantial question of law as to consti: The Article 132 threshold requirement — the case must turn on a genuinely significant, unsettled question about how a constitutional provision is to be interpreted, not a merely arguable or settled point, before the constitutional-appeal route can be certified.
glossary.High Court certification requirement (Ar: The precondition that the High Court itself must certify under Article 134A that the case involves a substantial question of constitutional interpretation before an Article 132 appeal can proceed to the Supreme Court.
glossary.'final order' extended meaning: The Explanation to Article 132 enlarging 'final order' to include an order deciding an issue which, had it been decided in the appellant's favour, would have finally disposed of the case — capturing preliminary-issue orders that dismiss on a threshold point without a full trial.
glossary.civil appeal to Supreme Court (Article 1: The Article 133 appellate route confined to civil matters, requiring the High Court's dual certification that the case involves a substantial question of law of general importance and that, in the High Court's opinion, the question needs to be decided by the Supreme Court.
glossary.substantial question of law of general i: The first limb of the Article 133 dual-certification test — the legal question must not only be substantial but of general importance transcending the particular parties' dispute, distinguishing it from Article 132's narrower constitutional-interpretation-only requirement.
glossary.High Court's opinion that the question n: The second, independently required limb of the Article 133 dual-certification test — the High Court must itself form the opinion that the identified substantial question of general importance needs to be decided by the Supreme Court, beyond merely existing.
glossary.single-Judge High Court order appeal bar: The Article 133(3) rule barring any appeal to the Supreme Court from a judgment, decree, or final order of a single High Court Judge, unless Parliament otherwise provides by law — closing off piecemeal appeals from single-Judge civil orders.
glossary.criminal appeal to Supreme Court (Articl: The Article 134 appellate route in criminal matters, combining two automatic rights of appeal tied to death-sentence outcomes with a third discretionary route via High Court 'fit case' certification under Article 134A, all subject to Supreme Court Rules made under Article 145 and any High Court-imposed conditions.
glossary.automatic appeal on reversal-of-acquitta: The Article 134(1)(a) automatic (certification-free) right of appeal to the Supreme Court arising when a High Court has, on appeal, reversed an accused's acquittal and sentenced him to death.
glossary.automatic appeal on withdrawn-case-trial: The Article 134(1)(b) automatic right of appeal arising when a High Court has withdrawn a case from a subordinate court for trial itself, convicted the accused, and sentenced him to death.
glossary.'fit case' certification (Article 134(1): The discretionary criminal-appeal route under Article 134(1)(c), permitting a High Court to certify a case as fit for appeal to the Supreme Court even outside the two automatic death-sentence triggers, following the Article 134A certification procedure.
glossary.Parliament's power to expand criminal ap: The Article 134(2) power letting Parliament by law confer on the Supreme Court further criminal appellate jurisdiction beyond the three routes textually specified in clause (1), exercised through legislation such as the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970.
glossary.unified High Court certification procedu: The Article 134A mechanism consolidating the certification process for Articles 132(1), 133(1), and 134(1)(c) appeals — the High Court, as soon as reasonably practicable after passing or making a qualifying judgment, decree, or order, either certifies on its own motion or determines the question upon the aggrieved party's application.
glossary.suo motu certification power: The Article 134A power letting a High Court certify a case as fit for Supreme Court appeal on its own motion, without waiting for either party to apply, immediately after delivering the qualifying judgment, decree, final order, or sentence.
glossary.aggrieved party's oral application for c: The Article 134A entitlement of a party aggrieved by a High Court judgment, decree, final order, or sentence to orally apply for a certificate immediately after the judgment is delivered, triggering the High Court's obligation to determine the certification question.
glossary.Federal Court residual jurisdiction tran: The Article 135 transitional rule automatically vesting the Supreme Court with any jurisdiction and powers the pre-Constitution Federal Court held under existing law that don't fall within Article 133 or Article 134, ensuring continuity during India's 1950 transition to the new constitutional order.
glossary.sunset clause pending Parliamentary legi: The built-in limit on Article 135's inherited Federal Court jurisdiction — it operates only 'until Parliament by law otherwise provides,' meaning any subsequent Parliamentary legislation on the subject supersedes the automatic inheritance.
glossary.special leave to appeal (Article 136): The Supreme Court's discretionary power under Article 136 to grant permission to appeal from any judgment, decree, determination, sentence, or order of any court or tribunal in India (except Armed Forces tribunals) — the broadest appellate gateway in the Constitution, commonly invoked through a Special Leave Petition (SLP).
glossary.SLP jurisdiction as residuary constituti: The characterization of Article 136's special leave power as a residuary, catch-all appellate jurisdiction that operates independently of and beyond the specific certification-gated routes in Articles 132-134A, available even where no other constitutional appeal route exists.
glossary.'notwithstanding anything in this Chapte: The non-obstante opening words of Article 136(1) confirming that the Supreme Court's special leave power is not constrained by, or dependent on, the certification requirements of Articles 132, 133, and 134 found elsewhere in the same Chapter.
glossary.any court or tribunal (Article 136 scope: The exceptionally wide class of forums from which Article 136 special leave may be sought — not limited to High Courts, but extending to subordinate courts and quasi-judicial tribunals exercising judicial or quasi-judicial functions anywhere in India.
glossary.Armed Forces tribunal exclusion (Article: The Article 136(2) carve-out removing judgments, determinations, sentences, or orders of any court or tribunal constituted under a law relating to the Armed Forces (such as court-martial proceedings) from the Supreme Court's special leave jurisdiction.
glossary.review jurisdiction of the Supreme Court: The Article 137 power letting the Supreme Court review and, where warranted, correct its own final judgments or orders — an exception to functus officio, exercised subject to Parliamentary law and the Supreme Court's own Article 145 Rules rather than on open-ended grounds.
glossary.grounds for review (developed through Su: The narrow grounds on which an Article 137 review petition is actually entertained in practice — chiefly discovery of new and important matter, a mistake or error apparent on the face of the record, or any other sufficient reason — sourced from Order XLVII of the Supreme Court Rules (mirroring Civil Procedure Code review principles) rather than spelled out in the constitutional text itself.
glossary.enlargement of Supreme Court's jurisdict: The Article 138 mechanism allowing the Supreme Court's jurisdiction to grow beyond Articles 131-137 through two routes — Parliamentary law over Union List subjects (clause 1), or a Centre-State special agreement backed by Parliamentary law (clause 2).
glossary.Union List jurisdiction conferment (Arti: The Article 138(1) route by which Parliament may, through ordinary legislation, confer on the Supreme Court further jurisdiction and powers over any subject falling within the Union List (List I of the Seventh Schedule).
glossary.special agreement jurisdiction confermen: The Article 138(2) route by which the Union and a State Government may agree to confer further jurisdiction on the Supreme Court over a matter — effective only once Parliament also passes a law providing for the Supreme Court to exercise that agreed jurisdiction.
glossary.conferment of additional writ power on t: The Article 139 mechanism letting Parliament extend the Supreme Court's writ-issuing power (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, certiorari) to purposes beyond Fundamental Rights enforcement under Article 32(2), which Parliament may exercise by law.
glossary.purposes other than Article 32(2) (Artic: The defining limitation of Article 139 — it concerns conferring Supreme Court writ power only for purposes outside Article 32(2)'s Fundamental-Rights-enforcement writ jurisdiction, which already exists independently and doesn't need Article 139 to operate.
glossary.transfer of cases between High Courts an: The Article 139A power letting the Supreme Court withdraw and consolidate cases raising the same substantial question of general importance that are pending across the Supreme Court and High Court(s), or across multiple High Courts, to avoid conflicting rulings on the same legal question.
glossary.withdrawal of cases involving common que: The Article 139A(1) power exercised by the Supreme Court, on its own motion or on application by the Attorney-General or a party, to withdraw to itself cases pending in one or more High Courts that involve the same or substantially the same substantial questions of law of general importance as a case already before it.
glossary.return of withdrawn case with binding ju: The proviso to Article 139A(1) letting the Supreme Court, after deciding the common legal question in a withdrawn case, send the case back to its originating High Court along with its judgment, binding the High Court to dispose of the remaining case in conformity with that ruling.
glossary.inter-High-Court transfer for ends of ju: The freestanding Article 139A(2) power letting the Supreme Court transfer any individual case, appeal, or proceeding from one High Court to another whenever it deems this expedient for the ends of justice, independent of any common-question-of-law requirement.
glossary.ancillary/supplemental powers of Supreme: The Article 140 power letting Parliament confer supplemental operational powers on the Supreme Court — powers that make its existing constitutional jurisdiction more effective in practice, provided they are consistent with the rest of the Constitution.
glossary.law declared by the Supreme Court bindin: The Article 141 rule making the ratio decidendi of every Supreme Court decision binding on all courts throughout India's territory — the constitutional foundation of India's unified, hierarchical system of binding judicial precedent.
glossary.doctrine of precedent (Indian constituti: The Indian legal system's version of stare decisis, textually rooted in Article 141, under which the Supreme Court's declared law binds every subordinate and High Court in the country, producing a single nationwide body of authoritative case law rather than fragmented regional interpretations.
glossary.'law declared' distinguished from obiter: The distinction, central to applying Article 141, between the ratio decidendi ('law declared' — the legal principle actually necessary to the decision, which binds) and obiter dicta (passing observations not essential to the decision, which are merely persuasive and not binding under Article 141).
glossary.complete justice power (Article 142): The extraordinary Article 142(1) power letting the Supreme Court pass any decree or order necessary for doing complete justice in a cause or matter pending before it, going beyond the strict letter of ordinary law where substantive justice requires — one of the Constitution's most distinctive and far-reaching judicial powers.
glossary.pan-India enforceability of Supreme Cour: The Article 142(1) rule that any decree or order the Supreme Court passes under its complete-justice power is enforceable throughout the whole territory of India, in a manner Parliament prescribes by law or, absent such law, as the President prescribes by order.
glossary.attendance/discovery/contempt investigat: The Article 142(2) bundle of practical powers — nationwide authority to compel attendance of persons, order discovery or production of documents, and investigate or punish contempt of itself — that keeps the Supreme Court's process effective across India, subject to any regulating Parliamentary law.
glossary.Presidential reference power (Article 14: The Article 143 mechanism letting the President formally refer a significant question of law or fact (clause 1) or a pre-Constitution treaty dispute otherwise excluded under Article 131's proviso (clause 2) to the Supreme Court for its opinion, activating the Court's advisory (non-adjudicatory) jurisdiction.
glossary.advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Cou: The Supreme Court's Article 143 function of giving the President a formal opinion on a referred question of law or fact outside the context of an actual adversarial dispute between parties — distinct from, and not binding in the same way as, its ordinary jurisdiction to decide live cases.
glossary.discretionary opinion under clause (1) v: The textual distinction within Article 143 — the Supreme Court 'may' report its opinion on a general public-importance reference under clause (1) (and may decline), but 'shall' report its opinion on a pre-Constitution treaty dispute reference under clause (2) (no discretion to decline).
glossary.pre-Constitution treaty dispute referenc: The specific Article 143(2) advisory-reference route letting the President send to the Supreme Court, for a mandatory opinion, the category of pre-Constitution treaty/instrument disputes that Article 131's proviso otherwise excludes from the Court's ordinary original jurisdiction.
glossary.duty to act in aid of the Supreme Court: The Article 144 mandatory obligation on all civil and judicial authorities throughout India's territory to actively cooperate with and support the Supreme Court's functioning, reinforcing its position at the apex of the Indian judicial hierarchy.
glossary.omitted Article 144A: A repealed constitutional provision — originally inserted by the Forty-second Amendment Act, 1976 to impose special restrictive procedures on courts deciding constitutional-validity questions, then omitted entirely by the Forty-third Amendment Act, 1977 (effective 13 April 1978) as part of the post-Emergency rollback of Emergency-era amendments; it has no current legal force.
glossary.Forty-third Amendment repeal of special: The 1977 constitutional amendment (effective 1978) that omitted Article 144A, removing the Emergency-era special procedural restrictions on judicial determination of a law's constitutional validity and restoring ordinary adjudicatory procedure.
glossary.Rules of Court (Article 145): The procedural rules the Supreme Court is empowered to make under Article 145(1), covering advocates' practice, appeal procedure, Fundamental Rights and Article 139A proceedings, review, costs, bail, stay, and summary dismissal of frivolous appeals — subject to Parliamentary law and Presidential approval.
glossary.Presidential approval requirement for Su: The Article 145(1) precondition that any rule the Supreme Court makes for regulating its own practice and procedure requires the President's approval before it can take effect, alongside remaining subject to any Parliamentary law on the subject.
glossary.Constitution Bench requirement (five-Jud: The Article 145(3) constitutional floor requiring at least five Judges to sit for deciding any case involving a substantial question of constitutional interpretation, or for hearing any Article 143 Presidential reference — commonly known in Indian practice as a 'Constitution Bench.'
glossary.mandatory reference of constitutional qu: The proviso to Article 145(3) requiring a smaller Bench (hearing an appeal under this Chapter other than under Article 132) that discovers a substantial constitutional question necessary for disposal of the appeal to refer that question to a properly constituted five-Judge Bench, and then dispose of the appeal in conformity with the opinion received.
glossary.open-court delivery requirement: The Article 145(4) rule that no Supreme Court judgment, and no Article 143 advisory report, may be delivered except in open court — barring private or informal issuance of the Court's decisions and opinions.
glossary.majority-concurrence requirement for jud: The Article 145(5) rule that no Supreme Court judgment or Article 143 opinion may be delivered without the concurrence of a majority of the Judges present at the hearing of the case.
glossary.dissenting judgment entitlement: The proviso within Article 145(5) expressly preserving the right of any Judge who does not concur with the majority to deliver a separate dissenting judgment or opinion — the constitutional foundation for India's tradition of published judicial dissents.
glossary.Chief Justice's appointment power over C: The Article 146(1) power vesting appointment of Supreme Court officers and servants in the Chief Justice of India (or a delegated Judge/officer), keeping the Court's administrative staffing outside ordinary executive control.
glossary.UPSC consultation proviso for outside ap: The proviso to Article 146(1) letting the President require, by rule, that appointment of an outsider (not already attached to the Court) to specified Court offices happen only after consultation with the Union Public Service Commission — a limited check on the Chief Justice's otherwise autonomous staffing power.
glossary.Charged expenditure (Supreme Court admin: The Article 146(3) rule making the Supreme Court's entire administrative budget — including staff salaries, allowances, and pensions — a charge on the Consolidated Fund of India, exempt from the annual Parliamentary voting process and thereby insulated from budgetary leverage over the judiciary.
glossary.extended meaning of 'constitutional inte: The Article 147 interpretive rule providing that, within the Union Judiciary Chapter and the parallel High Court appellate-jurisdiction Chapter, 'substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution' also includes substantial questions about interpreting the Government of India Act, 1935 and the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and instruments made under them.
glossary.Government of India Act 1935 interpretiv: The specific pre-Constitution statute (plus its amendments and Orders in Council) that Article 147 folds into the definition of 'constitutional interpretation' for purposes of Articles 132-145 and the parallel High Court Chapter, preserving continuity with India's immediately pre-1950 constitutional order.
glossary.Comptroller and Auditor-General of India: The Article 148 constitutional office responsible for auditing and reporting on the accounts of the Union and every State, appointed by the President and given independence protections closely modelled on those of a Supreme Court Judge.
glossary.removal safeguard equal to a Supreme Cou: The Article 148(1) guarantee that the CAG can only be removed from office in the same manner and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court Judge — i.e., via the Article 124(4) proved-misbehaviour-or-incapacity Parliamentary address procedure, not at executive discretion.
glossary.post-retirement office bar (CAG): The Article 148(4) permanent prohibition on a former CAG holding any further office under the Government of India or any State Government after ceasing to hold the post — preventing post-service inducements that could compromise independence while in office.
glossary.non-disadvantageous variation rule (CAG: The proviso to Article 148(3) guaranteeing that a CAG's salary and his rights regarding leave of absence, pension, or retirement age can never be varied to his disadvantage after his appointment — a financial-independence safeguard matching the pattern used for Judges and other high constitutional offices.
glossary.Indian Audit and Accounts Department: The professional cadre of government auditors and accountants whose conditions of service, and whose administrative oversight by the CAG, are governed by rules the President makes under Article 148(5) after consulting the Comptroller and Auditor-General.
glossary.charged expenditure (CAG office): The Article 148(6) rule making the administrative expenses of the CAG's office — including salaries, allowances, and pensions of its personnel — a charge on the Consolidated Fund of India, paralleling the same budget-insulation treatment given to the Supreme Court under Article 146(3).
glossary.CAG's duties and powers (Article 149): The Article 149 rule leaving the CAG's substantive audit duties and powers over Union, State, and other public accounts to be defined by Parliamentary law, defaulting in the interim to the powers the pre-Constitution Auditor-General of India held over the Dominion of India and the Provinces.
glossary.CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Se: The Parliamentary statute that comprehensively defines the CAG's audit jurisdiction over Union, State, and other publicly-financed bodies' accounts, superseding in practice the transitional pre-Constitution Auditor-General default preserved by Article 149.
glossary.pre-Constitution Auditor-General default: The Article 149 transitional rule that, until Parliament legislates on the CAG's duties and powers, the CAG exercises exactly the duties and powers the Auditor-General of India held over the Dominion of India and the Provinces immediately before the Constitution commenced.
glossary.form of Union and State accounts (Articl: The Article 150 rule empowering the President to prescribe the form in which Union and State government accounts are kept, ensuring a uniform, audit-compatible accounting format is used nationwide.
glossary.CAG's advisory role in prescribing accou: The requirement, strengthened from mere consultation (pre-1978) to binding advice (post-Forty-fourth Amendment, 1978), that the President prescribe the form of Union and State accounts only on the advice of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India.
glossary.CAG audit reports (Article 151): The formal reports the Comptroller and Auditor-General submits on Union accounts (to the President) and State accounts (to the respective Governor), which the President/Governor must in turn cause to be laid before Parliament or the State Legislature, completing the constitutional audit-accountability cycle.
glossary.laying of CAG reports before Parliament/: The mandatory Article 151 duty of the President (for Union accounts) and the Governor (for State accounts) to cause the CAG's submitted audit reports to be placed before the relevant legislature, converting independent audit findings into a basis for legislative accountability.
glossary.Public Accounts Committee scrutiny (inst: The parliamentary and State-legislative practice, not itself textually mandated by Article 151 but built around the reports it requires be laid, whereby a Public Accounts Committee examines CAG audit reports as its principal working material for holding the executive accountable for public expenditure.
glossary.definition of 'State' in Part VI: The Article 152 scoping rule that, throughout Part VI (The States), the expression 'State' does not include the State of Jammu and Kashmir, reflecting that State's historically distinct constitutional arrangement — now significantly altered by the 2019 abrogation of Article 370 and J&K's reorganisation into Union Territories.
glossary.Jammu and Kashmir exclusion (historical,: The textual carve-out of Jammu and Kashmir from the definition of 'State' in Part VI, rooted in that State's former special constitutional status under Article 370 — its practical significance has been overtaken by J&K's 2019 reorganisation into Union Territories, even though Article 152's text remains formally unamended.
glossary.Governor as head of State executive: The Article 153 constitutional requirement that every State have a Governor, serving as the State-level counterpart to the President — the formal head of the State's executive branch.
glossary.common Governor for multiple States: The proviso to Article 153, inserted by the Seventh Amendment Act, 1956, permitting the same individual to be appointed Governor of two or more States simultaneously, a practice occasionally used for administrative convenience though sometimes politically contentious.
glossary.executive power of the State (Article 15: The Article 154(1) formal vesting of a State's executive power in the Governor, exercisable directly or through subordinate officers in accordance with the Constitution — in practice exercised on the aid and advice of the State Council of Ministers, mirroring the President's position at the Union level under Article 53.
glossary.direct exercise vs delegation through su: The Article 154(1) flexibility letting the Governor exercise the State's executive power either personally or through officers subordinate to him, subject always to constitutional constraints — in ordinary practice channelled through ministerial advice rather than direct personal action.
glossary.existing-law functions preserved for oth: The Article 154(2) clarification that vesting executive power in the Governor does not disturb functions already conferred by existing law on some other authority, and does not prevent Parliament or the State Legislature from assigning functions to authorities subordinate to the Governor going forward.
glossary.Presidential appointment of Governor: The Article 155 rule vesting the power to appoint a State's Governor exclusively in the President, formalised by warrant under his hand and seal — exercised in practice on the advice of the Union Council of Ministers, with no textual requirement of consultation with the State concerned.
glossary.warrant under hand and seal (Governor ap: The formal instrument — a warrant bearing the President's hand (signature) and seal — through which a Governor's appointment under Article 155 is made, the same formal appointment mechanism used for Supreme Court and High Court Judges and other high constitutional offices.
glossary.Governor's tenure at President's pleasur: The Article 156(1) rule making a Governor's continuance in office entirely subject to the President's pleasure, allowing removal at any time without a stated cause — tempered in practice by evolving Supreme Court jurisprudence holding this discretion cannot be exercised arbitrarily.
glossary.Governor's resignation (Article 156(2)): The Article 156(2) power letting a Governor resign at will by writing under his hand addressed to the President, without needing to give reasons or obtain approval for the resignation to take effect.
glossary.five-year term subject to pleasure doctr: The Article 156(3) default tenure of five years from the date a Governor enters upon office, expressly made subject to the overriding 'pleasure of the President' rule in clause (1) and to voluntary resignation under clause (2) — the nominal term can be cut short by either.
glossary.hold-over rule pending successor's entry: The proviso to Article 156(3) requiring a Governor to continue holding office beyond the expiry of his five-year term until his successor actually enters upon office, ensuring the post is never left vacant.
glossary.Governor eligibility criteria: The Article 157 minimal qualification requirements for Governorship — Indian citizenship and completion of thirty-five years of age — with no further constitutional requirement of prior political, legal, or administrative experience.
glossary.minimum age thirty-five (Governor): The Article 157 minimum-age eligibility threshold of thirty-five completed years for appointment as Governor, matching the minimum age set for the President under Article 58 and for Rajya Sabha membership.
glossary.disqualification from legislative member: The Article 158(1) rule barring a Governor from simultaneously being a member of either House of Parliament or of any State Legislature's House, with any existing legislative seat automatically deemed vacated upon entering office as Governor.
glossary.automatic seat-vacation on becoming Gove: The Article 158(1) consequence that a sitting MP or MLA/MLC appointed Governor is automatically deemed to have vacated that legislative seat on the date he enters upon office as Governor, without needing any separate resignation formality.
glossary.office-of-profit bar (Governor): The Article 158(2) prohibition on a Governor holding any other office of profit while in office, protecting the full-time and independent character of the Governorship.
glossary.rent-free official residence entitlement: The Article 158(3) guarantee that a Governor is entitled, without payment of rent, to the use of his official residences, alongside emoluments, allowances, and privileges fixed by Parliament by law or defaulting to Second Schedule figures.
glossary.Second Schedule default (Governor's emol: The Article 158(3) fallback mechanism under which, absent a Parliamentary law fixing a Governor's emoluments, allowances, and privileges, the Second Schedule's specified figures apply by default — the same drafting pattern used for the President, Ministers, presiding officers, Supreme Court Judges, and the CAG.
glossary.emolument allocation for common Governor: The Article 158(3A) mechanism, inserted by the Seventh Amendment Act, 1956, letting the President by order allocate a common Governor's emoluments and allowances among the multiple States he serves, in whatever proportion the President determines.
glossary.non-diminution of Governor's emoluments: The Article 158(4) guarantee that a Governor's emoluments and allowances cannot be reduced during his term of office — a financial-independence safeguard, though textually narrower than equivalent Judge protections since it does not extend to 'privileges' or 'rights,' only emoluments and allowances.
glossary.Governor's oath of office: The Article 159 mandatory oath or affirmation every Governor (and anyone discharging the Governor's functions) must make before entering office, committing him to faithfully execute the office and preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution and the law.
glossary.administered by the High Court Chief Jus: The Article 159 requirement that a Governor's oath be administered by the Chief Justice of the State's High Court (or, in his absence, that Court's senior-most available Judge) — a judicial rather than political or executive functionary, underscoring the office's constitutional character.
glossary.content of Governor's oath — preserve, p: The substantive commitment in the Article 159 oath form — to faithfully execute the office of Governor, to the best of one's ability preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution and the law, and to devote oneself to the service and well-being of the State's people.
glossary.Presidential contingency-filling power (: The Article 160 residual power letting the President make whatever provision he thinks fit for discharging the Governor's functions in any contingency this Chapter doesn't already address — a safety-valve gap-filler for unanticipated situations.
glossary.residual gap-filling for unprovided cont: The characterization of Article 160 as operating only where a genuine gap exists in the constitutional scheme for the Governor's functioning — it supplements, rather than overrides, the specific succession and acting-arrangement rules this Chapter already provides.
glossary.Governor's pardoning power (Article 161): The State-level clemency power letting the Governor grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishment, or suspend, remit, or commute a sentence, for persons convicted of offences against laws relating to matters within the State's executive power — the State counterpart to the President's Article 72 power, though textually narrower in scope.
glossary.clemency power scope tied to State execu: The Article 161 limitation confining the Governor's pardoning power to offences against laws relating to matters to which the State's executive power extends, distinguishing it from the President's broader Article 72 clemency power over Union-law offences, death sentences, and court-martial sentences.
