Clause (1) still requires Presidential recommendation before introduction and still bars introduction in the Rajya Sabha for the fiscal-matter provisions specifically — but because it's not a pure Money Bill, once properly introduced in the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha thereafter participates as a co-equal House (unlike its weak Article 109 recommendatory role for true Money Bills). The proviso helpfully exempts tax-reduction/abolition amendments from needing fresh Presidential recommendation, since such amendments are revenue-friendly to the public rather than expenditure-risky. Clause (3) is a separate, broader rule — any Bill at all that would cause Consolidated Fund expenditure needs Presidential recommendation before either House passes it, even if it isn't otherwise a financial Bill under clause (1).
essential_elements: A Bill or amendment dealing with any Article 110(1)(a)-(f) matter requires Presidential recommendation before introduction/moving, and cannot be introduced in the Council of States
No fresh Presidential recommendation is needed for amendments that merely reduce or abolish a tax
Bills merely imposing fines, licence/service fees, or local-authority taxation are not treated as falling within the restricted fiscal matters, mirroring the Article 110(2) carve-out
Separately, any Bill (financial or not) that would involve expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India requires Presidential recommendation before either House passes it
exceptions_and_qualifications: Financial Bills under this article are structurally different from true Money Bills under Article 110 — only the fiscal-matter provisions trigger the introduction restrictions, and the Rajya Sabha retains its normal co-equal amending/passing role for the Bill as a whole once introduced (unlike its recommendation-only role under Article 109 for genuine Money Bills)

Clause (3)'s expenditure-recommendation requirement is broader and independent of clause (1) — it can apply even to a Bill that has nothing to do with the Article 110(1) fiscal-matter categories, simply because its enactment would cause Consolidated Fund spending
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish this article's 'financial Bill' from Article 110's 'Money Bill' — a financial Bill needs Presidential recommendation and Lok-Sabha-only introduction for its fiscal provisions but is otherwise processed as an ordinary Bill through both Houses, whereas a true Money Bill is entirely Lok-Sabha-controlled under Article 109.

sections.title: Rules of procedure
sections.raw_text: (1) Each House of Parliament may make rules for regulating, subject to the provisions of this Constitution, its procedure and the conduct of its business. (2) Until rules are made under clause (1), the rules of procedure and standing orders in force immediately before the commencement of this Constitution with respect to the Legislature of the Dominion of India shall have effect in relation to Parliament subject to such modifications and adaptations as may be made therein by the Chairman of the Council of States or the Speaker of the House of the People, as the case may be. (3) The President, after consultation with the Chairman of the Council of States and the Speaker of the House of the People, may make rules as to the procedure with respect to joint sittings of, and communications between, the two Houses. (4) At a joint sitting of the two Houses the Speaker of the House of the People, or in his absence such person as may be determined by rules of procedure made under clause (3), shall preside.
key_terms: each House's power to make its own procedural rules
transitional pre-Constitution standing orders
President's rules for joint sittings and inter-House communication
Speaker presides at joint sittings

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 118 gives each House of Parliament internal self-governance over its own procedure (subject to the Constitution itself) — this is the source of the Rajya Sabha's and Lok Sabha's own Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business, and of Speaker's/Chairman's rulings that shape day-to-day proceedings. Clause (2) was a one-time transitional bridge ensuring Parliament wasn't left without any procedural rules at all the moment the Constitution commenced, by carrying over the old Dominion Legislature's standing orders (as adapted). Clauses (3)-(4) specifically hand the President rule-making power for the cross-House mechanics of joint sittings and inter-House communication (the mechanics behind Article 108's joint sitting), and fix the Speaker (not the Rajya Sabha Chairman) as the default presiding officer whenever a joint sitting actually occurs — reflecting the Lok Sabha's numerically dominant position in that setting.
essential_elements: Each House has autonomous rule-making power over its own procedure and business conduct, always subject to the Constitution's overriding provisions
The pre-Constitution Dominion Legislature's standing orders filled the gap until each House made its own rules, as adapted by the Chairman or Speaker respectively
The President, after consulting both presiding officers, makes the rules specifically governing joint-sitting procedure and communications between the two Houses
The Speaker of the House of the People (or his rules-designated substitute) presides over any joint sitting, regardless of which House's Bill is under consideration
exceptions_and_qualifications: Each House's rule-making autonomy under clause (1) is expressly 'subject to the provisions of this Constitution' — internal rules cannot override or contradict any constitutional requirement (e.g., the quorum or voting rules of Article 100)

The President's joint-sitting rule-making power under clause (3) is confined to procedural/communication mechanics — it does not extend to the substantive voting or amendment rules for joint sittings, which are fixed directly by Article 108(4) itself
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat clause (1) as the general internal-autonomy rule (each House's own Rules of Procedure), clause (2) as a spent transitional bridge, and clauses (3)-(4) as the specific machinery provisions supporting Article 108's joint sitting mechanism — note the Speaker's default presiding role even over the combined Houses.

sections.title: Regulation by law of procedure in Parliament in relation to financial business
sections.raw_text: Parliament may, for the purpose of the timely completion of financial business, regulate by law the procedure of, and the conduct of business in, each House of Parliament in relation to any financial matter or to any Bill for the appropriation of moneys out of the Consolidated Fund of India, and, if and so far as any provision of any law so made is inconsistent with any rule made by a House of Parliament under clause (1) of article 118 or with any rule or standing order having effect in relation to Parliament under clause (2) of that article, such provision shall prevail.
key_terms: Parliament's law-making power over financial-business procedure
statutory override of internal House rules for financial business

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 119 lets Parliament, by ordinary legislation, impose binding time-limits and procedural discipline on how each House handles financial business specifically (Budget debates, grant votes, Appropriation Bills) — ensuring urgent fiscal matters like the annual Budget cannot be indefinitely stalled by internal procedural manoeuvring. Crucially, such a law trumps each House's own internal Rules of Procedure made under Article 118(1) (and the transitional standing orders under Article 118(2)) wherever there's a conflict — a rare instance of statute law overriding a House's own procedural autonomy, justified by the constitutional priority placed on timely fiscal governance.
essential_elements: Parliament may make a law specifically regulating the procedure and conduct of financial business (financial matters generally, or Appropriation Bills specifically) in either House
The stated purpose is ensuring timely completion of financial business, addressing the risk that ordinary procedural rules could be used to indefinitely delay Budget-related legislation
Where such a law conflicts with a House's own Article 118(1) rules, or with the transitional Article 118(2) standing orders, the statute prevails over the internal rule
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a narrow, purpose-specific override confined to financial business — it does not give Parliament general power to override each House's procedural autonomy on non-financial matters, which remains governed by Article 118(1) alone
In practice this power has rarely needed active exercise, since each House's own Rules of Procedure already build in Budget-session timelines, but the provision stands as a constitutional backstop
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this as a narrow, financial-business-specific exception to Article 118(1)'s internal-autonomy principle — the only context in which an ordinary Parliamentary statute can override a House's own procedural rules, justified by the urgency of timely Budget passage.

sections.title: Language to be used in Parliament
sections.raw_text: (1) Notwithstanding anything in Part XVII, but subject to the provisions of article 348, business in Parliament shall be transacted in Hindi or in English: Provided that the Chairman of the Council of States or Speaker of the House of the People, or person acting as such, as the case may be, may permit any member who cannot adequately express himself in Hindi or in English to address the House in his mother-tongue. (2) Unless Parliament by law otherwise provides, this article shall, after the expiration of a period of fifteen years from the commencement of this Constitution, have effect as if the words "or in English'' were omitted therefrom.
key_terms: language of Parliamentary business
mother-tongue proviso
fifteen-year sunset on English (unless extended by law)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 120 fixes Hindi and English as the two languages in which Parliament's business may be conducted, overriding the general official-language provisions of Part XVII except where Article 348 (language of the Supreme Court/High Courts and of authoritative legislative texts) specifically applies. The proviso is a practical accommodation letting a member who genuinely cannot manage either language address the House in his mother tongue, with the presiding officer's permission. Clause (2) originally set a 15-year sunset clock on English's constitutional status as a Parliamentary language (i.e., it would have automatically dropped out around 1965) — but Parliament has repeatedly exercised its 'unless Parliament by law otherwise provides' override, most notably via the Official Languages Act, 1963, so English remains fully valid today alongside Hindi.
essential_elements: Ordinary Parliamentary business must be transacted in Hindi or English
A member unable to adequately express himself in either language may, with the presiding officer's permission, address the House in his mother tongue

Clause (2)'s automatic removal of English after fifteen years from commencement is itself subject to Parliament's power to legislate otherwise — a power Parliament has exercised, keeping English available indefinitely
exceptions_and_qualifications: This article operates 'notwithstanding' Part XVII's general official-language scheme, but remains 'subject to' Article 348, which separately governs the language of the Supreme Court, High Courts, and authoritative legislative and judicial texts

The 15-year sunset in clause (2) never actually took effect in practice because Parliament passed overriding legislation (the Official Languages Act, 1963, as amended) before the deadline, preserving English's status
breakdown.how_to_read: Read clause (1) as the operative Hindi-or-English rule with a mother-tongue safety valve, and clause (2) as a dormant sunset clause that Parliament has continuously legislated around — in practice, both Hindi and English remain fully available today.

sections.title: Restriction on discussion in Parliament
sections.raw_text: No discussion shall take place in Parliament with respect to the conduct of any Judge of the Supreme Court or of a High Court in the discharge of his duties except upon a motion for presenting an address to the President praying for the removal of the Judge as hereinafter provided.
key_terms: bar on discussing judicial conduct in Parliament
removal-motion exception

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 121 protects judicial independence by generally barring Parliament from debating a sitting Supreme Court or High Court Judge's conduct in office at all — ordinary political criticism or discussion of a Judge's judicial performance is constitutionally off-limits. The sole exception is the formal, high-threshold removal process (the 'motion for presenting an address to the President praying for removal,' elaborated for Supreme Court Judges in Article 124(4)-(5) and applied to High Court Judges via Article 218) — only within that specific constitutional removal procedure may a Judge's conduct actually be discussed.
essential_elements: General Parliamentary discussion of a Judge's conduct in discharging judicial duties is prohibited
The only permitted forum for discussing a Judge's conduct is a formal removal motion (address to the President) under the procedure Article 124(4)-(5) establishes
exceptions_and_qualifications: This bar applies only to discussion of judicial conduct in the discharge of duties — it does not bar all reference to a Judge or to judicial decisions/judgments in Parliamentary debate generally, only conduct-focused discussion outside the formal removal process

The removal-motion procedure itself, including its supporting investigation machinery, is what Article 124(5) (Parliament's power to regulate the procedure) and equivalent High Court provisions govern
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as judicial-independence insulation — Parliament cannot casually debate a Judge's conduct; only the formal impeachment-style removal motion under Article 124(4)-(5) creates a lawful occasion to discuss it.

sections.title: Courts not to inquire into proceedings of Parliament
sections.raw_text: (1) The validity of any proceedings in Parliament shall not be called in question on the ground of any alleged irregularity of procedure. (2) No officer or member of Parliament in whom powers are vested by or under this Constitution for regulating procedure or the conduct of business, or for maintaining order, in Parliament shall be subject to the jurisdiction of any court in respect of the exercise by him of those powers.
key_terms: non-justiciability of Parliamentary procedural irregularity
immunity of presiding officers for procedural rulings

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 122 is the Parliamentary counterpart to the courts-not-to-inquire rule that protects legislative proceedings from being unpicked in litigation over mere procedural technicalities. Clause (1) means a court cannot invalidate an Act or Parliamentary proceeding just because internal procedure (e.g., a Rules of Procedure requirement) was allegedly not followed exactly. Clause (2) separately immunises the Speaker, Chairman, or any other officer/member exercising constitutionally-vested procedural or order-maintaining powers (such as suspending a disruptive member, or ruling on amendment admissibility under Articles 108(4) or 114(2)) from being hauled before a court over how they exercised that power.
essential_elements: Courts cannot invalidate Parliamentary proceedings merely for alleged procedural irregularity
Officers and members exercising constitutionally-vested procedural, business-conduct, or order-maintenance powers are immune from court jurisdiction over the exercise of those specific powers
exceptions_and_qualifications: This immunity concerns procedural regularity, not substantive constitutionality — it does not bar courts from reviewing whether a Parliamentary enactment itself is constitutionally valid on substantive grounds (that remains fully justiciable under the Constitution's ordinary judicial review framework)

The clause (2) immunity is confined to the exercise of powers 'vested by or under this Constitution' for procedure, business conduct, or order — it does not create a blanket immunity for every act of a Parliamentary officer unrelated to those specific functions
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish clause (1)'s narrow procedural-irregularity shield from full immunity from judicial review — substantive constitutional challenges to legislation remain fully available; only internal procedural regularity and presiding-officer discretion in exercising procedural powers are insulated.

sections.title: Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament
sections.raw_text: (1) If at any time, except when both Houses of Parliament are in session, the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require. (2) An Ordinance promulgated under this article shall have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, but every such Ordinance— (a) shall be laid before both Houses of Parliament and shall cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament, or, if before the expiration of that period resolutions disapproving it are passed by both Houses, upon the passing of the second of those resolutions; and (b) may be withdrawn at any time by the President. Explanation.—Where the Houses of Parliament are summoned to reassemble on different dates, the period of six weeks shall be reckoned from the later of those dates for the purposes of this clause. (3) If and so far as an Ordinance under this article makes any provision which Parliament would not under this Constitution be competent to enact, it shall be void.
key_terms: Presidential Ordinance-making power
recess precondition for Ordinances
six-week expiry after Parliament's reassembly
disapproval resolutions by both Houses
Ordinance void if beyond Parliament's legislative competence

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 123 lets the President — acting, in reality, on the Union Council of Ministers' aid and advice under Article 74 — legislate by Ordinance when Parliament is not in session and urgent action is needed, without waiting for Parliament to reconvene and pass an ordinary Act. An Ordinance has full force of law, identical to an Act of Parliament, the moment it's promulgated. But it is inherently temporary and provisional: it must be placed before both Houses once they reassemble, and automatically lapses six weeks after reassembly unless Parliament converts it into a permanent Act before then (or it can die sooner if both Houses pass disapproval resolutions). This power has generated significant constitutional controversy in India over 'Ordinance Raj' — repeated re-promulgation of Ordinances to indefinitely bypass Parliament — which the Supreme Court has held to be a fraud on the Constitution (D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar).
essential_elements: The Ordinance power can only be exercised when both Houses of Parliament are not simultaneously in session

The President must be satisfied that circumstances exist rendering immediate action necessary — a satisfaction that is subject to judicial review for mala fides or complete absence of relevant material, per later constitutional jurisprudence
An Ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament from the moment of promulgation
It must be laid before both Houses and automatically ceases to operate six weeks after Parliament's reassembly unless earlier converted into an Act or disapproved
The President retains an independent power to withdraw an Ordinance at any time before it would otherwise expire
exceptions_and_qualifications: Where Parliament's two Houses are summoned to reassemble on different dates, the six-week clock runs from the later of those two dates, not the earlier — ensuring the full Parliament (not just one House) gets a genuine opportunity to act

An Ordinance is void to the extent it contains any provision Parliament itself would lack competence to enact as an ordinary law — the Ordinance power cannot be used to legislate beyond Parliament's own constitutional limits

The repeated re-promulgation of an Ordinance without ever placing it before Parliament for a vote has been held unconstitutional as a colourable exercise of power circumventing the legislature (D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar, 1987) — the 'satisfaction' precondition and the six-week/disapproval safeguards are not meant to be indefinitely evaded
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Article 123 as a temporary, session-gap-filling legislative power fully co-extensive with (and bound by the same competence limits as) ordinary Parliamentary law-making — the six-week expiry and disapproval-resolution mechanisms are the built-in safeguards against it becoming a permanent substitute for legislation, and repeated re-promulgation to dodge those safeguards is itself unconstitutional per Wadhwa.

sections.title: Establishment and constitution of Supreme Court
sections.raw_text: (1) There shall be a Supreme Court of India consisting of a Chief Justice of India and, until Parliament by law prescribes a larger number, of not more than seven other Judges (now thirty-three other Judges per the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2019). (2) Every Judge of the Supreme Court shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal and shall hold office until he attains the age of sixty-five years. Provided that— (a) a Judge may, by writing under his hand addressed to the President, resign his office; (b) a Judge may be removed from his office in the manner provided in clause (4). (2A) The age of a Judge of the Supreme Court shall be determined by such authority and in such manner as Parliament may by law provide. (3) A person shall not be qualified for appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court unless he is a citizen of India and— (a) has been for at least five years a Judge of a High Court or of two or more such Courts in succession; or (b) has been for at least ten years an advocate of a High Court or of two or more such Courts in succession; or (c) is, in the opinion of the President, a distinguished jurist. Explanation I.—In this clause "High Court'' means a High Court which exercises, or which at any time before the commencement of this Constitution exercised, jurisdiction in any part of the territory of India. Explanation II.—In computing for the purpose of this clause the period during which a person has been an advocate, any period during which a person has held judicial office not inferior to that of a district judge after he became an advocate shall be included. (4) A Judge of the Supreme Court shall not be removed from his office except by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting has been presented to the President in the same session for such removal on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. (5) Parliament may by law regulate the procedure for the presentation of an address and for the investigation and proof of the misbehaviour or incapacity of a Judge under clause (4). (6) Every person appointed to be a Judge of the Supreme Court shall, before he enters upon his office, make and subscribe before the President, or some person appointed in that behalf by him, an oath or affirmation according to the form set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule. (7) No person who has held office as a Judge of the Supreme Court shall plead or act in any court or before any authority within the territory of India.
key_terms: composition of the Supreme Court of India
appointment of Supreme Court Judges
sixty-five-year retirement age (Supreme Court)
Supreme Court Judge eligibility criteria
distinguished jurist route to Supreme Court appointment
removal of a Supreme Court Judge (impeachment)
proved misbehaviour or incapacity standard
post-retirement practice bar (Supreme Court Judges)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 124 is the foundational provision establishing the Supreme Court of India itself — its composition (a Chief Justice plus a Parliament-expandable number of other Judges, now 33 following 2019 legislation, up from the original 7), how Judges are appointed and for how long they serve (until 65, unlike High Court Judges' 62 under Article 217), who is even eligible (a High Court Judge of 5+ years, a High Court advocate of 10+ years, or a 'distinguished jurist' in the President's opinion), and the extraordinarily high bar for removing one (a quasi-impeachment process requiring both an absolute majority AND a two-thirds present-and-voting majority in each House, on grounds of 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity' — no sitting Judge has ever actually been removed under this clause). Clause (2)'s original text envisioned appointment 'after consultation' with other Judges — but the Supreme Court's own jurisprudence (the 'Second' and 'Third Judges Cases,' 1993 and 1998) reinterpreted 'consultation' as requiring the Chief Justice's 'concurrence' via a collegium of senior Judges, effectively giving the judiciary primacy over the President/executive in appointments — the collegium system remains the operative practice today, since the 2014 attempt to replace it (Article 124A's National Judicial Appointments Commission) was itself struck down as unconstitutional in 2015.
essential_elements: The Supreme Court consists of the Chief Justice of India plus other Judges, a number Parliament may increase by law (now 33 additional Judges per 2019 legislation, up from the original ceiling of 7)
Judges are appointed by Presidential warrant and hold office until age 65 (clause 2A lets Parliament by law determine the authority/manner for determining that age, addressing age disputes)
Eligibility requires Indian citizenship plus one of three routes: 5+ years as a High Court Judge, 10+ years as a High Court advocate, or being a 'distinguished jurist' in the President's opinion

Removal requires proved misbehaviour or incapacity, established through an address by each House supported by an absolute majority of total membership AND a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, presented to the President in the same Parliamentary session
Every appointee must take the Third Schedule oath before the President (or his nominee) before entering office
A retired Supreme Court Judge is permanently barred from pleading or acting in any court or before any authority anywhere in India
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (2)'s original 'consultation' requirement has been judicially reinterpreted through the collegium system (Second and Third Judges Cases) to mean effective concurrence of the Chief Justice acting with a collegium of senior Judges, shifting real appointment power toward the judiciary — a purely judicially evolved gloss on the constitutional text, not itself a textual amendment to this article

The 2014 Ninety-Ninth Amendment's attempt to replace collegium-based appointments with the National Judicial Appointments Commission (Article 124A) was struck down by the Supreme Court in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) as violating the judicial-independence basic structure, restoring the collegium system as the operative practice

The two-thirds-plus-absolute-majority removal threshold in clause (4) is a deliberately near-impossible bar, distinct from and higher than ordinary legislative majorities, reflecting the framers' intent to insulate judicial tenure from political pressure — Parliament has attempted impeachment proceedings only a handful of times in India's history, none successfully completed to removal
breakdown.how_to_read: Read clause (2) alongside the historical note on collegium jurisprudence — the constitutional text alone (unamended since the 2015 NJAC judgment restored the pre-2014 position) still says 'consultation,' but in practice appointment power is exercised through the judicially evolved collegium mechanism, not literal Presidential discretion; clause (4)'s dual-supermajority is the key practitioner fact for any removal-related question.

sections.title: National Judicial Appointments Commission
sections.raw_text: (1) There shall be a Commission to be known as the National Judicial Appointments Commission consisting of the following, namely:— (a) the Chief Justice of India, Chairperson, ex officio; (b) two other senior Judges of the Supreme Court next to the Chief Justice of India — Members, ex officio; (c) the Union Minister in charge of Law and Justice — Member, ex officio; (d) two eminent persons to be nominated by the committee consisting of the Prime Minister, the Chief Justice of India and the Leader of Opposition in the House of the People or where there is no such Leader of Opposition, then, the Leader of single largest Opposition Party in the House of the People — Members: Provided that one of the eminent person shall be nominated from amongst the persons belonging to the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes, Minorities or Women: Provided further that an eminent person shall be nominated for a period of three years and shall not be eligible for renomination. (2) No act or proceedings of the National Judicial Appointments Commission shall be questioned or be invalidated merely on the ground of the existence of any vacancy or defect in the constitution of the Commission.
key_terms: National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC)
NJAC struck down as unconstitutional (2015)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 124A, inserted by the Ninety-Ninth Amendment in 2014, would have replaced the judicially-created collegium system with a six-member body (the Chief Justice, two senior Judges, the Law Minister, and two 'eminent persons') to jointly decide judicial appointments and transfers. It was designed to give the executive and civil society a formal seat at the table alongside the judiciary. However, the Supreme Court in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) struck down both this article and the companion Ninety-Ninth Amendment provisions as unconstitutional, holding that the NJAC's structure compromised judicial primacy in appointments and violated the basic structure doctrine's judicial-independence component. The text of Article 124A remains printed in the Constitution but is legally inoperative — the pre-2014 collegium system, described in the notes to Article 124, continues to operate in its place.
essential_elements: The NJAC as textually structured would have comprised the CJI, two senior-most Supreme Court Judges, the Union Law Minister, and two 'eminent persons' nominated by a Prime Minister-CJI-Leader of Opposition committee
One eminent person nominee was required to come from Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes, Minorities, or Women, with a fixed non-renewable three-year term
Clause (2) was a technical validity-preservation clause insulating NJAC actions from challenge merely for vacancies or constitutional defects in its own membership
exceptions_and_qualifications: This entire article, though still textually present in the Constitution, has been declared unconstitutional and struck down by the Supreme Court in the 2015 NJAC judgment — it has no current legal operation, and judicial appointments continue under the pre-existing collegium system

The 2015 judgment rested on the basic structure doctrine, holding that the NJAC's composition (particularly the Law Minister's presence and the eminent persons' effective veto power) compromised the judiciary's primacy in its own appointments, a core facet of judicial independence
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this article as constitutionally dead letter — its text survives in print but has zero legal effect after the 2015 Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association judgment; any question about how Supreme Court Judges are actually appointed today must be answered by reference to the collegium system, not this article.

sections.title: Functions of Commission
sections.raw_text: It shall be the duty of the National Judicial Appointments Commission to— (a) recommend persons for appointment as Chief Justice of India, Judges of the Supreme Court, Chief Justices of High Courts and other Judges of High Courts; (b) recommend transfer of Chief Justices and other Judges of High Courts from one High Court to any other High Court; and (c) ensure that the person recommended is of ability and integrity.
key_terms: NJAC's recommendation functions (inoperative)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 124B defined what the NJAC (had it survived) would actually do: recommend appointees for the CJI, Supreme Court Judges, and High Court Chief Justices/Judges, recommend inter-High-Court transfers, and vet nominees for ability and integrity. Like Article 124A itself, this provision was struck down in the 2015 NJAC judgment and has no current legal operation — these functions (recommending appointments and transfers) are instead performed today by the collegium system under the judicially evolved 'consultation' interpretation of Articles 124(2) and 217.
essential_elements: The NJAC's intended functions covered recommending appointments to the CJI-ship, Supreme Court Judgeships, and High Court Chief Justiceships/Judgeships, plus inter-High-Court transfers, with an ability-and-integrity screening duty
exceptions_and_qualifications: This article, like Article 124A, was struck down in the 2015 NJAC judgment and is legally inoperative — the functions it describes are in practice performed by the collegium system, not any NJAC
breakdown.how_to_read: Read alongside Article 124A as part of the same struck-down constitutional scheme — useful only for historical/comparative understanding of what the failed 2014 reform would have done, not as a description of current appointment practice.

sections.title: Power of Parliament to make law
sections.raw_text: Parliament may, by law, regulate the procedure for the appointment of Chief Justice of India and other Judges of the Supreme Court and Chief Justices and other Judges of High Courts and empower the Commission to lay down by regulations the procedure for the discharge of its functions, the manner of selection of persons for appointment and such other matters as may be considered necessary by it.
key_terms: Parliament's law-making power for NJAC procedure (inoperative)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 124C would have empowered Parliament to legislate the detailed appointment procedure and to let the NJAC itself frame supplementary regulations on selection methodology. Parliament did in fact pass the companion National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, 2014 pursuant to this power — but both that Act and this enabling constitutional provision were struck down together in the 2015 NJAC judgment, so neither has any current legal force.
essential_elements: The provision would have allowed Parliament to legislate NJAC appointment procedure in detail and to authorise the NJAC to make its own procedural regulations
exceptions_and_qualifications: Both this article and the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, 2014 passed under it were struck down together in the 2015 NJAC judgment and are legally inoperative
breakdown.how_to_read: The final piece of the now-defunct NJAC scheme (Articles 124A-124C) — read all three together as a single struck-down package superseded in practice by the pre-existing collegium system.

sections.title: Salaries, etc., of Judges
sections.raw_text: (1) There shall be paid to the Judges of the Supreme Court such salaries as may be determined by Parliament by law and, until provision in that behalf is so made, such salaries as are specified in the Second Schedule. (2) Every Judge shall be entitled to such privileges and allowances and to such rights in respect of leave of absence and pension as may from time to time be determined by or under law made by Parliament and, until so determined, to such privileges, allowances and rights as are specified in the Second Schedule: Provided that neither the privileges nor the allowances of a Judge nor his rights in respect of leave of absence or pension shall be varied to his disadvantage after his appointment.
key_terms: salaries of Supreme Court Judges
Second Schedule default (Judges' salaries)
non-disadvantageous variation rule (Judges' privileges)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 125 sets Supreme Court Judges' pay and benefits — a Parliament-by-law default backed by a Second Schedule fallback figure, the same drafting pattern used for the President (Article 59), Ministers (Article 75), and presiding officers (Article 97). The proviso's protection is the operative safeguard here: once a person is appointed a Judge, his privileges, allowances, leave, and pension rights can never be reduced to his disadvantage during his tenure — even if Parliament later revises the general scale downward, a sitting Judge's own terms are frozen at whatever was more favourable at (or after, if increased) his appointment. This financial security is a structural pillar of judicial independence, insulating Judges from any threat of retaliatory pay cuts.
essential_elements: Salaries are Parliament-determined by law, defaulting to Second Schedule figures absent such law
Privileges, allowances, leave-of-absence rights, and pension are likewise Parliament-determined by law, with Second Schedule defaults
The proviso locks in a non-disadvantageous floor — no Judge's privileges, allowances, leave, or pension rights may be varied to his disadvantage after his appointment
exceptions_and_qualifications: The non-disadvantage proviso applies only to privileges, allowances, leave, and pension under clause (2) — the raw salary figure under clause (1) carries no equivalent express non-disadvantage protection in the text, though salary reductions targeting sitting Judges would raise separate judicial-independence concerns

This financial-security structure mirrors the identical Second-Schedule-default-plus-law pattern used for other high constitutional offices, reinforcing a consistent constitutional design choice across the President, Ministers, presiding officers, and now the Judges
breakdown.how_to_read: Focus on the proviso's non-disadvantage guarantee as the practitioner-relevant protection — it is the textual anchor for judicial financial independence, distinguishing sitting Judges' locked-in terms from any general downward revision Parliament might later make to the salary/allowance scale.

sections.title: Appointment of acting Chief Justice
sections.raw_text: When the office of Chief Justice of India is vacant or when the Chief Justice is, by reason of absence or otherwise, unable to perform the duties of his office, the duties of the office shall be performed by such one of the other Judges of the Court as the President may appoint for the purpose.
key_terms: acting Chief Justice of India

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 126 ensures the Chief Justice of India's office never goes unattended — whether the post is genuinely vacant (e.g., between a CJI's retirement and the successor's appointment) or the sitting CJI is merely temporarily unable to function (absence, illness, etc.), the President appoints one of the other Supreme Court Judges to perform the CJI's duties in an acting capacity. In practice, by settled convention (not textual compulsion), the senior-most puisne Judge is appointed acting CJI, mirroring the seniority convention generally followed for the substantive CJI appointment itself.
essential_elements: The trigger is either an actual vacancy in the CJI's office or the sitting CJI's temporary inability to perform duties (absence or otherwise)
The President appoints one of the other sitting Supreme Court Judges to perform the CJI's duties during that period
exceptions_and_qualifications: The article itself gives the President unstructured discretion in choosing which Judge to appoint — the near-universal practice of appointing the senior-most Judge is a constitutional convention, not a textual requirement of this article
breakdown.how_to_read: A short, purely administrative continuity provision — the key fact is that it covers both true vacancy and mere temporary inability, and that the choice of acting CJI is textually open but conventionally seniority-based.

sections.title: Appointment of ad hoc Judges
sections.raw_text: (1) If at any time there should not be a quorum of the Judges of the Supreme Court available to hold or continue any session of the Court, the National Judicial Appointments Commission on a reference made to it by the Chief Justice of India, may with the previous consent of the President and after consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned, request in writing the attendance at the sittings of the Court, as an ad hoc Judge, for such period as may be necessary, of a Judge of a High Court duly qualified for appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court to be designated by the Chief Justice of India. (2) It shall be the duty of the Judge who has been so designated, in priority to other duties of his office, to attend the sittings of the Supreme Court at the time and for the period for which his attendance is required, and while so attending he shall have all the jurisdiction, powers and privileges, and shall discharge the duties, of a Judge of the Supreme Court.
key_terms: ad hoc Judge (Supreme Court)
quorum shortage trigger for ad hoc appointment

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 127 is a rarely-used stop-gap mechanism for the unusual situation where the Supreme Court cannot muster enough Judges to sit at all — a High Court Judge duly qualified for Supreme Court appointment can be temporarily drafted in as an 'ad hoc Judge' to fill the gap, with full Supreme Court jurisdiction and powers while sitting. Note that the article's text still refers to the National Judicial Appointments Commission, which was struck down in 2015 (see Article 124A) — in current practice, this function would be exercised through the collegium mechanism the CJI leads, since no NJAC exists to make the reference described here.
essential_elements: The trigger is an actual absence of quorum among sitting Supreme Court Judges needed to hold or continue a session

A duly qualified High Court Judge is designated by the Chief Justice of India and requested (with Presidential consent and consultation with the concerned High Court's Chief Justice) to attend as an ad hoc Judge for the necessary period
While attending, the designated Judge has the full jurisdiction, powers, privileges, and duties of a regular Supreme Court Judge, and must prioritise this attendance over his other High Court duties
exceptions_and_qualifications: The article's reference to the National Judicial Appointments Commission is a textual relic of the 2014 amendment that was struck down in 2015 — since the NJAC does not currently exist as a functioning body, this power in practice would need to be exercised through whatever appointment mechanism (the collegium) currently operates, an unresolved textual-practical gap

This mechanism has historically been used only rarely, since Supreme Court quorum shortages of the kind contemplated are uncommon given the Court's now much-enlarged sanctioned strength (33 Judges beyond the CJI)
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as an emergency quorum-filling device, but flag the NJAC textual reference as outdated in light of the 2015 judgment discussed under Article 124A — the mechanism's practical operating authority today would need to route through the collegium instead.

sections.title: Attendance of retired Judges at sittings of the Supreme Court
sections.raw_text: Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, the National Judicial Appointments Commission may at any time, with the previous consent of the President, request any person who has held the office of a Judge of the Supreme Court or of the Federal Court or who has held the office of a Judge of a High Court and is duly qualified for appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court to sit and act as a Judge of the Supreme Court, and every such person so requested shall, while so sitting and acting, be entitled to such allowances as the President may by order determine and have all the jurisdiction, powers and privileges of, but shall not otherwise be deemed to be, a Judge of that Court: Provided that nothing in this article shall be deemed to require any such person as aforesaid to sit and act as a Judge of that Court unless he consents so to do.
key_terms: retired Judge recalled to sit (Supreme Court)
consent requirement for recalled retired Judge

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 128 allows a retired Supreme Court Judge, a retired Federal Court Judge (a pre-Constitution transitional category), or a retired/qualified High Court Judge to be specially recalled to sit and act as a Supreme Court Judge, drawing on the deep bench of judicial experience among retirees. While sitting under this recall, the person exercises full Supreme Court jurisdiction and privileges — but is not thereby 'deemed to be' a permanent Judge of the Court, and critically, cannot be compelled to accept the recall; the proviso makes consent mandatory. As with Article 127, the text's reference to the National Judicial Appointments Commission is now a relic of the struck-down 2014 scheme.
essential_elements: Eligible recall candidates are retired Supreme Court Judges, retired Federal Court Judges, or retired/otherwise-qualified High Court Judges
The recall requires the President's previous consent, and the recalled Judge receives Presidentially-determined allowances while sitting
While sitting under recall, the person has full Supreme Court jurisdiction, powers, and privileges, but is not thereby deemed a permanent Judge of the Court
The recalled person's own consent is mandatory — nothing in the article compels attendance without it
exceptions_and_qualifications: Like Article 127, this article's reference to the National Judicial Appointments Commission reflects the struck-down 2014-2015 scheme and would need to be read today as operating through the collegium or whatever body currently exercises equivalent authority
The 'not otherwise deemed to be a Judge' language confines the recall strictly to the sitting/acting period — it creates no ongoing or permanent judicial status beyond that specific engagement
breakdown.how_to_read: Key practitioner distinction from Article 127: this covers retired Judges (Supreme Court, Federal Court, or High Court) rather than sitting High Court Judges, and uniquely requires the recalled individual's own consent as an express proviso — a safeguard against compelled post-retirement service.

sections.title: Supreme Court to be a court of record
sections.raw_text: The Supreme Court shall be a court of record and shall have all the powers of such a court including the power to punish for contempt of itself.
key_terms: Supreme Court as a court of record
contempt power (Supreme Court)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 129 confers two related but distinct attributes on the Supreme Court: first, being a 'court of record' means its proceedings and judgments are recorded for perpetual memory and its records carry evidentiary weight that cannot be questioned when produced elsewhere; second, and separately highlighted, the Court has the power to punish for contempt of itself — protecting the dignity and authority of the institution and the due administration of justice from actions that scandalise the Court, obstruct its process, or wilfully disobey its orders. This contempt power is a direct constitutional grant, not merely a statutory one (the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 supplements but does not create it).
essential_elements: The Supreme Court is constitutionally designated a court of record, giving its records unimpeachable evidentiary status
The Court possesses inherent power to punish for contempt of itself, sourced directly in this constitutional provision rather than solely in ordinary legislation
exceptions_and_qualifications: The contempt power under this article is available for contempt 'of itself' — the Supreme Court's own dignity and process — and operates alongside (not merely as a creature of) the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, which regulates procedure but cannot curtail the constitutional power itself
High Courts possess an equivalent court-of-record and contempt power under the parallel Article 215, reflecting the same institutional-dignity principle at the State level
breakdown.how_to_read: The two halves of this short article are both significant: 'court of record' has an evidentiary-status meaning practitioners should not conflate purely with the contempt power, which is the second, separately stated attribute.

sections.title: Seat of Supreme Court
sections.raw_text: The Supreme Court shall sit in Delhi or in such other place or places, as the Chief Justice of India may, with the approval of the President, from time to time, appoint.
key_terms: seat of the Supreme Court
Chief Justice's power to appoint alternate sitting places

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 130 fixes Delhi as the Supreme Court's default seat but keeps the location flexible — the Chief Justice of India, with the President's approval, may designate other places for the Court to sit from time to time. This provision has occasionally featured in public debate about establishing regional Supreme Court benches to improve access to justice outside Delhi, though no such regional bench has actually been constituted to date; any such move would require exactly this Chief-Justice-plus-Presidential-approval mechanism (or a constitutional amendment, depending on how it is structured).
essential_elements: Delhi is the Supreme Court's default and primary seat
The Chief Justice of India, with the President's approval, may appoint other places for the Court to sit from time to time
exceptions_and_qualifications: This flexibility has never in practice been exercised to establish a standing regional bench of the Supreme Court — proposals for regional benches remain a live but unimplemented policy debate, distinct from the National Court of Appeal proposals sometimes discussed alongside it
breakdown.how_to_read: A short but practically significant provision for the ongoing 'Supreme Court regional benches' debate — note the twin-consent structure (CJI plus Presidential approval) required for any change from the Delhi default.

sections.title: Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
sections.raw_text: Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, the Supreme Court shall, to the exclusion of any other court, have original jurisdiction in any dispute— (a) between the Government of India and one or more States; or (b) between the Government of India and any State or States on one side and one or more other States on the other; or (c) between two or more States, if and in so far as the dispute involves any question (whether of law or fact) on which the existence or extent of a legal right depends: Provided that the said jurisdiction shall not extend to a dispute arising out of any treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement, sanad or other similar instrument which, having been entered into or executed before the commencement of this Constitution, continues in operation after such commencement, or which provides that the said jurisdiction shall not extend to such a dispute.
key_terms: original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
exclusive federal-dispute jurisdiction
legal-right-dependent dispute requirement
pre-Constitution treaty/instrument exclusion

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 131 gives the Supreme Court sole, exclusive original jurisdiction over genuinely federal disputes — Centre versus State(s), Centre-plus-some-States versus other States, or State versus State — but only where the dispute actually turns on a question (of law or fact) affecting the existence or extent of a legal right, not mere political or policy disagreement between governments. No other court in India can entertain such a dispute at all; it is the Supreme Court's exclusive domain from the outset (unlike its appellate jurisdiction, which reviews lower-court decisions). The proviso carves out a historical category: disputes arising from pre-Constitution treaties, agreements, or similar instruments that continue in force are excluded from this jurisdiction, addressing legacy arrangements from the princely-state integration era.
essential_elements: Only three categories of parties qualify: Centre v. State(s), Centre-with-some-States v. other States, and State v. State
The dispute must involve a question of law or fact on which the existence or extent of a legal right depends — purely political disagreements between governments are not covered
The Supreme Court's jurisdiction here is exclusive — no other court may entertain such a dispute at all
This jurisdiction is 'subject to the provisions of this Constitution,' meaning other constitutional provisions can qualify or limit its reach
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso excludes disputes arising from pre-Constitution treaties, agreements, covenants, engagements, sanads, or similar instruments that continue in operation, or that themselves exclude Article 131 jurisdiction — a carve-out rooted in India's historical integration of princely states and their pre-existing legal arrangements

Disputes between private parties, or between a private party and a State/the Union, do not fall within Article 131 at all regardless of how significant the legal question, since the article is confined strictly to Centre-State or inter-State disputes

The former Article 131A (exclusive Supreme Court jurisdiction over the constitutional validity of Central laws) was inserted by the 42nd Amendment and later omitted by the 43rd Amendment (1977), so no such provision exists today
breakdown.how_to_read: The practitioner's checklist for Article 131: (1) are the parties confined to the Centre and/or States only; (2) does the dispute genuinely turn on a legal right rather than pure policy; (3) does the pre-Constitution-instrument proviso apply — all three gate whether this exclusive original jurisdiction is even available.

sections.title: Appellate jurisdiction of Supreme Court in appeals from High Courts in certain cases
sections.raw_text: (1) An appeal shall lie to the Supreme Court from any judgment, decree or final order of a High Court in the territory of India, whether in a civil, criminal or other proceeding, if the High Court certifies under article 134A that the case involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution. (3) Where such a certificate is given, any party in the case may appeal to the Supreme Court on the ground that any such question as aforesaid has been wrongly decided. Explanation.—For the purposes of this article, the expression "final order'' includes an order deciding an issue which, if decided in favour of the appellant, would be sufficient for the final disposal of the case.
key_terms: constitutional appeal (Article 132)
substantial question of law as to constitutional interpretation
High Court certification requirement (Article 132)
'final order' extended meaning

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 132 opens a Supreme Court appeal route for any High Court judgment, decree, or final order — in ANY kind of proceeding, civil, criminal, or other — provided it genuinely turns on a substantial question of constitutional interpretation. Unlike Article 133 (confined to civil matters) or Article 134 (confined to criminal matters), Article 132 is subject-matter-neutral; what matters is that the underlying issue is a substantial constitutional-interpretation question. The gatekeeping mechanism is a High Court certificate (now issued under the unified certification procedure of Article 134A) — without that certificate, no appeal lies under this article at all (though a party could still seek Supreme Court special leave under Article 136 in its absence). The Explanation broadens 'final order' beyond its natural meaning to include even an interlocutory-seeming order that, if it had gone the appellant's way, would have ended the case entirely — preventing procedural form from defeating substantively final rulings.
essential_elements: The appeal covers judgments, decrees, or final orders from any type of High Court proceeding — civil, criminal, or other — with no subject-matter restriction unlike Articles 133 and 134
The case must involve a substantial question of law specifically as to the interpretation of the Constitution — ordinary substantial questions of law (not constitutional) fall outside this article
A High Court certificate under Article 134A is the gatekeeping precondition for the appeal to lie under this article
Once certified, any party to the case (not only the party who sought the certificate) may appeal, arguing the constitutional question was wrongly decided
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Explanation's extended definition of 'final order' captures orders that decide an issue which, had it gone the appellant's way, would have been sufficient to finally dispose of the case — even if the order does not formally end all proceedings

The original clause (2), which once allowed a party to appeal directly to the Supreme Court without a High Court certificate if the High Court refused one, was omitted by the 44th Amendment (1978) — today, absent a High Court certificate, the only route is a discretionary special leave petition under Article 136
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 132's defining feature is subject-matter neutrality (civil/criminal/other) combined with strict subject-matter narrowness (constitutional interpretation only) — contrast this dual character with Articles 133 (civil-only, general substantial-question) and 134 (criminal-only, specific triggers).

sections.title: Appellate jurisdiction of Supreme Court in appeals from High Courts in regard to civil matters
sections.raw_text: (1) An appeal shall lie to the Supreme Court from any judgment, decree or final order in a civil proceeding of a High Court in the territory of India if the High Court certifies under article 134A— (a) that the case involves a substantial question of law of general importance; and (b) that in the opinion of the High Court the said question needs to be decided by the Supreme Court. (2) Notwithstanding anything in article 132, any party appealing to the Supreme Court under clause (1) may urge as one of the grounds in such appeal that a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution has been wrongly decided. (3) Notwithstanding anything in this article, no appeal shall, unless Parliament by law otherwise provides, lie to the Supreme Court from the judgment, decree or final order of one Judge of a High Court.
key_terms: civil appeal to Supreme Court (Article 133)
substantial question of law of general importance
High Court's opinion that the question needs Supreme Court decision
single-Judge High Court order appeal bar

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 133 is the general civil-appeal gateway to the Supreme Court — broader in subject matter than Article 132's constitutional-only focus, but requiring a dual certification: the High Court must certify both that a substantial question of law of general importance is involved AND that, in its own opinion, the Supreme Court specifically needs to decide it (a higher bar than merely 'substantial' — it must also be of general, not merely case-specific, importance). Clause (2) is a convenience provision letting an appellant who's already in the Supreme Court on a certified civil matter also raise a constitutional-interpretation argument without needing a separate Article 132 certificate for that specific point. Clause (3) closes off appeals from single-Judge High Court orders (Parliament could by law reopen this, but has generally not done so broadly) — reflecting that such orders are typically themselves appealable within the High Court (e.g., to a Division Bench) before any question of Supreme Court appeal arises.
essential_elements: The proceeding must be civil in nature (contrast with Article 134's criminal focus and Article 132's subject-matter neutrality)
The High Court must certify BOTH that a substantial question of law of general importance is involved AND that it needs Supreme Court determination — a conjunctive two-part test, not either alone
Clause (2) permits raising a constitutional-interpretation argument as an additional ground within an Article 133 appeal, without a separate Article 132 certificate
No appeal lies from a single Judge's judgment, decree, or final order unless Parliament has by law provided otherwise for that category of case
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'general importance' requirement distinguishes Article 133 from a pure error-correction appellate mechanism — the question must transcend the particular case's facts and matter for the wider development of law, not just for the litigants involved
The single-Judge bar in clause (3) is itself subject to Parliament's power to legislate exceptions, though such exceptions are the rarity rather than the rule in Indian civil procedure
breakdown.how_to_read: Remember the two-part conjunctive certification test in clause (1)(a)-(b) as the defining feature distinguishing Article 133 from a simple substantial-question test — both general importance AND the High Court's own view that Supreme Court resolution is needed must be satisfied.

sections.title: Appellate jurisdiction of Supreme Court in regard to criminal matters
sections.raw_text: (1) An appeal shall lie to the Supreme Court from any judgment, final order or sentence in a criminal proceeding of a High Court in the territory of India if the High Court— (a) has on appeal reversed an order of acquittal of an accused person and sentenced him to death; or (b) has withdrawn for trial before itself any case from any court subordinate to its authority and has in such trial convicted the accused person and sentenced him to death; or (c) certifies under article 134A that the case is a fit one for appeal to the Supreme Court: Provided that an appeal under sub-clause (c) shall lie subject to such provisions as may be made in that behalf under clause (1) of article 145 and to such conditions as the High Court may establish or require. (2) Parliament may by law confer on the Supreme Court any further powers to entertain and hear appeals from any judgment, final order or sentence in a criminal proceeding of a High Court in the territory of India subject to such conditions and limitations as may be specified in such law.
key_terms: criminal appeal to Supreme Court (Article 134)
automatic appeal on reversal-of-acquittal death sentence
automatic appeal on withdrawn-case-trial death sentence
'fit case' certification (Article 134(1)(c))
Parliament's power to expand criminal appellate jurisdiction

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 134 opens Supreme Court criminal appeals through three distinct routes. The first two are automatic, certificate-free 'as of right' appeals in the gravest scenario — a death sentence — triggered either when a High Court reverses a trial court's acquittal and itself imposes death, or when a High Court withdraws a case to try it directly and convicts with a death sentence; the logic is that a death sentence imposed for the first time (or on reversal of an acquittal) by a High Court warrants an automatic further layer of Supreme Court scrutiny given the finality and gravity of the punishment. The third route is discretionary High Court certification that a case is simply 'fit' for Supreme Court appeal — a broad, flexible catch-all for any other criminal matter the High Court considers appeal-worthy, though subject to Supreme Court Rules made under Article 145 and any conditions the High Court itself imposes. Clause (2) is a residual expansion power letting Parliament by ordinary law widen the Supreme Court's criminal appellate jurisdiction further — historically exercised, for instance, through provisions in the Code of Criminal Procedure enabling additional categories of criminal appeal.
essential_elements: Automatic appeal route one: the High Court, on appeal, reversed an acquittal and sentenced the accused to death
Automatic appeal route two: the High Court withdrew a case from a subordinate court, tried it itself, and sentenced the accused to death
Discretionary route: a High Court certificate under Article 134A that the case is a 'fit one' for Supreme Court appeal — a broad, undefined standard vesting real discretion in the High Court
Clause (2) lets Parliament by law confer further criminal appellate jurisdiction on the Supreme Court beyond what this article itself provides
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso to clause (1) subjects the discretionary 'fit case' certification route to Supreme Court Rules made under Article 145(1) and to any conditions the certifying High Court itself establishes or requires — the certification is not an unconditional, self-executing right of appeal

The two automatic death-sentence routes are narrowly confined to their specific fact patterns (acquittal-reversed-to-death, or withdrawn-case-tried-and-sentenced-to-death) — a death sentence confirmed on appeal from an original trial-court death sentence, without an intervening acquittal reversal, does not by itself trigger automatic Article 134 appeal (though such cases are typically covered by statutory appeal rights under the CrPC/BNSS and by Article 136 special leave in any event)
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish the two narrow, automatic 'as of right' death-sentence triggers in clauses (1)(a)-(b) from the broad, discretionary 'fit case' certification in clause (1)(c) — the former requires no certificate at all, while the latter is squarely a High Court discretionary judgment call subject to Article 145 Rules.

sections.title: Certificate for appeal to the Supreme Court
sections.raw_text: Every High Court, passing or making a judgment, decree, final order, or sentence, referred to in clause (1) of article 132 or clause (1) of article 133, or clause (1) of article 134,— (a) may, if it deems fit so to do, on its own motion; and (b) shall, if an oral application is made, by or on behalf of the party aggrieved, immediately after the passing or making of such judgment, decree, final order or sentence, determine, as soon as may be after such passing or making, the question whether a certificate of the nature referred to in clause (1) of article 132, or clause (1) of article 133 or, as the case may be, sub-clause (c) of clause (1) of article 134, may be given in respect of that case.
key_terms: unified High Court certification procedure
suo motu certification power
aggrieved party's oral application for certification

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 134A, inserted by the 44th Amendment (1978), streamlines and unifies the certificate-granting procedure across Articles 132, 133, and 134(1)(c) into a single mechanism, so a High Court follows one consistent process regardless of which appellate-gateway certificate is being sought. The High Court can certify on its own initiative (suo motu) if it thinks fit, but it MUST at least consider and rule on the question if the aggrieved party makes an oral application immediately after the judgment/order/sentence is passed — practically meaning counsel should orally request certification right there in court rather than filing a separate later application, a small but critical procedural trap for the unwary practitioner.
essential_elements: The article applies uniformly to certification requests under Article 132(1), Article 133(1), and Article 134(1)(c)
The High Court has discretionary suo motu power to grant certification on its own motion if it deems fit

The High Court has a mandatory duty to determine the certification question if an oral application is made by or on behalf of the aggrieved party immediately after the judgment/decree/order/sentence is passed
The determination should be made as soon as may be after the judgment is passed, reflecting the immediacy built into the oral-application mechanism
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'immediately after' timing requirement for the oral application is a strict practical trap — a party's counsel must be prepared to make the certification request right at the moment judgment is pronounced, not through a later formal written application, or risk losing this particular procedural route (though Article 136 special leave typically remains available as a fallback)

This article only unifies the certification PROCEDURE — it does not alter or relax the underlying substantive standards each article separately fixes (constitutional-interpretation-only under 132, general-importance-plus-needed under 133, or fit-case under 134(1)(c))
breakdown.how_to_read: The practitioner takeaway is procedural, not substantive: this article is the single certification gateway serving three different substantive tests (Articles 132, 133, 134(1)(c)) — and counsel must make any oral certification request immediately upon judgment being pronounced to preserve the right.

sections.title: Jurisdiction and powers of the Federal Court under existing law to be exercisable by the Supreme Court
sections.raw_text: Until Parliament by law otherwise provides, the Supreme Court shall also have jurisdiction and powers with respect to any matter to which the provisions of article 133 or article 134 do not apply if jurisdiction and powers in relation to that matter were exercisable by the Federal Court immediately before the commencement of this Constitution under any existing law.
key_terms: Federal Court residual jurisdiction transferred to Supreme Court
sunset clause pending Parliamentary legislation (Article 135)

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a transitional bridging provision. Before 1950, India's highest court was the Federal Court, which had certain jurisdiction and powers under pre-Constitution ('existing') law that don't neatly fall within the new Article 133 (civil appeals) or Article 134 (criminal appeals) categories. Article 135 simply carries that leftover Federal Court jurisdiction over to the Supreme Court automatically, so nothing falls through the cracks during the transition — but only until Parliament passes a law addressing the matter, at which point Parliament's law takes over.
essential_elements: The Supreme Court automatically inherits any Federal Court jurisdiction or power that isn't already covered by Article 133 or Article 134.
That inherited jurisdiction must have existed under 'existing law' — i.e., law in force immediately before the Constitution commenced on 26 January 1950.
The inheritance is a default rule, not a permanent guarantee — it operates only until Parliament by law otherwise provides.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Purely transitional: as decades pass and Parliament legislates over old Government of India Act, 1935-era jurisdictional pockets, Article 135's practical field of operation shrinks — it is largely of historical and residual interest today rather than a live litigation tool.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this as a 'nothing is lost in translation' clause bridging the Federal Court (pre-1950) to the Supreme Court (post-1950) — its practical importance has faded with time as Parliament has legislated over the relevant fields.

sections.title: Special leave to appeal by the Supreme Court
sections.raw_text:
(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, the Supreme Court may, in its discretion, grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, determination, sentence or order in any cause or matter passed or made by any court or tribunal in the territory of India.
(2) Nothing in clause (1) shall apply to any judgment, determination, sentence or order passed or made by any court or tribunal constituted by or under any law relating to the Armed Forces.
key_terms: special leave to appeal (Article 136)
SLP jurisdiction as residuary constitutional power
'notwithstanding anything in this Chapter' overriding clause (Article 136)
any court or tribunal (Article 136 scope)
Armed Forces tribunal exclusion (Article 136(2))

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 136 is the Supreme Court's broadest and most famous appellate tool — the Special Leave Petition (SLP). Unlike Articles 132-134A, which require High Court certification through fixed, technical gateways, Article 136 lets a litigant go straight to the Supreme Court and ask it, in its own discretion, for permission ('leave') to appeal from virtually any judgment, order, or sentence of virtually any court or tribunal in India — with only the Armed Forces tribunals carved out. It is not a right of appeal; it is a discretionary door the Supreme Court may open or shut as it sees fit, even in a case where no other appellate route under the Constitution exists.
essential_elements: The Supreme Court's power is entirely discretionary ('may, in its discretion') — there is no vested right in any party to demand that special leave be granted; refusal of an SLP is not itself a decision on the merits.

The overriding words 'notwithstanding anything in this Chapter' mean Article 136 operates independently of, and is not constrained by, the certification requirements of Articles 132, 133, and 134 — a litigant can seek Article 136 leave even where a 132/133/134 route was never invoked or was refused.

The words 'any court or tribunal in the territory of India' give Article 136 an exceptionally wide sweep — it covers not just High Courts but subordinate courts, quasi-judicial tribunals, and statutory adjudicatory bodies, subject to them being validly constituted courts or tribunals exercising judicial or quasi-judicial functions.
It reaches 'any judgment, decree, determination, sentence or order in any cause or matter' — civil, criminal, or otherwise — not limited to final orders the way Articles 132-134 are.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (2) excludes judgments, determinations, sentences, or orders passed by any court or tribunal constituted by or under any law relating to the Armed Forces — court-martial and similar military justice outcomes are outside Article 136's reach.

Despite its sweeping wording, the Supreme Court has self-imposed restraint through case law: it does not entertain SLPs as a matter of course, typically declines to interfere with concurrent findings of fact by two lower courts absent perversity or gross injustice, and reserves plenary exercise for cases involving substantial questions of law, grave miscarriage of justice, or violation of natural justice — a self-discipline that is judicial practice, not a textual limitation.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 136 as the Supreme Court's plenary safety-valve appellate power — broader than every other appellate Article in this Chapter combined, but tempered entirely by the Court's own discretion and self-restraint rather than by textual conditions (apart from the Armed Forces carve-out).

sections.title: Review of judgments or orders by the Supreme Court
sections.raw_text: Subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament or any rules made under article 145, the Supreme Court shall have power to review any judgment pronounced or order made by it.
key_terms: review jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (Article 137)
grounds for review (developed through Supreme Court Rules and practice)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 137 lets the Supreme Court revisit and correct its own final judgments and orders — an exception to the general principle that a court becomes functus officio (having no further authority) once it delivers a final judgment. This review power is not an appeal to a higher forum (there is none above the Supreme Court); it is the same Court re-examining its own decision, generally on narrow grounds, subject to whatever procedural rules Parliament or the Supreme Court's own Article 145 Rules prescribe.
essential_elements: The power applies to 'any judgment pronounced or order made by it' — the Supreme Court may review its own final civil or criminal decisions.

The power is expressly made subject to Parliamentary law and to rules made under Article 145 (the Supreme Court's own rule-making power) — meaning the detailed procedure, timelines, and grounds for review are not fixed by the constitutional text itself but by subordinate rules (principally Order XLVII of the Supreme Court Rules, which mirrors the Code of Civil Procedure's review grounds: discovery of new and important matter, a mistake or error apparent on the face of the record, or any other sufficient reason).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Review is narrower than an appeal — it is not an opportunity to re-argue the case or introduce fresh legal arguments merely because a party is dissatisfied with the outcome; it is confined to correcting manifest errors or addressing genuinely new material that could not have been produced earlier.

A review petition is ordinarily heard by the same Bench (or, for certain matters, a larger Bench) that delivered the original judgment, and is typically decided by circulation without oral hearing unless the Court directs otherwise.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this as the Supreme Court's narrow self-correction mechanism — a safety net against manifest error, not a second bite at the appellate apple, with its actual mechanics filled in by Supreme Court Rules rather than the constitutional text.

sections.title: Enlargement of the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
sections.raw_text:
(1) The Supreme Court shall have such further jurisdiction and powers with respect to any of the matters in the Union List as Parliament may by law confer.
(2) The Supreme Court shall have such further jurisdiction and powers with respect to any matter as the Government of India and the Government of any State may by special agreement confer, if Parliament by law provides for the exercise of such jurisdiction and powers by the Supreme Court.
key_terms: enlargement of Supreme Court's jurisdiction (Article 138)
Union List jurisdiction conferment (Article 138(1))
special agreement jurisdiction conferment (Article 138(2))

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 138 is an expansion valve: it lets the Supreme Court's jurisdiction grow beyond what Articles 131-137 already give it, through two distinct routes — ordinary Parliamentary legislation over Union List subjects, and a bilateral Centre-State 'special agreement' route (which still needs Parliament's backing law before it can operate). Neither route self-executes from the constitutional text alone; both require a further legislative act.
essential_elements: Clause (1): Parliament may, by ordinary law, confer further jurisdiction and powers on the Supreme Court over any subject in the Union List (List I of the Seventh Schedule) — the natural domain of central legislative competence.

Clause (2): the Union Government and a State Government may agree between themselves ('special agreement') to confer further jurisdiction and powers on the Supreme Court over any matter — but this agreement is not self-operative; it takes effect only if Parliament also passes a law providing for the Supreme Court to exercise that jurisdiction.
