(5) The salaries and allowances of Ministers shall be such as the Legislature of the State may from time to time by law determine and, until the Legislature of the State so determines, shall be as specified in the Second Schedule.
key_terms: Council of Ministers headed by Chief Minister (State)
tribal welfare Minister proviso (Article 164)
15% cap and 12-minimum Council of Ministers size (State)
Tenth Schedule disqualification bar on becoming a Minister
collective responsibility to Legislative Assembly
Minister's oath of office and secrecy (State)
six-consecutive-month non-membership cessation rule (Minister)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 164 fills out the operational rules for a State's Council of Ministers, mirroring Article 75's Union-level scheme almost provision-for-provision. The Governor appoints the Chief Minister and, on the Chief Minister's advice, the other Ministers, all holding office at the Governor's pleasure. Four States (Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha) are constitutionally required to have a dedicated tribal-welfare Minister. The Ninety-first Amendment (2003) capped Council size at 15% of the Legislative Assembly's total membership, with a floor of 12 members regardless of Assembly size. A defector disqualified under the Tenth Schedule's anti-defection paragraph 2 is barred from Ministerial appointment for a defined period. The Council is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly (not the Governor), Ministers take a Third Schedule oath before the Governor, must be or become a Legislature member within six months of appointment (else cease to hold office), and receive salaries fixed by State law or defaulting to Second Schedule figures.
essential_elements: Clause (1): Chief Minister appointed by the Governor; other Ministers appointed by the Governor on the Chief Minister's advice; all Ministers hold office during the Governor's pleasure.

Proviso to clause (1): Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, and Odisha must each have a Minister in charge of tribal welfare, who may additionally handle Scheduled Castes/backward classes welfare or other work.

Clause (1A) (Ninety-first Amendment, 2003): total Council of Ministers size (including the Chief Minister) capped at 15% of the Legislative Assembly's total membership, with a proviso setting an absolute floor of 12 Ministers regardless of how small that 15% figure would otherwise be.

Clause (1B) (Ninety-first Amendment, 2003): a Legislative Assembly or Legislative Council member disqualified under Tenth Schedule paragraph 2 (anti-defection) is also barred from Ministerial appointment for a defined period tied to the disqualification's duration or a fresh election, whichever comes first.
Clause (2): the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the State Legislative Assembly — the foundational responsible-government accountability rule.
Clause (3): before entering office, a Minister takes the oaths of office and secrecy administered by the Governor, in the Third Schedule forms.
Clause (4): a Minister who is not a Legislature member for six consecutive months automatically ceases to be a Minister at the expiry of that period.
Clause (5): Ministers' salaries and allowances are fixed by State law, defaulting to Second Schedule figures absent such law.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The tribal-welfare-Minister proviso applies only to the four named States — it is not a general requirement across all States.

The 15%-cap/12-minimum rule (clause 1A) was a post-2003 anti-defection-era reform aimed at curbing oversized Councils of Ministers used to accommodate factional politics; it did not exist in the Constitution's original 1950 text.

The Governor's 'pleasure' under clause (1) is, per established constitutional convention and Article 163, exercised on the Chief Minister's advice for removal of individual Ministers, not as an independent gubernatorial power — mirroring Article 75(2)'s Union-level pattern.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 164 as Article 75's State-level mirror — appointment, collective responsibility, oath, and the six-month membership rule track identically, with two State-specific additions (the four-State tribal-welfare proviso and, post-2003, the Council-size cap/floor and Tenth Schedule Ministerial-appointment bar) that have no Union-level counterpart in Article 75 as such, though the size-cap idea parallels Article 75(1A)'s identical Union-level formula.

sections.title: Advocate-General for the State
sections.raw_text:
(1) The Governor of each State shall appoint a person who is qualified to be appointed a Judge of a High Court to be Advocate-General for the State.
(2) It shall be the duty of the Advocate-General to give advice to the Government of the State upon such legal matters, and to perform such other duties of a legal character, as may from time to time be referred or assigned to him by the Governor, and to discharge the functions conferred on him by or under this Constitution or any other law for the time being in force.
(3) The Advocate-General shall hold office during the pleasure of the Governor, and shall receive such remuneration as the Governor may determine.
key_terms: Advocate-General for the State

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 165 creates the State-level counterpart to the Attorney-General for India (Article 76): a Governor-appointed Advocate-General, qualified to be a High Court Judge, who serves as the State Government's chief legal adviser. He advises on legal matters and performs other legal-character duties the Governor refers or assigns, plus any functions specifically conferred by the Constitution or other law, holding office at the Governor's pleasure with Governor-determined remuneration.
essential_elements: Appointment: made by the Governor, of a person qualified to be appointed a High Court Judge (the same qualification threshold as for the Attorney-General's Supreme-Court-Judge-qualification standard, but pegged one court level down).
Duties: giving legal advice to the State Government, performing other legal-character duties the Governor refers or assigns, and discharging functions conferred by the Constitution or other law.
Tenure and remuneration: office held during the Governor's pleasure; remuneration fixed at the Governor's discretion (unlike Ministers, no Second Schedule default applies to the Advocate-General).
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Advocate-General, like the Attorney-General at the Union level, is not a member of the Council of Ministers and not necessarily a member of the State Legislature — the office is a legal-adviser role distinct from a political/executive one, though he may be given rights to speak in the Legislature by State law (paralleling the Attorney-General's Article 88 rights) without being a member entitled to vote.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 165 as Article 76's precise State-level mirror — same qualification-by-reference-to-judicial-eligibility structure, same pleasure-tenure, same advisory-plus-assigned-duties job description, one court level down (High Court instead of Supreme Court).

sections.title: Conduct of business of the Government of a State
sections.raw_text:
(1) All executive action of the Government of a State shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the Governor.
(2) Orders and other instruments made and executed in the name of the Governor shall be authenticated in such manner as may be specified in rules to be made by the Governor, and the validity of an order or instrument which is so authenticated shall not be called in question on the ground that it is not an order or instrument made or executed by the Governor.
(3) The Governor shall make rules for the more convenient transaction of the business of the Government of the State, and for the allocation among Ministers of the said business in so far as it is not business with respect to which the Governor is by or under this Constitution required to act in his discretion.
(4) [Omitted]
key_terms: executive action expressed in Governor's name
authentication of orders/instruments (Governor) and non-questionability
Governor's rules for business transaction and Ministerial allocation

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 166 mirrors Article 77's Union-level machinery for how a State Government's decisions are formally expressed and internally organised. All executive action is formally taken 'in the name of the Governor,' even though in practice Ministers and officials act on his behalf. Orders and instruments in his name must be authenticated per rules the Governor himself makes, and once so authenticated their validity cannot be challenged merely on the basis that the Governor didn't personally make or execute them. The Governor also makes 'rules of business' — internal rules for efficiently transacting government business and allocating it among Ministers, except for matters falling within his own constitutionally-required discretionary zone. A former clause (4), inserted by the Forty-second Amendment (1976) and omitted by the Forty-fourth Amendment (1978), paralleled the similarly short-lived Article 77(4) at the Union level and has no current legal force.
essential_elements: Clause (1): all executive action of the State Government must be formally expressed as taken in the Governor's name — a legal fiction preserving the formal unity of the executive even though real decision-making rests with the Council of Ministers.

Clause (2): authentication of orders/instruments follows rules the Governor makes; once authenticated per those rules, an order's validity cannot be questioned on the ground that the Governor did not personally make or execute it — protecting the practical delegation of day-to-day government business to officials and Ministers.

Clause (3): the Governor makes 'rules of business' for convenient transaction of government business and its allocation among Ministers — but this rule-making excludes matters within the Governor's own constitutionally-required discretionary zone (per Article 163's carve-out).

Clause (4) (now omitted): originally inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) as part of the same Emergency-era package that inserted the parallel (and equally short-lived) Article 77(4) at the Union level; omitted by the 44th Amendment (1978) and carries no current legal force.
exceptions_and_qualifications: In practice, the Governor's rule-making under clause (3) is itself exercised on ministerial advice for ordinary business (not his personal discretion), consistent with Article 163's default rule — the discretionary carve-out in clause (3) is narrow and applies only where the Constitution specifically requires gubernatorial discretion.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 166 as Article 77's exact State-level mirror (including the same now-defunct, Emergency-era clause (4) history) — it is the internal 'plumbing' Article governing how State executive decisions are formally issued, authenticated, and organisationally allocated, distinct from Article 163's separate question of who actually decides.

sections.title: Duties of Chief Minister as respects the furnishing of information to Governor, etc.
sections.raw_text:
It shall be the duty of the Chief Minister of each State—
(a) to communicate to the Governor of the State all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to the administration of the affairs of the State and proposals for legislation;
(b) to furnish such information relating to the administration of the affairs of the State and proposals for legislation as the Governor may call for; and
(c) if the Governor so requires, to submit for the consideration of the Council of Ministers any matter on which a decision has been taken by a Minister but which has not been considered by the Council.
key_terms: Chief Minister's duty to communicate Council decisions to Governor
Governor's power to call for information (State)
Governor's power to require full-Council consideration of a Minister's individual decision

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 167 mirrors Article 78's Union-level scheme, casting the Chief Minister as the essential communication channel between the Council of Ministers and the Governor. Three specific duties are imposed: proactively communicate all Council decisions on State administration and legislative proposals to the Governor; supply whatever further information on administration or legislative proposals the Governor calls for; and, if the Governor requires it, bring before the full Council for its consideration any matter an individual Minister decided on his own that the Council as a body hasn't yet reviewed. Together these duties let the Governor stay informed and, where necessary, ensure collective Cabinet oversight of individually-taken decisions, without giving him a power to substitute his own judgment for the Council's.
essential_elements: Duty (a): proactive, without being asked — the Chief Minister must communicate all Council of Ministers decisions on State administration and legislative proposals to the Governor.
Duty (b): reactive — furnish administration/legislation-related information the Governor specifically calls for.

Duty (c): conditional on the Governor's requirement — submit an individual Minister's undecided-by-Council decision for full Council consideration, ensuring collective oversight where the Governor flags a concern.
exceptions_and_qualifications: These duties give the Governor an information and oversight channel but not a decision-making power of his own — he can require information and require Council-level reconsideration, but cannot substitute his own decision for the Council's on matters within its ordinary (non-discretionary) domain.

The duties run specifically to the Chief Minister personally, not to the Council of Ministers collectively or to individual Ministers — reflecting the Chief Minister's role as the constitutional link and spokesperson between Council and Governor.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 167 as Article 78's precise State-level mirror — it operationalises the Governor's right to be kept informed (paralleling the President's Article 78 rights vis-à-vis the Prime Minister) without disturbing Article 163's default rule that the Governor acts on ministerial aid and advice.

sections.title: Constitution of Legislatures in States
sections.raw_text:
(1) For every State there shall be a Legislature which shall consist of the Governor, and—
(a) in the States of Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh, two Houses;
(b) in other States, one House.
(2) Where there are two Houses of the Legislature of a State, one shall be known as the Legislative Council and the other as the Legislative Assembly, and where there is only one House, it shall be known as the Legislative Assembly.
key_terms: bicameral vs unicameral State Legislature
Legislative Council and Legislative Assembly (State)
Governor as constituent part of State Legislature

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 168 opens Chapter III (The State Legislature) by defining what a 'State Legislature' actually consists of: the Governor plus either one or two Houses, depending on the State. A fixed list of States (Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, and Uttar Pradesh) have bicameral Legislatures with both a Legislative Council and a Legislative Assembly; every other State has only a unicameral Legislature consisting of the Legislative Assembly alone. Just as with Parliament under Article 79, the Governor is formally reckoned a constituent part of the State Legislature even though he is not a member of either House.
essential_elements: The State Legislature always includes the Governor as a constituent part, exactly paralleling Article 79's structure for Parliament and the President.

Clause (1)(a) names eight specific States as having two Houses (a Legislative Council in addition to the Legislative Assembly) — this list has changed over time via specific constitutional amendments and State reorganisation/Council-abolition legislation.
Clause (1)(b) makes every other State unicameral, with only a Legislative Assembly.
Clause (2) fixes the naming convention: the upper House (where it exists) is the Legislative Council, the lower/sole House is always the Legislative Assembly.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The list of bicameral States in clause (1)(a) is not static — it has been amended multiple times as specific States' Legislative Councils were abolished or created under Article 169 (e.g., Tamil Nadu's Council was abolished in 1986, then later legislated to be recreated, and West Bengal's and Punjab's Councils were abolished in 1969 and 1970 respectively) or as States were reorganised (e.g., Telangana added after its 2014 creation).
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 168 as the State-level mirror of Article 79 — before drafting any State-legislative-process argument, first confirm from the current, amended text of clause (1)(a) whether the particular State is bicameral or unicameral, since that fundamentally changes which downstream Articles (bicameral-specific provisions on Money Bills, deadlock resolution, etc.) apply.

sections.title: Abolition or creation of Legislative Councils in States
sections.raw_text:
(1) Notwithstanding anything in article 168, Parliament may by law provide for the abolition of the Legislative Council of a State having such a Council or for the creation of such a Council in a State having no such Council, if the Legislative Assembly of the State passes a resolution to that effect by a majority of the total membership of the Assembly and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of the Assembly present and voting.
(2) Any law referred to in clause (1) shall contain such provisions for the amendment of this Constitution as may be necessary to give effect to the provisions of the law and may also contain such supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions as Parliament may deem necessary.
(3) No such law as aforesaid shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368.
key_terms: State-initiated request for Council abolition/creation
special State Assembly resolution majority (Article 169)
deemed non-amendment under Article 368 (Legislative Council law)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 169 lets Parliament abolish an existing Legislative Council or create a new one for a State — but only if that State's own Legislative Assembly first initiates the process by passing a special resolution, requiring both an absolute majority of the Assembly's total membership and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting. This dual-majority threshold ensures broad, considered State-level consent before Parliament acts on what is otherwise a matter altering the State's own constitutional structure. Strikingly, clause (3) declares that such a Parliamentary law is not deemed a constitutional amendment for Article 368 purposes, even though it may necessarily contain provisions amending the Constitution's own text (such as updating Article 168(1)(a)'s list) — meaning the ordinary Article 368 special-majority procedure doesn't independently apply; an ordinary Parliamentary law, passed after the State resolution, suffices.
essential_elements: Initiation must come from the State: the Legislative Assembly must pass a resolution by (a) a majority of its total membership, and (b) a majority of not less than two-thirds of members present and voting — a double-lock supermajority threshold.
Only after such a resolution can Parliament, by ordinary law, abolish an existing Council or create a new one for that State.

Clause (2) allows the Parliamentary law itself to contain whatever constitutional-amendment provisions are necessary to give effect to the change (e.g., updating Article 168's bicameral-States list), plus supplemental/incidental/consequential provisions.

Clause (3) is the key procedural shortcut: despite amending constitutional text, such a law is deemed NOT to be an amendment under Article 368 — so it need not go through Article 368's special procedure (no two-thirds Parliamentary majority or State ratification requirement beyond the State Assembly's own initiating resolution).
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is one of the Constitution's few provisions letting a State meaningfully drive a change to its own constitutional structure, though final legislative power still rests with Parliament — the State Assembly resolution is a precondition, not itself the operative law.

Examples of this Article's actual use include the abolition of Legislative Councils in states like West Bengal (1969), Punjab (1969/70), and Tamil Nadu (1986), and the (still not fully notified, per source-text footnotes) later legislation to recreate Tamil Nadu's Council.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 169 as the designated, self-contained mechanism for changing a State's bicameral/unicameral status — always check first whether the State Assembly's special-majority resolution preceded the Parliamentary law, since that resolution is the constitutional precondition validating the whole exercise.

sections.title: Composition of the Legislative Assemblies
sections.raw_text:
(1) Subject to the provisions of article 333, the Legislative Assembly of each State shall consist of not more than five hundred, and not less than sixty, members chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the State.
(2) For the purposes of clause (1), each State shall be divided into territorial constituencies in such manner that the ratio between the population of each constituency and the number of seats allotted to it shall, so far as practicable, be the same throughout the State.
Explanation.—In this clause, the expression "population" means the population as ascertained at the last preceding census of which the relevant figures have been published: Provided that the reference in this Explanation to the last preceding census of which the relevant figures have been published shall, until the relevant figures for the first census taken after the year 2026 have been published, be construed as a reference to the 2001 census.
(3) Upon the completion of each census, the total number of seats in the Legislative Assembly of each State and the division of each State into territorial constituencies shall be readjusted by such authority and in such manner as Parliament may by law determine:
Provided that such readjustment shall not affect representation in the Legislative Assembly until the dissolution of the then existing Assembly:
Provided further that such readjustment shall take effect from such date as the President may, by order, specify and until such readjustment takes effect, any election to the Legislative Assembly may be held on the basis of the territorial constituencies existing before such readjustment:
Provided also that until the relevant figures for the first census taken after the year 2026 have been published, it shall not be necessary to readjust—
(i) the total number of seats in the Legislative Assembly of each State as readjusted on the basis of the 1971 census; and
(ii) the division of such State into territorial constituencies as may be readjusted on the basis of the 2001 census,
under this clause.
key_terms: Legislative Assembly size range (60-500)
direct election from territorial constituencies (Assembly)
one-vote-one-value ratio principle (State Assembly)
delimitation freeze tied to 2026 census (State Assembly)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 170 mirrors Article 81's Lok Sabha composition rules at the State level: each Legislative Assembly must have between 60 and 500 members, all directly elected from territorial constituencies, subject to Article 333's separate rule on nominating an Anglo-Indian member where applicable (now spent following the 104th Amendment). Constituencies must be drawn so the population-to-seat ratio is, so far as practicable, uniform across the State — the same one-vote-one-value principle as at the Union level. And, exactly paralleling Article 82's delimitation freeze, seat totals and constituency boundaries are frozen at their 1971-census/2001-census-delimitation levels until the first census after 2026 is published, preventing States with faster population growth from gaining a proportionally larger Assembly (and hence political weight) before that freeze lifts.
essential_elements: Size range: not more than 500, not less than 60 members per Legislative Assembly — 'subject to Article 333,' which separately dealt with an Anglo-Indian nominated seat (now a spent provision after the Constitution (One Hundred and Fourth Amendment) Act, 2019 ended Anglo-Indian reservation/nomination).
All Assembly members are chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies within the State.
The population-to-seat ratio across constituencies within a State must be, so far as practicable, uniform — delimitation must avoid systematically over- or under-weighting particular constituencies.

Post-census readjustment of both total seats and constituency boundaries is mandated after each census, by authority and manner Parliament determines by law (in practice, the Delimitation Commission mechanism), but readjustment doesn't disturb an existing Assembly's composition until its dissolution, and only takes effect from a President-specified date.

The delimitation freeze: seat totals stay pegged to the 1971 census and constituency boundaries to the 2001-census-based delimitation, until the first census after 2026 is published — mirroring Article 82's identical freeze mechanism for the Lok Sabha.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The freeze's practical effect is that States with faster post-1971 population growth do not get additional Assembly seats relative to slower-growing States before the freeze lifts — a deliberate, controversial policy choice originally justified as an incentive not to penalise States for effective population-control policies, extended multiple times (originally to 2000, then 2026 via the Eighty-fourth and later amendments).
The 'subject to article 333' qualifier is now largely of historical interest only, since Anglo-Indian nomination itself lapsed with the One Hundred and Fourth Amendment Act, 2019.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 170 as Article 81's precise State-level mirror, right down to sharing the same 2026-census delimitation freeze — always check the current, amended figures (the freeze's end-year and reference census years have themselves been amended multiple times) rather than relying on the Constitution's original 1950 text.

sections.title: Composition of the Legislative Councils
key_terms: Legislative Council size cap (one-third of Assembly, minimum 40)
five-fold composition of Legislative Council (Article 171(3))
local authorities' constituency (Legislative Council)
graduates' constituency (Legislative Council)
teachers' constituency (Legislative Council)
MLA-elected Council seats (Article 171(3)(d))
Governor's nominated Council members — special knowledge/experience
proportional representation by single transferable vote (State Council)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 171 fixes how a State's Legislative Council (where one exists) is sized and composed — an intricate, multi-constituency design without a Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha parallel, reflecting the Council's role as a chamber representing specialised, local, and professional interests rather than pure population-based democracy. Size is capped at one-third of the Assembly's membership, with an absolute floor of 40. Absent a different Parliamentary law, composition follows a fixed five-part formula: one-third elected by local-body members (municipalities, district boards, etc.), one-twelfth by university graduates, one-twelfth by secondary-school-or-above teachers, one-third by MLAs voting for non-MLA candidates, and the remainder nominated by the Governor from persons with special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art, the co-operative movement, or social service. All the elected categories use proportional representation via the single transferable vote.
essential_elements: Clause (1): Council size capped at one-third of the Assembly's total membership, with a proviso guaranteeing a floor of at least 40 members regardless of how small a State's Assembly is.

Clause (2)-(3): absent a different Parliamentary law, the default five-category composition applies — local authorities' electorate (~1/3), graduates' electorate (~1/12), teachers' electorate (~1/12), MLA-elected non-MLA members (~1/3), and Governor-nominated members (the remainder).
Clause (4): elections under sub-clauses (a)-(d) are held via territorial constituencies (for (a)-(c)) and use the single-transferable-vote proportional representation system throughout.

Clause (5): Governor's nominated members (sub-clause (e)) must possess special knowledge or practical experience in one of five listed fields — literature, science, art, the co-operative movement, or social service — a closed, non-expandable list.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This entire composition scheme applies 'until Parliament by law otherwise provides' — Parliament retains full power to redesign a Council's composition by ordinary law, unlike the Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha's more constitutionally fixed structures.

Because Legislative Councils can be abolished or created under Article 169 on a State's own initiative, not every State has one — this Article only operates for the currently-bicameral States identified (as amended) under Article 168(1)(a).
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 171 as a self-contained, unusually granular composition code specific to the Legislative Council's function as a chamber of local, educational, and specialised representation — quite unlike the population-proportional design of Article 170's Legislative Assembly rules, and always check whether the default clause (3) formula still governs or whether Parliament has legislated a different composition for the particular State.

sections.title: Duration of State Legislatures
sections.raw_text:
(1) Every Legislative Assembly of every State, unless sooner dissolved, shall continue for five years from the date appointed for its first meeting and no longer and the expiration of the said period of five years shall operate as a dissolution of the Assembly:
Provided that the said period may, while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, be extended by Parliament by law for a period not exceeding one year at a time and not extending in any case beyond a period of six months after the Proclamation has ceased to operate.
(2) The Legislative Council of a State shall not be subject to dissolution, but as nearly as possible one-third of the members thereof shall retire as soon as may be on the expiration of every second year in accordance with the provisions made in that behalf by Parliament by law.
key_terms: five-year Legislative Assembly term (State)
Emergency extension of Assembly term (State)
Legislative Council permanence with one-third biennial retirement

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 172 fixes State Legislature terms, exactly mirroring Article 83's Parliament-level scheme. A Legislative Assembly's normal term is five years from its first meeting, automatically dissolving on expiry unless dissolved sooner (e.g., by the Governor). During a Proclamation of Emergency, Parliament can extend this term by law, one year at a time, but never beyond six months after the Emergency ends. A Legislative Council, by contrast, is a permanent body like the Rajya Sabha — never dissolved, with roughly one-third of its members retiring every two years per rules Parliament prescribes, ensuring continuous, staggered membership.
essential_elements: Legislative Assembly's default term: five years from the date appointed for its first meeting, with automatic dissolution on expiry — no further legislative act is needed to end the Assembly's life once the term runs out.
The Assembly may also be dissolved sooner (via the Governor's power under Article 174(2)(b)) — the five-year figure is a maximum, not a guarantee of tenure.

Emergency extension: Parliament may, by law, extend an Assembly's term beyond five years, one year at a time, only while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, with a hard outer limit of six months after the Emergency ceases.

Legislative Council: never dissolved as a body — it is a permanent, continuous chamber; instead, about one-third of its members retire every second year, per Parliament-made rules, creating staggered, overlapping terms (mirroring the Rajya Sabha's Article 83(1) design).
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Emergency-extension proviso has real historical precedent — Assembly terms were extended in several States during the Emergency era (1975-77) using the parallel Union-level mechanism, and equivalent State-level extensions have occurred under Article 172's own proviso.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 172 as Article 83's precise State-level mirror — five-year Assembly terms with an Emergency-only extension safety valve, and a permanent, one-third-biennial-retirement Legislative Council wherever one exists, structurally identical to the Rajya Sabha's design.

sections.title: Qualification for membership of the State Legislature
sections.raw_text:
A person shall not be qualified to be chosen to fill a seat in the Legislature of a State unless he—
(a) is a citizen of India, and makes and subscribes before some person authorised in that behalf by the Election Commission an oath or affirmation according to the form set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule;
(b) is, in the case of a seat in the Legislative Assembly, not less than twenty-five years of age and, in the case of a seat in the Legislative Council, not less than thirty years of age; and
(c) possesses such other qualifications as may be prescribed in that behalf by or under any law made by Parliament.
key_terms: Indian citizenship requirement (State Legislature membership)
pre-candidacy oath before Election-Commission-authorised person (State)
minimum age 25 (Assembly) / 30 (Council)
further qualifications by Parliamentary law (State Legislature)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 173 sets the baseline eligibility bar for State Legislature membership, mirroring Article 84's Parliament-membership qualifications almost exactly, just with different minimum ages matching each House's character. A candidate must be an Indian citizen who has made and subscribed the Third Schedule oath or affirmation before an Election-Commission-authorised person, meet the minimum age (25 for the Assembly, 30 for the Council — the same age gap as between the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha), and satisfy any further qualifications Parliament prescribes by law (principally the Representation of the People Act, 1951's disqualification and eligibility rules).
essential_elements: Citizenship: must be an Indian citizen.

Pre-candidacy oath: must make and subscribe the Third Schedule oath/affirmation before a person the Election Commission has authorised for that purpose — a mandatory precondition to candidacy, distinct from the post-election Article 188 oath taken before actually sitting.
Minimum age: 25 years for a Legislative Assembly seat, 30 years for a Legislative Council seat — the same differential reasoning as the Lok Sabha (25)/Rajya Sabha (30) age gap under Article 84.
Residual qualifications: whatever further qualifications Parliament prescribes by law — chiefly found in the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article sets only the affirmative eligibility floor — separate disqualification grounds (Article 191, covering office of profit, unsoundness of mind, insolvency, non-citizenship, and other Parliament-prescribed grounds including the Tenth Schedule) can still bar an otherwise-qualified person.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 173 as Article 84's State-level mirror — same oath-before-candidacy requirement and same structural logic behind the age differential, always cross-check against Article 191's separate disqualification grounds and the Representation of the People Act, 1951 for the complete eligibility-and-disqualification picture.

sections.title: Sessions of the State Legislature, prorogation and dissolution
sections.raw_text:
(1) The Governor shall from time to time summon the House or each House of the Legislature of the State to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit, but six months shall not intervene between its last sitting in one session and the date appointed for its first sitting in the next session.
(2) The Governor may from time to time—
(a) prorogue the House or either House;
(b) dissolve the Legislative Assembly.
key_terms: Governor's summoning power (State Legislature)
six-month maximum gap between sessions (State)
Governor's prorogation power (State Legislature)
Governor's dissolution power (Legislative Assembly)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 174 mirrors Article 85's Union-level rules on Parliament sessions, transposed to the State Legislature and the Governor. The Governor summons the House (or each House, for bicameral States) to meet, choosing the time and place, subject to the hard rule that no more than six months can elapse between one session's last sitting and the next session's first sitting — guaranteeing the Legislature meets at least twice a year. The Governor also holds the power to prorogue (formally end a session without dissolving the House) and, for the Legislative Assembly specifically, to dissolve it (only the Assembly can be dissolved — the Legislative Council, being a permanent body under Article 172(2), cannot be).
essential_elements: Clause (1): the Governor summons the House or each House at a time and place of his choosing, subject to the mandatory six-month maximum inter-session gap — the same rule Article 85(1) imposes on the President for Parliament.
Clause (2)(a): the Governor may prorogue the House or either House — ending a session's sittings without ending the House's life.

Clause (2)(b): the Governor may dissolve the Legislative Assembly specifically — the power to dissolve applies only to the Assembly, never to a Legislative Council, consistent with Article 172(2)'s rule that Councils are not subject to dissolution.
exceptions_and_qualifications: As with the President's equivalent powers under Article 85, the Governor's summoning, prorogation, and dissolution powers are, per Article 163's default rule, ordinarily exercised on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (specifically the Chief Minister), not as personal discretion — except in the narrow, well-recognised discretionary scenarios (e.g., a government that has lost its majority but declines to advise dissolution, or a hung Assembly).
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 174 as Article 85's precise State-level mirror — the six-month rule, prorogation power, and (Assembly-only) dissolution power all track identically, with the same underlying convention that these are ordinarily ministerial-advice powers, not personal gubernatorial discretion, save in genuinely exceptional situations.

sections.title: Right of Governor to address and send messages to the House or Houses
sections.raw_text:
(1) The Governor may address the Legislative Assembly or, in the case of a State having a Legislative Council, either House of the Legislature of the State, or both Houses assembled together, and may for that purpose require the attendance of members.
(2) The Governor may send messages to the House or Houses of the Legislature of the State, whether with respect to a Bill then pending in the Legislature or otherwise, and a House to which any message is so sent shall with all convenient despatch consider any matter required by the message to be taken into consideration.
key_terms: Governor's power to address the House(s)
Governor's power to send messages to the House(s)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 175 mirrors Article 86's Presidential powers at the State level, giving the Governor two distinct communication tools with the Legislature: the power to personally address the Legislative Assembly, either House (in a bicameral State), or both Houses assembled together — compelling member attendance for that purpose — and the separate power to send written messages to the House or Houses, whether about a pending Bill or any other matter, which the receiving House must then take up with all convenient despatch.
essential_elements: Clause (1): the Governor may address the Assembly, either House, or both Houses together, and may require members' attendance for that address.

Clause (2): the Governor may send messages to the House or Houses on a pending Bill or any other matter; the receiving House is obligated to consider the message's subject matter with all convenient despatch (though not bound to act on it in any particular way).
exceptions_and_qualifications: This power is distinct from the Special Address under Article 176, which is mandatory at fixed points (post-election, start of each year) — Article 175's address/message powers may be exercised at any time, at the Governor's own initiative (in practice, on ministerial advice).
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 175 as Article 86's State-level mirror — a general-purpose communication channel available at any time, distinct from Article 176's specific, calendar-triggered Special Address obligation.

sections.title: Special address by the Governor
sections.raw_text:
(1) At the commencement of the first session after each general election to the Legislative Assembly and at the commencement of the first session of each year, the Governor shall address the Legislative Assembly or, in the case of a State having a Legislative Council, both Houses assembled together and inform the Legislature of the causes of its summons.
(2) Provision shall be made by the rules regulating the procedure of the House or either House for the allotment of time for discussion of the matters referred to in such address.
key_terms: Special Address at each year's first session and post-election session (Governor)
allotted-time debate on Governor's Special Address

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 176 imposes a mandatory obligation on the Governor, mirroring the President's Article 87 duty: address the Assembly (or both Houses together, in bicameral States) at the start of the first session following each general election and at the start of each year's first session, explaining the causes of the Legislature's summons — in practice a policy-and-legislative-agenda-setting speech drafted by the Council of Ministers. House procedural rules must set aside dedicated time to debate the matters raised in that address.
essential_elements: Two mandatory trigger-points: the first session after each general election to the Assembly, and the first session of every calendar year — the Governor must address the Legislature (or both Houses together, if bicameral) at each.
The address must inform the Legislature of the causes of its summons — functioning, by convention, as a government policy statement for the year or new Assembly term.

Clause (2) requires House procedural rules to allot dedicated debate time for the matters the address raises — ensuring the Special Address triggers substantive legislative scrutiny, not just a ceremonial reading.
exceptions_and_qualifications: As with the President's Article 87 address, the Governor's Special Address content is, by settled constitutional convention, drafted by and reflects the policies of the Council of Ministers — it is not the Governor's personal statement of views.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 176 as Article 87's State-level mirror — a mandatory, calendar-triggered policy address (distinct from Article 175's general, any-time address/message powers), always followed by allotted-time legislative debate.

sections.title: Rights of Ministers and Advocate-General as respects the Houses
sections.raw_text: Every Minister and the Advocate-General for a State shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, the Legislative Assembly of the State or, in the case of a State having a Legislative Council, both Houses, and to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, any committee of the Legislature of which he may be named a member, but shall not, by virtue of this article, be entitled to vote.
key_terms: Ministers' and Advocate-General's floor rights without voting rights

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 177 mirrors Article 88's Union-level rule, giving every State Minister and the Advocate-General the right to speak and otherwise participate in proceedings of the Legislative Assembly, both Houses (in bicameral States), and any Legislature committee they're named to — regardless of whether they're actually elected members of that House. This lets a Minister who sits in the Council (or is not yet a Legislature member at all, within the Article 164(4) six-month grace period) still explain and defend government policy on the Assembly floor. The right stops short of voting — only House membership, not this Article, confers a vote.
essential_elements: Beneficiaries: every Minister (regardless of which House, if any, he belongs to) and the Advocate-General for the State.
Scope of rights: speaking and otherwise participating in proceedings of the Assembly, both Houses (bicameral States), and any committee they're named a member of.
Express limitation: this Article confers no voting right — voting remains tied to actual House membership.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is particularly significant for the Advocate-General, who is typically not an elected Legislature member at all, yet can still appear and speak on the floor to assist with legal matters or defend government legislation.

It is equally significant for a Minister drawn from the Legislative Council addressing the Assembly (or vice versa) in a bicameral State, and for a newly-appointed Minister who is not yet a sitting member within Article 164(4)'s six-month grace window.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 177 as Article 88's State-level mirror — it grants participation rights decoupled from membership, but never a vote; always distinguish a Minister/Advocate-General's floor rights under this Article from an actual member's full rights (including voting) under ordinary House membership.

sections.title: The Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Legislative Assembly
sections.raw_text: Every Legislative Assembly of a State shall, as soon as may be, choose two members of the Assembly to be respectively Speaker and Deputy Speaker thereof and, so often as the office of Speaker or Deputy Speaker becomes vacant, the Assembly shall choose another member to be Speaker or Deputy Speaker, as the case may be.
key_terms: Speaker and Deputy Speaker of Legislative Assembly (State)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 178 requires every State Legislative Assembly to elect two of its own members as Speaker and Deputy Speaker as soon as practicable after constitution, and to fill either office promptly by a fresh election from among its members whenever it falls vacant — mirroring the Lok Sabha's Article 93 requirement at the State level.
essential_elements: Both the Speaker and Deputy Speaker must be chosen from among the Assembly's own members — they are not outsiders or Governor-appointees.
The choice is made by the Assembly itself, 'as soon as may be' after the Assembly is constituted (i.e., after a general election).
Whenever either office falls vacant (resignation, removal, ceasing to be a member, or death), the Assembly must choose a replacement member for that office.
exceptions_and_qualifications: There is no constitutional requirement that the Speaker or Deputy Speaker belong to any particular party or coalition — the choice is entirely the Assembly's own, though by convention the Speaker is usually drawn from the ruling party/coalition and the Deputy Speaker sometimes from the opposition.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 178 as Article 93's State-level mirror — the Speaker and Deputy Speaker are always elected Assembly insiders, never Governor nominees, underscoring the Assembly's self-governing character over its own presiding officers.

sections.title: Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the offices of Speaker and Deputy Speaker
sections.raw_text:
A member holding office as Speaker or Deputy Speaker of an Assembly—
(a) shall vacate his office if he ceases to be a member of the Assembly;
(b) may at any time by writing under his hand addressed, if such member is the Speaker, to the Deputy Speaker, and if such member is the Deputy Speaker, to the Speaker, resign his office; and
(c) may be removed from his office by a resolution of the Assembly passed by a majority of all the then members of the Assembly:
Provided that no resolution for the purpose of clause (c) shall be moved unless at least fourteen days' notice has been given of the intention to move the resolution:
Provided further that, whenever the Assembly is dissolved, the Speaker shall not vacate his office until immediately before the first meeting of the Assembly after the dissolution.
key_terms: automatic vacation on ceasing Assembly membership (Speaker/Deputy Speaker)
resignation of Speaker/Deputy Speaker in writing
removal by absolute-majority Assembly resolution with 14-day notice
Speaker's continuation in office through dissolution

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 179 mirrors Article 94's rules for the Lok Sabha Speaker/Deputy Speaker, transposed to the State Assembly. The Speaker or Deputy Speaker automatically vacates office on ceasing to be an Assembly member, may resign in writing to the other officer, or may be removed by an absolute-majority Assembly resolution (of all then members, not just those present and voting), preceded by at least fourteen days' notice. Crucially, the second proviso ensures continuity: on Assembly dissolution, the Speaker does not vacate office immediately but continues until just before the newly-constituted Assembly's first meeting — so the Assembly is never left without a Speaker during the interregnum.
essential_elements: Clause (a): automatic vacation on ceasing to be an Assembly member — the office is inseparable from membership.
Clause (b): resignation by writing under hand, addressed to the counterpart officer (Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker, and vice versa).

Clause (c): removal by an Assembly resolution requiring an absolute majority of all then members (not merely a majority of those present and voting) — a deliberately high bar protecting the Speaker's independence from transient majorities.
First proviso: at least fourteen days' notice of intention to move a removal resolution is mandatory before it can be moved.

Second proviso: the Speaker (notably, not the Deputy Speaker) continues in office through an Assembly's dissolution, vacating only immediately before the newly-elected Assembly's first meeting — ensuring institutional continuity.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The continuity proviso in clause (c) applies specifically to the Speaker, not the Deputy Speaker — on dissolution, only the Speaker's tenure is extended this way.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 179 as Article 94's precise State-level mirror — the absolute-majority-plus-14-day-notice removal threshold is a significant procedural safeguard, and the dissolution-continuity proviso for the Speaker (but not the Deputy Speaker) is a frequently tested distinction.

sections.title: Power of the Deputy Speaker or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Speaker
sections.raw_text:
(1) While the office of Speaker is vacant, the duties of the office shall be performed by the Deputy Speaker or, if the office of Deputy Speaker is also vacant, by such member of the Assembly as the Governor may appoint for the purpose.
(2) During the absence of the Speaker from any sitting of the Assembly the Deputy Speaker or, if he is also absent, such person as may be determined by the rules of procedure of the Assembly, or, if no such person is present, such other person as may be determined by the Assembly, shall act as Speaker.
key_terms: Deputy Speaker filling a vacant Speaker's office
Governor-appointed member filling both offices vacant
acting Speaker for a single sitting's absence

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 180 mirrors Article 95's Lok Sabha continuity mechanism, ensuring the Assembly always has someone presiding. If the Speaker's office itself is vacant, the Deputy Speaker performs its duties; if both offices are vacant simultaneously, the Governor appoints an Assembly member to perform them. Separately, for a mere temporary absence of the Speaker from a particular sitting (offices not vacant, Speaker just not present that day), a cascading fallback applies: the Deputy Speaker acts, or if he too is absent, whoever the Assembly's procedural rules designate, or failing that, whoever the Assembly itself determines for that sitting.
essential_elements: Clause (1) addresses office vacancy: Deputy Speaker steps in first; only if both Speaker and Deputy Speaker offices are simultaneously vacant does the Governor appoint an Assembly member to perform the Speaker's duties.
Clause (2) addresses mere sitting-by-sitting absence (not vacancy): Deputy Speaker acts first, then a rules-designated person, then an Assembly-determined person for that sitting.
The Governor's appointment power under clause (1) is a narrow, last-resort mechanism — it only engages when both offices are vacant, not whenever the Speaker happens to be unavailable.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (1)'s Governor-appointment power is exceptional and narrow — it applies only when both the Speaker's and Deputy Speaker's offices are simultaneously vacant, not to routine day-to-day absences, which clause (2) handles entirely within the Assembly without any gubernatorial role.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 180 as Article 95's exact State-level mirror — carefully distinguish clause (1)'s office-vacancy scenario (where the Governor may eventually get involved) from clause (2)'s mere sitting-absence scenario (purely an internal Assembly matter, no gubernatorial role at all).

sections.title: The Speaker or the Deputy Speaker not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration
sections.raw_text:
(1) At any sitting of the Legislative Assembly, while any resolution for the removal of the Speaker from his office is under consideration, the Speaker, or while any resolution for the removal of the Deputy Speaker from his office is under consideration, the Deputy Speaker, shall not, though he is present, preside, and the provisions of clause (2) of article 180 shall apply in relation to every such sitting as they apply in relation to a sitting from which the Speaker or, as the case may be, the Deputy Speaker, is absent.
(2) The Speaker shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, the Legislative Assembly while any resolution for his removal from office is under consideration in the Assembly and shall, notwithstanding anything in article 189, be entitled to vote only in the first instance on such resolution or on any other matter during such proceedings but not in the case of an equality of votes.
key_terms: disqualification from presiding during own removal resolution (Speaker/Deputy Speaker)
Speaker's first-instance-only voting right during own removal debate

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 181 mirrors Article 96's natural-justice safeguard: a Speaker or Deputy Speaker facing his own removal resolution cannot preside over that sitting (even if physically present), with Article 180(2)'s absence-fallback rules kicking in instead. The Speaker retains the right to speak and participate in the debate on his own removal, and — departing from Article 189's normal no-casting-vote-unless-tied rule for the Speaker — may vote in the first instance on the resolution or any other matter during those proceedings, but is barred from exercising the tie-breaking casting vote he would ordinarily hold.
essential_elements: Clause (1): the Speaker (or Deputy Speaker) cannot preside over a sitting considering his own removal — a basic natural-justice rule against being judge in one's own cause — and Article 180(2)'s absence-fallback mechanism applies as if he were absent.
Clause (2): despite not presiding, the Speaker keeps full speaking and participation rights in the debate on his own removal.

Clause (2)'s voting carve-out: the Speaker may vote in the first instance during such proceedings (unlike his ordinary no-vote-except-on-a-tie position under Article 189), but is still denied the casting/tie-breaking vote.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Speaker's loss of presiding function during his own removal debate is temporary and proceeding-specific — once the resolution is disposed of (whether it succeeds or fails), his ordinary presiding role resumes if he remains in office.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 181 as Article 96's precise State-level mirror — note carefully that clause (2)'s voting rule is a narrow, proceeding-specific exception to Article 189's general rule, not a general expansion of the Speaker's voting rights.

sections.title: The Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Legislative Council
sections.raw_text: The Legislative Council of every State having such Council shall, as soon as may be, choose two members of the Council to be respectively Chairman and Deputy Chairman thereof and, so often as the office of Chairman or Deputy Chairman becomes vacant, the Council shall choose another member to be Chairman or Deputy Chairman, as the case may be.
key_terms: Chairman and Deputy Chairman of Legislative Council (State)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 182 is the Legislative Council's counterpart to Article 178 — every bicameral State's Legislative Council must choose two of its own members to serve as Chairman and Deputy Chairman, refilling either office by fresh election from among its members whenever it falls vacant, mirroring the Rajya Sabha's Vice-Chairman arrangement under Article 89(1) (the Council's Chairman role is distinct from the ex officio Vice-President-as-Rajya-Sabha-Chairman pattern — a State Legislative Council chooses its own Chairman from its own members, with no Governor-equivalent-of-Vice-President ex officio role here).
essential_elements: Both the Chairman and Deputy Chairman must be chosen from among the Legislative Council's own members.
The Council itself makes the choice, as soon as may be after being constituted, and refills either office promptly whenever it becomes vacant.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Unlike the Rajya Sabha (where the Vice-President serves ex officio as Chairman under Article 89(1)), a State Legislative Council has no equivalent ex officio presiding officer — its Chairman is always elected from among its own members, making Article 182 closer in structure to Article 93 (Speaker) than to Article 89(1) (Rajya Sabha Chairman).
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 182 as structurally closer to Article 178's Speaker-selection model than to the Rajya Sabha's ex officio Vice-President-as-Chairman arrangement — a State's Legislative Council Chairman is always one of its own elected members.

sections.title: Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the offices of Chairman and Deputy Chairman
sections.raw_text:
A member holding office as Chairman or Deputy Chairman of a Legislative Council—
(a) shall vacate his office if he ceases to be a member of the Council;
(b) may at any time by writing under his hand addressed, if such member is the Chairman, to the Deputy Chairman, and if such member is the Deputy Chairman, to the Chairman, resign his office; and
(c) may be removed from his office by a resolution of the Council passed by a majority of all the then members of the Council:
Provided that no resolution for the purpose of clause (c) shall be moved unless at least fourteen days' notice has been given of the intention to move the resolution.
key_terms: automatic vacation on ceasing Council membership (Chairman/Deputy Chairman)
resignation of Chairman/Deputy Chairman in writing
removal of Chairman/Deputy Chairman by absolute-majority resolution with 14-day notice

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 183 is the Legislative Council's precise counterpart to Article 179, applying the identical vacation/resignation/removal scheme to the Chairman and Deputy Chairman: automatic vacation on ceasing Council membership, resignation by writing to the counterpart officer, and removal only by an absolute-majority resolution of all then Council members, preceded by at least fourteen days' notice. Unlike Article 179, there is no dissolution-continuity proviso here, because a Legislative Council — being a permanent body under Article 172(2) — is never dissolved in the first place, so no such safeguard is needed.
essential_elements: Clause (a): automatic vacation on ceasing to be a Council member.
Clause (b): resignation by writing under hand to the counterpart officer (Chairman resigns to Deputy Chairman, and vice versa).
Clause (c): removal requires an absolute majority of all then Council members, with the same mandatory fourteen-day advance notice requirement as for the Speaker/Deputy Speaker.
exceptions_and_qualifications: No dissolution-continuity proviso exists here (unlike Article 179's second proviso for the Speaker) — because the Legislative Council is a permanent, non-dissolvable body under Article 172(2), there is no dissolution event that could otherwise leave the Chairman's office in limbo.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 183 as Article 179's Council-level twin, minus the dissolution-continuity proviso — the absence of that proviso is a direct, logical consequence of the Council's permanence under Article 172(2), not an oversight.

sections.title: Power of the Deputy Chairman or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Chairman
sections.raw_text:
(1) While the office of Chairman is vacant, the duties of the office shall be performed by the Deputy Chairman or, if the office of Deputy Chairman is also vacant, by such member of the Council as the Governor may appoint for the purpose.
(2) During the absence of the Chairman from any sitting of the Council the Deputy Chairman or, if he is also absent, such person as may be determined by the rules of procedure of the Council, or, if no such person is present, such other person as may be determined by the Council, shall act as Chairman.
key_terms: Deputy Chairman filling a vacant Chairman's office
Governor-appointed Council member filling both offices vacant
acting Chairman for a single sitting's absence

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 184 is the Legislative Council's precise counterpart to Article 180, ensuring the Council always has someone presiding. If the Chairman's office is vacant, the Deputy Chairman performs its duties; if both offices are simultaneously vacant, the Governor appoints a Council member to perform them. For a mere temporary absence of the Chairman from a particular sitting (office not vacant, just not present), a cascading fallback applies: Deputy Chairman first, then a rules-designated person, then whoever the Council itself determines for that sitting.
essential_elements: Clause (1) addresses office vacancy: Deputy Chairman steps in first; only if both offices are simultaneously vacant does the Governor appoint a Council member to perform the Chairman's duties.
Clause (2) addresses mere sitting-by-sitting absence (office not vacant): Deputy Chairman acts first, then a rules-designated person, then an Council-determined person for that sitting.
exceptions_and_qualifications: As with Article 180's Assembly equivalent, the Governor's appointment power under clause (1) is narrow and last-resort — engaged only when both Chairman and Deputy Chairman offices are simultaneously vacant.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 184 as Article 180's exact Council-level twin — same office-vacancy-versus-sitting-absence distinction, same narrow gubernatorial fallback role.

sections.title: The Chairman or the Deputy Chairman not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration
sections.raw_text:
(1) At any sitting of the Legislative Council, while any resolution for the removal of the Chairman from his office is under consideration, the Chairman, or while any resolution for the removal of the Deputy Chairman from his office is under consideration, the Deputy Chairman, shall not, though he is present, preside, and the provisions of clause (2) of article 184 shall apply in relation to every such sitting as they apply in relation to a sitting from which the Chairman or, as the case may be, the Deputy Chairman is absent.
(2) The Chairman shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, the Legislative Council while any resolution for his removal from office is under consideration in the Council and shall, notwithstanding anything in article 189, be entitled to vote only in the first instance on such resolution or on any other matter during such proceedings but not in the case of an equality of votes.
key_terms: disqualification from presiding during own removal resolution (Chairman/Deputy Chairman)
Chairman's first-instance-only voting right during own removal debate

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 185 is the Legislative Council's precise counterpart to Article 181, applying the same natural-justice rule: a Chairman or Deputy Chairman facing his own removal resolution cannot preside over that sitting even if present, with Article 184(2)'s absence-fallback rules applying instead. The Chairman retains the right to speak and participate in the debate on his own removal and may vote in the first instance on the resolution or any other matter during those proceedings (departing from Article 189's ordinary rule), but is barred from the tie-breaking casting vote.
essential_elements: Clause (1): the Chairman (or Deputy Chairman) cannot preside over a sitting considering his own removal, and Article 184(2)'s absence-fallback mechanism applies as if he were absent.
Clause (2): the Chairman keeps speaking/participation rights and a first-instance vote during such proceedings, but not the tie-breaking casting vote.
exceptions_and_qualifications: As with the Speaker's equivalent position under Article 181, the Chairman's loss of presiding function during his own removal debate is temporary and confined to that proceeding — his ordinary presiding role resumes once the resolution is disposed of, if he remains in office.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 185 as Article 181's exact Council-level twin — identical natural-justice logic and identical narrow voting carve-out.

sections.title: Salaries and allowances of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker and the Chairman and Deputy Chairman
sections.raw_text: There shall be paid to the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the Legislative Assembly, and to the Chairman and the Deputy Chairman of the Legislative Council, such salaries and allowances as may be respectively fixed by the Legislature of the State by law and, until provision in that behalf is so made, such salaries and allowances as are specified in the Second Schedule.
key_terms: salaries and allowances of presiding officers (State Legislature)
Second Schedule default (State presiding officers)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 186 guarantees the four State Legislature presiding officers — Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Chairman, and Deputy Chairman — salaries and allowances fixed by State legislative law, defaulting to Second Schedule figures absent such law, following the same drafting pattern used throughout the Constitution for high constitutional offices (the President, Governor, Judges, CAG, Union presiding officers).
essential_elements: Covers all four State Legislature presiding/deputy-presiding officers: Speaker and Deputy Speaker (Assembly), Chairman and Deputy Chairman (Council).
Primary source of salary/allowance figures: State legislative law.
Default fallback: Second Schedule figures apply until the State Legislature enacts its own law.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The salaries/allowances of these presiding officers are distinct from, and additional to, any salary they might separately draw as an ordinary Legislature member — this Article specifically compensates the presiding/deputy-presiding role itself.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 186 as following the Constitution's standard Second-Schedule-default salary pattern — cross-reference the Second Schedule itself for the actual fallback figures if no State law has been made.

sections.title: Secretariat of State Legislature
sections.raw_text:
(1) The House or each House of the Legislature of a State shall have a separate secretarial staff:
Provided that nothing in this clause shall, in the case of the Legislature of a State having a Legislative Council, be construed as preventing the creation of posts common to both Houses of such Legislature.
(2) The Legislature of a State may by law regulate the recruitment, and the conditions of service of persons appointed, to the secretarial staff of the House or Houses of the Legislature of the State.
(3) Until provision is made by the Legislature of the State under clause (2), the Governor may, after consultation with the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly or the Chairman of the Legislative Council, as the case may be, make rules regulating the recruitment, and the conditions of service of persons appointed, to the secretarial staff of the Assembly or the Council, and any rules so made shall have effect subject to the provisions of any law made under the said clause.
key_terms: separate secretarial staff per House (State Legislature)
common posts across both Houses proviso (State Secretariat)
State law regulating Legislature secretarial staff recruitment/conditions
Governor's interim rules for Secretariat staff (post-Speaker/Chairman consultation)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 187 mirrors Article 98's Union-level rule, guaranteeing each House of a State Legislature its own secretarial staff (though bicameral States may create posts common to both Houses for efficiency). The State Legislature can regulate recruitment and service conditions for this staff by law; until it does, the Governor fills the gap by making rules — but only after consulting the Speaker (for Assembly staff) or the Chairman (for Council staff) — and any such rules yield to a later State law on the subject.
essential_elements: Clause (1): each House gets its own secretarial staff, with a proviso permitting common posts across both Houses in bicameral States (administrative efficiency, avoiding needless duplication).
Clause (2): the State Legislature may regulate recruitment and service conditions for this staff by law — the primary, preferred source of regulation.

Clause (3): absent such a State law, the Governor makes interim rules on the same subject, but only after consulting the relevant presiding officer (Speaker for the Assembly, Chairman for the Council) — and those rules remain subject to (i.e., are overridden by) any subsequent State law.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The consultation requirement in clause (3) is a meaningful procedural safeguard — it ensures the Secretariat, which serves the Legislature and must remain institutionally independent of the executive, isn't staffed or regulated by the Governor unilaterally.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 187 as Article 98's precise State-level mirror — the Secretariat's institutional independence from the executive (Governor) is protected both by the State-law-primacy structure and by the mandatory presiding-officer consultation requirement for any interim gubernatorial rules.

sections.title: Oath or affirmation by members
sections.raw_text: Every member of the Legislative Assembly or the Legislative Council of a State shall, before taking his seat, make and subscribe before the Governor, or some person appointed in that behalf by him, an oath or affirmation according to the form set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule.
key_terms: member's oath before taking seat (State Legislature)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 188 mirrors Article 99's Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha rule, requiring every State Legislature member — Assembly or Council — to make and subscribe the Third Schedule oath or affirmation before the Governor (or his appointed delegate) before actually taking his seat. This is distinct from the pre-candidacy oath under Article 173(a): that earlier oath is a precondition to being chosen for the seat at all, while this Article 188 oath is a precondition to actually sitting and functioning as a member once chosen.
essential_elements: Applies to every member of either House — Assembly or Council.
Must occur before the member takes his seat — a precondition to functioning as a member, not to being elected/chosen.
Administered by the Governor or a person he appoints for the purpose, in the Third Schedule's prescribed form.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article 188 oath is textually and functionally distinct from the Article 173(a) pre-candidacy oath — the latter must be made before an Election-Commission-authorised person as a condition of candidacy itself; this one is made before the Governor (or his delegate) as a condition of actually sitting after being duly chosen.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 188 as Article 99's precise State-level mirror — always distinguish it from Article 173(a)'s earlier, differently-administered pre-candidacy oath; a member takes two separate oaths at two separate stages of the process.

sections.title: Voting in Houses, power of Houses to act notwithstanding vacancies and quorum
sections.raw_text:
(1) Save as otherwise provided in this Constitution, all questions at any sitting of a House of the Legislature of a State shall be determined by a majority of votes of the members present and voting, other than the Speaker or Chairman, or person acting as such.
The Speaker or Chairman, or person acting as such, shall not vote in the first instance, but shall have and exercise a casting vote in the case of an equality of votes.
(2) A House of the Legislature of a State shall have power to act notwithstanding any vacancy in the membership thereof, and any proceedings in the Legislature of a State shall be valid notwithstanding that it is discovered subsequently that some person who was not entitled so to do sat or voted or otherwise took part in the proceedings.
(3) Until the Legislature of the State by law otherwise provides, the quorum to constitute a meeting of a House of the Legislature of a State shall be ten members or one-tenth of the total number of members of the House, whichever is greater.
(4) If at any time during a meeting of the Legislative Assembly or the Legislative Council of a State there is no quorum, it shall be the duty of the Speaker or Chairman, or person acting as such, either to adjourn the House or to suspend the meeting until there is a quorum.
key_terms: ordinary-majority voting rule (State Legislature)
Speaker/Chairman's no-vote-except-casting-vote rule
House's power to act despite vacancies/ineligible participants
quorum: 10 members or one-tenth, whichever greater (State House)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 189 mirrors Article 100's Union-level rules on voting, quorum, and procedural validity, transposed to State Houses. Ordinary questions are decided by simple majority of members present and voting, excluding the presiding officer, who votes only to break a tie (never in the first instance). Houses can validly function despite membership vacancies, and proceedings remain valid even if it later emerges an ineligible person sat or voted. Quorum, absent State legislation otherwise, is 10 members or one-tenth of total House membership (whichever is greater); if quorum is lost mid-meeting, the presiding officer must adjourn or suspend until quorum is restored.
essential_elements: Clause (1): simple majority of members present and voting decides ordinary questions, excluding the Speaker/Chairman (or acting equivalent), who has only a casting vote in case of a tie — never a first-instance vote.

Clause (2): vacancies in House membership don't disable the House from acting, and later-discovered participation by an ineligible person doesn't retroactively invalidate proceedings — protecting institutional stability against technical challenges.
Clause (3): default quorum is 10 members or one-tenth of total House membership, whichever is greater, until the State Legislature legislates a different figure.
Clause (4): losing quorum mid-meeting obliges the presiding officer to either adjourn the House or suspend the meeting until quorum is restored — not to continue proceedings without quorum.
exceptions_and_qualifications: 'Save as otherwise provided in this Constitution' in clause (1) flags that some specific matters require a different (often higher) voting threshold elsewhere in the Constitution — e.g., the absolute-majority-plus-14-day-notice threshold for removing a Speaker/Chairman under Articles 179(c)/183(c).
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 189 as Article 100's precise State-level mirror — the quorum and casting-vote rules are frequently tested distinctions from ordinary parliamentary procedure, and the clause (2) validity-preservation rule is an important practical safeguard against procedural challenges to legislative business.

sections.title: Vacation of seats
sections.raw_text:
(1) No person shall be a member of both Houses of the Legislature of a State and provision shall be made by the Legislature of the State by law for the vacation by a person who is chosen a member of both Houses of his seat in one house or the other.
(2) No person shall be a member of the Legislatures of two or more States specified in the First Schedule and if a person is chosen a member of the Legislatures of two or more such States, then, at the expiration of such period as may be specified in rules made by the President, that person's seat in the Legislatures of all such States shall become vacant, unless he has previously resigned his seat in the Legislatures of all but one of the States.
(3) If a member of a House of the Legislature of a State—
(a) becomes subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in clause (1) or clause (2) of article 191; or
(b) resigns his seat by writing under his hand addressed to the Speaker or the Chairman, as the case may be, and his resignation is accepted by the Speaker or the Chairman, as the case may be,
his seat shall thereupon become vacant:
Provided that in the case of any resignation referred to in sub-clause (b), if from information received or otherwise and after making such inquiry as he thinks fit, the Speaker or the Chairman, as the case may be, is satisfied that such resignation is not voluntary or genuine, he shall not accept such resignation.
(4) If for a period of sixty days a member of a House of the Legislature of a State is without permission of the House absent from all meetings thereof, the House may declare his seat vacant:
Provided that in computing the said period of sixty days no account shall be taken of any period during which the House is prorogued or is adjourned for more than four consecutive days.
key_terms: bar on dual-House membership within one State
bar on membership across multiple States' Legislatures
