sections.raw_text: Every High Court shall be a court of record and shall have all the powers of such a court including the power to punish for contempt of itself.
key_terms: High Court as a court of record
High Court's contempt-of-itself punishment power

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 215 is the High Court's precise counterpart to Article 129's Supreme Court guarantee, declaring every High Court a 'court of record' — meaning its proceedings and judgments are authoritatively recorded and admitted as evidence without further proof, and its decisions carry precedential weight within its jurisdiction. This status inherently includes the power to punish for contempt of itself, an essential self-protective power ensuring the Court's authority and the administration of justice within its jurisdiction cannot be undermined by defiance or scandalising conduct.
essential_elements: Every High Court is constitutionally a court of record — its records are authoritative and self-proving.
This status carries with it the inherent power to punish for contempt of itself, without needing separate statutory conferral.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The contempt power is constitutionally inherent (not statutorily conferred), but its actual exercise is procedurally regulated by the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, which prescribes procedure, defences (including truth as a valid defence in the public interest, added by a 2006 amendment), and punishment limits — the Act channels the power's exercise without being its constitutional source.

'Court of record' status fixes only the High Court's evidentiary/precedential standing, not its substantive jurisdiction — a High Court's actual subject-matter and territorial jurisdiction is separately defined by other Articles and statutes, and is not enlarged by Article 215 itself.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 215 as Article 129's precise High-Court-level mirror — like the Supreme Court's contempt power, this is a constitutionally inherent power, not one merely granted by ordinary legislation (though the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 regulates its exercise procedurally).

sections.title: Constitution of High Courts
sections.raw_text: Every High Court shall consist of a Chief Justice and such other Judges as the President may from time to time deem it necessary to appoint.
key_terms: Chief Justice plus President-determined additional Judges (High Court composition)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 216 is the High Court's counterpart to Article 124(1) (Supreme Court composition), leaving a High Court's exact strength deliberately flexible: every High Court has a Chief Justice, plus as many other Judges as the President, from time to time, deems necessary to appoint. This flexibility lets the Union executive scale each High Court's Judge strength to its actual and evolving caseload without needing a constitutional amendment for every adjustment — unlike the Supreme Court, whose Judge count is fixed by Parliamentary law under Article 124(1), a High Court's sanctioned strength is set by executive determination.
essential_elements: Every High Court has a Chief Justice as a constitutional minimum.
The number of additional (puisne) Judges is determined by the President from time to time, based on need — not fixed by any Article or Parliamentary law the way the Supreme Court's strength is.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'other Judges' contemplated here are permanent Judges; additional and acting Judges appointed to meet temporary increases in business or arrears of work are separately provided for under Article 224, and do not count toward the permanent sanctioned strength fixed under this Article.

Though the President formally determines the number of Judges, this determination is in practice an executive administrative exercise made on the Union Government's assessment of a High Court's workload (typically following the recommendation of the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned) — not an unfettered personal discretion.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 216 as the High Court's answer to the Supreme Court's composition Article, but note the structural difference: High Court strength is executively flexible (President's determination), whereas Supreme Court strength is fixed by Parliamentary law under Article 124(1) — a deliberate design choice reflecting the more variable, State-specific caseload pressures High Courts face.

sections.title: Appointment and conditions of the office of a Judge of a High Court
key_terms: High Court Judge's appointment by President's warrant after consultation
sixty-two-year retirement age (High Court Judges)
Judge's voluntary resignation by writing to President
removal via Article 124(4) impeachment procedure (High Court Judges)
office vacation on Supreme Court elevation or inter-High-Court transfer
ten-year judicial office or ten-year High Court advocate qualification
Explanation-inclusive service-period computation rules
President's final age-dispute determination after CJI consultation
NJAC amendment struck down — collegium consultation practice restored

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 217 is the High Court's counterpart to Articles 124(2)/(4) combined, governing appointment, tenure, and removal of High Court Judges. Appointment is by Presidential warrant after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the State Governor, and (for puisne Judges) the High Court's own Chief Justice — the 2014 Ninety-ninth Amendment's attempt to replace this consultative process with a National Judicial Appointments Commission was struck down by the Supreme Court in October 2015 as unconstitutional, so the original collegium-consultation process remains operative in practice. A regular Judge holds office until 62 (raised from 60 by the Fifteenth Amendment, 1963), while additional/acting Judges' tenure is separately governed by Article 224. Removal follows the identical rigorous Article 124(4) Supreme-Court-Judge impeachment procedure. Eligibility requires Indian citizenship plus either ten years as a judicial officer or ten years as a High Court advocate, with generous Explanation-based rules crediting mixed judicial/advocate/tribunal service and pre-Independence service toward these thresholds.
essential_elements: Clause (1): appointment by Presidential warrant after the CJI/Governor/Chief-Justice-of-the-High-Court consultation (the NJAC's attempted replacement of this was struck down); tenure until 62 for regular Judges (Article 224 governs additional/acting Judges separately).
Provisos (a)-(c): resignation by writing to the President; removal only via the Article 124(4) procedure; automatic vacation on Supreme Court elevation or inter-High-Court transfer.
Clause (2): the alternative ten-year judicial-office or ten-year High-Court-advocate eligibility tracks, open only to Indian citizens.

Explanation (a)/(aa)/(b): generous service-computation rules letting mixed judicial/advocate/tribunal/special-legal-knowledge service, and pre-15-August-1947 service in comparable roles, count toward the ten-year thresholds.
Clause (3): any age dispute about a sitting Judge is finally decided by the President after CJI consultation.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 2014 Ninety-ninth Amendment's NJAC-based appointment mechanism, though textually substituted into clause (1), was struck down by the Supreme Court in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) — the pre-amendment consultative process (with the judiciary's collegium exercising primacy per subsequent case law) governs appointments in actual practice despite the amendment's text remaining formally on the books.

Clause (2)(c) — a 42nd Amendment (1976) insertion adding a residual Parliamentary-law eligibility ground — was itself omitted by the 44th Amendment (1978) and does not currently form part of the operative eligibility criteria.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 217 as the High-Court-level counterpart to Article 124(2) and (4) combined — always flag the NJAC/collegium history explicitly, since the Article's literal text and the operative constitutional practice currently diverge due to the 2015 Supreme Court ruling.

sections.title: Application of certain provisions relating to Supreme Court to High Courts
sections.raw_text: The provisions of clauses (4) and (5) of article 124 shall apply in relation to a High Court as they apply in relation to the Supreme Court with the substitution of references to the High Court for references to the Supreme Court.
key_terms: Article 124(4)/(5) removal procedure extended to High Court Judges

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 218 is a short cross-referencing Article that avoids restating the entire Judge-removal machinery a second time: it simply extends Article 124(4) (the special-majority Parliamentary address procedure for removing a Judge on proved misbehaviour or incapacity) and Article 124(5) (Parliament's power to regulate the investigation/proof procedure by law) to High Court Judges, with 'High Court' substituted wherever 'Supreme Court' appears. This is why Article 217(1) proviso (b) can simply say a High Court Judge is removed 'in the manner provided in clause (4) of article 124' — Article 218 is what makes that cross-reference textually complete and operative.
essential_elements: Article 124(4)'s special-majority Parliamentary address procedure for removing a Judge on proved misbehaviour or incapacity applies to High Court Judges exactly as it applies to Supreme Court Judges.
Article 124(5)'s power for Parliament to regulate by law the procedure for presentation of the address and investigation/proof of misbehaviour or incapacity likewise applies to High Court Judges.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article only imports clauses (4) and (5) of Article 124 — not the whole of Article 124; the High Court Judge appointment process, retirement age, and other conditions of service are separately and specifically governed by Article 217, not by cross-reference to Article 124's other clauses.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 218 as a pure drafting-economy cross-reference Article — always trace it back to Article 124(4)/(5) to see the actual substantive removal procedure text, and read it together with Article 217(1) proviso (b), which is what actually triggers this Article's application in the context of a specific High Court Judge's removal.

sections.title: Oath or affirmation by Judges of High Courts
sections.raw_text: Every person appointed to be a Judge of a High Court shall, before he enters upon his office, make and subscribe before the Governor of the State, or some person appointed in that behalf by him, an oath or affirmation according to the form set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule.
key_terms: Judge's oath before Governor per Third Schedule form

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 219 is the High Court's counterpart to Article 124(6), requiring every newly appointed High Court Judge to make and subscribe an oath or affirmation, in the precise form set out in the Third Schedule, before entering upon office. Unlike a Supreme Court Judge (who takes the oath before the President or a person appointed by the President), a High Court Judge takes the oath before the State Governor, or a person the Governor appoints for that purpose — reflecting the High Court's institutional placement within State-level constitutional machinery even though it remains part of the single unified national judiciary.
essential_elements: The oath/affirmation must be made and subscribed before entering upon office — it is a precondition to validly functioning as a Judge, not a mere formality performed afterward.
It must be administered by the Governor of the State (or the Governor's appointee) — not the President, in contrast to the Supreme Court Judge's oath under Article 124(6).
The oath's content must follow the exact form prescribed in the Third Schedule — there is no discretion to vary its wording.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The oath is administered by the Governor or the Governor's appointee, not by the Chief Justice of the High Court or the Chief Justice of India — the Governor's involvement here is a formal, ministerial act distinct from the Governor's substantive consultative role in the Judge's appointment under Article 217(1).
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 219 as Article 124(6)'s precise High-Court-level mirror, with the one structural substitution worth remembering: the oath-administering authority is the State Governor, not the President — always cross-read the Third Schedule itself to see the oath's actual prescribed wording.

sections.title: Restriction on practice after being a permanent Judge
sections.raw_text:
No person who, after the commencement of this Constitution, has held office as a permanent Judge of a High Court shall plead or act in any court or before any authority in India except the Supreme Court and the other High Courts.
Explanation.—In this article, the expression "High Court" does not include a High Court for a State specified in Part B of the First Schedule as it existed before the commencement of the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956.
key_terms: post-retirement practice ban on former permanent High Court Judges
Part-B-State High Court exclusion from Article 220's practice ban

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 220 imposes a post-retirement practice restriction unique to High Court Judges, with no Supreme Court equivalent (a retired Supreme Court Judge faces no comparable constitutional bar on legal practice): a person who has held office as a permanent Judge of a High Court is barred for life from pleading or acting in any court or before any authority in India, except the Supreme Court itself and other High Courts. This prevents a retired High Court Judge from practising before the very High Court (or its subordinate courts) where his own former colleagues and successors sit, guarding against the appearance of undue influence, while still permitting appearance before the Supreme Court and sister High Courts where no such familiarity concern arises.
essential_elements: The bar applies only to a person who held office as a permanent Judge of a High Court — additional or acting Judges are not automatically covered by this specific Article's express language (though other rules of professional conduct may separately apply to them).
The bar is total as to ordinary courts/authorities in India generally, but expressly carved out for the Supreme Court and the other High Courts, where the retired Judge may plead or act freely.
The restriction is lifelong and applies to any court or authority in India, not merely the specific High Court the person served on.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Explanation excludes from the definition of 'High Court' (for this Article's purposes only) a High Court for a State specified in Part B of the First Schedule as that Schedule existed before the Seventh Amendment Act, 1956 — a transitional, now largely historical carve-out tied to the pre-1956 Part A/Part B/Part C State classification abolished by the States Reorganisation Act.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 220 as a distinctive High-Court-specific post-retirement integrity safeguard with no Supreme Court parallel — the key operative distinction to hold onto is the permanent-Judge-only scope and the Supreme-Court-and-other-High-Courts carve-out; the Part B State Explanation is chiefly of historical interest today.

sections.title: Salaries, etc., of Judges
sections.raw_text:
(1) There shall be paid to the Judges of each High Court such salaries as may be determined by Parliament by law and, until provision in that behalf is so made, such salaries as are specified in the Second Schedule.
(2) Every Judge shall be entitled to such allowances and to such rights in respect of leave of absence and pension as may from time to time be determined by or under law made by Parliament and, until so determined, to such allowances and rights as are specified in the Second Schedule:
Provided that neither the allowances of a Judge nor his rights in respect to leave of absence or pension shall be varied to his disadvantage after his appointment.
key_terms: Parliament-law-determined High Court Judge salaries (Second Schedule default)
no-disadvantage protection for Judge's allowances/leave/pension

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 221 is the High Court's counterpart to Article 125, fixing Judges' salaries by Parliamentary law (defaulting to the Second Schedule's figures until Parliament legislates) and likewise letting Parliament determine allowances, leave, and pension rights by law (again defaulting to the Second Schedule). Clause (1) was substituted by the Fifty-fourth Amendment Act, 1986 to let Parliament revise salaries by ordinary law rather than needing a constitutional amendment each time. The proviso to clause (2) carries over the same disadvantage-protection safeguard found in Article 125 — a sitting Judge's allowances, leave, or pension rights cannot be reduced to his disadvantage after his appointment, insulating judicial remuneration from post-appointment political pressure.
essential_elements: Salaries are fixed by Parliamentary law, defaulting to the Second Schedule's specified figures absent such law.
Allowances, leave-of-absence rights, and pension rights are likewise Parliament-law-determined, with the same Second Schedule default.
The proviso bars any disadvantageous variation of a Judge's allowances or leave/pension rights after his appointment — a protection that does not extend to salary itself under this Article's text.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The disadvantage-protection proviso textually covers only allowances and leave/pension rights, not salary itself — though in practice, salary changes enacted by Parliament have generally been upward revisions, so this textual asymmetry has rarely been tested.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 221 as Article 125's precise High-Court-level mirror — always check whether Parliament has in fact legislated current salary/allowance figures (it regularly has, via High Court and Supreme Court Judges (Salaries and Conditions of Service) Acts) rather than relying on the Second Schedule's default figures, which are frequently superseded.

sections.title: Transfer of a Judge from one High Court to another
sections.raw_text:
(1) The President may, on the recommendation of the National Judicial Appointments Commission referred to in article 124A, transfer a Judge from one High Court to any other High Court.
(2) When a Judge has been or is so transferred, he shall, during the period he serves, after the commencement of the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963, as a Judge of the other High Court, be entitled to receive in addition to his salary such compensatory allowance as may be determined by Parliament by law and, until so determined, such compensatory allowance as the President may by order fix.
key_terms: President's power to transfer a Judge between High Courts
compensatory allowance for transferred Judges

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 222 lets the President transfer a sitting Judge from one High Court to any other High Court — a power distinct from, and additional to, the automatic office-vacation-on-transfer rule in Article 217(1) proviso (c) (that proviso addresses the consequence for the vacated office; this Article is the source of the transfer power itself). The 2014 Ninety-ninth Amendment substituted 'on the recommendation of the National Judicial Appointments Commission' for the original 'after consultation with the Chief Justice of India,' but since the NJAC amendment was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015, the pre-amendment CJI-consultation practice (with collegium primacy per subsequent case law) governs transfers in actual operation today, exactly as with Article 217(1) appointments. Clause (2), inserted by the Fifteenth Amendment (1963), compensates a transferred Judge with a compensatory allowance — recognising that an inter-State transfer typically involves real personal and financial disruption — determined by Parliament by law or, absent such law, fixed by Presidential order.
essential_elements: The President holds the power to transfer a Judge from one High Court to any other High Court in India.
A transferred Judge is entitled to a compensatory allowance in addition to his ordinary salary, determined by Parliament by law or, absent such law, fixed by Presidential order.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 2014 Ninety-ninth Amendment's NJAC-recommendation requirement, though textually substituted into clause (1), was struck down by the Supreme Court in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) — the original CJI-consultation process (with collegium primacy) governs transfers in practice, exactly as with Article 217(1) appointments, despite the amended text remaining formally on the books.

This Article is distinct from Article 217(1) proviso (c): that proviso addresses the vacation of the Judge's original office upon transfer, while this Article is the actual source of the President's power to order the transfer in the first place.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 222 alongside Article 217(1) proviso (c) (the consequence of transfer) and Article 217's NJAC/collegium history (the same 2015 strike-down governs how transfers are actually decided today, regardless of this Article's amended text) — the compensatory allowance in clause (2) is a distinct, purely financial protection worth remembering separately.

sections.title: Appointment of acting Chief Justice
sections.raw_text: When the office of Chief Justice of a High Court is vacant or when any such Chief Justice is, by reason of absence or otherwise, unable to perform the duties of his office, the duties of the office shall be performed by such one of the other Judges of the Court as the President may appoint for the purpose.
key_terms: President's appointment of acting Chief Justice

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 223 is the High Court's counterpart to Article 126, ensuring a High Court is never left without someone performing the Chief Justice's duties — whether because the office is genuinely vacant or because the sitting Chief Justice is temporarily unable to act (absence, illness, or other cause). The President appoints one of the High Court's own other Judges to perform those duties in the interim, keeping the Court's essential administrative and judicial leadership functions running without interruption.
essential_elements: Triggered either by a genuine vacancy in the office of Chief Justice, or by the sitting Chief Justice's temporary inability to perform his duties (for any reason, including absence).
The President appoints one of the High Court's own existing Judges (not an outsider) to perform the Chief Justice's duties on an acting basis.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a duties-performing arrangement, not a substantive appointment to the office of Chief Justice itself — the appointed Judge performs the Chief Justice's duties without necessarily being formally appointed Chief Justice under Article 217(1)'s regular process.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 223 as Article 126's precise High-Court-level mirror — a short stopgap-continuity provision, best remembered alongside Article 224's additional/acting Judge provisions as part of the Constitution's toolkit for keeping a High Court's bench fully functional despite vacancies or temporary absences.

sections.title: Appointment of additional and acting Judges
sections.raw_text:
(1) If by reason of any temporary increase in the business of a High Court or by reason of arrears of work therein, it appears to the President that the number of the Judges of that Court should be for the time being increased, the President may, in consultation with the National Judicial Appointments Commission, appoint duly qualified persons to be additional Judges of the Court for such period not exceeding two years as he may specify.
(2) When any Judge of a High Court other than the Chief Justice is by reason of absence or for any other reason unable to perform the duties of his office or is appointed to act temporarily as Chief Justice, the President may, in consultation with the National Judicial Appointments Commission, appoint a duly qualified person to act as a Judge of that Court until the permanent Judge has resumed his duties.
(3) No person appointed as an additional or acting Judge of a High Court shall hold office after attaining the age of sixty-two years.
key_terms: additional Judges for temporary High Court caseload increase
acting Judge appointment during Chief Justice/Judge absence
sixty-two-year cap for additional/acting Judges

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 224 lets the President appoint two categories of non-permanent Judges to a High Court, each addressing a distinct operational need. Additional Judges (clause (1)) address a temporary increase in business or arrears of work, appointed for a fixed period not exceeding two years — a flexible tool for surging a High Court's capacity without permanently enlarging its sanctioned strength under Article 216. Acting Judges (clause (2)) fill in for a specific Judge (other than the Chief Justice) who is temporarily unable to perform his duties, or who has himself been appointed to act temporarily as Chief Justice under Article 223 — serving only until the permanent Judge resumes duties. Both categories are capped by the same sixty-two-year retirement age applicable to regular Judges under Article 217(1). As with Articles 217(1) and 222, the 2014 NJAC amendment's consultation mechanism was struck down in 2015, so the pre-amendment consultative practice governs these appointments in operation.
essential_elements: Clause (1): additional Judges are appointed for a fixed term not exceeding two years, specifically to address temporary business increases or arrears — not to permanently expand the Court's sanctioned strength.

Clause (2): acting Judges are appointed to substitute for a specific Judge (other than the Chief Justice) who is temporarily unable to act, or who is himself acting temporarily as Chief Justice — service ends when the permanent Judge resumes duties.
Clause (3): both additional and acting Judges are subject to the same sixty-two-year age cap as regular Judges, and cannot hold office past that age regardless of their appointment term.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 2014 Ninety-ninth Amendment's NJAC-consultation requirement in clauses (1) and (2), though textually substituted into the Article, was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015 along with the rest of the NJAC scheme — the pre-amendment consultative practice (collegium-based) governs these appointments in actual operation.

An additional or acting Judge appointed under this Article is distinct from a permanent Judge appointed under Article 217(1) — this distinction matters for eligibility computations (Article 217(2) Explanation), for the post-retirement practice restriction (Article 220, which textually addresses permanent Judges), and for tenure security generally.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 224 as the operational flexibility counterpart to Article 216's fixed-strength composition and Article 217's permanent-Judge appointment process — remember the two-year cap on additional Judges, the resumption-of-duties trigger for acting Judges ending, the shared sixty-two-year ceiling, and the same NJAC/collegium historical divergence that runs through Articles 217, 222, and this Article alike.

sections.title: Appointment of retired Judges at sittings of High Courts
sections.raw_text:
Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, the National Judicial Appointments Commission on a reference made to it by the Chief Justice of a High Court for any State, may with the previous consent of the President, request any person who has held the office of a Judge of that Court or of any other High Court to sit and act as a Judge of the High Court for that State, and every such person so requested shall, while so sitting and acting, be entitled to such allowances as the President may by order determine and have all the jurisdiction, powers and privileges of, but shall not otherwise be deemed to be, a Judge of that High Court:
Provided that nothing in this article shall be deemed to require any such person as aforesaid to sit and act as a Judge of that High Court unless he consents so to do.
key_terms: recall of retired Judges to sit and act in High Courts
retired Judge's consent precondition for recall

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 224A, inserted by the Fifteenth Amendment (1963), is a further caseload-management tool distinct from both Article 224's additional/acting Judges and Article 128's Supreme Court equivalent: it lets a retired Judge (of that High Court or any other High Court) be requested to sit and act as a Judge again, notwithstanding anything else in this Chapter. While so sitting, the retired Judge has all the jurisdiction, powers, and privileges of a regular Judge of that High Court, drawing allowances the President determines by order, but is not otherwise deemed to actually be a Judge of that Court (e.g., for purposes like seniority or the sanctioned strength under Article 216). The overriding safeguard is the proviso: no retired Judge can be compelled to accept the request — the recall is entirely consent-based, respecting the individual's post-retirement autonomy.
essential_elements: The recall targets specifically a retired Judge — someone who has already held office as a Judge of that High Court or of any other High Court, not a fresh appointee.
While sitting and acting under a recall, the retired Judge has the full jurisdiction, powers, and privileges of a regular Judge of that High Court, and receives Presidentially-determined allowances.

The recalled Judge is not otherwise deemed to be a Judge of that Court — the recall confers functional judicial authority for the sitting without converting the person into a permanent or additional Judge for other constitutional purposes.
The proviso makes the recall entirely voluntary: the retired Judge's consent is an absolute precondition, and nothing in this Article can compel him to sit and act.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The recall mechanism, as originally enacted, operated on the Chief Justice of the High Court's own reference with the President's previous consent; the 2014 Ninety-ninth Amendment substituted a National Judicial Appointments Commission reference-and-consent mechanism, which — like the rest of the NJAC scheme — was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015, restoring the original Chief-Justice-of-the-High-Court-reference practice in operation.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 224A as a distinctly consent-gated recall mechanism — the opening 'notwithstanding anything in this Chapter' signals it operates as a standalone override, and the proviso's voluntariness requirement is the single most important operative safeguard to remember; the same NJAC/collegium historical divergence documented under Articles 217, 222, and 224 applies here too.

sections.title: Jurisdiction of existing High Courts
sections.raw_text:
Subject to the provisions of this Constitution and to the provisions of any law of the appropriate Legislature made by virtue of powers conferred on that Legislature by this Constitution, the jurisdiction of, and the law administered in, any existing High Court, and the respective powers of the Judges thereof in relation to the administration of justice in the Court, including any power to make rules of Court and to regulate the sittings of the Court and of members thereof sitting alone or in Division Courts, shall be the same as immediately before the commencement of this Constitution:
Provided that any restriction to which the exercise of original jurisdiction by any of the High Courts with respect to any matter concerning the revenue or concerning any act ordered or done in the collection thereof was subject immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall no longer apply to the exercise of such jurisdiction.
key_terms: continuity of existing High Court jurisdiction post-Constitution
removal of pre-Constitution revenue-jurisdiction restrictions

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 225 is a continuity provision preventing a jurisdictional vacuum at the Constitution's commencement: rather than re-legislating every existing High Court's jurisdiction, administered law, and Judges' administrative powers (including rule-making and sitting arrangements, whether sitting alone or in Division Courts) from scratch, it simply carries forward whatever existed immediately before the Constitution commenced — subject to the Constitution itself and to competent legislation made under it. The proviso makes one deliberate substantive change on top of that continuity baseline: any pre-Constitution restriction on a High Court's original jurisdiction over revenue matters or revenue-collection acts is abolished, reflecting the framers' view that colonial-era revenue-jurisdiction limitations had no place in the new constitutional order.
essential_elements: An existing High Court's jurisdiction, administered law, and Judges' administrative/rule-making powers continue unchanged from immediately before the Constitution's commencement.

This continuity is expressly subject to the Constitution's own provisions and to any law validly made by a competent Legislature under constitutional authority — it is a default baseline, not an entrenched immunity from change.
The proviso abolishes, going forward, any pre-Constitution restriction on a High Court's original jurisdiction concerning revenue matters or revenue-collection acts.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article addresses only jurisdiction, administered law, and judicial administrative powers as they existed pre-Constitution — it does not itself confer any new powers (such as the Article 226 writ power, which is a fresh constitutional grant, not a continuation of pre-existing jurisdiction).
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 225 as a housekeeping continuity Article establishing the jurisdictional baseline from which the Constitution's other High Court Articles (226, 227, 228) then add fresh, constitutionally original powers — the revenue-jurisdiction proviso is its one substantive change, not a mere continuity statement.

sections.title: Power of High Courts to issue certain writs
sections.raw_text:
(1) Notwithstanding anything in article 32, every High Court shall have power, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction, to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases, any Government, within those territories directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose.
(2) The power conferred by clause (1) to issue directions, orders or writs to any Government, authority or person may also be exercised by any High Court exercising jurisdiction in relation to the territories within which the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises for the exercise of such power, notwithstanding that the seat of such Government or authority or the residence of such person is not within those territories.
(3) Where any party against whom an interim order, whether by way of injunction or stay or in any other manner, is made on, or in any proceedings relating to, a petition under clause (1), without—
(a) furnishing to such party copies of such petition and all documents in support of the plea for such interim order; and
(b) giving such party an opportunity of being heard,
makes an application to the High Court for the vacation of such order and furnishes a copy of such application to the party in whose favour such order has been made or the counsel of such party, the High Court shall dispose of the application within a period of two weeks from the date on which it is received or from the date on which the copy of such application is so furnished, whichever is later, or where the High Court is closed on the last day of that period, before the expiry of the next day afterwards on which the High Court is open; and if the application is not so disposed of, the interim order shall, on the expiry of that period, or, as the case may be, the expiry of the said next day, stand vacated.
(4) The power conferred on a High Court by this article shall not be in derogation of the power conferred on the Supreme Court by clause (2) of article 32.
key_terms: High Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 226
Article 226 writs for 'any other purpose' beyond Part III rights
cause-of-action-based territorial writ jurisdiction
two-week interim-order vacation hearing rule
Article 226 not in derogation of Supreme Court's Article 32(2) power

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 226 is, in practical litigation terms, India's single most heavily invoked constitutional provision — it empowers every High Court to issue the five prerogative writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, certiorari) or any other direction/order, both to enforce Part III Fundamental Rights and, distinctively, 'for any other purpose' — a phrase with no Article 32 equivalent that lets a High Court issue writs for enforcing ordinary legal rights and correcting jurisdictional/legal errors by any person, authority, or Government, not just Fundamental Rights violations. This makes Article 226 jurisdiction textually wider than Article 32's, even though Article 32 alone is itself a Fundamental Right guaranteeing direct Supreme Court access. Clause (2) lets a High Court exercise this power based on where the cause of action arises, not just where the respondent is seated or resides — a deliberate access-to-justice expansion. Clause (3), inserted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978 in reaction to Emergency-era interim-order abuses, imposes a strict two-week timeline for disposing of a vacation application against an ex parte interim order, automatically vacating the order if the deadline is missed. Clause (4) confirms this power supplements, rather than derogates from, the Supreme Court's parallel Article 32(2) writ power.
essential_elements: Clause (1): every High Court may issue directions, orders, or writs (including the five named prerogative writs) to any person, authority, or Government within its territorial jurisdiction, both to enforce Part III rights and for any other legal purpose — a textually broader mandate than Article 32.

Clause (2): territorial jurisdiction to issue such writs extends to any High Court within whose territory the cause of action wholly or partly arises, even if the respondent's seat or residence lies elsewhere.

Clause (3): a strict two-week (or next-court-working-day) deadline for disposing of an application to vacate an ex parte interim order, with automatic vacation of the order if the deadline is missed — a procedural check against indefinite unchallenged interim relief.
Clause (4): Article 226 operates alongside, not in derogation of, the Supreme Court's own Article 32(2) writ power — the two are concurrent, not mutually exclusive, jurisdictions.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The original 1950 Article 226 was substantially curtailed by the Forty-second Amendment (1976) — which limited writs to the enforcement of Fundamental Rights alone and added several restrictive conditions — but this curtailment was itself reversed by the Forty-fourth Amendment (1978), which restored the broader 'enforcement of Part III rights and for any other purpose' formulation seen in the current text.

A short-lived Article 226A ('Constitutional validity of Central laws not to be considered in proceedings under article 226'), inserted by the Forty-second Amendment (1976), was omitted by the Forty-third Amendment (1977) and does not currently form part of the Constitution's text.

Despite Article 226's textually wider 'any other purpose' scope, courts have developed the discretionary and self-imposed rule that ordinarily an alternative statutory remedy should be exhausted first — Article 226 relief is discretionary, not a matter of right, unlike (in principle) Article 32's Fundamental Right status.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 226 as the practical engine of most Indian administrative-law and constitutional litigation — always note the 'any other purpose' clause's textually wider scope than Article 32, the cause-of-action territorial rule in clause (2), and the clause (3) interim-order-vacation timeline as a distinctly practitioner-relevant procedural safeguard against runaway ex parte orders.

sections.title: Power of superintendence over all courts by the High Court
sections.raw_text:
(1) Every High Court shall have superintendence over all courts and tribunals throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction.
(2) Without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing provision, the High Court may—
(a) call for returns from such courts;
(b) make and issue general rules and prescribe forms for regulating the practice and proceedings of such courts; and
(c) prescribe forms in which books, entries and accounts shall be kept by the officers of any such courts.
(3) The High Court may also settle tables of fees to be allowed to the sheriff and all clerks and officers of such courts and to attorneys, advocates and pleaders practising therein:
Provided that any rules made, forms prescribed or tables settled under clause (2) or clause (3) shall not be inconsistent with the provision of any law for the time being in force, and shall require the previous approval of the Governor.
(4) Nothing in this article shall be deemed to confer on a High Court powers of superintendence over any court or tribunal constituted by or under any law relating to the Armed Forces.
key_terms: High Court's power of superintendence over subordinate courts/tribunals
Governor's previous-approval requirement for HC superintendence rules
Armed Forces tribunal exclusion from HC superintendence

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 227 gives every High Court general administrative and judicial superintendence over all courts and tribunals within its territorial jurisdiction — a power distinct from, and broader in kind than, Article 226's writ jurisdiction: while Article 226 is exercised case-by-case in response to a specific petition, Article 227 superintendence includes systemic administrative oversight (calling for returns, issuing general practice/procedure rules, prescribing record-keeping forms, and settling court-officer fee schedules) as well as judicial correction of subordinate courts' and tribunals' errors. Clause (2)'s list is expressly non-exhaustive ('without prejudice to the generality'), confirming clause (1)'s general superintendence power is the true source of authority, with clause (2) merely illustrating specific instances. The proviso requires the Governor's previous approval for any rules, forms, or fee tables made under clauses (2)-(3), and clause (4) carves out courts/tribunals constituted under Armed Forces law entirely from this Article's reach.
essential_elements: Clause (1): general, broad superintendence over all courts and tribunals within the High Court's territorial jurisdiction — the foundational grant, not limited to the illustrative powers listed afterward.
Clause (2): specific (non-exhaustive) administrative powers — calling for returns, making general practice/procedure rules, and prescribing record-keeping forms.
Clause (3): power to settle fee tables for court officers, sheriffs, clerks, and practising legal professionals.
Clause (4): courts/tribunals constituted under Armed Forces law are entirely excluded from the High Court's superintendence under this Article.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Any rules made, forms prescribed, or fee tables settled under clauses (2) or (3) must be consistent with existing law and require the Governor's previous approval — the High Court's rule-making power here is not unilateral.

Superintendence over tribunals specifically (as opposed to courts) is a comparatively later and judicially significant extension — clause (1)'s original 1950 text was substituted by the Forty-second Amendment (1976) and further refined by the Forty-fourth Amendment (1978) to arrive at the current 'courts and tribunals' formulation, reflecting the growing importance of the tribunal system in Indian administrative adjudication.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 227 as the administrative/supervisory counterpart to Article 226's case-specific writ power — remember that clause (1)'s general superintendence, not the clause (2) list, is the true source of authority, and that superintendence exercised judicially (correcting jurisdictional errors of subordinate courts/tribunals) is narrower in scope than ordinary appellate review, a distinction courts have repeatedly emphasised to prevent Article 227 from becoming a backdoor substitute for appeal.

sections.title: Transfer of certain cases to High Court
sections.raw_text:
If the High Court is satisfied that a case pending in a court subordinate to it involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution the determination of which is necessary for the disposal of the case, it shall withdraw the case and may—
(a) either dispose of the case itself, or
(b) determine the said question of law and return the case to the court from which the case has been so withdrawn together with a copy of its judgment on such question, and the said court shall on receipt thereof proceed to dispose of the case in conformity with such judgment.
key_terms: mandatory case withdrawal for substantial constitutional-interpretation questions

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 228 ensures that genuinely significant constitutional-interpretation questions arising in a subordinate court are resolved at the High Court level rather than left to a lower court's determination: once the High Court is satisfied that a pending subordinate-court case involves a substantial question of law about the Constitution's interpretation whose determination is necessary to dispose of the case, withdrawal is mandatory ('it shall withdraw the case'), not discretionary. After withdrawal, the High Court has a genuine choice on disposal method — it may either decide the whole case itself, or confine itself to determining just the constitutional question and remit the rest of the case back to the subordinate court, which must then dispose of the case in conformity with the High Court's ruling on that question.
essential_elements: Withdrawal is triggered only where the case involves a substantial question of law on constitutional interpretation, and that determination is necessary for disposing of the case — not any incidental or trivial constitutional point.
Once that threshold is satisfied, withdrawal is mandatory on the High Court ('shall withdraw'), removing the case entirely from the subordinate court's hands at that stage.

After withdrawal, the High Court chooses between two disposal paths: deciding the entire case itself, or deciding only the constitutional question and remitting the remainder to the subordinate court, which is then bound to follow that determination.
exceptions_and_qualifications: A related Article 228A ('Special provisions as to disposal of questions relating to constitutional validity of State laws'), inserted by the Forty-second Amendment (1976), was omitted by the Forty-third Amendment (1977) and does not currently form part of the Constitution's operative text.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 228 as ensuring genuine constitutional questions get decided at the High Court level rather than by a subordinate court, and note carefully the mandatory-withdrawal-but-discretionary-disposal-method structure — the High Court cannot decline to withdraw a qualifying case, but retains full choice over whether to decide the whole matter itself or send it back after ruling only on the constitutional point.

sections.title: Officers and servants and the expenses of High Courts
sections.raw_text:
(1) Appointments of officers and servants of a High Court shall be made by the Chief Justice of the Court or such other Judge or officer of the Court as he may direct:
Provided that the Governor of the State may by rule require that in such cases as may be specified in the rule no person not already attached to the Court shall be appointed to any office connected with the Court save after consultation with the State Public Service Commission.
(2) Subject to the provisions of any law made by the Legislature of the State, the conditions of service of officers and servants of a High Court shall be such as may be prescribed by rules made by the Chief Justice of the Court or by some other Judge or officer of the Court authorised by the Chief Justice to make rules for the purpose:
Provided that the rules made under this clause shall, so far as they relate to salaries, allowances, leave or pensions, require the approval of the Governor of the State.
(3) The administrative expenses of a High Court, including all salaries, allowances and pensions payable to or in respect of the officers and servants of the Court, shall be charged upon the Consolidated Fund of the State, and any fees or other moneys taken by the Court shall form part of that Fund.
key_terms: Chief Justice's power to appoint High Court officers/servants
Governor's rule-making for State Public Service Commission consultation on HC appointments
Governor's approval requirement for HC service-condition rules on pay/pension
High Court administrative expenses charged on State Consolidated Fund

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 229 secures a High Court's administrative and financial independence from the State executive in its day-to-day staffing and functioning — a structural safeguard for judicial independence at the institutional level, complementing the individual Judge-independence protections elsewhere in this Chapter. The Chief Justice (or a delegate) appoints the Court's own officers and servants, subject only to a Governor's rule specifically requiring State Public Service Commission consultation for outside appointments in specified cases. Service conditions are similarly Chief-Justice-rule-governed, subject to State legislation and (for pay/pension matters specifically) Governor approval. Clause (3) is the key financial-independence guarantee: the High Court's administrative expenses are charged directly upon the State's Consolidated Fund — meaning they are non-votable, not subject to the annual appropriation vote that ordinary government expenditure requires (paralleling Article 202(3)(d)'s charged-expenditure list, which includes High Court administrative expenses), insulating the Court's operational budget from potential legislative pressure.
essential_elements: Clause (1): the Chief Justice (or his delegate) has the primary power to appoint the Court's officers and servants, subject to a Governor's rule mandating State Public Service Commission consultation for specified outside appointments.

Clause (2): the Chief Justice (or an authorised delegate) makes rules governing officers'/servants' conditions of service, subject to State legislation generally and Governor approval specifically for pay/pension/leave/allowance rules.

Clause (3): all High Court administrative expenses (including officer/servant salaries, allowances, and pensions) are charged upon the State's Consolidated Fund, and any Court-collected fees/moneys likewise form part of that Fund.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Chief Justice's appointment and rule-making powers under clauses (1) and (2) are not unfettered — clause (1)'s proviso allows a Governor's rule requiring Public Service Commission consultation for specified outside appointments, and clause (2)'s proviso requires Governor approval specifically for salary/allowance/leave/pension rules, so the High Court's administrative autonomy operates within these defined checks rather than being absolute.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 229 as the institutional-independence counterpart to Articles 217/218's individual-Judge-independence provisions — the charged-upon-the-Consolidated-Fund rule in clause (3) is the single most practically important guarantee here, since it removes the High Court's own operating budget from the ordinary annual appropriation-vote process that Article 203 makes non-votable for other charged items.

sections.title: Extension of jurisdiction of High Courts to Union territories
sections.raw_text:
(1) Parliament may by law extend the jurisdiction of a High Court to, or exclude the jurisdiction of a High Court from, any Union territory.
(2) Where the High Court of a State exercises jurisdiction in relation to a Union territory,—
(a) nothing in this Constitution shall be construed as empowering the Legislature of the State to increase, restrict or abolish that jurisdiction; and
(b) the reference in article 227 to the Governor shall, in relation to any rules, forms or tables for subordinate courts in that territory, be construed as a reference to the President.
key_terms: Parliament's power to extend/exclude HC jurisdiction over Union territories
State Legislature's inability to alter HC's Union-territory jurisdiction
President substituted for Governor in Union-territory subordinate-court rules

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 230 addresses a structural gap: Union territories generally lack their own High Court, so this Article lets Parliament, by law, extend an existing State High Court's jurisdiction to cover a Union territory (or conversely exclude it) — this is how, for example, the Punjab and Haryana High Court's jurisdiction extends to Chandigarh, and the Bombay High Court's to certain Union territories. Because this jurisdiction flows from a Union-Parliament law rather than the State's own legislative authority, clause (2)(a) expressly bars the State Legislature from touching that Union-territory jurisdiction in any way (increase, restrict, or abolish) — keeping control over the Union territory link exclusively with Parliament. Clause (2)(b) makes a necessary substitution: since a Union territory typically has no Governor of its own, any Article 227 reference to 'the Governor' for subordinate-court rules/forms/tables in that territory is read instead as a reference to the President.
essential_elements: Clause (1): only Parliament, by law, can extend a High Court's jurisdiction to, or exclude it from, a Union territory — this is not something achievable by executive action or State legislation.

Clause (2)(a): once such jurisdiction exists, the State Legislature (of the State whose High Court is exercising the extended jurisdiction) has no power whatsoever to increase, restrict, or abolish it.

Clause (2)(b): for the purposes of Article 227's Governor-approval requirement over subordinate-court rules/forms/tables in that Union territory specifically, 'the Governor' is read as 'the President.'
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article deals only with extending/excluding an existing State High Court's jurisdiction over a Union territory — it is not the mechanism for creating a dedicated High Court for a Union territory (some larger Union territories, like Delhi, do have their own dedicated High Court established by separate legislation).
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 230 as the jurisdictional-bridge Article connecting State High Courts to Union territories lacking their own — the Governor-to-President substitution in clause (2)(b) is a small but easy-to-miss detail worth remembering whenever Article 227 issues arise in a Union-territory context.

sections.title: Establishment of a common High Court for two or more States
sections.raw_text:
(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the preceding provisions of this Chapter, Parliament may by law establish a common High Court for two or more States or for two or more States and a Union territory.
(2) In relation to any such High Court,—
(b) the reference in article 227 to the Governor shall, in relation to any rules, forms or tables for subordinate courts, be construed as a reference to the Governor of the State in which the subordinate courts are situate; and
(c) the references in articles 219 and 229 to the State shall be construed as a reference to the State in which the High Court has its principal seat:
Provided that if such principal seat is in a Union territory, the references in articles 219 and 229 to the Governor, Public Service Commission, Legislature and Consolidated Fund of the State shall be construed respectively as references to the President, Union Public Service Commission, Parliament and Consolidated Fund of India.
key_terms: Parliament's power to establish a common High Court for two or more States
principal-seat State substitution for Article 219/229 State references
Union-territory principal-seat substitution rule (President/UPSC/Parliament/CFI)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 231 is the express exception to Article 214's one-High-Court-per-State default, promised in that Article's own text: it lets Parliament, by law, establish a single common High Court serving two or more States (or States plus a Union territory) — the historical and continuing example being the Punjab and Haryana High Court, serving both Punjab and Haryana (and Chandigarh) from one common institution. Because a common High Court by definition spans multiple States, several other Articles' single-State references need interpretive substitution to function sensibly: clause (2)(b) reads Article 227's Governor-approval reference as the Governor of whichever State the specific subordinate court is actually situated in (not a single common Governor, since none exists for the joint High Court as such), while clause (2)(c) reads Article 219's and Article 229's 'the State' references as the State where the common High Court has its principal seat. The proviso further substitutes Union-level authorities (President, Union Public Service Commission, Parliament, Consolidated Fund of India) wherever that principal seat happens to be located in a Union territory rather than a State.
essential_elements: Clause (1): Parliament alone, by law, may establish a common High Court for two or more States or for two or more States plus a Union territory — overriding, notwithstanding, the Chapter's otherwise State-specific default structure.
Clause (2)(b): Article 227's Governor reference, for subordinate-court rules/forms/tables, is read State-by-State according to where the particular subordinate court is actually situated.
Clause (2)(c): Article 219's (oath) and Article 229's (officers/expenses) 'the State' references are read as the single State where the common High Court has its principal seat.

Proviso: if that principal seat is itself in a Union territory, the Article 219/229 references to Governor, Public Service Commission, Legislature, and State Consolidated Fund are substituted with President, Union Public Service Commission, Parliament, and Consolidated Fund of India respectively.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (2) originally had a sub-clause (a) reading Article 217's Governor reference as referring collectively to the Governors of all States the common High Court serves; this sub-clause was omitted by the 2014 Ninety-ninth Amendment as part of the broader NJAC restructuring, but since the NJAC amendment itself was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015, the pre-amendment position (treating Article 217 consultation as involving all relevant States' Governors for a common High Court) continues to reflect actual operative practice despite the amended text's formal omission.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 231 directly alongside Article 214 — this is the promised exception to the one-State-one-High-Court default, and the mechanical State-substitution rules in clause (2) and its proviso are essential whenever applying Articles 219, 227, or 229 to a common High Court like Punjab and Haryana's; also cross-read the NJAC/collegium historical divergence already familiar from Articles 217, 222, 224, and 224A, which recurs here for clause (2)(a).

sections.title: Appointment of district judges
sections.raw_text:
(1) Appointments of persons to be, and the posting and promotion of, district judges in any State shall be made by the Governor of the State in consultation with the High Court exercising jurisdiction in relation to such State.
(2) A person not already in the service of the Union or of the State shall only be eligible to be appointed a district judge if he has been for not less than seven years an advocate or a pleader and is recommended by the High Court for appointment.
key_terms: Governor's district judge appointment power via HC consultation
seven-year advocate/pleader eligibility plus HC recommendation (outside appointees)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 233 opens Chapter VI (Subordinate Courts), governing the apex tier of a State's subordinate judiciary — district judges. Appointment, posting, and promotion of district judges is a Governor's power, but never exercised unilaterally: it requires consultation with the High Court exercising jurisdiction over that State, reflecting the same judiciary-executive collaborative appointment model seen at the High Court level itself, adapted downward to the district judiciary. Clause (2) opens a direct entry route into the district judiciary for practising lawyers (as opposed to promotion from within the judicial service): a person not already in Union or State service can only be appointed a district judge after at least seven years as an advocate or pleader, and only on the High Court's recommendation — ensuring even direct-entry candidates are vetted by the judiciary itself, not appointed on executive discretion alone.
essential_elements: Clause (1): appointment, posting, and promotion of district judges is a Governor's power exercised in consultation with the relevant High Court — a mandatory consultative step, not a mere courtesy.

Clause (2): a person from outside Union/State service is eligible for direct appointment as a district judge only with at least seven years' standing as an advocate or pleader, and only if the High Court itself recommends the appointment.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (2)'s seven-year-advocate/High-Court-recommendation route applies specifically to persons not already in Union or State service — a person already within the judicial service (i.e., promoted internally) is not subject to this particular eligibility gateway, though internal promotion is separately regulated by service rules and Article 235's High Court control.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 233 as the foundational appointment provision for the district judiciary — always note the mandatory High Court consultation in clause (1) (echoing the judiciary-executive collaboration seen in Article 217) and the distinct direct-entry eligibility gateway in clause (2), which is a separate route from internal promotion within the judicial service.

sections.title: Validation of appointments of, and judgments, etc., delivered by, certain district judges
sections.raw_text:
Notwithstanding any judgment, decree or order of any court,—
(a) (i) no appointment of any person already in the judicial service of a State or of any person who has been for not less than seven years an advocate or a pleader, to be a district judge in that State, and
(ii) no posting, promotion or transfer of any such person as a district judge,
made at any time before the commencement of the Constitution (Twentieth Amendment) Act, 1966, otherwise than in accordance with the provisions of article 233 or article 235 shall be deemed to be illegal or void or ever to have become illegal or void by reason only of the fact that such appointment, posting, promotion or transfer was not made in accordance with the said provisions;
(b) no jurisdiction exercised, no judgment, decree, sentence or order passed or made, and no other act or proceeding done or taken, before the commencement of the Constitution (Twentieth Amendment) Act, 1966 by, or before, any person appointed, posted, promoted or transferred as a district judge in any State otherwise than in accordance with the provisions of article 233 or article 235 shall be deemed to be illegal or invalid or ever to have become illegal or invalid by reason only of the fact that such appointment, posting, promotion or transfer was not made in accordance with the said provisions.
key_terms: retrospective validation of pre-1966 district judge appointment irregularities

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 233A, inserted by the Twentieth Amendment Act, 1966, is a curative validation provision responding directly to a specific judicial crisis: the Supreme Court's decision in Chandra Mohan v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1966) had held certain district judge appointments made without following Article 233's consultation procedure to be constitutionally invalid, throwing into legal doubt not just those appointments but every judgment, order, and proceeding those judges had ever handled. Parliament responded with this retrospective validating Article: notwithstanding any court's contrary judgment, decree, or order, both the pre-1966 appointments/postings/promotions/transfers themselves (clause (a)) and every act of jurisdiction, judgment, decree, sentence, or proceeding those judges conducted (clause (b)) are deemed never to have been illegal or void purely on account of the Article 233/235 procedural non-compliance — protecting the enormous volume of litigation these judges had already decided from being reopened or invalidated wholesale.
essential_elements: Clause (a): retrospectively validates pre-Twentieth-Amendment (1966) district judge appointments, postings, promotions, and transfers that did not strictly follow Article 233 or Article 235's procedure — they are deemed never to have been illegal or void on that ground alone.

Clause (b): separately and additionally validates every judicial act — jurisdiction exercised, judgments, decrees, sentences, orders, and other proceedings — conducted by such improperly-appointed district judges before that same 1966 cutoff date.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This validation operates only for the specific procedural defect of Article 233/235 non-compliance and only for actions/appointments before the Constitution (Twentieth Amendment) Act, 1966's commencement — it is a historically bounded curative fix, not an open-ended or forward-looking immunity for future procedural irregularities.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 233A as a classic post-judgment legislative validation Article, directly traceable to the Supreme Court's Chandra Mohan ruling — a useful illustration for understanding how Parliament can retrospectively cure a specific class of procedural constitutional defects without amending the substantive rule (Article 233 itself) going forward.

sections.title: Recruitment of persons other than district judges to the judicial service
sections.raw_text: Appointments of persons other than district judges to the judicial service of a State shall be made by the Governor of the State in accordance with rules made by him in that behalf after consultation with the State Public Service Commission and with the High Court exercising jurisdiction in relation to such State.
key_terms: Governor's judicial service recruitment power via PSC and HC consultation

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 234 governs recruitment into the State judicial service below the district judge level — the entry-level civil judges who form the bulk of the subordinate judiciary. Unlike Article 233's ad hoc consultation for individual district judge appointments, Article 234 recruitment is rule-based: the Governor makes recruitment rules after consulting both the State Public Service Commission (the standard body for State civil service recruitment generally) and the relevant High Court (reflecting the judiciary's specific interest in who enters judicial service), and appointments are then made in accordance with those rules — typically through a competitive examination process (the Judicial Service Examination) conducted under High Court oversight in most States.
essential_elements: Covers recruitment of persons other than district judges — the entry-level tier of the State judicial service, distinct from Article 233's district-judge-specific appointment process.
Recruitment is rule-based: the Governor first makes rules after consulting both the State Public Service Commission and the relevant High Court, and then appointments follow those rules.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article addresses initial recruitment into the judicial service below district judge level — subsequent posting, promotion, and leave for these officers is separately governed by Article 235's High Court control provision, not by this Article.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 234 as the recruitment-stage counterpart to Article 235's control-stage provision — Article 234 governs how junior judicial officers enter service, while Article 235 governs how the High Court subsequently controls their careers; the twin consultation requirement (Public Service Commission plus High Court) is the key procedural safeguard to remember.

sections.title: Control over subordinate courts
sections.raw_text: The control over district courts and courts subordinate thereto including the posting and promotion of, and the grant of leave to, persons belonging to the judicial service of a State and holding any post inferior to the post of district judge shall be vested in the High Court, but nothing in this article shall be construed as taking away from any such person any right of appeal which he may have under the law regulating the conditions of his service or as authorising the High Court to deal with him otherwise than in accordance with the conditions of his service prescribed under such law.
key_terms: High Court's control over subordinate judiciary (posting/promotion/leave)
subordinate judicial officer's service-law appeal right preserved

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 235 is the cornerstone provision securing the subordinate judiciary's operational independence from the State executive: control over district courts and all courts subordinate to them — specifically including posting, promotion, and grant of leave for judicial officers below district judge rank — is vested in the High Court, not in the State's executive or administrative machinery. This gives the High Court comprehensive day-to-day administrative authority over the entire subordinate judicial hierarchy within its jurisdiction, ensuring judicial officers' careers are managed by the judiciary itself rather than by executive officials who might otherwise exert improper influence over decisions through career-related leverage. The concluding clause carefully balances this control against individual officers' rights: the High Court's control does not strip a judicial officer of any service-law appeal right, nor authorise the High Court to treat him inconsistently with his prescribed conditions of service — the High Court's control power is substantial but not a license to bypass established service jurisprudence.
essential_elements: The High Court holds control over district courts and all courts subordinate to them, specifically including posting, promotion, and leave for judicial officers below district judge rank.
This control is comprehensive administrative authority over the subordinate judiciary's day-to-day career management, vested exclusively in the High Court rather than the State executive.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The High Court's control does not extinguish any right of appeal a judicial officer has under the law regulating his service conditions — service-law appellate remedies survive this Article's grant of control.

The High Court's control power does not authorise treating a judicial officer otherwise than in accordance with his prescribed conditions of service — the control is exercised within, not above, the applicable service-rules framework.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 235 as the single most important judicial-independence guarantee for the subordinate judiciary — courts have interpreted 'control' here broadly (encompassing disciplinary matters, though subject to Article 311's civil-servant safeguards for major penalties), and the concluding proviso-like clause is essential for correctly balancing High Court authority against individual judicial officers' service-law protections.

sections.title: Interpretation
key_terms: 'district judge' definitional scope (Chapter VI)
'judicial service' definitional scope (Chapter VI)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 236 is the interpretation clause fixing the precise scope of two terms used throughout Chapter VI. 'District judge' is defined expansively to include not just the officer formally titled district judge, but a wide range of functionally equivalent posts — city civil court judges, additional/joint/assistant district judges, small cause court chief judges, presidency magistrates, and sessions judges at various levels — ensuring Chapter VI's protections and procedures apply uniformly across this whole cluster of senior subordinate judicial posts regardless of local title variations. 'Judicial service' is defined narrowly as a service consisting exclusively of persons intended to fill district-judge-and-below civil judicial posts — deliberately excluding criminal-side magistracy from the core definition (which is why Article 237 separately addresses extending the Chapter's provisions to magistrates).
essential_elements: Clause (a): 'district judge' is defined to include a specified list of functionally equivalent civil and criminal court posts, not just the literally-titled district judge post.
Clause (b): 'judicial service' is defined as a service consisting exclusively of persons intended for district-judge-and-below civil judicial posts.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'judicial service' definition's exclusivity to civil judicial posts is precisely why Article 237 is needed as a separate mechanism — magistrates (a criminal-side function) are not automatically covered by Chapter VI's provisions absent the Governor's Article 237 notification.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 236 as the definitional key that determines exactly who Articles 233 through 235 actually cover — the deliberately civil-judicial-service-only scope of 'judicial service' is the essential fact that makes Article 237's separate magistrate-extension mechanism necessary, rather than redundant.

sections.title: Application of the provisions of this Chapter to certain class or classes of magistrates
sections.raw_text: The Governor may by public notification direct that the foregoing provisions of this Chapter and any rules made thereunder shall with effect from such date as may be fixed by him in that behalf apply in relation to any class or classes of magistrates in the State as they apply in relation to persons appointed to the judicial service of the State subject to such exceptions and modifications as may be specified in the notification.
key_terms: Governor's power to extend Chapter VI to specified magistrates

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 237 closes Chapter VI by letting the Governor extend the Chapter's entire protective and administrative framework (recruitment via Article 234, High Court control via Article 235, and so on) to specified classes of magistrates by public notification — necessary precisely because Article 236(b)'s 'judicial service' definition is limited to civil judicial posts and does not automatically capture magistrates exercising criminal jurisdiction. This mechanism became especially significant after the separation of the judiciary from the executive (implementing Article 50's Directive Principle) in most States, when judicial magistrates were brought under High Court control via Article 237 notifications, completing the structural independence of the criminal-side subordinate judiciary from executive administration.
essential_elements: The Governor may, by public notification, extend Chapter VI's provisions (and any rules made under it) to any specified class or classes of magistrates in the State.

The extension takes effect from a date the Governor fixes in the notification, and may be made subject to exceptions and modifications specified in that same notification — it need not be a wholesale, unmodified extension.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The extension is discretionary and selective — the Governor may choose which classes of magistrates to cover and may tailor the extension with exceptions/modifications, rather than being bound to extend the Chapter uniformly to every magistrate in the State.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 237 as the mechanism that completed the separation-of-judiciary-from-executive project (Article 50's Directive Principle) for the criminal-side magistracy — cross-read it with Article 236(b)'s civil-only 'judicial service' definition to see exactly why this separate extension power was constitutionally necessary rather than superfluous.

sections.title: Administration of Union territories
sections.raw_text:
(1) Save as otherwise provided by Parliament by law, every Union territory shall be administered by the President acting, to such extent as he thinks fit, through an administrator to be appointed by him with such designation as he may specify.
(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in Part VI, the President may appoint the Governor of a State as the administrator of an adjoining Union territory, and where a Governor is so appointed, he shall exercise his functions as such administrator independently of his Council of Ministers.
key_terms: President's administration of Union territories via appointed administrator
Governor as ex officio Union territory administrator (adjoining UT)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 239 opens Part VIII by establishing the default administrative model for Union territories, which structurally differs from Part VI's State model: instead of a Governor acting on the aid and advice of an elected State Council of Ministers, a Union territory is administered directly by the President (in practice, the Union Council of Ministers) acting through an appointed administrator (variously designated Lieutenant Governor, Administrator, or Chief Commissioner depending on the territory) — reflecting Parliament's plenary Article 246/Seventh Schedule List I control over Union territories generally. Clause (2) permits administrative efficiency: the President may appoint an existing State's Governor as the administrator of an adjoining Union territory (e.g., Punjab's Governor for Chandigarh), but critically requires that Governor to act as administrator independently of that State's Council of Ministers — the dual-hat arrangement does not import the State's aid-and-advice constraint into the Union territory role, keeping the two capacities constitutionally separate.
essential_elements: Clause (1): the default rule — a Union territory is administered by the President, acting to whatever extent he thinks fit through an appointed administrator with a designation of the President's choosing, unless Parliament has by law provided otherwise (as it has for territories covered by Articles 239A, 239AA, and dedicated Union territory legislation).
