In practice, most States designate the Examiner of Local Fund Accounts, the Director of Local Fund Audit, or a similar State-level local-audit authority — sometimes working alongside the Comptroller and Auditor-General under supplementary arrangements — to audit Panchayat accounts pursuant to the State's own Panchayati Raj or local-fund-audit legislation made under this Article.
essential_elements: The Legislature of a State may, by law, prescribe how Panchayats maintain their accounts and how those accounts are audited — the Constitution leaves the entire substantive and procedural framework to State legislative design.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Unlike Article 148 (Comptroller and Auditor-General), Article 243J does not itself create or designate any particular auditing authority for Panchayat accounts — the actual auditing body (commonly a State-level Local Fund Audit authority, sometimes working with the CAG under separate technical guidance and support arrangements) is a matter of State legislative and administrative choice, not constitutional mandate.

This Article's brevity (a single enabling sentence, with no clauses) stands in deliberate contrast to the more elaborate Article 243I immediately preceding it — audit was left as a comparatively lighter-touch, State-legislative-discretion matter rather than being built out with the same institutional detail (fixed periodicity, mandatory legislative laying) given to the Finance Commission mechanism.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243J as the final, deliberately minimal accountability provision in the Panchayat-finance cluster (Articles 243H-243J) — cross-reference it against Article 148's CAG framework to appreciate what this Article does not itself do: it delegates audit design to State law rather than constitutionally entrenching any specific auditing institution the way Article 148 does at the Union/State level.

sections.title: Elections to the Panchayats
sections.raw_text:
243K. Elections to the Panchayats.—(1) The superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls for, and the conduct of, all elections to the Panchayats shall be vested in a State Election Commission consisting of a State Election Commissioner to be appointed by the Governor.
(2) Subject to the provisions of any law made by the Legislature of a State, the conditions of service and tenure of office of the State Election Commissioner shall be such as the Governor may by rule determine: Provided that the State Election Commissioner shall not be removed from his office except in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of a High Court and the conditions of service of the State Election Commissioner shall not be varied to his disadvantage after his appointment.
(3) The Governor of a State shall, when so requested by the State Election Commission, make available to the State Election Commission such staff as may be necessary for the discharge of the functions conferred on the State Election Commission by clause (1).
(4) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, the Legislature of a State may, by law, make provision with respect to all matters relating to, or in connection with, elections to the Panchayats.
key_terms: State Election Commission for Panchayat elections
High-Court-Judge-equivalent removal protection for the State Election Commissioner

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243K creates a dedicated State Election Commission — headed by a Governor-appointed State Election Commissioner — to superintend, direct, and control the preparation of Panchayat electoral rolls and the conduct of Panchayat elections, and insulates that Commissioner's tenure with High-Court-Judge-equivalent removal protection.
essential_elements: Clause (1) vests superintendence, direction, and control of Panchayat electoral-roll preparation and election conduct in a State Election Commission.
The State Election Commission consists of a State Election Commissioner appointed by the Governor.
Clause (2) leaves the Commissioner's service conditions and tenure to Governor's rules, subject to any State law.
The proviso to clause (2) bars removal except in like manner and on like grounds as a High Court Judge, and bars disadvantageous variation of service conditions after appointment.
Clause (3) obliges the Governor to furnish necessary staff to the Commission on request.
Clause (4) leaves the entire substantive law of Panchayat elections to State legislation, subject to the Constitution.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is the State-tier structural mirror of Article 324's Election Commission of India, but the two are entirely distinct bodies — a State Election Commission under Article 243K has no role in Parliamentary or State Legislature elections, which remain with the Election Commission of India under Article 324.

A single State Election Commissioner (not a multi-member body, unlike the Election Commission of India's Chief Election Commissioner plus Election Commissioners structure) is contemplated by this Article's text.

The independence architecture (Judge-equivalent removal protection, non-variation of service conditions) mirrors Article 324(5)'s protection for the Chief Election Commissioner, underscoring that Panchayat election administration was deliberately insulated from executive control just as national/State election administration is.

Article 243ZA later extends this same State Election Commission's jurisdiction to Municipal elections as well, so in practice a single State Election Commission typically administers both Panchayat and Municipal elections in a State.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243K as the institutional-independence guarantee underlying every election held under this Part — without a constitutionally insulated Election Commissioner, the detailed seat-reservation and duration rules in Articles 243D and 243E would be unenforceable in practice.

sections.title: Application to Union territories
sections.raw_text: 243L. Application to Union territories.—The provisions of this Part shall apply to the Union territories and shall, in their application to a Union territory, have effect as if the references to the Governor of a State were references to the Administrator of the Union territory appointed under article 239 and references to the Legislature or the legislative Assembly of a State were references, in relation to a Union territory having a Legislative Assembly, to that Legislative Assembly: Provided that the President may, by public notification, direct that the provisions of this Part shall apply to any Union territory or part thereof subject to such exceptions and modifications as he may specify in the notification.
key_terms: Union-territory extension of Part IX with Governor-to-Administrator substitution

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243L extends the entire Panchayat Part to Union territories by textually substituting 'Administrator appointed under article 239' for every reference to 'Governor,' and substituting a Union territory's own Legislative Assembly (where one exists) for every reference to a State Legislature, while letting the President modify or except provisions for particular territories by notification.
essential_elements: The Part applies to Union territories by a substitution formula, not a freestanding separate text.
'Governor of a State' reads as 'Administrator of the Union territory appointed under article 239.'
'Legislature or Legislative Assembly of a State' reads as the Union territory's own Legislative Assembly, where one exists.
The proviso lets the President tailor the Part's application to a specific Union territory or part thereof by public notification, specifying exceptions and modifications.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is the same substitution technique used elsewhere for extending State-oriented constitutional provisions to Union territories (compare Article 239's Governor-as-adjoining-UT-administrator arrangement), rather than a bespoke Union-territory Panchayat scheme.

Where a Union territory has no Legislative Assembly at all, the Legislature-substitution formula has nothing to substitute in for — Panchayat law-making in such territories functions through the Article 239/240 administrator/regulation mechanisms instead.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243L as a drafting-economy device: rather than re-writing Articles 243 through 243-O for Union territories, it simply swaps two defined terms so the same text governs both States and Union territories, subject to Presidential fine-tuning.

sections.title: Part not to apply to certain areas
sections.raw_text:
243M. Part not to apply to certain areas.—(1) Nothing in this Part shall apply to the Scheduled Areas referred to in clause (1), and the tribal areas referred to in clause (2), of article 244.
(2) Nothing in this Part shall apply to—
(a) the States of Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram;
(b) the hill areas in the State of Manipur for which District Councils exist under any law for the time being in force.
(3) Nothing in this Part—
(a) relating to Panchayats at the district level shall apply to the hill areas of the District of Darjeeling in the State of West Bengal for which Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council exists under any law for the time being in force;
(b) shall be construed to affect the functions and powers of the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council constituted under such law.
(3A) Nothing in article 243D, relating to reservation of seats for the Scheduled Castes, shall apply to the State of Arunachal Pradesh.
(4) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution,—
(a) the Legislature of a State referred to in sub-clause (a) of clause (2) may, by law, extend this Part to that State, except the areas, if any, referred to in clause (1), if the Legislative Assembly of that State passes a resolution to that effect by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting;
(b) Parliament may, by law, extend the provisions of this Part to the Scheduled Areas and the tribal areas referred to in clause (1) subject to such exceptions and modifications as may be specified in such law, and no such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368.
key_terms: blanket carve-out of Fifth/Sixth Schedule and tribal Northeast areas from Part IX
special-majority State-Assembly resolution route to opt in to Part IX
PESA extension route for Scheduled/tribal areas

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243M carves an entire category of areas out of Part IX by default — Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas, Sixth Schedule tribal areas, Nagaland/Meghalaya/Mizoram, the District-Council hill areas of Manipur, the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council's district-level jurisdiction, and (for SC reservation specifically) Arunachal Pradesh — while opening two distinct routes back in: a State's own special-majority Assembly resolution for the Nagaland/Meghalaya/Mizoram category, or a Parliamentary law (with tailored exceptions/modifications) for Scheduled/tribal areas.
essential_elements: Clause (1) excludes Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas and Sixth Schedule tribal areas outright.
Clause (2) excludes Nagaland, Meghalaya, and Mizoram, plus Manipur's District-Council hill areas.
Clause (3) excludes only the district-level Panchayat tier from applying to Darjeeling's hill areas, preserving the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council's own functions and powers.
Clause (3A) is a narrower, single-subject carve-out exempting Arunachal Pradesh specifically from Article 243D's SC seat-reservation rule.

Clause (4)(a) lets a Nagaland/Meghalaya/Mizoram Legislature opt the whole Part back in via a resolution passed by a majority of total membership plus a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.

Clause (4)(b) lets Parliament extend the Part to Scheduled/tribal areas by ordinary law (not a constitutional amendment) with its own exceptions and modifications, and expressly this is not an Article 368 amendment.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article is the constitutional gateway that necessitated the Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA) — the Parliamentary law made under clause (4)(b) that extends a modified Panchayat scheme (with enhanced Gram Sabha powers over natural resources, minor forest produce, money-lending, etc.) to Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas across several States.
The clause (4)(a) route requires a genuinely supermajoritarian internal decision by the excluded State's own Assembly — Part IX cannot be imposed on Nagaland, Meghalaya, or Mizoram from outside.

The Sixth Schedule areas (parts of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram) already have their own autonomous district/regional council government structure under the Sixth Schedule itself, which is why Part IX simply does not apply there rather than needing an opt-out mechanism.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243M as defining the outer geographic boundary of ordinary Part IX Panchayati Raj — it does not mean these areas have no local self-government, but that their local self-government runs on separate constitutional tracks (Sixth Schedule councils, PESA-modified Panchayats, or State-specific arrangements) rather than the standard Article 243B-243-O scheme.

sections.title: Continuance of existing laws and Panchayats
sections.raw_text: 243N. Continuance of existing laws and Panchayats.—Notwithstanding anything in this Part, any provision of any law relating to Panchayats in force in a State immediately before the commencement of the Constitution (Seventy-third Amendment) Act, 1992, which is inconsistent with the provisions of this Part, shall continue to be in force until amended or repealed by a competent Legislature or other competent authority or until the expiration of one year from such commencement, whichever is earlier: Provided that all the Panchayats existing immediately before such commencement shall continue till the expiration of their duration, unless sooner dissolved by a resolution passed to that effect by the Legislative Assembly of that State or, in the case of a State having a Legislative Council, by each House of the Legislature of that State.
key_terms: one-year transitional continuance of pre-1993 inconsistent Panchayat laws

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243N is a transitional savings clause: pre-existing State Panchayat laws that conflict with the new Part IX scheme stay valid for up to one year after the Seventy-third Amendment's commencement (or until sooner amended/repealed), and Panchayats already sitting when the Amendment commenced continue for their existing duration unless the State Legislature affirmatively dissolves them.
essential_elements: Inconsistent pre-commencement Panchayat laws continue notwithstanding Part IX, but only temporarily.
That continuance ends at the earlier of: competent amendment/repeal, or one year from the Seventy-third Amendment's commencement.
The proviso separately protects already-existing Panchayats themselves (not just the laws), letting them run out their existing term.
Early dissolution of such a continuing Panchayat requires an affirmative Legislative Assembly resolution (both Houses, if the State has a Legislative Council).
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a one-time historical transitional provision tied to the 1992-93 commencement date and has no ongoing operative significance for law made after that one-year window closed — it is retained in the constitutional text as a historical record of how the transition to Part IX was managed.

It parallels the standard constitutional drafting technique of giving States a grace period to align pre-existing law with a newly inserted constitutional scheme, rather than causing an abrupt legal vacuum on commencement.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243N as a now-largely-spent transitional bridge — useful for understanding the 1992-93 changeover, but not a source of any live legal rule today.

sections.title: Bar to interference by courts in electoral matters
key_terms: delimitation-law judicial-review bar for Panchayat elections
election-petition-only channel for challenging Panchayat elections

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243-O closes Part IX with the same two-part electoral-non-interference bar familiar from Article 329 for Parliamentary/State Legislature elections: delimitation and seat-allotment laws made under Article 243K cannot be challenged in any court at all, and an actual Panchayat election can only be challenged through an election petition under State-enacted procedure — never through ordinary writ or civil litigation.
essential_elements: Clause (a) is an absolute bar — delimitation/seat-allotment law validity under Article 243K cannot be questioned in any court.
Clause (b) channels all election-validity challenges exclusively through an election petition mechanism.
The election petition's presenting authority and procedure are left entirely to State legislation.

The 'notwithstanding anything in this Constitution' opening overrides even the general writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 and the Supreme Court under Article 32 for these specific matters.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This directly mirrors Article 329(b)'s bar on questioning Parliamentary/State Legislature elections outside an election petition — the Supreme Court's Article 329 jurisprudence (holding that the bar operates only once the electoral process has actually begun, and that pre-election stages can still be challenged by writ) is the natural interpretive analogy courts draw on for Article 243-O.

The bar targets election validity specifically — it does not oust judicial review of the underlying State Panchayat election law's constitutionality on grounds unrelated to a specific election's conduct.

Because the election petition authority and procedure are State-law creatures under clause (b), the specific forum (a civil court, a tribunal, or an Election Commission-designated authority) varies by State.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243-O as Part IX's finality guarantee for the electoral process — it protects the tight election timelines mandated by Articles 243C-243E from being derailed by litigation, by confining all electoral disputes to a single, State-prescribed post-election channel.

sections.title: Definitions (Part IXA — The Municipalities)
key_terms: Metropolitan area definition (ten-lakh population threshold)
Municipality definition (self-government institution under Article 243Q)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243P opens Part IXA (inserted by the Seventy-fourth Amendment Act, 1992, effective 1 June 1993) by defining the Part's core vocabulary — most significantly 'Metropolitan area' (a Governor-notified area of at least ten lakh population spanning multiple Municipalities/Panchayats) and 'Municipality' (an urban self-government institution constituted under Article 243Q) — establishing the urban-local-government counterpart to Part IX's rural Panchayat definitions.
essential_elements: 'Committee' means a Committee constituted under Article 243S (Wards Committees and similar bodies).
'Metropolitan area' requires a ten-lakh-or-more population threshold, spanning one or more districts and two or more Municipalities/Panchayats/contiguous areas, and must be Governor-notified.
'Municipal area' is the Governor-notified territorial area of a specific Municipality.
'Municipality' is defined by cross-reference to Article 243Q's constitution mechanism.
'population' is anchored to the last published preceding census, exactly as Article 243(f) does for Part IX.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This structurally mirrors Article 243's Part IX definitions almost term-for-term (compare 'Gram Sabha'/'Panchayat'/'population' there with 'Committee'/'Municipality'/'population' here), reflecting that the Seventy-fourth Amendment was drafted as the urban companion to the Seventy-third Amendment's rural scheme, enacted together as a package.
The 'Metropolitan area' concept has no Part IX analogue — it is a distinctly urban-governance innovation tied to Article 243ZE's Metropolitan Planning Committee mechanism for large conurbations.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243P as the glossary for the entire Municipalities Part — in particular, note that 'Metropolitan area' and 'Municipal area' are two different, non-interchangeable defined terms, the former being a larger multi-Municipality planning unit and the latter being a single Municipality's own territorial jurisdiction.

sections.title: Constitution of Municipalities
sections.raw_text:
243Q. Constitution of Municipalities.—(1) There shall be constituted in every State,—
(a) a Nagar Panchayat (by whatever name called) for a transitional area, that is to say, an area in transition from a rural area to an urban area;
(b) a Municipal Council for a smaller urban area; and
(c) a Municipal Corporation for a larger urban area,
in accordance with the provisions of this Part: Provided that a Municipality under this clause may not be constituted in such urban area or part thereof as the Governor may, having regard to the size of the area and the municipal services being provided or proposed to be provided by an industrial establishment in that area and such other factors as he may deem fit, by public notification, specify to be an industrial township.
(2) In this article, “a transitional area”, “a smaller urban area” or “a larger urban area” means such area as the Governor may, having regard to the population of the area, the density of the population therein, the revenue generated for local administration, the percentage of employment in non-agricultural activities, the economic importance or such other factors as he may deem fit, specify by public notification for the purposes of this Part.
key_terms: three-tier Municipality structure (Nagar Panchayat/Municipal Council/Municipal Corporation)
industrial-township exemption from Municipality constitution

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243Q requires every State to constitute a three-tier urban local-government structure — a Nagar Panchayat for transitional (rural-to-urban) areas, a Municipal Council for smaller urban areas, and a Municipal Corporation for larger urban areas — with the Governor empowered to draw the boundaries between these categories using population, density, revenue, and non-agricultural-employment criteria, and to exempt genuine industrial townships from having a Municipality at all.
essential_elements: Clause (1) mandates all three tiers exist in every State: Nagar Panchayat (transitional), Municipal Council (smaller urban), Municipal Corporation (larger urban).

The proviso lets the Governor notify an area as an 'industrial township' and thereby exempt it from Municipality constitution, based on area size and municipal services already provided by an industrial establishment.

Clause (2) leaves the criteria distinguishing 'transitional,' 'smaller urban,' and 'larger urban' areas to Governor's notification, using population, density, local-revenue generation, non-agricultural employment percentage, and economic importance as guiding (non-exhaustive) factors.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Unlike Article 243B's Part IX three-tier rule (which allows a small-population State to skip the intermediate tier entirely), Article 243Q contains no population-based exemption for any of its three tiers generally — the only exemption mechanism is the narrower industrial-township proviso.

The industrial-township exemption is commonly invoked for company townships built and serviced by large industrial or public-sector undertakings (e.g., steel-plant townships), where the employer already functions as a de facto municipal-service provider.

Because the Governor's notification power under clause (2) uses open-ended, multi-factor criteria rather than fixed numeric thresholds, classification disputes (is a given area 'transitional' or already 'smaller urban'?) are a recurring source of litigation and rest heavily on the Governor's discretion, though not entirely beyond judicial review for arbitrariness.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243Q as the urban parallel to Article 243B, but notice the structural difference: Part IX's three tiers are rural-hierarchy tiers (village/intermediate/district) covering the same population at different scales, while Part IXA's three tiers are urban-classification tiers (Nagar Panchayat/Council/Corporation) covering different, non-overlapping areas by size and urbanization stage.

sections.title: Composition of Municipalities
key_terms: ward-based direct election as the default Municipality composition rule
non-voting expert-member representation in a Municipality

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243R mandates direct election by ward-based territorial constituencies as the default rule for filling all Municipality seats, while letting State law optionally add non-voting expert members and ex officio MP/MLA/MLC/Committee-Chairperson representation, and leaving the Chairperson's election method to State legislation.
essential_elements: Clause (1) is the default: every Municipality seat is filled by direct election from wards, the Municipal area being divided into wards for this purpose.
Clause (2)(a)(i) permits State law to add municipal-administration experts as members, but the proviso strips them of voting rights in Municipality meetings.
Clause (2)(a)(ii)-(iii) permits State law to add overlapping-constituency MPs, MLAs, MPs of the Council of States, and MLCs registered as electors in the Municipal area.
Clause (2)(a)(iv) permits State law to add Article 243S(5) Committee Chairpersons as members.

Clause (2)(b) leaves the Chairperson's election method entirely to State law — unlike Article 243C(5)(b)'s mandatory indirect election for intermediate/district Panchayat Chairpersons, Article 243R imposes no default rule at all for Municipality Chairpersons.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Compare this closely with Article 243C's Panchayat composition rule: both mandate direct ward/constituency election as the baseline and both permit optional ex officio legislator representation, but Article 243R additionally permits non-voting subject-matter experts (no Part IX equivalent), and leaves Chairperson election method entirely open rather than mandating direct election at the lowest tier and indirect election above it as Article 243C(5) does.

The non-voting proviso for clause (2)(a)(i) experts is a deliberate safeguard ensuring unelected members cannot out-vote the directly elected ward representatives, preserving the democratic character of Municipal decision-making.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243R alongside Article 243C — the direct-election baseline is identical in spirit to Part IX, but track the specific differences (voting-rights proviso for experts, and the complete absence of a default Chairperson-election rule) since these are natural comparison points in any bare-act reading of the two Parts side by side.

sections.title: Constitution and composition of Wards Committees, etc.
sections.raw_text:
243S. Constitution and composition of Wards Committees, etc.—(1) There shall be constituted Wards Committees, consisting of one or more wards, within the territorial area of a Municipality having a population of three lakhs or more.
(2) The Legislature of a State may, by law, make provision with respect to—
(a) the composition and the territorial area of a Wards Committee;
(b) the manner in which the seats in a Wards Committee shall be filled.
(3) A member of a Municipality representing a ward within the territorial area of the Wards Committee shall be a member of that Committee.
(4) Where a Wards Committee consists of—
(a) one ward, the member representing that ward in the Municipality; or
(b) two or more wards, one of the members representing such wards in the Municipality elected by the members of the Wards Committee,
shall be the Chairperson of that Committee.
(5) Nothing in this article shall be deemed to prevent the Legislature of a State from making any provision for the constitution of Committees in addition to the Wards Committees.
key_terms: mandatory Wards Committee for three-lakh-plus-population Municipalities

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243S requires every Municipality with a population of three lakhs or more to break itself down further into Wards Committees (each covering one or more wards), automatically seats each ward's elected Municipality member on the corresponding Committee, fixes a default Chairperson rule (the sole ward member, or an internally elected Chairperson for multi-ward Committees), and expressly permits States to create still further sub-Municipal Committees beyond Wards Committees.
essential_elements: Clause (1) makes Wards Committees mandatory only for Municipalities at or above three lakh population — smaller Municipalities have no Article 243S obligation.
Clause (2) leaves Committee composition, territorial area, and seat-filling method to State law.
Clause (3) automatically makes the relevant ward's elected Municipality member a member of that Wards Committee.
Clause (4) supplies a default Chairperson rule: the single member for a one-ward Committee, or a Committee-internal election among members for a multi-ward Committee.
Clause (5) is a non-obstante-style clarification that the Article does not cap State power to create additional Committees beyond Wards Committees.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The three-lakh population threshold is a hard numeric trigger (unlike Article 243B's more flexible twenty-lakh exemption for the Panchayat intermediate tier), so smaller Municipal Councils and Nagar Panchayats below this threshold are never obligated to create Wards Committees at all, though nothing stops a State from mandating them anyway by its own law.

Article 243S(5)'s additional-Committees clause is the enabling basis for ward sub-committees, area sabhas, or similar micro-local bodies some States have created by statute beyond the constitutionally mandated Wards Committee.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243S as creating a second, more granular tier of urban representation below the Municipality itself — necessary because a large Municipal Corporation's ward count can run into the hundreds, making a single Municipality-wide body too remote for genuinely local ward-level concerns.

sections.title: Reservation of seats (Municipalities)
sections.raw_text:
243T. Reservation of seats.—(1) Seats shall be reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in every Municipality and the number of seats so reserved shall bear, as nearly as may be, the same proportion to the total number of seats to be filled by direct election in that Municipality as the population of the Scheduled Castes in the Municipal area or of the Scheduled Tribes in the Municipal area bears to the total population of that area and such seats may be allotted by rotation to different constituencies in a Municipality.
(2) Not less than one-third of the total number of seats reserved under clause (1) shall be reserved for women belonging to the Scheduled Castes or, as the case may be, the Scheduled Tribes.
(3) Not less than one-third (including the number of seats reserved for women belonging to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes) of the total number of seats to be filled by direct election in every Municipality shall be reserved for women and such seats may be allotted by rotation to different constituencies in a Municipality.
(4) The offices of Chairpersons in the Municipalities shall be reserved for the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes and women in such manner as the Legislature of a State may, by law, provide.
(5) The reservation of seats under clauses (1) and (2) and the reservation of offices of Chairpersons (other than the reservation for women) under clause (4) shall cease to have effect on the expiration of the period specified in article 334.
(6) Nothing in this Part shall prevent the Legislature of a State from making any provision for reservation of seats in any Municipality or offices of Chairpersons in the Municipalities in favour of backward class of citizens.
key_terms: population-proportionate SC/ST seat reservation in Municipalities
one-third overall women reservation in Municipalities (inclusive of SC/ST women)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243T reproduces Article 243D's Panchayat reservation scheme for the urban context essentially clause-for-clause: population-proportionate SC/ST seat reservation with rotation, a one-third SC/ST-women sub-reservation, an inclusive one-third overall women's reservation, State-law-governed Chairperson-office reservation, an Article 334 sunset for SC/ST (but not women's) reservation, and a permissive backward-class reservation enabling clause.
essential_elements: Clause (1) reserves Municipality seats for SC/ST in proportion to their population share of the Municipal area, with rotation among constituencies.
Clause (2) sub-reserves at least one-third of those SC/ST seats for SC/ST women.
Clause (3) reserves at least one-third of all directly elected Municipality seats for women overall, inclusive of the SC/ST women already counted under clause (2).
Clause (4) mirrors the reservation scheme for the office of Chairperson, per State-law-determined manner.
Clause (5) sunsets SC/ST seat and (non-women) Chairperson-office reservation at the Article 334 expiry date, expressly excluding women's reservation from that sunset.
Clause (6) permissively allows additional State-law backward-class reservation.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article is textually near-identical to Article 243D, confirming the Seventy-third and Seventy-fourth Amendments were designed as a deliberately parallel rural/urban reservation package — any interpretive principle settled for Article 243D (e.g., the K. Krishna Murthy v. Union of India, (2010) 7 SCC 202 empirical-justification standard and 50% aggregate cap for clause (6) backward-class reservation) applies with equal force to Article 243T.

As with Article 243D, the 106th Amendment Act, 2023's new Lok Sabha/Assembly women's-reservation Articles (330A/332A) are structurally distinct and leave this Municipality women's-reservation scheme untouched.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243T side by side with Article 243D — treat any analysis or case law developed under the Panchayat reservation Article as directly transferable to the Municipality reservation Article, since the two provisions were drafted to be substantively identical.

sections.title: Duration of Municipalities, etc.
sections.raw_text:
243U. Duration of Municipalities, etc.—(1) Every Municipality, unless sooner dissolved under any law for the time being in force, shall continue for five years from the date appointed for its first meeting and no longer: Provided that a Municipality shall be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before its dissolution.
(2) No amendment of any law for the time being in force shall have the effect of causing dissolution of a Municipality at any level, which is functioning immediately before such amendment, till the expiration of its duration specified in clause (1).
(3) An election to constitute a Municipality shall be completed,—
(a) before the expiry of its duration specified in clause (1);
(b) before the expiration of a period of six months from the date of its dissolution: Provided that where the remainder of the period for which the dissolved Municipality would have continued is less than six months, it shall not be necessary to hold any election under this clause for constituting the Municipality for such period.
(4) A Municipality constituted upon the dissolution of a Municipality before the expiration of its duration shall continue only for the remainder of the period for which the dissolved Municipality would have continued under clause (1) had it not been so dissolved.
key_terms: fixed five-year Municipality term with hearing-before-dissolution right

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243U reproduces Article 243E's Panchayat duration scheme for Municipalities essentially clause-for-clause: a fixed five-year term from the first meeting, protection against dissolution by mere legislative amendment, a mandatory six-month re-election deadline after dissolution, and a reconstituted Municipality inheriting only its predecessor's remaining term — with one textual addition, an explicit proviso guaranteeing the Municipality a reasonable hearing before dissolution.
essential_elements: Clause (1) fixes the term at five years from the first-meeting date, 'and no longer,' subject to earlier dissolution under existing law.
The proviso to clause (1) guarantees the Municipality a reasonable opportunity of being heard before dissolution — a right with no explicit textual counterpart in Article 243E for Panchayats.
Clause (2) prevents a mere legislative amendment from itself dissolving an already-functioning Municipality before its term expires.
Clause (3) mandates fresh elections within six months of dissolution, subject to the de minimis exception where under six months of the term would have remained anyway.
Clause (4) confirms a reconstituted Municipality serves only the remainder of its predecessor's original term.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The reasonable-opportunity-of-hearing proviso is the one substantive textual difference from Article 243E — its absence from the Panchayat provision does not necessarily mean Panchayats lack any analogous natural-justice protection (general administrative-law principles may still apply), but Article 243U makes the protection explicit and constitutionally guaranteed for Municipalities specifically.
As with Article 243E, this Article imports timing discipline analogous to Article 172's fixed Legislative Assembly term and Article 356's structured dissolution/reconstitution scheme.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243U side by side with Article 243E, and specifically flag the added hearing-before-dissolution proviso as the one point of textual divergence worth remembering between the rural and urban duration schemes.

sections.title: Disqualifications for membership (Municipalities)
sections.raw_text:
243V. Disqualifications for membership.—(1) A person shall be disqualified for being chosen as, and for being, a member of a Municipality—
(a) if he is so disqualified by or under any law for the time being in force for the purposes of elections to the Legislature of the State concerned: Provided that no person shall be disqualified on the ground that he is less than twenty-five years of age, if he has attained the age of twenty-one years;
(b) if he is so disqualified by or under any law made by the Legislature of the State.
(2) If any question arises as to whether a member of a Municipality has become subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in clause (1), the question shall be referred for the decision of such authority and in such manner as the Legislature of a State may, by law, provide.
key_terms: State-Legislature-election disqualification grounds imported for Municipality membership
twenty-one-year minimum age floor for Municipality membership

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243V reproduces Article 243F's Panchayat disqualification scheme for Municipalities word-for-word in substance: State Legislature election disqualification grounds import by default (subject to the twenty-one-year age-floor proviso lowering the usual candidacy age), plus any additional State-law-specific disqualification, with the adjudicating authority and procedure for disqualification disputes left entirely to State legislation.
essential_elements: Clause (1)(a) imports the disqualification grounds applicable to that State's own Legislature elections as the default rule for Municipality membership.
The proviso to clause (1)(a) ensures no one is disqualified merely for being under twenty-five, provided they have attained twenty-one — the same age-floor exception as Article 243F(1)(a)'s proviso.
Clause (1)(b) allows additional State-law-specific disqualification grounds beyond the imported Legislature-election grounds.
Clause (2) leaves the adjudicating authority and procedure for disqualification disputes entirely to State legislation, just as Article 243F(2) does for Panchayats.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is textually identical in structure and substance to Article 243F, differing only in referring to 'member of a Municipality' rather than 'member of a Panchayat' — any interpretive principle under Article 243F transfers directly.

As with Article 243F, the State-law-designated disqualification authority contrasts with Article 192's constitutionally fixed Governor-plus-Election-Commission mechanism for State Legislature members themselves.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243V as Article 243F's urban mirror — the twenty-one-year age floor and State-law dispute-forum design are the two features worth remembering, both carried over unchanged from the Panchayat scheme.

sections.title: Powers, authority and responsibilities of Municipalities, etc.
key_terms: State-law devolution of self-government powers to Municipalities
Twelfth Schedule as the illustrative subject-matter list for Municipal devolution

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243W mirrors Article 243G's Panchayat devolution enabling provision for the urban context: State Legislatures may, by law, endow Municipalities (and, separately, the Article 243S Committees) with the powers and authority needed to function as genuine self-government institutions, including devolving economic-development/social-justice planning and scheme implementation drawn from the Twelfth Schedule's illustrative subject list.
essential_elements: The power is permissive ('may'), not mandatory — a State is not constitutionally compelled to devolve any specific power to its Municipalities.
Clause (a) covers Municipalities themselves, including plan preparation for economic development/social justice and scheme implementation.
Clause (a)(ii) cross-references the Twelfth Schedule as the illustrative area list for Municipal devolution.
Clause (b) separately empowers devolution to the Article 243S Committees (Wards Committees and others), also with Twelfth Schedule cross-reference.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is the direct urban counterpart of Article 243G, sharing the identical 'illustrative, not authority-transferring' character — the Twelfth Schedule's eighteen entries (urban planning, land-use regulation, roads, water supply, public health, slum upgradation, urban poverty alleviation, fire services, etc.) do not by themselves confer legislative competence; actual devolution requires specific State legislation.

The separate treatment of Committees under clause (b) has no precise Part IX analogue, reflecting that Part IX's devolution clause (Article 243G) does not separately address sub-Panchayat committees the way Article 243W addresses Article 243S Wards Committees.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243W together with the Twelfth Schedule exactly as Article 243G is read together with the Eleventh Schedule — the Schedule supplies subject-matter examples, the Article supplies the enabling legal mechanism, and actual power transfer requires a third ingredient: specific State legislation.

sections.title: Power to impose taxes by, and Funds of, the Municipalities
key_terms: Municipality's own tax/toll/fee levy authorisation power
State-collected tax assignment to Municipalities

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243X reproduces Article 243H's Panchayat finance-enabling scheme for Municipalities: State law may authorise a Municipality's own-source taxation, assign State-collected levies to Municipalities, provide Consolidated-Fund grants-in-aid, and constitute dedicated Municipal Funds for crediting and withdrawing money — the complete four-part urban local-finance toolkit mirroring the rural one.
essential_elements: Clause (a) enables own-source Municipal taxation, subject to State-specified procedure and limits.
Clause (b) enables revenue-sharing via assignment of State-levied/collected taxes to Municipalities.
Clause (c) enables Consolidated Fund of the State grants-in-aid to Municipalities.
Clause (d) enables constitution of dedicated Municipal Funds for crediting and withdrawal of Municipal moneys.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is textually parallel to Article 243H across all four sub-clauses, differing only in substituting 'Municipality/Municipalities' for 'Panchayat' — the same practical reality applies that grants-in-aid under clause (c) are typically the dominant revenue source given limited own-source taxation potential, especially for smaller Municipalities.

Larger Municipal Corporations (e.g., in major metropolitan cities) often have comparatively stronger own-source revenue bases (property tax, octroi/local body tax where retained, etc.) than most rural Panchayats, making clause (a) practically more significant for urban local bodies than its Article 243H(a) Panchayat counterpart.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243X as Article 243H's direct urban mirror — the four-part own-tax/assigned-tax/grants-in-aid/dedicated-Fund structure is identical, only the institutional beneficiary changes from Panchayat to Municipality.

sections.title: Finance Commission (Municipalities)
key_terms: single Finance Commission reviewing both Panchayat and Municipal finances

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243Y does not create a second Finance Commission — it extends the same Article 243-I State Finance Commission's mandate to also review Municipal finances and recommend on State-Municipality revenue distribution, tax assignment, and grants-in-aid, with the same mandatory laying-before-Legislature transparency obligation as Article 243I(4).
essential_elements: The Article 243-I Finance Commission is a single body reviewing both Panchayat (under 243-I) and Municipal (under 243Y) finances — there is no separate Municipal Finance Commission.

Clause (1)(a) mandates recommendations on State-Municipality revenue division, inter-Municipality-tier allocation, tax assignment, and grants-in-aid — mirroring Article 243I(1)(a)'s Panchayat-side mandate.
Clause (1)(b) additionally mandates recommendations on measures to improve Municipal financial position generally.
Clause (1)(c) allows the Governor to refer any other sound-finance matter to the Commission.
Clause (2) mandates the Governor lay every recommendation, with an action-taken explanatory memorandum, before the State Legislature.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The unification of the Panchayat and Municipal finance-review function in a single Article 243-I Commission (rather than two separate bodies) is a deliberate design choice ensuring a coherent, single view of the State's overall local-government finance picture across both rural and urban tiers.
As with Article 243I(4), the recommendations are not textually made binding on the State Government — only the laying-before-Legislature transparency obligation is mandatory.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243Y not as a standalone institution-creating provision but as a mandate-extension clause bolted onto the Article 243-I Commission — always read the two Articles together to get the complete picture of a State Finance Commission's full jurisdiction.

sections.title: Audit of accounts of Municipalities
sections.raw_text: 243Z. Audit of accounts of Municipalities.—The Legislature of a State may, by law, make provisions with respect to the maintenance of accounts by the Municipalities and the auditing of such accounts.
key_terms: State-law Municipal account-maintenance and audit framework

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243Z is the brief urban mirror of Article 243J — it leaves the entire framework for Municipal account-keeping and auditing to State legislation, without constitutionally designating any specific auditing authority.
essential_elements: The power is permissive State legislative competence, not a mandatory constitutional audit mechanism.
Both account-maintenance standards and the audit process itself are left to State law.
exceptions_and_qualifications: As with Article 243J, no constitutional counterpart to Article 148's entrenched Comptroller and Auditor-General is designated here — States commonly designate Directors of Local Fund Audit, examiners of local accounts, or similar State-created authorities by ordinary statute.
This is the shortest substantive Article across both Part IX and Part IXA, textually near-identical to Article 243J save for the Municipality/Panchayat substitution.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243Z as confirming that, just as with Panchayats, Municipal financial accountability runs through State-created audit machinery rather than any constitutionally fixed national auditor.

sections.title: Elections to the Municipalities
sections.raw_text:
243ZA. Elections to the Municipalities.—(1) The superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls for, and the conduct of, all elections to the Municipalities shall be vested in the State Election Commission referred to in article 243K.
(2) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, the Legislature of a State may, by law, make provision with respect to all matters relating to, or in connection with, elections to the Municipalities.
key_terms: shared State Election Commission for Municipal elections

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243ZA does not create a second election-management body — it places Municipal elections under the same Article 243K State Election Commission that already administers Panchayat elections, and leaves the substantive law of Municipal elections to State legislation.
essential_elements: Clause (1) vests superintendence, direction, and control of Municipal electoral rolls and election conduct in the same Article 243K State Election Commission used for Panchayat elections.
Clause (2) leaves substantive Municipal election law to State legislation, subject to the Constitution.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This confirms the single-Commission design already implicit from Article 243K's drafting — one State Election Commissioner administers both rural (Panchayat) and urban (Municipal) local body elections in a State, rather than two separate bodies.
As with Article 243K, this Commission is entirely distinct from the Election Commission of India under Article 324, which has no role in Panchayat or Municipal elections.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243ZA as a short mandate-extension clause, exactly like Article 243Y's relationship to Article 243-I's Finance Commission — always read it together with Article 243K to see the complete picture of the State Election Commission's jurisdiction.

sections.title: Application to Union territories (Municipalities)
sections.raw_text: 243ZB. Application to Union territories.—The provisions of this Part shall apply to the Union territories and shall, in their application to a Union territory, have effect as if the references to the Governor of a State were references to the Administrator of the Union territory appointed under article 239 and references to the Legislature or the Legislative Assembly of a State were references in relation to a Union territory having a Legislative Assembly, to that Legislative Assembly: Provided that the President may, by public notification, direct that the provisions of this Part shall apply to any Union territory or part thereof subject to such exceptions and modifications as he may specify in the notification.
key_terms: Union-territory extension of Part IXA with Governor-to-Administrator substitution

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243ZB extends the entire Municipalities Part to Union territories using the identical Governor-to-Administrator, Legislature-to-Legislative-Assembly substitution formula that Article 243L uses for Part IX, again subject to Presidential tailoring by public notification.
essential_elements: 'Governor of a State' reads as 'Administrator of the Union territory appointed under article 239.'
'Legislature or Legislative Assembly of a State' reads as the Union territory's own Legislative Assembly, where one exists.
The proviso lets the President tailor the Part's application to a specific Union territory by public notification.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is textually identical to Article 243L save for the Part IXA cross-reference, confirming the same drafting-economy technique was reused for the urban local-government Part.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243ZB as Article 243L's exact urban mirror — no substantive analysis differs between the two beyond which Part is being extended.

sections.title: Part not to apply to certain areas (Municipalities)
sections.raw_text:
243ZC. Part not to apply to certain areas.—(1) Nothing in this Part shall apply to the Scheduled Areas referred to in clause (1), and the tribal areas referred to in clause (2) of article 244.
(2) Nothing in this Part shall be construed to affect the functions and powers of the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council constituted under any law for the time being in force for the hill areas of the district of Darjeeling in the State of West Bengal.
(3) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may, by law, extend the provisions of this Part to the Scheduled Areas and the tribal areas referred to in clause (1) subject to such exceptions and modifications as may be specified in such law, and no such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368.
key_terms: Scheduled/tribal-area and Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council carve-out from Part IXA

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243ZC excludes Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas and Sixth Schedule tribal areas from Part IXA by default, protects the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council's functions and powers from being affected by the Part, and gives Parliament the same PESA-style ordinary-law extension route Article 243M(4)(b) gives for Part IX.
essential_elements: Clause (1) excludes Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas and Sixth Schedule tribal areas outright.
Clause (2) protects the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council's functions and powers from being affected by this Part.
Clause (3) lets Parliament extend the Part to Scheduled/tribal areas by ordinary law (not an Article 368 amendment) with tailored exceptions and modifications.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 243ZC is a noticeably shorter carve-out than Article 243M — it has no counterpart to Article 243M(2)'s exclusion of Nagaland/Meghalaya/Mizoram/Manipur hill areas, and no counterpart to the clause (4)(a) special-majority Assembly opt-in route, reflecting that those particular exclusions were specific to Panchayati Raj's rural character rather than to urban local government generally.

The Darjeeling protection here is framed slightly differently from Article 243M(3) — Article 243M(3)(a) excludes only the district-level Panchayat tier from Darjeeling, while Article 243ZC(2) protects the Hill Council's functions/powers generally without a tier-specific carve-out, since Part IXA's Municipality structure does not have a directly analogous district-level tier concept.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243ZC as a shorter, urban-tailored version of Article 243M — same Scheduled/tribal-area logic and same PESA-style Parliamentary extension route, but without the Northeast-hill-State-specific clauses that have no urban-local-government equivalent.

sections.title: Committee for district planning
key_terms: mandatory District Planning Committee consolidating rural and urban plans
four-fifths rural/urban-elected-member composition floor for District Planning Committees

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243ZD is the constitutional hinge connecting Part IX and Part IXA — it mandates a District Planning Committee in every State to consolidate the separate plans prepared by district Panchayats and Municipalities into one integrated district development plan, with at least four-fifths of the Committee's membership drawn proportionately from elected rural and urban local-body members, and forwards the resulting plan to the State Government.
essential_elements: Clause (1) mandates a District Planning Committee in every State at the district level, with the dual function of consolidating Panchayat/Municipality plans and preparing a whole-district development plan.

Clause (2)'s proviso fixes a hard floor: at least four-fifths of Committee members must be elected members of the district-level Panchayat and district Municipalities, apportioned by rural/urban population ratio.
Clause (2)(a),(c),(d) otherwise leave composition, assigned functions, and Chairperson-selection method to State law.

Clause (3) requires the Committee to have regard to spatial planning, shared natural resources, infrastructure integration, and available resources, and to consult Governor-specified institutions/organisations.
Clause (4) requires the Chairperson to forward the recommended plan to the State Government.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is the first Article in either Part IX or Part IXA that operates across both Parts simultaneously — it is the structural bridge ensuring rural and urban local planning are not developed in silos within a single district.

The four-fifths elected-member floor is unusually high compared to most other composition rules in this Part, signalling a strong constitutional preference for genuinely local, elected-body-driven district planning over bureaucratic or nominated control.

Neither Article 243ZD nor Article 243ZE creates a body with binding decision-making power over Panchayats/Municipalities themselves — their output is a consolidated 'draft development plan' forwarded to the State Government, not a directly enforceable order.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243ZD as evidence that Parts IX and IXA, though textually separate, were designed as a single integrated decentralization scheme — the District Planning Committee is where the rural and urban tracks formally converge.

sections.title: Committee for Metropolitan planning
key_terms: mandatory Metropolitan Planning Committee for ten-lakh-plus conurbations
two-thirds elected-member composition floor for Metropolitan Planning Committees

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243ZE requires every Article 243P(c) Metropolitan area (ten-lakh-plus conurbations spanning multiple Municipalities/Panchayats) to have its own Metropolitan Planning Committee, with at least two-thirds elected membership proportionate to Municipal/Panchayat population, tasked with producing an integrated draft development plan that also factors in Union and State government investment priorities — reflecting that large metropolitan regions need planning coordination beyond what a single Municipality or district can provide.
essential_elements: Clause (1) mandates a Metropolitan Planning Committee in every Metropolitan area (as defined in Article 243P(c)) to prepare a whole-area draft development plan.

Clause (2)'s proviso fixes at least two-thirds elected membership, drawn from Municipality members and Panchayat Chairpersons in the Metropolitan area, proportionate to Municipal/Panchayat population ratio.

Clause (2)(c) uniquely allows representation of the Government of India itself on this Committee — no equivalent Union-Government representation appears in Article 243ZD's District Planning Committee scheme.

Clause (3) requires regard to existing Municipal/Panchayat plans, shared-resource coordination, Union/State objectives and priorities, and likely Union/State investment levels, plus consultation with Governor-specified institutions.
Clause (4) requires the Chairperson to forward the plan to the State Government.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The two-thirds elected-member floor here is lower than Article 243ZD's four-fifths floor for District Planning Committees — reflecting that Metropolitan Planning Committees are expected to also seat a meaningful share of non-elected institutional/expert/Union-Government representation given the scale and complexity of metropolitan-region planning.

The explicit Union-Government representation clause reflects the practical reality that metropolitan-region infrastructure (e.g., transport, water, environment) often involves Union agencies and Union-funded schemes, unlike ordinary district-level planning.

As with Article 243ZD, the Metropolitan Planning Committee's output is a non-binding draft development plan forwarded to the State Government, not an order enforceable directly against Municipalities or Panchayats.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243ZE alongside Article 243ZD as a matched pair — compare the different elected-member thresholds (two-thirds vs. four-fifths) and the Metropolitan Committee's additional Union-Government representation clause as the two clauses' main points of structural divergence.

sections.title: Continuance of existing laws and Municipalities
sections.raw_text: 243ZF. Continuance of existing laws and Municipalities.—Notwithstanding anything in this Part, any provision of any law relating to Municipalities in force in a State immediately before the commencement of the Constitution (Seventy-fourth Amendment) Act, 1992, which is inconsistent with the provisions of this Part, shall continue to be in force until amended or repealed by a competent Legislature or other competent authority or until the expiration of one year from such commencement, whichever is earlier: Provided that all the Municipalities existing immediately before such commencement shall continue till the expiration of their duration, unless sooner dissolved by a resolution passed to that effect by the Legislative Assembly of that State or, in the case of a State having a Legislative Council, by each House of the Legislature of that State.
key_terms: one-year transitional continuance of pre-1993 inconsistent Municipal laws

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243ZF is the transitional savings clause for Part IXA, mirroring Article 243N for Part IX: pre-existing State Municipal laws inconsistent with the new scheme continue for up to one year after the Seventy-fourth Amendment's commencement, and already-sitting Municipalities continue for their existing term absent affirmative Legislative Assembly dissolution.
essential_elements: Inconsistent pre-commencement Municipal laws continue notwithstanding Part IXA, but only until the earlier of competent amendment/repeal or one year from the Seventy-fourth Amendment's commencement.
The proviso protects already-existing Municipalities' current terms, subject to early dissolution only via an affirmative Legislative Assembly resolution.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a now-largely-spent, purely historical transitional provision tied to the 1992-93 commencement, exactly like Article 243N — retained in the text as a record of the transition, with no ongoing operative significance today.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243ZF as Article 243N's exact urban mirror — no substantive analysis differs beyond which Amendment and which institution it references.

sections.title: Bar to interference by courts in electoral matters (Municipalities)
key_terms: delimitation-law judicial-review bar for Municipal elections
election-petition-only channel for challenging Municipal elections

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243ZG closes Part IXA with the identical electoral-non-interference bar Article 243-O provides for Panchayats: Municipal delimitation/seat-allotment laws made under Article 243ZA cannot be questioned in any court, and Municipal election validity can only be challenged via a State-law-governed election petition.
essential_elements: Clause (a) is an absolute bar on questioning delimitation/seat-allotment law validity under Article 243ZA.
Clause (b) channels all Municipal election-validity challenges exclusively through an election petition mechanism under State-enacted procedure.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is textually identical to Article 243-O save for the Article 243ZA cross-reference in place of Article 243K, and 'Municipality' in place of 'Panchayat' — the same Article 329 interpretive analogy applies with equal force here.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243ZG as Article 243-O's exact urban mirror, completing Part IXA's parallel structure with Part IX — with this Article, both the rural (Part IX) and urban (Part IXA) local self-government Parts of the Constitution are now fully captured.

sections.title: Definitions (Part IXB — The Co-operative Societies)
key_terms: multi-State co-operative society definition
dual Central/State Registrar definition for co-operative societies

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243ZH opens Part IXB (inserted by the Ninety-seventh Amendment Act, 2011, effective 15 February 2012) by defining its core vocabulary, most significantly distinguishing an ordinary State-registered 'co-operative society' from a 'multi-State co-operative society' (objects not confined to one State) and correspondingly defining 'Registrar' as either a Central Registrar (for multi-State societies) or a State-appointed Registrar (for ordinary societies) — the dual Union/State jurisdictional split that runs through this entire Part.
essential_elements: 'co-operative society' is any society registered (or deemed registered) under State co-operative-society law.
'multi-State co-operative society' is a society whose objects are not confined to one State, registered under law relating to such multi-State co-operatives.

'Registrar' bifurcates into a Central Registrar (multi-State societies) and a State-appointed Registrar (ordinary societies) — reflecting that this single Part governs both Union and State legislative competence over co-operatives.
'board' is the governing body, by whatever name called, entrusted with management direction and control.
'office bearer' is defined by an illustrative list (President, Vice-President, Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, Secretary, Treasurer) plus any other board-elected person.
'State level co-operative society' is one whose area of operation extends to the whole State, as defined by State law.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is the third and final self-government-institution Part inserted into the Constitution's local/associational-governance cluster (following Part IX's 1992 Panchayats and Part IXA's 1992 Municipalities), but co-operative societies are member-owned economic associations rather than units of political local self-government, making Part IXB's subject matter meaningfully different in character despite the parallel drafting structure.

The multi-State/State co-operative distinction reflects the underlying Entry 44 of List I (Union List, corporations other than co-operative societies... actually multi-State co-operative societies specifically) versus Entry 32 of List II (State List, co-operative societies) division of legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule — Part IXB does not itself allocate this competence but operates within that pre-existing division.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243ZH's Registrar/multi-State definitions as the key that unlocks the rest of Part IXB — nearly every subsequent Article's operative rule shifts depending on whether a co-operative society is an ordinary State-registered society or a multi-State co-operative society, as made explicit later by Article 243ZR's Parliament/Central-Act/Central-Government substitution rule.

sections.title: Incorporation of co-operative societies
sections.raw_text: 243ZI. Incorporation of co-operative societies.—Subject to the provisions of this Part, the Legislature of a State may, by law, make provisions with respect to the incorporation, regulation and winding up of co-operative societies based on the principles of voluntary formation, democratic member-control, member-economic participation and autonomous functioning.
key_terms: four co-operative principles constitutionally anchoring State incorporation law (voluntary formation, democratic member-control, member-economic participation, autonomous functioning)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243ZI grants State Legislatures the power to legislate on co-operative society incorporation, regulation, and winding up, but constitutionally anchors that legislative power to four internationally recognized co-operative principles — voluntary formation, democratic member-control, member-economic participation, and autonomous functioning — meaning State co-operative law must operate consistently with these principles rather than being entirely unconstrained.
essential_elements: The power is a State legislative competence ('Legislature of a State may, by law'), covering incorporation, regulation, and winding up.
That competence is expressly made 'subject to the provisions of this Part' — i.e., constrained by the rest of Part IXB's mandatory rules (board composition, elections, audit, etc.).

The four named principles (voluntary formation, democratic member-control, member-economic participation, autonomous functioning) are built directly into the constitutional text as the values State co-operative legislation must be based on.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is the enabling foundation for the entire Part, comparable in structural role to Article 243B (Panchayats) and Article 243Q (Municipalities), but unlike those Articles it does not mandate any specific institutional tiers — co-operative societies remain voluntary member associations, not units of compulsory local government.

The stated principles mirror the internationally recognized Statement on the Co-operative Identity's core co-operative principles, reflecting that the Ninety-seventh Amendment was partly motivated by concerns over excessive government control and politicization of co-operative societies, aiming to constitutionally guarantee their autonomous, member-driven character.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243ZI as Part IXB's foundational values clause — every subsequent provision in this Part (board composition, election timing, supersession limits, audit requirements) should be understood as an attempt to operationalize these four principles, particularly democratic member-control and autonomous functioning.

sections.title: Number and term of members of board and its office bearers
sections.raw_text:
243ZJ. Number and term of members of board and its office bearers.—(1) The board shall consist of such number of directors as may be provided by the Legislature of a State, by law: Provided that the maximum number of directors of a co-operative society shall not exceed twenty-one: Provided further that the Legislature of a State shall, by law, provide for the reservation of one seat for the Scheduled Castes or the Scheduled Tribes and two seats for women on board of every co-operative society consisting of individuals as members and having members from such class of category of persons.
(2) The term of office of elected members of the board and its office bearers shall be five years from the date of election and the term of office bearers shall be conterminous with the term of the board: Provided that the board may fill a casual vacancy on the board by nomination out of the same class of members in respect of which the casual vacancy has arisen, if the term of office of the board is less than half of its original term.
(3) The Legislature of a State shall, by law, make provisions for co-option of persons to be members of the board having experience in the field of banking, management, finance or specialisation in any other field relating to the objects and activities undertaken by the co-operative society, as members of the board of such society: Provided that the number of such co-opted members shall not exceed two in addition to twenty-one directors specified in the first proviso to clause (1): Provided further that such co-opted members shall not have the right to vote in any election of the co-operative society in their capacity as such member or to be eligible to be elected as office bearers of the board: Provided also that the functional directors of a co-operative society shall also be the members of the board and such members shall be excluded for the purpose of counting the total number of directors specified in the first proviso to clause (1).
key_terms: twenty-one-director maximum board-size cap
mandatory SC/ST and women board-seat reservation on co-operative societies
five-year board term with casual-vacancy nomination-fill exception
non-voting co-opted expert directors on co-operative boards

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243ZJ constitutionally fixes the ceiling and internal composition of a co-operative society's board — a hard twenty-one-director cap, mandatory reservation of one SC/ST seat and two women's seats where the society has members from those categories, a five-year board term (with a nomination-based casual-vacancy fill mechanism only in the term's second half), and up to two additional non-voting expert co-opted directors alongside functional directors who sit on the board without counting against the twenty-one-director cap.
essential_elements: Clause (1) leaves director count to State law but caps it at twenty-one directors maximum.
The second proviso to clause (1) mandates reservation of one SC/ST seat and two women's seats on boards of individual-membership societies with members from those categories.

Clause (2) fixes a five-year board term, office-bearer terms conterminous with the board's term, and permits casual-vacancy filling by nomination (from the same member class) only if less than half the original term remains.

Clause (3) mandates State-law provision for co-opting up to two additional expert directors (banking/management/finance/specialised fields), who are denied voting rights and ineligible for office-bearer election.
Functional directors are counted as board members but excluded from the twenty-one-director cap calculation.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The twenty-one-director cap and mandatory SC/ST/women reservation directly constrain State legislative discretion in a way that has no precise analogue in Part IX/IXA's more open-ended composition provisions — Part IXB is markedly more prescriptive and detailed about internal board mechanics than the Panchayat/Municipality Parts are about their own bodies.

The non-voting co-opted-expert-director design mirrors Article 243R(2)(a)(i)'s non-voting Municipal expert-member provision, again ensuring unelected specialists cannot outvote elected member-representatives — a recurring constitutional design pattern across all three self-government Parts.

The casual-vacancy nomination exception is itself a deliberate carve-out from the 'democratic member-control' principle of Article 243ZI, justified only for the practical case where so little of the term remains that a fresh election would be disproportionate.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243ZJ as the single most detailed internal-governance Article across Parts IX, IXA, and IXB — its numeric specificity (twenty-one directors, five years, two co-opted members, one SC/ST plus two women's seats) reflects Parliament's intent to directly constitutionalize co-operative board mechanics rather than leave them entirely to State discretion, a notably stronger intervention than the corresponding Panchayat/Municipality provisions.

sections.title: Election of members of board
sections.raw_text:
243ZK. Election of members of board.—(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any law made by the Legislature of a State, the election of a board shall be conducted before the expiry of the term of the board so as to ensure that the newly elected members of the board assume office immediately on the expiry of the term of the office of members of the outgoing board.
(2) The superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls for, and the conduct of, all elections to a co-operative society shall vest in such an authority or body, as may be provided by the Legislature of a State, by law: Provided that the Legislature of a State may, by law, provide for the procedure and guidelines for the conduct of such elections.
key_terms: seamless board-transition election-timing mandate for co-operative societies
State-law-designated election authority for co-operative societies

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 243ZK mandates that co-operative board elections be conducted before the outgoing board's term expires, so the newly elected board can assume office immediately without any administrative gap, and leaves the identity of the election-conducting authority (unlike Article 243K's constitutionally fixed State Election Commission for Panchayats/Municipalities) entirely to State law.
essential_elements: Clause (1) mandates election completion before the outgoing board's term expires, ensuring immediate, gap-free handover — this overrides any contrary State law ('notwithstanding').
Clause (2) vests superintendence, direction, and control of co-operative electoral rolls and election conduct in whatever authority or body State law designates.
The proviso to clause (2) allows State law to further prescribe procedure and guidelines for conducting such elections.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a deliberate structural departure from both Article 243K (Panchayats) and Article 243ZA (Municipalities), which vest election administration in a single constitutionally created State Election Commission — Article 243ZK leaves the choice of election authority to ordinary State legislation, reflecting that co-operative societies are member-owned economic bodies rather than units of political government, so a less constitutionally rigid election-administration structure was considered appropriate.

The seamless-transition mandate directly serves the Article 243ZI 'democratic member-control' principle and the Article 243ZL six-month supersession cap by preventing administrative or political actors from indefinitely delaying board elections to prolong an outgoing board's (or an appointed administrator's) control.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 243ZK's clause (1) timing mandate together with Article 243ZL's supersession cap — together they form the two-part guarantee against a co-operative society being left without a genuinely elected board for any extended period.

sections.title: Supersession and suspension of board and interim management
sections.raw_text:
243ZL. Supersession and suspension of board and interim management.—(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any law for the time being in force, no board shall be superseded or kept under suspension for a period exceeding six months: Provided that the board may be superseded or kept under suspension in a case—
(i) of its persistent default; or
(ii) of negligence in the performance of its duties; or
(iii) the board has committed any act prejudicial to the interests of the co-operative society or its members; or
(iv) there is stalemate in the constitution or functions of the board; or
