Article 257A (which once dealt with deployment of Union armed/other forces to assist States) was inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) and later omitted by the 44th Amendment (1978) — now a spent, omitted provision with no current legal effect, reflecting the post-Emergency (1975-77) rollback of centralizing amendments.

This Article's directions are backed by the same Article 365 consequence as Article 256 — non-compliance with a lawful Union direction can expose a State Government to a claim that its governance is not being carried on in accordance with the Constitution.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 257 as the specific-subject elaboration of Article 256's general compliance obligation — pay attention to clause (4)'s cost-reimbursement guarantee, which tempers what would otherwise be an unfunded-mandate-style burden on States, and note that Article 257A is now an inert historical relic.

sections.title: Power of the Union to confer powers, etc., on States in certain cases
sections.raw_text:
258. Power of the Union to confer powers, etc., on States in certain cases.—(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may, with the consent of the Government of a State, entrust either conditionally or unconditionally to that Government or to its officers functions in relation to any matter to which the executive power of the Union extends.
(2) A law made by Parliament which applies in any State may, notwithstanding that it relates to a matter with respect to which the Legislature of the State has no power to make laws, confer powers and impose duties, or authorise the conferring of powers and the imposition of duties, upon the State or officers and authorities thereof.
(3) Where by virtue of this article powers and duties have been conferred or imposed upon a State or officers or authorities thereof, there shall be paid by the Government of India to the State such sum as may be agreed, or, in default of agreement, as may be determined by an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Justice of India, in respect of any extra costs of administration incurred by the State in connection with the exercise of those powers and duties.
key_terms: Presidential entrustment of Union executive functions to a consenting State
Parliament's power to confer State-implementation duties even on non-State-List matters
Union's reimbursement obligation for extra administrative costs under Article 258

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 258 lets the Union delegate downward: the President may, with a State's consent, entrust Union executive functions to that State's Government or officers (clause (1)), and Parliament may, by law, confer powers/duties on a State or its officers to help implement Union laws even on matters outside the State Legislature's own competence (clause (2)) — again backed by a Union reimbursement guarantee for extra administrative costs, using the same Chief-Justice-arbitrator mechanism as Article 257(4).
essential_elements: Clause (1) is a President-to-State-Government entrustment power, requiring the State's consent, and covering any matter within the Union's executive power — conditional or unconditional.

Clause (2) is a Parliament-to-State-Government/officers conferral power via ordinary legislation, notably not requiring State consent (unlike clause (1)) and applicable even to matters where the State Legislature itself has no law-making competence.
Clause (3) mirrors Article 257(4)'s cost-reimbursement guarantee and Chief-Justice-of-India arbitration mechanism for extra administrative costs incurred under either clause (1) or clause (2).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (1)'s consent requirement versus clause (2)'s absence of an explicit consent requirement is a meaningful textual distinction — clause (2) operates through ordinary Parliamentary legislation applicable in the State, which itself supplies the legal authority without needing separate State Government consent for each instance.

Article 258A (inserted by the 7th Amendment, 1956) is the mirror-image power for a State to entrust its own executive functions to the Union (with the Governor entrusting, subject to Union Government consent) — together, Articles 258 and 258A create a genuinely bidirectional executive-function-sharing mechanism between Union and States.

This is a practical, commonly used delegation mechanism (Union schemes and programmes are frequently implemented through State machinery under Article 258 entrustment) that avoids the Union needing to build entirely separate administrative infrastructure in every State.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 258 (and its mirror, Article 258A) as the Constitution's administrative-delegation toolkit — Union-to-State under Article 258, State-to-Union under Article 258A — both cost-reimbursed via the same Chief-Justice-arbitrator mechanism used in Article 257(4).

sections.title: Power of the States to entrust functions to the Union
sections.raw_text: 258A. Power of the States to entrust functions to the Union.—Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the Governor of a State may, with the consent of the Government of India, entrust either conditionally or unconditionally to that Government or to its officers functions in relation to any matter to which the executive power of the State extends.
key_terms: Gubernatorial entrustment of State executive functions to the Union

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 258A (inserted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956) is the precise mirror-image of Article 258(1): it lets a State's Governor, with the consent of the Government of India, entrust State executive functions to the Union Government or its officers, conditionally or unconditionally.
essential_elements: The entrusting authority is the State's Governor (not the State Government or Legislature directly, though the Governor acts on the State Council of Ministers' aid and advice per ordinary constitutional practice).
Union consent is required — the reciprocal requirement to Article 258(1)'s State-consent requirement.
The functions entrusted must be ones to which the State's own executive power extends.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article completes the bidirectional entrustment scheme with Article 258 — Union-to-State entrustment needs State consent (Article 258(1)); State-to-Union entrustment needs Union consent (Article 258A) — a symmetric federal cooperation design.

Unlike Article 258, Article 258A has no separate cost-reimbursement clause of its own; in practice, cost arrangements for State-to-Union entrustments would need to be separately negotiated or provided for, since Article 258(3)'s reimbursement mechanism is textually tied to 'this article' (Article 258), not Article 258A.
This provision was added relatively early (1956) alongside the broader post-States-Reorganisation-Act constitutional adjustments of that period.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 258A immediately alongside Article 258(1) as a matched pair — same conditional/unconditional entrustment structure, opposite direction, and note the absence of an explicit Article 258A cost-reimbursement clause as a genuine asymmetry between the two provisions.

sections.title: Jurisdiction of the Union in relation to territories outside India
sections.raw_text: 260. Jurisdiction of the Union in relation to territories outside India.—The Government of India may by agreement with the Government of any territory not being part of the territory of India undertake any executive, legislative or judicial functions vested in the Government of such territory, but every such agreement shall be subject to, and governed by, any law relating to the exercise of foreign jurisdiction for the time being in force.
key_terms: Union's power to undertake executive/legislative/judicial functions in foreign territory by agreement

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 260 lets the Government of India, by agreement with the government of a foreign territory (not part of India), undertake executive, legislative, or judicial functions otherwise vested in that foreign territory's government — subject always to any law on the exercise of foreign jurisdiction then in force.
essential_elements: The mechanism requires an agreement with the foreign territory's government — it is consensual, not unilateral.
The functions that may be undertaken span all three branches (executive, legislative, judicial) of the foreign territory's governance.
Any such agreement operates subject to, and is governed by, existing foreign-jurisdiction law (historically, legislation like the Foreign Jurisdiction Act, 1947).
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article has had limited but real historical application — for instance, arrangements involving Sikkim before its 1975 accession as a full State, or certain protectorate/agency-style historical arrangements with neighbouring territories.

Article 260 is functionally distinct from Article 1's definition of India's own territory and from Article 2/3's admission/formation of new States — it deals with the Union exercising governmental functions in territory that remains outside India, rather than incorporating new territory into India.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 260 as a specialized, agreement-based extension of Indian governmental functions into foreign territory — distinct from and narrower than actual territorial incorporation, and always bounded by prevailing foreign-jurisdiction law.

sections.title: Public acts, records and judicial proceedings
sections.raw_text:
261. Public acts, records and judicial proceedings.—(1) Full faith and credit shall be given throughout the territory of India to public acts, records and judicial proceedings of the Union and of every State.
(2) The manner in which and the conditions under which the acts, records and proceedings referred to in clause (1) shall be proved and the effect thereof determined shall be as provided by law made by Parliament.
(3) Final judgments or orders delivered or passed by civil courts in any part of the territory of India shall be capable of execution anywhere within that territory according to law.
key_terms: full faith and credit for public acts/records/judicial proceedings across India
Parliament's power to prescribe proof/effect procedure
pan-India executability of civil court final judgments

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 261 guarantees that public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of the Union and every State are given full faith and credit throughout India's territory — so a document or judgment valid in one State is recognized throughout the country — with Parliament empowered to legislate on how such acts/records/proceedings are proved and their legal effect, and with a specific guarantee that final civil-court judgments/orders are executable anywhere in India according to law.
essential_elements: Clause (1) is the core full-faith-and-credit guarantee, borrowed conceptually from the analogous US constitutional clause, ensuring inter-State/Union legal recognition rather than treating each State as a separate legal universe.
Clause (2) delegates the proof-and-effect mechanics (how such acts/records/proceedings are established in evidence and what legal weight they carry) to Parliamentary legislation.

Clause (3) specifically guarantees pan-India executability of final civil judgments/orders — a litigant who wins a civil decree in one State's courts can enforce it anywhere in India, subject to applicable procedural law (principally the Code of Civil Procedure's provisions on execution of decrees, including transfer of decrees for execution in another court).
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article underpins the practical operation of India's unified judicial system despite its federal political structure — unlike the US, where full faith and credit was historically more contested for certain matters, India's single integrated judiciary (with the Supreme Court at its apex over all State High Courts) gives this guarantee a comparatively smoother practical application.

Clause (3)'s execution guarantee is what makes decree-transfer provisions under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (e.g., Section 39, execution of decrees by courts which passed them or by transferee courts) constitutionally grounded and mandatory in their pan-India reach.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 261 as the constitutional foundation for treating India's legal landscape as a single, mutually-recognizing system — clause (3) in particular is the direct constitutional root of the CPC's decree-execution-transfer machinery familiar from civil procedure practice.

sections.title: Adjudication of disputes relating to waters of inter-State rivers or river valleys
sections.raw_text:
262. Adjudication of disputes relating to waters of inter-State rivers or river valleys.—(1) Parliament may by law provide for the adjudication of any dispute or complaint with respect to the use, distribution or control of the waters of, or in, any inter-State river or river valley.
(2) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may by law provide that neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction in respect of any such dispute or complaint as is referred to in clause (1).
key_terms: Parliament's power to legislate inter-State river water dispute adjudication mechanisms
Parliament's power to oust Supreme Court/all-court jurisdiction over such disputes

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 262 gives Parliament exclusive power to create special adjudication mechanisms for inter-State river/river-valley water disputes, and — remarkably — lets Parliament by law bar even the Supreme Court (and all other courts) from exercising jurisdiction over such disputes, channeling them instead into the specialized tribunal mechanisms Parliament creates (principally under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956).
essential_elements: Clause (1) empowers Parliament to legislate on adjudicating disputes over the use, distribution, or control of inter-State river/river-valley waters.

Clause (2) is the unusual ouster clause: 'notwithstanding anything in this Constitution,' Parliament may exclude both the Supreme Court's and every other court's jurisdiction over such disputes — a rare express constitutional authorization to oust even Supreme Court jurisdiction, which otherwise enjoys broad original jurisdiction under Article 131 over Centre-State/inter-State disputes.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is one of the very few provisions in the Constitution expressly permitting exclusion of the Supreme Court's jurisdiction — a significant departure from the Court's ordinarily entrenched role, reflecting the framers' judgment that river-water disputes (often highly technical, politically sensitive, and multi-State) are better resolved through specialized tribunals than ordinary adversarial litigation.

The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 (enacted under Article 262) establishes the tribunal mechanism actually used for major disputes (e.g., Cauvery, Krishna, Narmada water disputes) — tribunal awards under that Act have historically been treated as having the same practical force as a Supreme Court decree once notified, though litigation over the scope of the jurisdictional bar and the tribunals' functioning has repeatedly reached the Supreme Court on related/collateral questions.

Whether Article 262(2)'s ouster is absolute in practice has been contested — courts have entertained certain collateral challenges (e.g., procedural fairness, tribunal composition) even while broadly respecting the jurisdictional bar on the merits of water allocation itself.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 262 as a deliberately specialized federal-dispute carve-out — its clause (2) ouster power is exceptional constitutional text, and should be read alongside the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956's tribunal mechanism to understand how the power has actually been exercised.

sections.title: Provisions with respect to an inter-State Council
sections.raw_text:
263. Provisions with respect to an inter-State Council.—If at any time it appears to the President that the public interests would be served by the establishment of a Council charged with the duty of—
(a) inquiring into and advising upon disputes which may have arisen between States;
(b) investigating and discussing subjects in which some or all of the States, or the Union and one or more of the States, have a common interest; or
(c) making recommendations upon any such subject and, in particular, recommendations for the better co-ordination of policy and action with respect to that subject,
it shall be lawful for the President by order to establish such a Council, and to define the nature of the duties to be performed by it and its organisation and procedure.
key_terms: Presidential power to establish an Inter-State Council
Inter-State Council's three-fold advisory/investigative/recommendatory functions

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 263 closes Part XI by empowering the President, whenever the public interest would be served, to establish an Inter-State Council by order — a cooperative-federalism body charged with inquiring into and advising on inter-State disputes, investigating/discussing matters of common Union-State or inter-State interest, and making policy-coordination recommendations, with its organisation and procedure defined by the same Presidential order.
essential_elements: The power is discretionary and conditional on the President's assessment that public interest would be served — there is no mandatory obligation to establish such a Council.
Clause (a) empowers the Council to inquire into and advise on inter-State disputes.
Clause (b) empowers it to investigate and discuss subjects of common interest among States, or between the Union and States.
Clause (c) empowers it to make recommendations, particularly for better policy/action coordination, on such subjects.
The President's order also fixes the Council's organisation and procedure — Article 263 itself does not prescribe a fixed composition.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The actual Inter-State Council was established by Presidential Order in 1990 (following the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation), decades after the Constitution's commencement — illustrating that this is a genuinely discretionary, not self-executing, power.

The Inter-State Council is advisory and consultative only — it has no binding decision-making or adjudicatory power (contrast Article 262's binding-tribunal river-dispute mechanism) — its value lies in fostering cooperative federalism dialogue rather than legal compulsion.

Article 263 is functionally complementary to, but distinct from, Article 131's Supreme Court original jurisdiction over Centre-State/inter-State legal disputes — Article 263 addresses political/policy coordination and dispute resolution outside formal adjudication, while Article 131 addresses genuine legal disputes.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 263 as Part XI's cooperative-federalism capstone — a flexible, non-binding, dialogue-oriented mechanism (contrast the binding Article 262 river-tribunal power) whose actual institutional form (the Inter-State Council) was only established decades after the Constitution's commencement, on the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation.

sections.title: Interpretation
sections.raw_text: 264. Interpretation.—In this Part, "Finance Commission" means a Finance Commission constituted under article 280.
key_terms: Finance Commission defined for Part XII purposes

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 264 opens Part XII (Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits) with a single interpretive definition: wherever 'Finance Commission' appears in this Part, it means the Finance Commission constituted under Article 280.
essential_elements: This is a pure definitional/interpretive clause with no substantive rule of its own.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The current text was substituted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, replacing an earlier, more elaborate original Article 264 that dealt with transitional financial arrangements no longer needed after the 1956 States Reorganisation.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 264 as a simple cross-reference anchor — whenever 'Finance Commission' appears anywhere in Part XII, trace it back to Article 280's constitutional body.

sections.title: Taxes not to be imposed save by authority of law
sections.raw_text: 265. Taxes not to be imposed save by authority of law.—No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law.
key_terms: no taxation without law — constitutional foundation of Indian tax law

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 265 states, in a single sweeping sentence, one of the most foundational principles of Indian public finance law: no tax can be levied or collected except under the authority of law — meaning a validly enacted statute (not executive fiat, custom, or mere administrative practice) must authorize every tax.
essential_elements: 'Levied' and 'collected' are both covered — both the imposition and the actual collection of a tax require legal authority; a tax validly imposed but collected in excess of or contrary to that legal authority is equally unconstitutional.

'Law' here means a validly enacted statute (by Parliament or a State Legislature, within their respective competence under Article 246) — executive circulars, notifications without statutory backing, or mere government policy cannot themselves impose a tax.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This principle is the Indian analogue to the international 'no taxation without representation'/rule-of-law principle, and grounds the extensive body of Indian tax litigation testing whether a particular levy has valid legislative authority, is within the taxing Legislature's competence under the Seventh Schedule, and is collected strictly per the statute's terms.

A tax that is otherwise validly imposed by law but administered in a manner exceeding statutory authority (e.g., collecting more than the law permits, or via an unauthorized procedure) can still be challenged under this Article even though the underlying taxing statute itself is valid.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 265 as Indian tax law's foundational constitutional pillar — virtually every tax dispute ultimately traces back to whether the specific levy and its collection are backed by valid, competent legislative authority under this Article.

sections.title: Consolidated Funds and public accounts of India and of the States
sections.raw_text:
266. Consolidated Funds and public accounts of India and of the States.—(1) Subject to the provisions of article 267 and to the provisions of this Chapter with respect to the assignment of the whole or part of the net proceeds of certain taxes and duties to States, all revenues received by the Government of India, all loans raised by that Government by the issue of treasury bills, loans or ways and means advances and all moneys received by that Government in repayment of loans shall form one consolidated fund to be entitled "the Consolidated Fund of India", and all revenues received by the Government of a State, all loans raised by that Government by the issue of treasury bills, loans or ways and means advances and all moneys received by that Government in repayment of loans shall form one consolidated fund to be entitled "the Consolidated Fund of the State".
(2) All other public moneys received by or on behalf of the Government of India or the Government of a State shall be credited to the public account of India or the public account of the State, as the case may be.
(3) No moneys out of the Consolidated Fund of India or the Consolidated Fund of a State shall be appropriated except in accordance with law and for the purposes and in the manner provided in this Constitution.
key_terms: Consolidated Fund of India
Consolidated Fund of a State
public account of India/State
no appropriation from Consolidated Fund except by law

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 266 creates the two foundational public-money repositories for every government in India: the Consolidated Fund (of India, and separately of each State), which pools all revenues, loan proceeds, and loan repayments received by that government, and the public account, which catches all other public moneys — and mandates that no money leaves a Consolidated Fund except strictly in accordance with law and for constitutionally provided purposes/manner.
essential_elements: Clause (1) defines the Consolidated Fund of India/of a State as pooling: all revenues received, all loans raised via treasury bills/loans/ways-and-means advances, and all loan-repayment receipts — the Union's and each State's respective 'main bank account.'

Clause (2) defines the public account as the catch-all for other public moneys (e.g., moneys held in a fiduciary/trust capacity, such as provident fund deposits, small savings collections) not part of the Consolidated Fund.

Clause (3) is the critical control mechanism: no appropriation (withdrawal/spending) from a Consolidated Fund is permitted except in accordance with law and for purposes/in a manner the Constitution provides — this is what makes the annual Appropriation Act (following the budget/Demands for Grants process under Articles 112-114/202-204) constitutionally mandatory.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Consolidated Fund/public account distinction matters because withdrawal rules differ sharply: Consolidated Fund withdrawals require Parliamentary/Legislative appropriation via law (clause (3)), while public account moneys (since the government holds them essentially as a banker/trustee for the true owner, not as the government's own revenue) do not require the same appropriation process.

This Article is the structural foundation for the entire budget process detailed later in Part V (Articles 112-117, Union) and Part VI (Articles 202-207, States) — the Consolidated Fund is the fund those budget/appropriation provisions actually govern.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 266 as the plumbing beneath India's entire public-finance constitutional architecture — Consolidated Fund withdrawals need a law (Appropriation Act), the public account does not, and virtually every subsequent financial provision in Part XII operates on, or interacts with, one or both of these two funds.

sections.title: Contingency Fund
sections.raw_text:
267. Contingency Fund.—(1) Parliament may by law establish a Contingency Fund in the nature of an imprest to be entitled "the Contingency Fund of India" into which shall be paid from time to time such sums as may be determined by such law, and the said Fund shall be placed at the disposal of the President to enable advances to be made by him out of such Fund for the purposes of meeting unforeseen expenditure pending authorisation of such expenditure by Parliament by law under article 115 or article 116.
(2) The Legislature of a State may by law establish a Contingency Fund in the nature of an imprest to be entitled "the Contingency Fund of the State" into which shall be paid from time to time such sums as may be determined by such law, and the said Fund shall be placed at the disposal of the Governor of the State to enable advances to be made by him out of such Fund for the purposes of meeting unforeseen expenditure pending authorisation of such expenditure by the Legislature of the State by law under article 205 or article 206.
key_terms: Contingency Fund of India
Contingency Fund of a State
imprest advances for unforeseen expenditure pending Parliamentary/Legislative authorisation

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 267 lets Parliament (and separately, each State Legislature) establish a Contingency Fund — an 'imprest' (standing advance fund) placed at the President's (or Governor's) disposal specifically to meet genuinely unforeseen expenditure quickly, before Parliament or the State Legislature has had the chance to formally authorize that spending through the ordinary supplementary/additional grants process under Articles 115-116 (Union) or 205-206 (States).
essential_elements: Clause (1) establishes the Contingency Fund of India, a Parliament-created imprest fund at the President's disposal for urgent unforeseen expenditure pending formal Parliamentary authorisation.
Clause (2) establishes the parallel Contingency Fund of the State mechanism, at the Governor's disposal, pending State Legislature authorisation.

In both cases, the fund exists specifically to bridge the gap between an emergent, unforeseen spending need and the time it takes to secure formal legislative authorisation — it is not itself a substitute for that authorisation, only a temporary advance mechanism pending it.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Unlike the Consolidated Fund (Article 266), a Contingency Fund advance does not require prior specific legislative appropriation for that expenditure — that is precisely its point (speed in emergencies) — but the expenditure must still eventually be regularized: once Parliament/the Legislature authorizes the expenditure via a supplementary/additional grant, the amount advanced from the Contingency Fund is recouped back into it from the Consolidated Fund.

The Contingency Fund of India Act, 1950 is the Parliamentary law actually establishing and governing the Union's Contingency Fund under clause (1); each State similarly has its own Contingency Fund Act.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 267 as the constitutional 'emergency cash reserve' mechanism — distinct from and smaller in ambit than the Consolidated Fund, existing purely to bridge genuinely unforeseen spending needs pending the ordinary Article 115/116 (or 205/206) authorisation process, with amounts advanced later recouped once that authorisation is secured.

sections.title: Duties levied by the Union but collected and appropriated by the States
sections.raw_text:
268. Duties levied by the Union but collected and appropriated by the States.—(1) Such stamp duties as are mentioned in the Union List shall be levied by the Government of India but shall be collected—
(a) in the case where such duties are leviable within any Union territory, by the Government of India, and
(b) in other cases, by the States within which such duties are respectively leviable.
(2) The proceeds in any financial year of any such duty leviable within any State shall not form part of the Consolidated Fund of India, but shall be assigned to that State.
key_terms: Union-List stamp duties levied by Union, collected by States, proceeds assigned to States

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 268 sets up a specific revenue-sharing arrangement for Union List stamp duties: the Union levies (imposes) these duties, but the actual collection happens locally — by the Union Government itself within Union territories, or by the respective States elsewhere — and every rupee collected within a State's territory is assigned entirely to that State rather than flowing into the Consolidated Fund of India.
essential_elements: The duties in question are specifically Union-List stamp duties (Union List Entry 91-type duties) — a narrow, specific category, not general taxation.
Levy (legal imposition) remains with the Union, but collection is bifurcated: Union Government for Union territories, respective States for their own territories.
Proceeds collected within a State go entirely to that State — bypassing the Consolidated Fund of India altogether (contrast Article 270's shared-distribution mechanism).
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a 'levy-collect' split unique among Article 268-270's several distinct revenue-sharing models — Article 268A (service tax, now omitted after GST subsumed it) and Article 269/269A (inter-State sales tax/IGST) each use different splits; Article 268 is the simplest, oldest model (Union levies, State collects and keeps 100%).

Because the Union sets the rate/law but the State collects and keeps the proceeds, this creates an interesting federal dynamic: the State has an administrative incentive to collect efficiently (it keeps everything) while having no legislative control over the duty's rate or structure (which remains Parliament's exclusive Union List domain).
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 268 as the first (and simplest) of several distinct Union-State revenue-sharing models in this Chapter — Union levies, State collects and keeps all proceeds — and contrast it against Article 270's shared-net-proceeds-distribution model that follows shortly after.

sections.title: Taxes levied and collected by the Union but assigned to the States
sections.raw_text:
269. Taxes levied and collected by the Union but assigned to the States.—(1) Taxes on the sale or purchase of goods and taxes on the consignment of goods except as provided in article 269A shall be levied and collected by the Government of India but shall be assigned and shall be deemed to have been assigned to the States on or after the 1st day of April, 1996 in the manner provided in clause (2).
Explanation.—For the purposes of this clause,—
(a) the expression "taxes on the sale or purchase of goods" shall mean taxes on sale or purchase of goods other than newspapers, where such sale or purchase takes place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce;
(b) the expression "taxes on the consignment of goods" shall mean taxes on the consignment of goods (whether the consignment is to the person making it or to any other person), where such consignment takes place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce.
(2) The net proceeds in any financial year of any such tax, except in so far as those proceeds represent proceeds attributable to Union territories, shall not form part of the Consolidated Fund of India, but shall be assigned to the States within which that tax is leviable in that year, and shall be distributed among those States in accordance with such principles of distribution as may be formulated by Parliament by law.
(3) Parliament may by law formulate principles for determining when a sale or purchase of, or consignment of goods takes place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce.
key_terms: inter-State sale/purchase and consignment taxes levied+collected by Union, assigned to States
Parliament's power to formulate inter-State-sale/consignment situs principles

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 269 covers taxes on inter-State sale/purchase of goods and inter-State consignment of goods: the Union both levies and collects these taxes (unlike Article 268's Union-levy/State-collect split), but the entire net proceeds (except the Union-territory-attributable portion) are assigned to the States where the tax is leviable and distributed among them per Parliament-formulated principles — with Article 269A now carving GST-covered inter-State supplies out of this Article's scope.
essential_elements: Clause (1) covers two specific tax categories — inter-State sale/purchase-of-goods tax and inter-State consignment-of-goods tax — now expressly excluding whatever Article 269A (GST) covers.

Clause (2) directs the entire net proceeds (minus the Union-territory-attributable share) to the States where leviable, distributed per Parliament-formulated principles — a full assignment, not a partial share.

Clause (3) empowers Parliament to formulate the legal principles determining when a sale/purchase/consignment counts as occurring 'in the course of inter-State trade or commerce' — a historically contentious situs question resolved via the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956's principles.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Post-GST (2017), Article 269's practical scope has shrunk dramatically, since GST subsumed most inter-State sale/purchase taxation into Article 269A's IGST mechanism — Article 269 now mainly retains relevance for goods still outside GST (e.g., certain petroleum products, alcoholic liquor for human consumption).

The 'Union levies and collects, but proceeds fully assigned to States' model here is distinct from both Article 268's Union-levy/State-collect model and Article 270's shared-distribution-between-Union-and-States model — Article 269 gives States effectively 100% of the relevant proceeds.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 269 as historically central to India's pre-GST inter-State sales-tax regime (via the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956) — recognize that its practical field of operation has been substantially displaced by Article 269A's GST mechanism for most goods and services since 2017.

sections.title: Levy and collection of goods and services tax in course of inter-State trade or commerce
sections.raw_text:
269A. Levy and collection of goods and services tax in course of inter-State trade or commerce.—(1) Goods and services tax on supplies in the course of inter-State trade or commerce shall be levied and collected by the Government of India and such tax shall be apportioned between the Union and the States in the manner as may be provided by Parliament by law on the recommendations of the Goods and Services Tax Council.
Explanation.—For the purposes of this clause, supply of goods, or of services, or both in the course of import into the territory of India shall be deemed to be supply of goods, or of services, or both in the course of inter-State trade or commerce.
(2) The amount apportioned to a State under clause (1) shall not form part of the Consolidated Fund of India.
(3) Where an amount collected as tax levied under clause (1) has been used for payment of the tax levied by a State under article 246A, such amount shall not form part of the Consolidated Fund of India.
(4) Where an amount collected as tax levied by a State under article 246A has been used for payment of the tax levied under clause (1), such amount shall not form part of the Consolidated Fund of the State.
(5) Parliament may, by law, formulate the principles for determining the place of supply, and when a supply of goods, or of services, or both takes place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce.
key_terms: Integrated GST (IGST) levied by Union, apportioned between Union and States on GST Council recommendation
imports deemed inter-State supply for IGST purposes
cross-utilisation of IGST/State-GST amounts kept outside Consolidated Funds
Parliament's power to formulate place-of-supply principles

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 269A (inserted by the 101st Amendment, 2016) is the constitutional foundation for Integrated GST (IGST): the Union levies and collects GST on inter-State supplies (and on imports into India, which are deemed inter-State supplies), then apportions it between the Union and the States per Parliament-made law based on the GST Council's recommendations — with careful accounting rules ensuring that cross-utilised IGST/State-GST credits never get double-counted into either the Consolidated Fund of India or of a State.
essential_elements: Clause (1) vests IGST levy-and-collection exclusively with the Union, with apportionment governed by Parliamentary law following GST Council recommendations — a genuinely novel three-step process (levy → collect → apportion by recommendation-driven law).
The Explanation deems imports into India as inter-State supply for IGST purposes — extending the same apportionment mechanism to import transactions.

Clauses (2)-(4) are technical fund-accounting rules preventing IGST-State apportionment amounts and cross-utilised IGST/State-GST credit amounts from artificially inflating either Consolidated Fund — necessary because GST's input-tax-credit mechanism allows taxpayers to offset IGST liability against State-GST credit and vice versa across jurisdictions.

Clause (5) empowers Parliament to formulate 'place of supply' principles — the modern GST-era successor to Article 269(3)'s older inter-State-sale-situs principles, now implemented via the IGST Act, 2017's place-of-supply provisions.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article, together with Article 246A and Article 279A, forms the complete constitutional GST trio inserted by the 101st Amendment — 246A grants concurrent legislative competence, 279A creates the GST Council as the recommending body, and 269A specifically handles the inter-State/IGST apportionment mechanics.

The clauses (2)-(4) accounting rules reflect a genuinely new fiscal-federalism challenge GST created: because a single transaction's tax can, through credit mechanisms, effectively move value between Union and State fiscal accounts, the Constitution had to be amended with specific rules to prevent that movement from being double-counted or misallocated.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 269A as the specific inter-State/import leg of India's post-2017 GST architecture — always read it together with Article 246A (competence) and Article 279A (the GST Council that drives the apportionment formula this Article requires).

sections.title: Taxes levied and distributed between the Union and the States
sections.raw_text:
270. Taxes levied and distributed between the Union and the States.—(1) All taxes and duties referred to in the Union List, except the duties and taxes referred to in articles 268, 269 and 269A, respectively, surcharge on taxes and duties referred to in article 271 and any cess levied for specific purposes under any law made by Parliament shall be levied and collected by the Government of India and shall be distributed between the Union and the States in the manner provided in clause (2).
(1A) The tax collected by the Union under clause (1) of article 246A shall also be distributed between the Union and the States in the manner provided in clause (2).
(1B) The tax levied and collected by the Union under clause (2) of article 246A and article 269A, which has been used for payment of the tax levied by the Union under clause (1) of article 246A, and the amount apportioned to the Union under clause (1) of article 269A, shall also be distributed between the Union and the States in the manner provided in clause (2).
(2) Such percentage, as may be prescribed, of the net proceeds of any such tax or duty in any financial year shall not form part of the Consolidated Fund of India, but shall be assigned to the States within which that tax or duty is leviable in that year, and shall be distributed among those States in such manner and from such time as may be prescribed in the manner provided in clause (3).
(3) In this article, "prescribed" means, —
(i) until a Finance Commission has been constituted, prescribed by the President by order, and
(ii) after a Finance Commission has been constituted, prescribed by the President by order after considering the recommendations of the Finance Commission.
key_terms: general Union-List tax/duty pool shared between Union and States by prescribed percentage
Union's own-GST and IGST-derived amounts also brought into the shared-distribution pool
'prescribed' percentage set by President, post-Finance-Commission on its recommendations

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 270 is the Constitution's general revenue-sharing mechanism for most Union List taxes and duties (everything not already carved out to Articles 268, 269, 269A, or surcharges/cesses): the Union levies and collects them, but a President-prescribed percentage of the net proceeds — set with Finance Commission input once one exists — is distributed to the States rather than retained wholly by the Union, with clauses (1A) and (1B) extending the same shared-distribution treatment to the Union's own GST collections and certain IGST-derived amounts.
essential_elements: Clause (1) is the residual/general sharing rule: Union List taxes/duties not otherwise specifically allocated (excluding Articles 268/269/269A items, Article 271 surcharges, and Parliament-law-specific cesses) are levied/collected by the Union and distributed per clause (2)'s mechanism.

Clauses (1A) and (1B) (added by the 101st Amendment) extend the same distribution treatment to the Union's own-GST (CGST) collections and to certain amounts the Union collects/retains under the IGST mechanism — ensuring GST-era revenues flow through the same sharing formula as traditional Union List taxes.
Clause (2) sets the mechanics: a 'prescribed' percentage of net proceeds is carved out of the Consolidated Fund of India and assigned to States, distributed among them per a prescribed manner/timing.
Clause (3) defines 'prescribed': before any Finance Commission exists, the President alone prescribes by order; afterward, the President must consider the Finance Commission's recommendations first.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Surcharges (Article 271) and specific-purpose cesses are deliberately excluded from this sharing pool — meaning the Union can retain 100% of surcharge/cess revenue exclusively, a frequently criticized practice since it lets the Union increase its effective revenue share without triggering the Article 270 sharing formula, reducing the States' effective share of the divisible pool.

The Finance Commission's recommended 'vertical devolution' percentage (e.g., the 15th Finance Commission recommended 41% of the divisible pool to States) is exactly the 'prescribed' percentage under clause (2) — this Article is the constitutional hook implementing that number once the President accepts (or modifies) the Finance Commission's recommendation.

The 1996 shift (via the 80th Amendment) from a scheme where only specifically enumerated taxes were shared to today's 'all Union List taxes except carved-out categories are shared' scheme was a major fiscal-federalism reform, significantly broadening States' revenue base.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 270 as the central engine of India's vertical fiscal devolution — pair it directly with Article 280 (Finance Commission) to understand how the 'prescribed percentage' actually gets set in practice, and note how surcharges/cesses (Article 271) sit deliberately outside this sharing pool.

sections.title: Surcharge on certain duties and taxes for purposes of the Union
sections.raw_text: 271. Surcharge on certain duties and taxes for purposes of the Union.—Notwithstanding anything in articles 269 and 270, Parliament may at any time increase any of the duties or taxes referred to in those articles except the goods and services tax under article 246A, by a surcharge for purposes of the Union and the whole proceeds of any such surcharge shall form part of the Consolidated Fund of India.
key_terms: Parliament's surcharge power on Article 269/270 duties/taxes exclusively for the Union
GST expressly excluded from the surcharge power

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 271 lets Parliament, at any time and notwithstanding the Article 269/270 sharing schemes, add a surcharge on top of any Article 269 or 270 duty/tax — but that surcharge's entire proceeds go exclusively to the Union's own Consolidated Fund of India, bypassing the States entirely (GST is expressly excluded from this surcharge power since the 101st Amendment).
essential_elements: The surcharge power applies to duties/taxes referred to in Articles 269 and 270 specifically, expressly excluding GST under Article 246A.
The surcharge's entire proceeds go into the Consolidated Fund of India exclusively — none is shared with States, unlike the base duty/tax itself.
This is a Parliament-only power ('Parliament may at any time') — an ordinary Parliamentary law suffices, no Finance Commission or State-consultation process is constitutionally mandated.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is precisely the mechanism referenced in Article 270's exceptions-and-qualifications discussion above as a frequently criticized fiscal tool — because surcharge/cess revenue entirely bypasses the States' constitutionally guaranteed sharing formula, its increasing use over time (relative to base tax rates) has been a persistent source of Centre-State fiscal federalism tension, even though it is fully constitutional under this Article.

The GST exclusion (added by the 101st Amendment) reflects that GST already has its own dedicated apportionment mechanism (Article 246A/269A/279A) — layering an Article 271 surcharge on top of GST would conflict with that separate, GST-Council-driven scheme.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 271 as the Union's unilateral fiscal lever for retaining 100% of incremental revenue — always distinguish a 'surcharge' (Union-only, Article 271) from the 'base' duty/tax rate (shared per Article 270) when analyzing the real fiscal split between Union and States on any given levy.

sections.title: Grants in lieu of export duty on jute and jute products
sections.raw_text:
273. Grants in lieu of export duty on jute and jute products.—(1) There shall be charged on the Consolidated Fund of India in each year as grants-in-aid of the revenues of the States of Assam, Bihar, Odisha and West Bengal, in lieu of assignment of any share of the net proceeds in each year of export duty on jute and jute products to those States, such sums as may be prescribed.
(2) The sums so prescribed shall continue to be charged on the Consolidated Fund of India so long as any export duty on jute or jute products continues to be levied by the Government of India or until the expiration of ten years from the commencement of this Constitution whichever is earlier.
(3) In this article, the expression "prescribed" has the same meaning as in article 270.
key_terms: jute-export-duty compensatory grants to Assam/Bihar/Odisha/West Bengal
ten-year-or-earlier sunset tied to continued jute export duty levy

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 273 provides a historical compensatory-grant mechanism for the four jute-producing/exporting States (Assam, Bihar, Odisha, West Bengal): since jute export duty proceeds are not shared with States under the ordinary Article 269/270 mechanisms, this Article instead charges compensatory grants-in-aid directly on the Consolidated Fund of India, but only for as long as jute export duty continues to be levied or ten years from the Constitution's commencement (26 January 1950), whichever comes first.
essential_elements: The grant is charged automatically on the Consolidated Fund of India — no separate appropriation vote is needed each year since it is a charged (not voted) expenditure, similar in character to other charged expenditures under Articles 112(3)/202(3).
The named beneficiary States are specifically Assam, Bihar, Odisha, and West Bengal — India's principal historical jute-growing regions.
The duration is capped by whichever comes first: continued levy of jute export duty, or ten years from commencement (i.e., by 26 January 1960).
'Prescribed' carries the same meaning as in Article 270 — President-set, with Finance Commission input once constituted.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is now a spent, purely historical provision — the ten-year cap (or earlier cessation of jute export duty) means this Article has had no practical operative effect for decades, remaining in the constitutional text as a historical artifact of India's immediate post-independence jute-export economy.

It illustrates a broader pattern in Part XII of narrow, sector/region-specific compensatory provisions (paralleling Article 275's Assam tribal-area grants) addressing particular historical revenue-distribution anomalies rather than general principles.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 273 as a spent, time-barred historical relic — useful for understanding the immediate post-independence jute economy and Assam/Bihar/Odisha/West Bengal's specific fiscal concerns in 1950, but with no ongoing practical legal effect today.

sections.title: Prior recommendation of President required to Bills affecting taxation in which States are interested
sections.raw_text:
274. Prior recommendation of President required to Bills affecting taxation in which States are interested.—(1) No Bill or amendment which imposes or varies any tax or duty in which States are interested, or which varies the meaning of the expression "agricultural income" as defined for the purposes of the enactments relating to Indian income-tax, or which affects the principles on which under any of the foregoing provisions of this Chapter moneys are or may be distributable to States, or which imposes any such surcharge for the purposes of the Union as is mentioned in the foregoing provisions of this Chapter, shall be introduced or moved in either House of Parliament except on the recommendation of the President.
(2) In this article, the expression "tax or duty in which States are interested" means—
(a) a tax or duty the whole or part of the net proceeds whereof are assigned to any State; or
(b) a tax or duty by reference to the net proceeds whereof sums are for the time being payable out of the Consolidated Fund of India to any State.
key_terms: Presidential-recommendation precondition for Bills touching State-interested taxation
'tax or duty in which States are interested' defined
'agricultural income' definitional-change Bills require Presidential recommendation too

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 274 imposes a procedural gatekeeping requirement protecting States' fiscal interests in Parliament: no Bill or amendment touching a tax/duty in which States have a financial stake (or that redefines 'agricultural income' for income-tax purposes, or that affects Chapter I's State-distribution principles, or that imposes an Article 271 surcharge) can even be introduced in either House of Parliament without the President's prior recommendation.
essential_elements: The Presidential-recommendation requirement applies at the introduction/moving stage — before the Bill can even be formally taken up, not merely before passage.

It covers four distinct categories: Bills imposing/varying a 'tax or duty in which States are interested,' Bills redefining 'agricultural income' for income-tax purposes, Bills affecting the Chapter's State-distribution principles, and Bills imposing an Article 271 surcharge.

Clause (2) precisely defines 'tax or duty in which States are interested' as one whose net proceeds are wholly/partly assigned to States (Article 268/269/269A/270-type), or whose net proceeds trigger Consolidated-Fund-of-India payments to States (e.g., Article 275 grants).
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'agricultural income' redefinition trigger exists because agricultural income tax is constitutionally a State List subject (Entry 46) — yet 'agricultural income' as defined for central income-tax purposes affects the boundary between Union and State taxing fields, so States have a direct interest in how Parliament defines that boundary even though Parliament cannot itself tax agricultural income.

This Article operationalizes cooperative fiscal federalism procedurally — it ensures the executive (specifically the President, who by convention acts on Union Council of Ministers' advice, itself informed by inter-governmental fiscal consultation) has vetted any Bill with real State-fiscal-interest implications before Parliament can even debate it, rather than leaving States to challenge such legislation only after enactment.

Note this differs from the broader Article 117/207 Money Bill recommendation requirements — Article 274 is specifically targeted at the narrower category of State-interested taxation Bills, applicable regardless of whether the Bill otherwise qualifies as a Money Bill.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 274 as a State-fiscal-interest procedural safeguard operating at the Bill-introduction stage — always check clause (2)'s precise definition of 'tax or duty in which States are interested' before concluding a particular taxation Bill triggers this Presidential-recommendation requirement.

sections.title: Grants from the Union to certain States
sections.raw_text:
275. Grants from the Union to certain States.—(1) Such sums as Parliament may by law provide shall be charged on the Consolidated Fund of India in each year as grants-in-aid of the revenues of such States as Parliament may determine to be in need of assistance, and different sums may be fixed for different States:
Provided that there shall be paid out of the Consolidated Fund of India as grants-in-aid of the revenues of a State such capital and recurring sums as may be necessary to enable that State to meet the costs of such schemes of development as may be undertaken by the State with the approval of the Government of India for the purpose of promoting the welfare of the Scheduled Tribes in that State or raising the level of administration of the Scheduled Areas therein to that of the administration of the rest of the areas of that State:
Provided further that there shall be paid out of the Consolidated Fund of India as grants-in-aid of the revenues of the State of Assam sums, capital and recurring, equivalent to—
(a) the average excess of expenditure over the revenues during the two years immediately preceding the commencement of this Constitution in respect of the administration of the tribal areas specified in Part I of the table appended to paragraph 20 of the Sixth Schedule; and
(b) the costs of such schemes of development as may be undertaken by that State with the approval of the Government of India for the purpose of raising the level of administration of the said areas to that of the administration of the rest of the areas of that State.
(1A) On and from the formation of the autonomous State under article 244A,—
(i) any sums payable under clause (a) of the second proviso to clause (1) shall, if the autonomous State comprises all the tribal areas referred to therein, be paid to the autonomous State, and, if the autonomous State comprises only some of those tribal areas, be apportioned between the State of Assam and the autonomous State as the President may, by order, specify;
(ii) there shall be paid out of the Consolidated Fund of India as grants-in-aid of the revenues of the autonomous State sums, capital and recurring, equivalent to the costs of such schemes of development as may be undertaken by the autonomous State with the approval of the Government of India for the purpose of raising the level of administration of that State to that of the administration of the rest of the State of Assam.
(2) Until provision is made by Parliament under clause (1), the powers conferred on Parliament under that clause shall be exercisable by the President by order and any order made by the President under this clause shall have effect subject to any provision so made by Parliament:
Provided that after a Finance Commission has been constituted no order shall be made under this clause by the President except after considering the recommendations of the Finance Commission.
key_terms: general need-based Union grants-in-aid to States
mandatory Scheduled Tribes/Scheduled Areas welfare-and-administration grants proviso
Assam Sixth Schedule tribal-area special grant
Article 244A autonomous State grant apportionment
President's stand-in power pending Parliamentary provision, subject to Finance Commission consultation

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 275 is the Constitution's needs-based (as opposed to Article 270's formula-based, share-of-taxes) Union-to-State grant mechanism: Parliament may charge sums on the Consolidated Fund of India as grants-in-aid for States it determines need assistance (with different amounts for different States), with two mandatory provisos guaranteeing specific grants for Scheduled Tribes welfare/Scheduled Areas administration generally, and for Assam's Sixth Schedule tribal areas specifically (with apportionment rules if an Article 244A autonomous State is later formed) — and pending Parliamentary legislation, the President exercises this power by order, subject to Finance Commission consultation once one exists.
essential_elements: Clause (1)'s main body is discretionary and needs-based: Parliament decides which States need assistance and how much, unlike Article 270's formula-driven universal sharing.

The first proviso is mandatory, not discretionary: capital/recurring sums must be paid for Scheduled Tribes welfare and Scheduled Area administration-levelling schemes, wherever a State has such areas — a guaranteed minimum, not left to Parliament's needs-assessment discretion.

The second proviso is Assam-specific and mandatory: grants covering both a historical administration-deficit calculation (pre-Constitution expenditure-over-revenue excess for the Sixth Schedule Part I tribal areas) and ongoing development-scheme costs for those areas.

Clause (1A) (added alongside Article 244A by the 22nd Amendment) governs how these Assam-specific grants get apportioned or redirected if an Article 244A autonomous State is later carved out of those tribal areas.

Clause (2) is the same President-as-stand-in-legislator mechanism seen elsewhere in this Chapter — pending Parliamentary law under clause (1), the President exercises the power by order, subject to mandatory Finance Commission consultation once one exists.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 275 grants are the primary constitutional channel for the 'non-formula' component of Union-State fiscal transfers — contrast with Article 270's automatic, formula-driven tax-devolution share; both are typically discussed together as forming India's overall vertical fiscal transfer architecture, alongside Finance-Commission-recommended grants and Planning-Commission/NITI-Aayog-era scheme-based transfers (the latter not constitutionally mandated).

The Scheduled Tribes/Scheduled Areas proviso directly implements the Fifth Schedule's substantive tribal-welfare mandate with fiscal teeth — connecting back to Article 244(1)'s Fifth Schedule routing and giving it a concrete funding guarantee.

The Assam-specific proviso and clause (1A) directly cross-reference Article 244(2)'s Sixth Schedule routing and Article 244A's autonomous-State mechanism, illustrating how Part X's tribal-area administrative scheme and Part XII's fiscal scheme are deliberately interlocked.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 275 as the needs-based counterpart to Article 270's formula-based tax-sharing — pay special attention to how its two provisos convert what would otherwise be pure Parliamentary discretion into binding, cross-referenced obligations tied directly back to the Fifth/Sixth Schedule tribal-administration scheme in Part X.

sections.title: Taxes on professions, trades, callings and employments
sections.raw_text:
276. Taxes on professions, trades, callings and employments.—(1) Notwithstanding anything in article 246, no law of the Legislature of a State relating to taxes for the benefit of the State or of a municipality, district board, local board or other local authority therein in respect of professions, trades, callings or employments shall be invalid on the ground that it relates to a tax on income.
(2) The total amount payable in respect of any one person to the State or to any one municipality, district board, local board or other local authority in the State by way of taxes on professions, trades, callings and employments shall not exceed two thousand and five hundred rupees per annum.
(3) The power of the Legislature of a State to make laws as aforesaid with respect to taxes on professions, trades, callings and employments shall not be construed as limiting in any way the power of Parliament to make laws with respect to taxes on income accruing from or arising out of professions, trades, callings and employments.
key_terms: State/local-authority profession tax validated despite income-tax overlap
₹2,500 per annum aggregate profession-tax cap per person
Parliament's income-tax power over professions unaffected by State profession tax

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 276 resolves a potential Union-State taxing-power overlap: even though income tax (including income from professions/trades/callings/employments) is exclusively a Union List/Parliament subject, this Article validates State (or local-authority) laws taxing professions, trades, callings, and employments for the State's or a local body's benefit, capping the aggregate amount any one person can be charged across all such State/local profession taxes at ₹2,500 per annum, while confirming Parliament's own income-tax power over the same professions/trades is completely unaffected by this State taxing power.
essential_elements: Clause (1) is the validating, Article-246-overriding rule: a State/local profession tax law is not invalid merely because it 'relates to' income tax (a Union List subject) — resolving what would otherwise be a competence conflict given income tax is Union List Entry 82 while State List Entry 60 covers 'taxes on professions, trades, callings and employments.'

Clause (2) fixes a hard aggregate cap of ₹2,500 per annum per person across all State/local-authority profession taxes combined — a rare instance of the Constitution itself fixing a specific rupee ceiling rather than leaving the amount entirely to legislative discretion.
Clause (3) is a savings clause confirming Parliament's own separate income-tax competence over professional/trade/employment income remains completely intact and unlimited by this Article.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The ₹2,500 cap was raised from an original ₹250 to the current ₹2,500 by the Constitution (Sixtieth Amendment) Act, 1988 — one of the few instances where the Constitution itself fixes and periodically revises (via formal amendment) a specific monetary figure, rather than delegating amount-setting entirely to ordinary legislation.

This Article is the direct constitutional basis for the commonly encountered 'Professional Tax' levied by many Indian States (e.g., Maharashtra, Karnataka, West Bengal) on salaried employees and professionals — a State List Entry 60 tax whose validity depends specifically on Article 276's overlap-resolution and rate-cap rules.

Because any further increase to the cap requires a full constitutional amendment (not ordinary legislation), the ₹2,500 figure has remained static since 1988 despite decades of inflation — a frequently noted practical limitation on States' profession-tax revenue potential.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 276 as a narrow but practically significant overlap-resolution-plus-rate-cap provision — remember the ₹2,500 aggregate annual cap applies per person across all State/local profession taxes combined, and that changing this figure requires nothing less than a constitutional amendment.

sections.title: Savings
sections.raw_text: 277. Savings.—Any taxes, duties, cesses or fees which, immediately before the commencement of this Constitution, were being lawfully levied by the Government of any State or by any municipality or other local authority or body for the purposes of the State, municipality, district or other local area may, notwithstanding that those taxes, duties, cesses or fees are mentioned in the Union List, continue to be levied and to be applied to the same purposes until provision to the contrary is made by Parliament by law.
key_terms: transitional savings for pre-Constitution State/local levies mentioned in Union List

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 277 is a transitional savings clause protecting a State's or local authority's pre-existing (as of 26 January 1950) taxes, duties, cesses, or fees from being immediately invalidated merely because the new Constitution's Union List happens to cover the same subject — such pre-Constitution levies may continue to be collected and applied to their original purposes until Parliament affirmatively legislates to the contrary.
essential_elements: The levy must have been lawfully in force immediately before the Constitution's commencement (26 January 1950) — a levy introduced afterward gets no protection under this Article.
The protection covers State Government levies as well as municipal/local-authority/other local-body levies.
Protection continues only until Parliament makes contrary provision by law — this is a default continuation rule, not a permanent immunity; Parliament can end it at will.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article performs the same 'grandfather clause' function for Part XII's Union-State fiscal reallocation that similar transitional-savings provisions perform elsewhere in the Constitution (e.g., the Article 372 general savings of pre-Constitution laws) — preventing a jarring, immediate fiscal disruption to States/local bodies from the Constitution's new Union List allocations.

In practice, this Article has had limited long-run significance since three-quarters of a century have passed since 1950, and most States/local bodies have long since had their tax structures reorganized through subsequent legislation — but it remains textually significant for understanding the Constitution's careful transition-management approach to fiscal federalism at the founding moment.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 277 as a founding-era transitional bridge, not a source of ongoing contemporary tax authority — it protected the fiscal status quo at the moment of transition from British India's/princely states' pre-existing arrangements into the new constitutional order, subject always to Parliament's power to override it by law.

sections.title: Calculation of "net proceeds", etc.
sections.raw_text:
279. Calculation of "net proceeds", etc.—(1) In the foregoing provisions of this Chapter, "net proceeds" means in relation to any tax or duty the proceeds thereof reduced by the cost of collection, and for the purposes of those provisions the net proceeds of any tax or duty, or of any part of any tax or duty, in or attributable to any area shall be ascertained and certified by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, whose certificate shall be final.
(2) Subject as aforesaid, and to any other express provision of this Chapter, a law made by Parliament or an order of the President may, in any case where under this Part the proceeds of any duty or tax are, or may be, assigned to any State, provide for the manner in which the proceeds are to be calculated, for the time from or at which and the manner in which any payments are to be made, for the making of adjustments between one financial year and another, and for any other incidental or ancillary matters.
key_terms: "net proceeds" defined as gross proceeds minus cost of collection
CAG's certification of net proceeds is final
Parliament/Presidential order power over calculation/payment/adjustment mechanics

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 279 supplies the precise technical definition underlying every 'net proceeds' reference across this entire Chapter (Articles 268-278): net proceeds means gross tax/duty proceeds minus collection costs, with the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India (CAG) ascertaining and certifying the figure — and that certificate is made final and unchallengeable — while also empowering Parliament (or, pending Parliamentary law, the President by order) to set the detailed mechanics of how proceeds are calculated, when/how payments are made, and how inter-year adjustments are handled.
essential_elements: Clause (1) defines 'net proceeds' as gross proceeds reduced by cost of collection, with the CAG empowered to ascertain and certify the figure for any tax/duty or portion attributable to any area — and that CAG certificate is expressly made final (not subject to further challenge or recalculation).

Clause (2) is a technical implementation-mechanics clause: Parliament (or the President by order, pending Parliamentary law) may fill in calculation methodology, payment timing/manner, and inter-year adjustment rules for any Chapter I revenue-assignment provision.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The CAG's role here (Article 279(1)) is a distinct, narrower function from the CAG's general audit function under Article 148 — here the CAG acts as the authoritative, final certifier of a specific financial figure (net proceeds) that directly drives how much money flows to which State under Articles 268-270 and 275, making this a quietly consequential fiscal-federalism role.

Because the CAG's certificate is 'final,' States have historically had limited formal legal recourse to directly contest the CAG's net-proceeds calculation through ordinary litigation — disputes instead tend to surface through political/Finance-Commission channels rather than judicial review of the certificate itself.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 279 as the definitional/mechanical backbone underlying the whole Chapter's revenue-sharing arithmetic — whenever any preceding Article refers to 'net proceeds,' trace back to this Article's gross-minus-collection-cost definition and the CAG's final-certificate role.

sections.title: Goods and Services Tax Council
sections.raw_text:
279A. Goods and Services Tax Council.—(1) The President shall, within sixty days from the date of commencement of the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, by order, constitute a Council to be called the Goods and Services Tax Council.
(2) The Goods and Services Tax Council shall consist of the following members, namely:—
(a) the Union Finance Minister — Chairperson;
(b) the Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance — Member;
(c) the Minister in charge of Finance or Taxation or any other Minister nominated by each State Government — Members.
(3) The Members of the Goods and Services Tax Council referred to in sub-clause (c) of clause (2) shall, as soon as may be, choose one amongst themselves to be the Vice-Chairperson of the Council for such period as they may decide.
(4) The Goods and Services Tax Council shall make recommendations to the Union and the States on—
(a) the taxes, cesses and surcharges levied by the Union, the States and the local bodies which may be subsumed in the goods and services tax;
(b) the goods and services that may be subjected to, or exempted from, the goods and services tax;
(c) model Goods and Services Tax Laws, principles of levy, apportionment of Goods and Services Tax levied on supplies in the course of inter-State trade or commerce under article 269A and the principles that govern the place of supply;
(d) the threshold limit of turnover below which goods and services may be exempted from goods and services tax;
(e) the rates including floor rates with bands of goods and services tax;
(f) any special rate or rates for a specified period, to raise additional resources during any natural calamity or disaster;
(g) special provision with respect to the States of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Jammu and Kashmir, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand; and
(h) any other matter relating to the goods and services tax, as the Council may decide.
(5) The Goods and Services Tax Council shall recommend the date on which the goods and services tax be levied on petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit (commonly known as petrol), natural gas and aviation turbine fuel.
(6) While discharging the functions conferred by this article, the Goods and Services Tax Council shall be guided by the need for a harmonised structure of goods and services tax and for the development of a harmonised national market for goods and services.
(7) One-half of the total number of Members of the Goods and Services Tax Council shall constitute the quorum at its meetings.
(8) The Goods and Services Tax Council shall determine the procedure in the performance of its functions.
(9) Every decision of the Goods and Services Tax Council shall be taken at a meeting, by a majority of not less than three-fourths of the weighted votes of the members present and voting, in accordance with the following principles, namely:—
(a) the vote of the Central Government shall have a weightage of one-third of the total votes cast, and
(b) the votes of all the State Governments taken together shall have a weightage of two-thirds of the total votes cast,
in that meeting.
(10) No act or proceedings of the Goods and Services Tax Council shall be invalid merely by reason of—
(a) any vacancy in, or any defect in, the constitution of the Council; or
(b) any defect in the appointment of a person as a Member of the Council; or
(c) any procedural irregularity of the Council not affecting the merits of the case.
(11) The Goods and Services Tax Council shall establish a mechanism to adjudicate any dispute—
(a) between the Government of India and one or more States; or
(b) between the Government of India and any State or States on one side and one or more other States on the other side; or
(c) between two or more States,
arising out of the recommendations of the Council or implementation thereof.
key_terms: GST Council composition — Union Finance Minister as Chairperson plus State Finance/Taxation Ministers
GST Council's broad recommendatory mandate over rates/exemptions/thresholds/model laws
weighted voting formula — Centre 1/3, States combined 2/3, 3/4 majority threshold
GST Council's mandatory inter-governmental dispute-adjudication mechanism

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 279A (inserted by the 101st Amendment, 2016) constitutes the Goods and Services Tax Council — a unique constitutional body chaired by the Union Finance Minister and composed of each State's Finance/Taxation Minister, tasked with recommending virtually every substantive parameter of India's GST regime (what gets subsumed, exemptions, model laws, rates, special provisions for hill/border States, and the petroleum-products commencement date), deciding by a weighted three-fourths-majority vote (Centre 1/3 weight, States combined 2/3 weight), and required to establish its own dispute-resolution mechanism for Centre-State or inter-State GST disputes.
essential_elements: Clauses (1)-(3) establish the Council's composition: Union Finance Minister (Chairperson), Union Minister of State for Revenue/Finance (Member), and one nominated Minister from each State (Members, who elect a Vice-Chairperson among themselves).

Clause (4) lists the Council's wide recommendatory jurisdiction — essentially every substantive design parameter of the GST system, from what taxes get subsumed to rates, thresholds, exemptions, and model legislation.

Clause (5) singles out petroleum crude, diesel, petrol, natural gas, and aviation turbine fuel as items the Council must separately recommend a commencement date for — these remain outside GST until that recommendation is made and acted on.

Clauses (7)-(9) set the Council's internal procedure: half its members form quorum, and every decision requires a three-fourths weighted-majority vote under the fixed 1/3 Centre-2/3 States weighting formula — meaning neither the Centre alone nor the States alone can force a decision through without the other's substantial cooperation.
Clause (10) is a validating/curative provision immunizing Council actions from challenge over mere vacancies, appointment defects, or non-merits procedural irregularities.
Clause (11) mandates the Council itself to set up a dispute-adjudication mechanism for Centre-State and inter-State GST disputes arising from its recommendations or their implementation.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The weighted-voting formula (Centre 1/3, States 2/3, three-fourths threshold) means no single State can block a decision, but the States acting together can outvote the Centre, and the Centre alone can never pass a decision without at least some State support — a deliberately balanced federal design praised and litigated over since 2017.

In Union of India v.
