essential_elements: The freedom guaranteed spans three overlapping concepts: 'trade,' 'commerce,' and 'intercourse' — broadly interpreted by courts to cover the movement of goods, persons, and economic activity throughout Indian territory, not merely formal commercial transactions.
The freedom is nationwide/inter-territorial in character — its central target is barriers between States/regions, not (primarily) purely local regulation with no inter-State dimension.

The opening qualifier 'subject to the other provisions of this Part' is critical: Article 301 does not stand alone as an absolute guarantee — it must always be read together with Articles 302-307, which authorize various restrictions.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The landmark Atiabari Tea Co. v. State of Assam (1961) and Automobile Transport (Rajasthan) v. State of Rajasthan (1962) decisions established that Article 301 targets only restrictions that directly and immediately impede the free movement of trade (not every tax or regulation that merely touches trade incidentally) — a 'direct and immediate effect' test that has shaped decades of subsequent litigation over State taxation and regulatory measures.

The Supreme Court's 9-judge bench in Jindal Stainless Ltd. v. State of Haryana (2016) significantly refined this doctrine, holding that non-discriminatory compensatory taxes do not violate Article 301 at all, and that only discriminatory or protectionist barriers (not mere revenue-raising taxes with no protectionist intent) genuinely offend the freedom of trade guarantee — considerably narrowing the earlier 'direct and immediate effect' test's practical reach.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 301 as the opening, general-principle provision of a five-Article interlocking scheme (301-305, plus the enforcement Article 307) — never analyze Article 301 in isolation from Articles 302-305's restriction-permitting powers, and apply the Jindal Stainless (2016) discriminatory/protectionist-barrier test as the modern operative standard rather than the older, broader Atiabari 'direct and immediate effect' formulation.

sections.title: Power of Parliament to impose restrictions on trade, commerce and intercourse
sections.raw_text: 302. Power of Parliament to impose restrictions on trade, commerce and intercourse.—Parliament may by law impose such restrictions on the freedom of trade, commerce or intercourse between one State and another or within any part of the territory of India as may be required in the public interest.
key_terms: Parliament's public-interest-justified power to restrict inter-State/intra-territory trade freedom

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 302 lets Parliament impose restrictions on the Article 301 freedom of trade, commerce, and intercourse — both between States and within any part of India's territory — wherever required in the public interest, giving the Union legislature the primary, general power to qualify the trade-freedom guarantee for the whole country.
essential_elements: The restricting power belongs to Parliament alone under this specific Article (State Legislatures get their own, narrower restricting power under Article 304).
The restriction must be justified as 'required in the public interest' — a substantive, judicially reviewable standard, not an unlimited discretion.

The power covers both inter-State trade restrictions and restrictions 'within any part of the territory of India' — meaning Parliament's Article 302 power is not limited to cross-border/inter-State measures alone.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 302's 'public interest' restriction power is itself subject to Article 303's non-discrimination bar (discussed next) — Parliament cannot use Article 302 to give one State a preference over another or discriminate between States, except in the narrow scarcity-related circumstance Article 303(2) allows.

In practice, Article 302 restrictions are relatively rare compared to State-level Article 304 restrictions, since most day-to-day trade regulation affecting inter-State commerce (like State-level entry taxes, mandi/APMC regulations, or check-post requirements) has historically arisen at the State level, testing Article 304 rather than Article 302.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 302 as Parliament's general trade-restriction power, but always cross-check any purported Article 302 restriction against Article 303(1)'s discrimination bar — a 'public interest' restriction under 302 cannot itself become a preference/discrimination device between States except under Article 303(2)'s narrow scarcity exception.

sections.title: Restrictions on the legislative powers of the Union and of the States with regard to trade and commerce
sections.raw_text:
303. Restrictions on the legislative powers of the Union and of the States with regard to trade and commerce.—(1) Notwithstanding anything in article 302, neither Parliament nor the Legislature of a State shall have power to make any law giving, or authorising the giving of, any preference to one State over another, or making, or authorising the making of, any discrimination between one State and another, by virtue of any entry relating to trade and commerce in any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule.
(2) Nothing in clause (1) shall prevent Parliament from making any law giving, or authorising the giving of, any preference or making, or authorising the making of, any discrimination if it is declared by such law that it is necessary to do so for the purpose of dealing with a situation arising from scarcity of goods in any part of the territory of India.
key_terms: blanket bar on Parliament/State trade-and-commerce laws that prefer or discriminate between States
Parliament-only scarcity exception, requiring express legislative declaration of necessity

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 303 imposes a strict non-discrimination/non-preference rule on both Parliament and every State Legislature: neither may use any Seventh Schedule trade-and-commerce entry to make a law that prefers one State over another or discriminates between States — even Parliament's own Article 302 public-interest restriction power is expressly overridden by this bar — with a single, narrow exception letting Parliament (not States) legislate preference/discrimination specifically to address goods scarcity in part of India's territory, provided the law itself expressly declares that necessity.
essential_elements: Clause (1)'s bar operates 'notwithstanding anything in article 302' — meaning it overrides even Parliament's general public-interest restriction power, making non-discrimination a stronger, near-absolute constitutional principle within its scope.
The bar applies to both Parliament and State Legislatures equally — no level of government may prefer or discriminate between States via trade-and-commerce legislative entries.

Clause (2)'s exception is deliberately narrow and Parliament-only (States get no equivalent scarcity exception): it applies solely to addressing goods scarcity, and the law itself must expressly declare that the preference/discrimination is necessary for that purpose — a mandatory, judicially checkable self-declaration requirement, not an implied or inferred justification.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article reflects the Constituent Assembly's deliberate design choice to make India an economically unified 'common market' where the Centre cannot play favorites among States through ordinary trade legislation — a foundational commitment to inter-State economic equality distinct from (and stronger than) the general Article 301 freedom-of-trade guarantee.

The scarcity exception in clause (2) has historically been invoked in the context of essential-commodities legislation (like the Essential Commodities Act framework) permitting geographically differentiated distribution/rationing measures during shortages — but any such law must carry the express necessity declaration or risk being struck down under clause (1)'s general bar.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 303 as a stronger, near-absolute non-discrimination principle sitting above even Article 302's public-interest restriction power — remember the scarcity exception in clause (2) is available to Parliament only (never States) and requires an express statutory declaration of necessity, not merely a de facto scarcity-response effect.

sections.title: Restrictions on trade, commerce and intercourse among States
sections.raw_text:
304. Restrictions on trade, commerce and intercourse among States.—Notwithstanding anything in article 301 or article 303, the Legislature of a State may by law—
(a) impose on goods imported from other States or the Union territories any tax to which similar goods manufactured or produced in that State are subject, so, however, as not to discriminate between goods so imported and goods so manufactured or produced; and
(b) impose such reasonable restrictions on the freedom of trade, commerce or intercourse with or within that State as may be required in the public interest:
Provided that no Bill or amendment for the purposes of clause (b) shall be introduced or moved in the Legislature of a State without the previous sanction of the President.
key_terms: State's power to tax imported goods on par with local goods, non-discriminatorily
State's public-interest reasonable-restriction power, subject to mandatory Presidential prior sanction

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 304 grants State Legislatures two specific powers, notwithstanding Articles 301 and 303: first, to tax goods imported from other States/Union territories at the same rate as similar locally-produced goods (a non-discriminatory equalization tax, not a protectionist import tax), and second, to impose reasonable public-interest restrictions on trade/commerce/intercourse with or within that State — but any Bill for the second power requires the President's prior sanction before it can even be introduced in the State Legislature.
essential_elements: Clause (a) permits a State to tax imported goods, but strictly on a non-discriminatory, equal-treatment basis — the imported-goods tax rate cannot exceed what similar locally-manufactured/produced goods already bear; this is an anti-protectionism safeguard built directly into the taxing power itself.

Clause (b) is a general reasonable-restriction power for trade/commerce/intercourse 'with or within' the State, justified by public interest — narrower in formal scope than Parliament's Article 302 power (State-specific rather than nationwide) but requiring an extra procedural safeguard.

The proviso is a mandatory prior-sanction requirement specifically for clause (b) Bills (not clause (a) taxing Bills) — the President's sanction must be obtained before the Bill is even introduced or moved, not merely before it takes effect, making this a stronger procedural check than an assent-stage requirement.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (a)'s 'discriminate' bar has generated extensive litigation testing whether a State tax scheme genuinely equalizes imported and local goods or covertly favors local production through exemptions, rebates, or differential administrative treatment — courts scrutinize the practical/economic effect, not just the formal tax rate, to detect disguised protectionism.

The Presidential-prior-sanction requirement for clause (b) Bills exists precisely because such restrictions could otherwise be used by a State to erect protectionist barriers against other States' trade — requiring Union-level vetting before the Bill even enters the legislative process, a stronger safeguard than the ordinary Article 200 assent-stage reservation mechanism used elsewhere.

Post-GST (101st Amendment), clause (a)'s practical significance for goods taxation has substantially diminished since State-level differential goods taxation is now largely subsumed into the unified GST framework — but the Article remains textually intact and potentially relevant to non-GST-covered goods or other trade-restriction contexts.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 304 as the States' counterpart to Parliament's Article 302 power — note its two distinct sub-powers have different safeguards: clause (a)'s built-in non-discrimination requirement versus clause (b)'s external Presidential-prior-sanction requirement, and recognize clause (a)'s practical significance has shrunk considerably in the post-GST goods-taxation landscape.

sections.title: Saving of existing laws and laws providing for State monopolies
sections.raw_text: 305. Saving of existing laws and laws providing for State monopolies.—Nothing in articles 301 and 303 shall affect the provisions of any existing law except in so far as the President may by order otherwise direct; and nothing in article 301 shall affect the operation of any law made before the commencement of the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, in so far as it relates to, or prevent Parliament or the Legislature of a State from making any law relating to, any such matter as is referred to in sub-clause (ii) of clause (6) of article 19.
key_terms: general savings of pre-Constitution existing laws from Articles 301/303, Presidential-order-overridable
specific savings protecting State-monopoly legislation from Article 301

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 305 (substituted by the Fourth Amendment, 1955) is a savings clause with two limbs: first, it generally protects any 'existing law' (pre-Constitution law) from being struck down under Articles 301 or 303's trade-freedom/non-discrimination principles, unless the President specifically orders otherwise; second, it specifically protects laws (whenever made, before or after the Fourth Amendment for the Article 19(6)(ii) category) establishing State monopolies in any trade/business/industry/service from Article 301 challenge, reflecting the Constitution's accommodation of State-run monopoly enterprises.
essential_elements: The first limb's general 'existing law' savings applies to both Articles 301 and 303, but the President retains power to lift the savings by order for any specific existing law — a case-by-case override mechanism.

The second limb specifically cross-references Article 19(6)(ii) — the fundamental-rights provision (Part III) permitting the State to carry on any trade/business/industry/service to the partial or complete exclusion of citizens (i.e., State monopolies) — and ensures Article 301's trade-freedom guarantee cannot be used to challenge legislation creating or continuing such State monopolies.

This second limb's protection extends beyond merely pre-1955 laws: it also 'prevent[s]... Parliament or the Legislature of a State from making any law relating to' such State-monopoly matters, meaning future State-monopoly legislation is also protected from Article 301 challenge, not just historical laws.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article explains the constitutional coexistence of India's historically extensive public-sector monopolies/near-monopolies (e.g., railways, and formerly banking, insurance, and various other sectors before liberalization) with the Article 301 free-trade guarantee — State monopoly creation is a deliberate carve-out, not an accidental gap, in the free-trade scheme.

The Article 19(6)(ii) cross-reference means this Article must be read together with Part III's fundamental-rights framework (specifically the reasonable-restrictions-on-trade provision) to fully understand its scope — it is one of relatively few Part XIII provisions that explicitly interlocks with a Part III fundamental right provision.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 305 as protecting two distinct categories from Article 301/303 challenge — general pre-Constitution existing laws (Presidential-order-overridable) and State-monopoly legislation specifically (protected via the Article 19(6)(ii) cross-reference, extending to future as well as past legislation) — and always trace the second limb back to Part III's Article 19(6)(ii) to fully understand this Article's scope.

sections.title: Appointment of authority for carrying out the purposes of articles 301 to 304
sections.raw_text: 307. Appointment of authority for carrying out the purposes of articles 301 to 304.—Parliament may by law appoint such authority as it considers appropriate for carrying out the purposes of articles 301, 302, 303 and 304, and confer on the authority so appointed such powers and such duties as it thinks necessary.
key_terms: Parliament's power to create an implementing/enforcement authority for the Part XIII trade-freedom scheme

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 307 lets Parliament establish, by law, a dedicated authority to carry out the purposes of Articles 301-304 (the core trade-freedom, restriction, and non-discrimination scheme), and to confer on that authority whatever powers and duties Parliament considers necessary — envisioning an institutional enforcement/oversight mechanism for India's internal common-market guarantee, though this power has famously never been exercised.
essential_elements: The authority-creation power is entirely discretionary ('Parliament may') — there is no constitutional mandate that such an authority actually be created.

The authority's purposes are tied specifically to Articles 301-304 (not 305-306) — i.e., enforcing/implementing the freedom-of-trade guarantee, the Parliament/State restriction powers, and the non-discrimination principle.
Parliament has full discretion over what powers/duties to confer on any such authority — the Article itself specifies no minimum institutional design.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Despite being in the Constitution since 1950, Parliament has never actually exercised this Article 307 power to create a dedicated trade-freedom-enforcement authority — meaning Part XIII's Article 301 guarantee has been enforced entirely through ordinary judicial review (the Atiabari/Automobile Transport/Jindal Stainless line of cases) rather than through any specialized administrative body, a notable and long-standing implementation gap.

This mirrors the similar non-implementation of the GST Council's Article 279A(11) dispute-mechanism mandate — both are examples of constitutionally-authorized-but-never-created institutional mechanisms in the fiscal/trade-federalism space, with courts filling the resulting gap through ordinary litigation instead.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 307 as the (never-exercised) institutional-enforcement power closing out Part XIII's trade-freedom scheme — note its purposes are limited to Articles 301-304, and recognize this as one of several 'authorized but never implemented' institutional powers scattered through the Constitution's fiscal/trade provisions.

sections.title: Interpretation
sections.raw_text: In this Part, unless the context otherwise requires, the expression "State" does not include the State of Jammu and Kashmir.
key_terms: Part XIV-specific narrowed definition of 'State' excluding Jammu and Kashmir

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 308 fixes a special, Part-XIV-only meaning of the word 'State': everywhere Part XIV (Services Under the Union and the States) uses 'State', it excludes Jammu and Kashmir, unlike the general Article 12 definition used elsewhere in the Constitution.
essential_elements: Applies only within Part XIV (Articles 308-323)
Excludes the State of Jammu and Kashmir from 'State' for these purposes
exceptions_and_qualifications: A historical special-status carve-out originally tied to Jammu and Kashmir's now-abrogated special constitutional position under the former Article 370
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as a pure interpretation clause — it doesn't create any right or duty itself, but silently narrows every other Part XIV article's use of 'State'.

sections.title: Recruitment and conditions of service of persons serving the Union or a State
sections.raw_text: Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, Acts of the appropriate Legislature may regulate the recruitment, and conditions of service of persons appointed, to public services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of any State: Provided that it shall be competent for the President or such person as he may direct in the case of services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union, and for the Governor of a State or such person as he may direct in the case of services and posts in connection with the affairs of the State, to make rules regulating the recruitment, and the conditions of service of persons appointed, to such services and posts until provision in that behalf is made by or under an Act of the appropriate Legislature under this article, and any rules so made shall have effect subject to the provisions of any such Act.
key_terms: Legislature's primary power to regulate public-service recruitment and conditions of service
President's/Governor's interim rule-making power pending legislation, subordinate to any later Act

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 309 is the foundational civil-service law-making power: Parliament (for Union services) and State Legislatures (for State services) may pass Acts governing recruitment and conditions of service of government employees, but until such an Act exists the President or Governor may make rules to cover the gap — and those rules automatically yield once the Legislature actually legislates.
essential_elements: Primary power vests in the 'appropriate Legislature' (Parliament for Union affairs, State Legislature for State affairs)
President/Governor's rule-making power is only a stopgap, operative 'until provision...is made by or under an Act'
Rules made under the proviso remain subject to, and are overridden by, any subsequently enacted Act
exceptions_and_qualifications: The power is itself 'subject to the provisions of this Constitution' — so it cannot override other constitutional guarantees such as Articles 14, 16, or 311
The President/Governor may delegate this rule-making power to 'such person as he may direct'
breakdown.how_to_read: The classic Government-servant conditions-of-service source: most civil service rules (e.g., All India Services Rules) trace their authority to this article's proviso, since Parliament has enacted only framework legislation rather than comprehensive service codes for most cadres.

sections.title: Tenure of office of persons serving the Union or a State
sections.raw_text: (1) Except as expressly provided by this Constitution, every person who is a member of a defence service or of a civil service of the Union or of an all-India service or holds any post connected with defence or any civil post under the Union holds office during the pleasure of the President, and every person who is a member of a civil service of a State or holds any civil post under a State holds office during the pleasure of the Governor of the State. (2) Notwithstanding that a person holding a civil post under the Union or a State holds office during the pleasure of the President or, as the case may be, of the Governor of the State, any contract under which a person, not being a member of a defence service or of an all-India service or of a civil service of the Union or a State, is appointed under this Constitution to hold such a post may, if the President or the Governor, as the case may be, deems it necessary in order to secure the services of a person having special qualifications, provide for the payment to him of compensation, if before the expiration of an agreed period that post is abolished or he is, for reasons not connected with any misconduct on his part, required to vacate that post.
key_terms: 'doctrine of pleasure' — Union/State civil and defence servants hold office at the President's/Governor's pleasure
compensation-for-early-termination clause for specially contracted appointees, overriding the pleasure doctrine only as to money

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 310(1) enshrines India's version of the English 'doctrine of pleasure': defence personnel and civil servants of the Union and States hold their posts at the pleasure of the President or Governor respectively, meaning they can in principle be dismissed without a fixed-term contractual right to the post. Clause (2) softens this for specially recruited contract appointees (not regular service members) by allowing a compensation clause if their post is abolished or they're removed early through no fault of their own.
essential_elements: Clause (1)'s pleasure doctrine applies to defence services, all-India services, civil services of the Union, and civil services/posts of a State
The pleasure doctrine operates 'except as expressly provided by this Constitution' — Article 311's procedural safeguards are the principal express qualification
Clause (2)'s compensation mechanism is limited to specially-qualified contract appointees, not regular service members
Compensation under clause (2) is triggered only by post-abolition or blameless removal before an agreed period ends
exceptions_and_qualifications: The pleasure doctrine does not mean arbitrary or unlimited dismissal power — it is always read subject to Article 311's procedural protections and Articles 14/16's non-arbitrariness guarantee
Constitutional functionaries with their own removal procedures (e.g., Supreme Court/High Court judges, Comptroller and Auditor-General) are outside Article 310's pleasure doctrine entirely
breakdown.how_to_read: Always read Article 310 together with Article 311 — 310 states the general 'at pleasure' baseline, while 311 immediately fences it in with mandatory inquiry and hearing safeguards for civil servants; courts treat the pleasure doctrine as heavily circumscribed in practice, not literal at-will termination.

sections.title: Dismissal, removal or reduction in rank of persons employed in civil capacities under the Union or a State
sections.raw_text: (1) No person who is a member of a civil service of the Union or an all-India service or a civil service of a State or holds a civil post under the Union or a State shall be dismissed or removed by an authority subordinate to that by which he was appointed. (2) No such person as aforesaid shall be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank except after an inquiry in which he has been informed of the charges against him and given a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges: Provided that where it is proposed after such inquiry, to impose upon him any such penalty, such penalty may be imposed on the basis of the evidence adduced during such inquiry and it shall not be necessary to give such person any opportunity of making representation on the penalty proposed: Provided further that this clause shall not apply— (a) where a person is dismissed or removed or reduced in rank on the ground of conduct which has led to his conviction on a criminal charge; or (b) where the authority empowered to dismiss or remove a person or to reduce him in rank is satisfied that for some reason, to be recorded by that authority in writing, it is not reasonably practicable to hold such inquiry; or (c) where the President or the Governor, as the case may be, is satisfied that in the interest of the security of the State it is not expedient to hold such inquiry. (3) If, in respect of any such person as aforesaid, a question arises whether it is reasonably practicable to hold such inquiry as is referred to in clause (2), the decision thereon of the authority empowered to dismiss or remove such person or to reduce him in rank shall be final.
key_terms: no-dismissal-by-subordinate-authority rule
mandatory inquiry-plus-hearing safeguard before dismissal/removal/reduction in rank
penalty-stage representation dispensed with once the merits inquiry is complete
criminal-conviction, impracticability, and State-security exceptions removing the inquiry requirement entirely

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 311 is the core constitutional job-security shield for civil servants: clause (1) bars a junior authority from dismissing someone appointed by a senior authority, and clause (2) requires a proper disciplinary inquiry (charges communicated, reasonable hearing opportunity) before dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank — though the employee need not additionally be heard on the penalty itself once the inquiry is done. Three exceptions let the government skip the inquiry altogether: a prior criminal conviction, a documented practical impossibility, or a Presidential/Gubernatorial national-security finding.
essential_elements: Clause (1)'s protection: dismissal/removal must be by an authority equal to or senior to the appointing authority
Clause (2)'s protection: charges communicated + reasonable opportunity to be heard, before any dismissal/removal/reduction in rank
The second proviso's three exceptions ((a) criminal conviction, (b) recorded impracticability, (c) security-of-the-State satisfaction) each independently dispense with the inquiry requirement
Clause (3) makes the dismissing/removing authority's own 'impracticability' determination final and unreviewable on that specific question
exceptions_and_qualifications: The penalty-stage representation requirement was itself removed by the 42nd Amendment (1976) — only the charge-and-hearing stage is now mandatory, not a second round on quantum of punishment
'Reduction in rank' as a stigmatic/punitive measure attracts Article 311(2); a genuine non-punitive reversion (e.g., end of a probationary promotion) does not
Clause (3)'s 'finality' has been read by courts as not completely ousting judicial review for mala fides or complete absence of material
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the single most litigated service-law provision in the Constitution — always check first whether the impugned action is 'dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank' in substance (not just label), since only those three actions trigger the clause (2) inquiry requirement; a genuinely non-punitive termination (e.g., simple probation discharge) falls outside it entirely.

sections.title: All-India services
sections.raw_text: (1) Notwithstanding anything in Chapter VI of Part VI or Part XI, if the Council of States has declared by resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest so to do, Parliament may by law provide for the creation of one or more all India services (including an all-India judicial service) common to the Union and the States, and, subject to the other provisions of this Chapter, regulate the recruitment, and the conditions of service of persons appointed, to any such service. (2) The services known at the commencement of this Constitution as the Indian Administrative Service and the Indian Police Service shall be deemed to be services created by Parliament under this article. (3) The all-India judicial service referred to in clause (1) shall not include any post inferior to that of a district judge as defined in article 236. (4) The law providing for the creation of the all-India judicial service aforesaid may contain such provisions for the amendment of Chapter VI of Part VI as may be necessary for giving effect to the provisions of that law and no such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368.
key_terms: Rajya Sabha two-thirds resolution precondition for Parliament to create new all-India services
deemed-created status for the pre-existing IAS and IPS
district-judge-or-above floor for any future all-India judicial service

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 312 lets Parliament create 'all-India services' — cadres shared between the Union and every State, like the IAS and IPS — but only after the Rajya Sabha (as the House representing the States) passes a special two-thirds resolution declaring it nationally necessary or expedient; this Rajya Sabha check protects State autonomy over their own civil services from unilateral Union override. The IAS and IPS are grandfathered in as if already created this way, and any future all-India judicial service (long proposed but never created) could not include posts below district judge.
essential_elements: Precondition: Rajya Sabha resolution supported by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, declaring national necessity/expediency
Overrides Chapter VI of Part VI (State judiciary provisions) and Part XI (Centre-State relations) 'notwithstanding' anything therein
IAS and IPS are deemed created under this article without needing a fresh resolution
A hypothetical all-India judicial service is capped at district-judge-and-above posts only
Enabling amendments to Chapter VI of Part VI for the judicial service are deemed ordinary legislation, not Article 368 constitutional amendments
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Rajya Sabha-origination requirement is a deliberate federalism safeguard — it cannot begin in the Lok Sabha
An all-India judicial service remains constitutionally authorized under clause (3)-(4) but has never actually been created despite decades of proposals
breakdown.how_to_read: Note the deliberate procedural asymmetry: unlike ordinary Union List legislation, creating a new all-India service needs prior Rajya Sabha political buy-in — a recurring pattern (compare Article 249's similar Rajya Sabha-resolution gateway for Parliament to legislate on State List subjects in the national interest).

sections.title: Power of Parliament to vary or revoke conditions of service of officers of certain services
sections.raw_text: (1) Parliament may by law— (a) vary or revoke, whether prospectively or retrospectively, the conditions of services as respects remuneration, leave and pension and the rights as respects disciplinary matters of persons who, having been appointed by the Secretary of State or Secretary of State in Council to a civil service of the Crown in India before the commencement of this Constitution, continue on and after the commencement of the Constitution (Twenty-eighth Amendment) Act, 1972, to serve under the Government of India or of a State in any service or post; (b) vary or revoke, whether prospectively or retrospectively, the conditions of service as respects pension of persons who, having been appointed by the Secretary of State or Secretary of State in Council to a civil service of the Crown in India before the commencement of this Constitution, retired or otherwise ceased to be in service at any time before the commencement of the Constitution (Twenty-eighth Amendment) Act, 1972: Provided that in the case of any such person who is holding or has held the office of the Chief Justice or other Judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court, the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, the Chairman or other member of the Union or a State Public Service Commission or the Chief Election Commissioner, nothing in sub-clause (a) or sub-clause (b) shall be construed as empowering Parliament to vary or revoke, after his appointment to such post, the conditions of his service to his disadvantage except in so far as such conditions of service are applicable to him by reason of his being a person appointed by the Secretary of State or Secretary of State in Council to a civil service of the Crown in India. (2) Except to the extent provided for by Parliament by law under this article, nothing in this article shall affect the power of any Legislature or other authority under any other provision of this Constitution to regulate the conditions of service of persons referred to in clause (1). (3) Neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall have jurisdiction in— (a) any dispute arising out of any provision of, or any endorsement on, any covenant, agreement or other similar instrument which was entered into or executed by any person referred to in clause (1), or arising out of any letter issued to such person, in relation to his appointment to any civil service of the Crown in India or his continuance in service under the Government of the Dominion of India or a Province thereof; (b) any dispute in respect of any right, liability or obligation under article 314 as originally enacted. (4) The provisions of this article shall have effect notwithstanding anything in article 314 as originally enacted or in any other provision of this Constitution.
key_terms: Parliament's retrospective power to vary Secretary-of-State-appointed 'Crown in India' officers' pay/leave/pension/disciplinary terms
protected-office proviso shielding sitting/former constitutional-post holders from disadvantageous variation
court-jurisdiction bar over Crown-in-India-era covenant/appointment disputes and Article-314-original disputes

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 312A, inserted by the 28th Amendment (1972), let Parliament retrospectively rewrite the service conditions of the last holdover pre-Independence 'Secretary of State' civil servants (a small, shrinking group appointed under British colonial authority before 1950) — including cutting their pay, leave, pension, or disciplinary rights — while specially protecting anyone who went on to hold high constitutional office (Supreme Court/High Court judges, CAG, Public Service Commission members, Chief Election Commissioner) from having their terms worsened on that specific ground. It also strips courts of jurisdiction over disputes arising from these old Crown-in-India appointment covenants.
essential_elements: Clause (1)(a): covers serving officers as of the 28th Amendment's commencement (29-8-1972)
Clause (1)(b): covers officers who had already retired/ceased service by that date, but only as to pension

Proviso: protects Chief Justice/Judges, CAG, Public Service Commission Chairman/members, and Chief Election Commissioner from disadvantageous variation of their service conditions in that later office
Clause (3) ousts all court jurisdiction over Crown-in-India covenant disputes and original-Article-314 disputes
Clause (4) gives this article overriding effect over original Article 314 and any other constitutional provision
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is now a historically spent provision in practical effect — the covered class of pre-1950 Secretary-of-State appointees has long since retired or passed away
The proviso's protection is narrow: it only shields the disadvantage arising 'by reason of' the Crown-in-India appointment status, not disadvantage from any other source
breakdown.how_to_read: A historical curiosity today — relevant mainly for understanding how the Constitution handled the last vestiges of colonial-era civil service appointments; rarely if ever invoked in modern practice.

sections.title: Transitional provisions
sections.raw_text: Until other provision is made in this behalf under this Constitution, all the laws in force immediately before the commencement of this Constitution and applicable to any public service or any post which continues to exist after the commencement of this Constitution, as an all-India service or as service or post under the Union or a State shall continue in force so far as consistent with the provisions of this Constitution.
key_terms: automatic continuation of pre-Constitution service laws until superseded, subject to Constitutional consistency

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 313 is a standard transitional bridge: pre-Constitution laws governing public services and posts that still exist after 26 January 1950 keep operating exactly as before, until Parliament or the appropriate authority makes fresh provision under the new constitutional scheme — and even then, only to the extent those old laws don't conflict with the Constitution itself.
essential_elements: Applies only to services/posts that 'continue to exist' after the Constitution's commencement
Continuation is automatically displaced once 'other provision is made in this behalf under this Constitution'
Continued laws remain valid only 'so far as consistent with the provisions of this Constitution'
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a gap-filling, not a permanently operative, provision — in practice almost entirely superseded today by Article 309 legislation and rules made over the past seven-plus decades
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as part of the Constitution's broader family of continuity clauses (compare Articles 372's general law-continuation rule) — it prevented an administrative vacuum at the Constitution's birth, not a standing source of authority today.

sections.title: Public Service Commissions for the Union and for the States
sections.raw_text: (1) Subject to the provisions of this article, there shall be a Public Service Commission for the Union and a Public Service Commission for each State. (2) Two or more States may agree that there shall be one Public Service Commission for that group of States, and if a resolution to that effect is passed by the House or, where there are two Houses, by each House of the Legislature of each of those States, Parliament may by law provide for the appointment of a Joint State Public Service Commission (referred to in this Chapter as Joint Commission) to serve the needs of those States. (3) Any such law as aforesaid may contain such incidental and consequential provisions as may be necessary or desirable for giving effect to the purposes of the law. (4) The Public Service Commission for the Union, if requested so to do by the Governor of a State, may, with the approval of the President, agree to serve all or any of the needs of the State. (5) References in this Constitution to the Union Public Service Commission or a State Public Service Commission shall, unless the context otherwise requires, be construed as references to the Commission serving the needs of the Union or, as the case may be, the State as respects the particular matter in question.
key_terms: mandatory one-Commission-per-Union/per-State baseline structure
opt-in Joint State Public Service Commission mechanism via State Legislature resolutions plus Parliamentary law
UPSC-serving-a-State option via Governor's request and Presidential approval

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 315 sets up India's public-service-recruitment institutional architecture: one Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) plus one Commission per State by default, with two flexibility mechanisms — States can pool resources into a shared 'Joint Commission' (via their own Legislatures' resolutions and a Parliament law), or a State can simply ask the UPSC itself to serve its needs, with the President's approval.
essential_elements: Baseline: one UPSC for the Union, one Commission per State
Joint Commission route requires each participating State's Legislature (both Houses, if bicameral) to pass a resolution, followed by a Parliament law
UPSC-serving-a-State route requires the State Governor's request plus the President's approval — no State Legislature resolution needed for this route
Clause (5) makes constitutional references to 'the' Commission context-sensitive, pointing to whichever Commission actually serves the matter in question
exceptions_and_qualifications: Smaller States or those wanting cost savings commonly use the UPSC-serving-a-State route (clause 4) rather than establishing their own full Commission
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as the structural map before reading the substantive powers/functions articles (316-323) — establishing whether a matter is being handled by the UPSC, a State Commission, or a Joint Commission determines which appointing/removing authority (President vs. Governor) applies throughout the rest of the Chapter.

sections.title: Appointment and term of office of members
sections.raw_text: (1) The Chairman and other members of a Public Service Commission shall be appointed, in the case of the Union Commission or a Joint Commission, by the President, and in the case of a State Commission, by the Governor of the State: Provided that as nearly as may be one-half of the members of every Public Service Commission shall be persons who at the dates of their respective appointments have held office for at least ten years either under the Government of India or under the Government of a State, and in computing the said period of ten years any period before the commencement of this Constitution during which a person has held office under the Crown in India or under the Government of an Indian State shall be included. (1A) If the office of the Chairman of the Commission becomes vacant or if any such Chairman is by reason of absence or for any other reason unable to perform the duties of his office, those duties shall, until some person appointed under clause (1) to the vacant office has entered on the duties thereof or, as the case may be, until the Chairman has resumed his duties, be performed by such one of the other members of the Commission as the President, in the case of the Union Commission or a Joint Commission, and the Governor of the State in the case of a State Commission, may appoint for the purpose. (2) A member of a Public Service Commission shall hold office for a term of six years from the date on which he enters upon his office or until he attains, in the case of the Union Commission, the age of sixty-five years, and in the case of a State Commission or a Joint Commission, the age of sixty-two years, whichever is earlier: Provided that— (a) a member of a Public Service Commission may, by writing under his hand addressed, in the case of the Union Commission or a Joint Commission, to the President, and in the case of a State Commission, to the Governor of the State, resign his office; (b) a member of a Public Service Commission may be removed from his office in the manner provided in clause (1) or clause (3) of article 317. (3) A person who holds office as a member of a Public Service Commission shall, on the expiration of his term of office, be ineligible for re-appointment to that office.
key_terms: President's/Governor's appointment power depending on Commission type
roughly-half-experienced-officers composition requirement
acting-Chairman mechanism for vacancy/incapacity
six-year-term or age-cap (65 UPSC / 62 State) tenure formula, whichever comes first
resignation and Article 317 removal as the only exit routes; no re-appointment after term expiry

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 316 governs who appoints Public Service Commission members and how long they serve: the President appoints UPSC/Joint Commission members while Governors appoint State Commission members, with roughly half of every Commission required to be experienced government officers (at least ten years' service, counting pre-Constitution Crown/Indian-State service too). Members serve a fixed six-year term or until a fixed retirement age (65 for UPSC, 62 for State/Joint Commissions), whichever arrives first, and once their term ends they can never be re-appointed to that same office — the only earlier exits are voluntary resignation or Article 317 removal.
essential_elements: Appointment authority tracks Commission type: President for UPSC/Joint Commission, Governor for State Commission
Composition proviso: 'as nearly as may be' one-half of members must have at least 10 years' prior government service (Union or State, including pre-Constitution Crown/Indian-State service)
Tenure: six years from entering office, or the applicable age cap, whichever is earlier
Resignation is by writing to the appointing authority (President or Governor as applicable)
Absolute bar on re-appointment to the same Commission office after term expiry
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (1A)'s acting-Chairman mechanism is triggered only by vacancy or the Chairman's inability to perform duties (absence or other reason), not by mere disagreement or policy differences
The re-appointment bar in clause (3) is specific to 'that office' — a former member is not barred from being appointed Chairman of a different Commission (see Article 319's cross-eligibility rules)
breakdown.how_to_read: The composition proviso (half experienced officers) and the absolute no-re-appointment rule are both designed to insulate Commission membership from becoming a political reward or a stepping-stone for repeat appointments — read them together with Article 319's post-tenure employment restrictions for the full independence-protection picture.

sections.title: Removal and suspension of a member of a Public Service Commission
sections.raw_text: (1) Subject to the provisions of clause (3), the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Commission shall only be removed from his office by order of the President on the ground of misbehaviour after the Supreme Court, on reference being made to it by the President, has, on inquiry held in accordance with the procedure prescribed in that behalf under article 145, reported that the Chairman or such other member, as the case may be, ought on any such ground to be removed. (2) The President, in the case of the Union Commission or a Joint Commission, and the Governor in the case of a State Commission, may suspend from office the Chairman or any other member of the Commission in respect of whom a reference has been made to the Supreme Court under clause (1) until the President has passed orders on receipt of the report of the Supreme Court on such reference. (3) Notwithstanding anything in clause (1), the President may by order remove from office the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Commission if the Chairman or such other member, as the case may be,— (a) is adjudged an insolvent; or (b) engages during his term of office in any paid employment outside the duties of his office; or (c) is, in the opinion of the President, unfit to continue in office by reason of infirmity of mind or body. (4) If the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Commission is or becomes in any way concerned or interested in any contract or agreement made by or on behalf of the Government of India or the Government of a State or participates in any way in the profit thereof or in any benefit or emolument arising therefrom otherwise than as a member and in common with the other members of an incorporated company, he shall, for the purposes of clause (1), be deemed to be guilty of misbehaviour.
key_terms: Supreme-Court-inquiry-plus-Presidential-order mechanism for misbehaviour-based removal, even for State Commission members
Union-exclusive suspension power pending the Supreme Court's reference report
no-inquiry Presidential removal for insolvency, outside paid employment, or mental/physical unfitness
deemed-misbehaviour rule for improper government-contract interest

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 317 protects Public Service Commission independence the same way judges are protected: even a State Commission member can only be removed for 'misbehaviour' after the Supreme Court itself holds an inquiry and reports that removal is warranted, with the President then issuing the actual removal order — notably, only the President (never a Governor) can suspend or remove, even for State Commissions. Three narrower situations (insolvency, taking outside paid work, or mental/physical unfitness) let the President remove without any Supreme Court inquiry at all, and having an improper personal stake in a government contract is automatically treated as 'misbehaviour' for these purposes.
essential_elements: Clause (1): misbehaviour-based removal requires a Supreme Court Article-145 inquiry and report before the President's removal order — applies uniformly to Union, Joint, and State Commission members
Clause (2): only the President may suspend a member pending the Supreme Court's report, even for a State Commission member
Clause (3): insolvency, outside paid employment, or Presidentially-assessed mental/physical unfitness allow direct Presidential removal with no Supreme Court inquiry
Clause (4): improper contractual/financial interest in a government contract or agreement is deemed 'misbehaviour' under clause (1), triggering the full Supreme Court inquiry route
exceptions_and_qualifications: The exception in clause (4) preserves ordinary shareholding in an incorporated company ('in common with the other members of an incorporated company') as not constituting disqualifying misbehaviour
breakdown.how_to_read: The centralisation of both suspension and removal power in the President alone — never the Governor, even for a purely State-level Commission — is a deliberate design choice protecting State Public Service Commissions from removal-related pressure by their own State Government; this parallels the similarly centralised removal mechanism for High Court judges.

sections.title: Power to make regulations as to conditions of service of members and staff of the Commission
sections.raw_text: In the case of the Union Commission or a Joint Commission, the President and, in the case of a State Commission, the Governor of the State may by regulations— (a) determine the number of members of the Commission and their conditions of service; and (b) make provision with respect to the number of members of the staff of the Commission and their conditions of service: Provided that the conditions of service of a member of a Public Service Commission shall not be varied to his disadvantage after his appointment.
key_terms: President's/Governor's regulation-making power over Commission size, member conditions, and staff
no-disadvantageous-variation guarantee for a member's own conditions of service post-appointment

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 318 lets the President (for the UPSC/Joint Commission) or the Governor (for a State Commission) fix, by regulation, how many members a Commission has and what its members' and staff's conditions of service are — but once a particular person is appointed as a member, their own conditions of service can never afterward be changed to their disadvantage.
essential_elements: Regulation-making authority tracks Commission type (President for Union/Joint, Governor for State)
Covers both (a) the Commission's own membership size/conditions and (b) its supporting staff's numbers/conditions
The proviso's protection is member-specific and appointment-date-anchored: conditions in force at the time of a member's appointment cannot later be worsened for that member
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso protects only the appointed member personally — it does not freeze the regulations for future appointees, who take office under whatever conditions apply when they join
breakdown.how_to_read: This is another independence-protection device in the same family as Article 316's fixed-tenure structure and Article 322's charged-Fund financing — insulating an individual member's terms from being punitively altered mid-tenure by the appointing government.

sections.title: Prohibition as to the holding of offices by members of Commission on ceasing to be such members
sections.raw_text: On ceasing to hold office— (a) the Chairman of the Union Public Service Commission shall be ineligible for further employment either under the Government of India or under the Government of a State; (b) the Chairman of a State Public Service Commission shall be eligible for appointment as the Chairman or any other member of the Union Public Service Commission or as the Chairman of any other State Public Service Commission, but not for any other employment either under the Government of India or under the Government of a State; (c) a member other than the Chairman of the Union Public Service Commission shall be eligible for appointment as the Chairman of the Union Public Service Commission or as the Chairman of a State Public Service Commission, but not for any other employment either under the Government of India or under the Government of a State; (d) a member other than the Chairman of a State Public Service Commission shall be eligible for appointment as the Chairman or any other member of the Union Public Service Commission or as the Chairman of that or any other State Public Service Commission, but not for any other employment either under the Government of India or under the Government of a State.
key_terms: absolute post-tenure employment bar for a former UPSC Chairman
cross-Commission-Chairman/membership eligibility ladder for former State Chairmen and non-Chairman members, coupled with a bar on all other government employment

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 319 stops Public Service Commission members from using their post as a springboard to another government job: a former UPSC Chairman can never again work for any government (Union or State) in any capacity, while former State Chairmen and ordinary (non-Chairman) members may only move sideways into another listed Commission role (UPSC membership/chairmanship or another State Commission's chairmanship/membership as applicable) — any other government employment is off-limits for all of them.
essential_elements: (a) Former UPSC Chairman: no further Union or State government employment of any kind
(b) Former State Commission Chairman: eligible only for UPSC Chairman/member or another State Commission's Chairman role; barred from any other government employment
(c) Former UPSC non-Chairman member: eligible only for UPSC Chairman or a State Commission Chairman role; barred from any other government employment
(d) Former State Commission non-Chairman member: eligible for UPSC Chairman/member or that/another State Commission's Chairman/member role; barred from any other government employment
exceptions_and_qualifications: The bar covers only 'employment... under the Government of India or under the Government of a State' — it does not restrict purely private-sector employment after demitting office
breakdown.how_to_read: A graduated independence safeguard: the most senior/visible role (UPSC Chairman) gets the strictest post-tenure bar, while lower-tier roles retain limited lateral mobility only within the closed circle of Public Service Commission appointments themselves — memorize the asymmetry between (a) and (b)-(d) rather than treating all four sub-clauses as identical.

sections.title: Functions of Public Service Commissions
sections.raw_text: (1) It shall be the duty of the Union and the State Public Service Commissions to conduct examinations for appointments to the services of the Union and the services of the State respectively. (2) It shall also be the duty of the Union Public Service Commission, if requested by any two or more States so to do, to assist those States in framing and operating schemes of joint recruitment for any services for which candidates possessing special qualifications are required. (3) The Union Public Service Commission or the State Public Service Commission, as the case may be, shall be consulted— (a) on all matters relating to methods of recruitment to civil services and for civil posts; (b) on the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers from one service to another and on the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers; (c) on all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Government of India or the Government of a State in a civil capacity, including memorials or petitions relating to such matters; (d) on any claim by or in respect of a person who is serving or has served under the Government of India or the Government of a State or under the Crown in India or under the Government of an Indian State, in a civil capacity, that any costs incurred by him in defending legal proceedings instituted against him in respect of acts done or purporting to be done in the execution of his duty should be paid out of the Consolidated Fund of India, or, as the case may be, out of the Consolidated Fund of the State; (e) on any claim for the award of a pension in respect of injuries sustained by a person while serving under the Government of India or the Government of a State or under the Crown in India or under the Government of an Indian State, in a civil capacity, and any question as to the amount of any such award, and it shall be the duty of a Public Service Commission to advise on any matter so referred to them and on any other matter which the President, or, as the case may be, the Governor of the State, may refer to them: Provided that the President as respects the all-India services and also as respects other services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union, and the Governor, as respects other services and posts in connection with the affairs of a State, may make regulations specifying the matters in which either generally, or in any particular class of case or in any particular circumstances, it shall not be necessary for a Public Service Commission to be consulted. (4) Nothing in clause (3) shall require a Public Service Commission to be consulted as respects the manner in which any provision referred to in clause (4) of article 16 may be made or as respects the manner in which effect may be given to the provisions of article 335. (5) All regulations made under the proviso to clause (3) by the President or the Governor of a State shall be laid for not less than fourteen days before each House of Parliament or the House or each House of the Legislature of the State, as the case may be, as soon as possible after they are made, and shall be subject to such modifications, whether by way of repeal or amendment, as both Houses of Parliament or the House or both Houses of the Legislature of the State may make during the session in which they are so laid.
key_terms: core examination-conducting duty for Union/State civil-service appointments
UPSC's optional joint-recruitment assistance role for States needing specially-qualified candidates
mandatory consultation duty on recruitment methods, appointment/promotion/transfer principles, disciplinary matters, litigation-cost claims, and injury-pension claims
President's/Governor's regulation-making power to exempt specified matters from the consultation requirement, subject to mandatory legislative laying

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 320 lists what Public Service Commissions actually do day-to-day: conduct recruitment examinations (clause 1), optionally help States run joint recruitment drives for specialist posts (clause 2), and — most importantly — serve as the mandatory consultative body on recruitment methods, appointment/promotion/transfer principles, disciplinary matters, and certain litigation-cost and injury-pension claims involving civil servants (clause 3). The government can carve out specific categories from this consultation duty by regulation, but any such carve-out regulation must be laid before Parliament or the State Legislature for at least 14 days and remains subject to being modified or repealed there.
essential_elements: Clause (1)'s examination duty is mandatory and unqualified for both UPSC and State Commissions
Clause (2)'s joint-recruitment-assistance duty triggers only 'if requested by any two or more States'
Clause (3)'s five consultation categories ((a)-(e)) are the default consultation duty, itself subject to the proviso's carve-out power
Any consultation-exemption regulation must be laid before the relevant Legislature for at least 14 days and remains amendable/repealable by that Legislature
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (4) exempts reservation-related matters under Article 16(4) and Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes representation matters under Article 335 from the consultation requirement entirely, without needing any regulation

Consultation is advisory, not binding — the government may decline to accept a Commission's advice, though (per Article 323) it must then explain the non-acceptance in its annual report to the Legislature
breakdown.how_to_read: The functional heart of the Chapter — when a recruitment or disciplinary dispute turns on 'was the Commission properly consulted', go straight to clause (3)'s five categories and then check whether the proviso's exemption regulations (duly laid under clause 5) actually covered that specific matter.

sections.title: Power to extend functions of Public Service Commissions
sections.raw_text: An Act made by Parliament or, as the case may be, the Legislature of a State may provide for the exercise of additional functions by the Union Public Service Commission or the State Public Service Commission as respects the services of the Union or the State and also as respects the services of any local authority or other body corporate constituted by law or of any public institution.
key_terms: legislative power to expand Commission functions beyond Article 320's baseline, including to local authorities/body corporates/public institutions

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 321 lets Parliament or a State Legislature, by ordinary Act, hand Public Service Commissions extra functions beyond what Article 320 already requires — including recruitment-related work for local authorities, statutory body corporates, or public institutions, not just the Union or State government itself.
essential_elements: Extension requires an Act of the appropriate Legislature (Parliament for UPSC, State Legislature for a State Commission)
Extended functions can reach beyond Union/State government services to local authorities, body corporates constituted by law, and public institutions
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a pure enabling power — Commissions gain no additional functions automatically; a specific Act must actually confer them
breakdown.how_to_read: Useful whenever a Commission is asked to recruit for a statutory corporation or public institution — check first whether an Article 321 Act actually extends the Commission's Article 320 functions to that body, since the baseline duty otherwise covers only Union/State civil services.

sections.title: Expenses of Public Service Commissions
sections.raw_text: The expenses of the Union or a State Public Service Commission, including any salaries, allowances and pensions payable to or in respect of the members or staff of the Commission, shall be charged on the Consolidated Fund of India or, as the case may be, the Consolidated Fund of the State.
key_terms: charged-expenditure status for Commission expenses, salaries, allowances, and pensions

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 322 guarantees Public Service Commission funding independence by making all Commission expenses — including members' and staff salaries, allowances, and pensions — 'charged' expenditure on the Consolidated Fund of India or the relevant State's Consolidated Fund, meaning they are paid without needing an annual vote in the Legislature (see Article 112/202's charged-vs-voted distinction).
essential_elements: Covers Commission expenses generally, plus specifically salaries, allowances, and pensions of both members and staff
Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Union Commission) or the Consolidated Fund of the relevant State (State Commission)
exceptions_and_qualifications: Unlike most other charged items which are individually itemised, Article 322's charge is a blanket one covering the Commission's entire expense base, not merely a fixed sum
breakdown.how_to_read: Part of the same institutional-independence design family as the charged salaries of judges, the CAG, and the Election Commission — funding security removes one lever governments might otherwise use to pressure the Commission.

sections.title: Reports of Public Service Commissions
sections.raw_text: (1) It shall be the duty of the Union Commission to present annually to the President a report as to the work done by the Commission and on receipt of such report the President shall cause a copy thereof together with a memorandum explaining, as respects the cases, if any, where the advice of the Commission was not accepted, the reasons for such non-acceptance to be laid before each House of Parliament. (2) It shall be the duty of a State Commission to present annually to the Governor of the State a report as to the work done by the Commission, and it shall be the duty of a Joint Commission to present annually to the Governor of each of the States the needs of which are served by the Joint Commission a report as to the work done by the Commission in relation to that State, and in either case the Governor shall, on receipt of such report, cause a copy thereof together with a memorandum explaining, as respects the cases, if any, where the advice of the Commission was not accepted, the reasons for such non-acceptance to be laid before the Legislature of the State.
key_terms: mandatory annual UPSC report to the President, tabled before Parliament with a non-acceptance memorandum
mandatory annual State/Joint Commission report to the Governor(s), tabled before the State Legislature with a non-acceptance memorandum

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 323 builds in public accountability for Public Service Commissions: each Commission must submit an annual work report to its appointing head of state (President for UPSC, Governor for State/Joint Commissions), who must then table that report before the Legislature together with a memorandum explaining every instance where the government declined to follow the Commission's advice — making non-acceptance politically visible rather than silent.
essential_elements: Reporting duty is annual and mandatory for every Commission type (Union, State, Joint)
A Joint Commission reports separately to the Governor of each State it serves, on the work done 'in relation to that State'
The tabling head of state must attach a memorandum explaining reasons for any non-acceptance of Commission advice
UPSC reports go before both Houses of Parliament; State/Joint Commission reports go before the State Legislature
exceptions_and_qualifications: The article only mandates disclosure of non-acceptance reasons — it does not compel the government to actually accept or implement the Commission's advice on any matter
breakdown.how_to_read: This transparency mechanism is what gives Article 320's advisory (non-binding) consultation teeth in practice — a government can reject a Commission's advice, but only at the cost of having to publicly justify the rejection in the tabled memorandum.

sections.title: Administrative tribunals
sections.raw_text: (1) Parliament may, by law, provide for the adjudication or trial by administrative tribunals of disputes and complaints with respect to recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed to public services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of any State or of any local or other authority within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India or of any corporation owned or controlled by the Government. (2) A law made under clause (1) may— (a) provide for the establishment of an administrative tribunal for the Union and a separate administrative tribunal for each State or for two or more States; (b) specify the jurisdiction, powers (including the power to punish for contempt) and authority which may be exercised by each of the said tribunals; (c) provide for the procedure (including provisions as to limitation and rules of evidence) to be followed by the said tribunals; (d) exclude the jurisdiction of all courts, except the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under article 136, with respect to the disputes or complaints referred to in clause (1); (e) provide for the transfer to each such administrative tribunal of any cases pending before any court or other authority immediately before the establishment of such tribunal as would have been within the jurisdiction of such tribunal if the causes of action on which such suits or proceedings are based had arisen after such establishment; (f) repeal or amend any order made by the President under clause (3) of article 371D; (g) contain such supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions (including provisions as to fees) as Parliament may deem necessary for the effective functioning of, and for the speedy disposal of cases by, and the enforcement of the orders of, such tribunals. (3) The provisions of this article shall have effect notwithstanding anything in any other provision of this Constitution or in any other law for the time being in force.
key_terms: Parliament-exclusive power to create administrative tribunals for public-service recruitment/conditions-of-service disputes
near-total ouster of ordinary-court jurisdiction, preserving only Supreme Court Article 136 special leave
overriding effect notwithstanding any other constitutional provision or law

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 323A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976), lets Parliament create specialised administrative tribunals — like the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) — to handle disputes over recruitment and conditions of service of Union, State, and local-authority/government-corporation employees, instead of those disputes going through the regular High Courts/civil courts. Once such a tribunal law is made, it can almost completely oust the ordinary courts' jurisdiction over those service disputes, leaving only the Supreme Court's discretionary Article 136 special-leave power intact.
essential_elements: Power vests exclusively in Parliament, not State Legislatures (unlike Article 323B)
Covers recruitment and conditions-of-service disputes/complaints for Union, State, local-authority, or government-corporation public servants
Clause (2)(d) permits excluding all court jurisdiction except the Supreme Court's Article 136 special leave power
Clause (3) gives the article overriding effect over any other constitutional provision or law
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Supreme Court in L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) held that clause (2)(d)'s exclusion of High Courts' Article 226/227 judicial review power over tribunal decisions is unconstitutional, since that power is part of the Constitution's basic structure — tribunals now function as courts of first instance, subject to a Division Bench of the jurisdictional High Court
Clause (2)(f) lets a tribunal law repeal/amend Presidential orders made under Article 371D(3) (the analogous Andhra Pradesh/Telangana administrative tribunal special provision)
breakdown.how_to_read: Read alongside L. Chandra Kumar (1997) as the decisive gloss: despite clause (2)(d)'s literal text excluding 'all courts', tribunals cannot be the final word — their orders remain subject to High Court judicial review, preserving the basic-structure guarantee of judicial review while still channelling first-instance service disputes away from crowded civil courts.

sections.title: Tribunals for other matters
sections.raw_text: (1) The appropriate Legislature may, by law, provide for the adjudication or trial by tribunals of any disputes, complaints, or offences with respect to all or any of the matters specified in clause (2) with respect to which such Legislature has power to make laws. (2) The matters referred to in clause (1) are the following, namely:— (a) levy, assessment, collection and enforcement of any tax; (b) foreign exchange, import and export across customs frontiers; (c) industrial and labour disputes; (d) land reforms by way of acquisition by the State of any estate as defined in article 31A or of any rights therein or the extinguishment or modification of any such rights or by way of ceiling on agricultural land or in any other way; (e) ceiling on urban property; (f) elections to either House of Parliament or the House or either House of the Legislature of a State, but excluding the matters referred to in article 329 and article 329A; (g) production, procurement, supply and distribution of food-stuffs (including edible oilseeds and oils) and such other goods as the President may, by public notification, declare to be essential goods for the purpose of this article and control of prices of such goods; (h) rent, its regulation and control and tenancy issues including the right, title and interest of landlords and tenants; (i) offences against laws with respect to any of the matters specified in sub-clauses (a) to (h) and fees in respect of any of those matters; (j) any matter incidental to any of the matters specified in sub-clauses (a) to (i). (3) A law made under clause (1) may— (a) provide for the establishment of a hierarchy of tribunals; (b) specify the jurisdiction, powers (including the power to punish for contempt) and authority which may be exercised by each of the said tribunals; (c) provide for the procedure (including provisions as to limitation and rules of evidence) to be followed by the said tribunals; (d) exclude the jurisdiction of all courts, except the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under article 136, with respect to all or any of the matters falling within the jurisdiction of the said tribunals; (e) provide for the transfer to each such tribunal of any cases pending before any court or any other authority immediately before the establishment of such tribunal as would have been within the jurisdiction of such tribunal if the causes of action on which such suits or proceedings are based had arisen after such establishment; (f) contain such supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions (including provisions as to fees) as the appropriate Legislature may deem necessary for the effective functioning of, and for the speedy disposal of cases by, and the enforcement of the orders of, such tribunals. (4) The provisions of this article shall have effect notwithstanding anything in any other provision of this Constitution or in any other law for the time being in force. Explanation.—In this article, "appropriate Legislature", in relation to any matter, means Parliament or, as the case may be, a State Legislature competent to make laws with respect to such matter in accordance with the provisions of Part XI.
key_terms: appropriate-Legislature (Parliament or State) power to create subject-specific tribunals for a defined list of ten matter-categories
taxation, foreign exchange/customs, industrial/labour, land reform, urban property ceiling, non-329/329A elections, essential-goods, and rent-control tribunal subjects
hierarchy-of-tribunals structure with near-total court-jurisdiction exclusion, subject to Article 136
'appropriate Legislature' defined by ordinary Part XI legislative competence

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 323B, also inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976), broadens the Article 323A model beyond service disputes: whichever Legislature (Parliament or a State Legislature) already has law-making competence over a listed subject — taxation, customs/foreign exchange, industrial disputes, land reforms, urban property ceilings, non-electoral-petition election matters, essential-goods price control, or rent control — may also set up tribunals (potentially a whole hierarchy of them) to adjudicate disputes in that subject, again largely displacing the ordinary courts subject only to the Supreme Court's Article 136 power.
essential_elements: Legislative competence for the tribunal tracks ordinary Part XI competence over the underlying subject-matter (the 'appropriate Legislature')
Ten enumerated matter-categories in clause (2), (a) through (j), define the outer limit of what Article 323B tribunals can cover
Clause (3)(a) uniquely allows a 'hierarchy of tribunals' (unlike Article 323A's single-tier model)
Clause (3)(d) again permits excluding all court jurisdiction except the Supreme Court's Article 136 power
Clause (4) gives overriding effect over any other constitutional provision or law
exceptions_and_qualifications: Election matters covered by Articles 329 and 329A (election-dispute bars/special provisions) are expressly excluded from clause (2)(f), preventing overlap with those dedicated election-dispute mechanisms
